title: Use MPI I/O on IU research supercomputers
content:
MPI I/O is an API standard for parallel I/O that allows multiple processes of a parallel program to access data in a common file simultaneously. MPI I/O maps I/O reads and writes to message-passing sends and receives. Implementing parallel I/O can improve the performance of your parallel application.
Ideally, MPI I/O should be used on a parallel file system (such as
Slate
,
Slate-Project
, or
Slate-Scratch
). Common systems (for example,
NFS
, EXT3FS) do not provide the MPI I/O API. However, a popular MPI I/O implementation, ROMIO, allows MPI I/O to work on NFS.
The following example uses MPI I/O functions to copy files. Short explanations for each step are provided below:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <mpi.h>       /* Include the MPI definitions */
void ErrorMessage(int error, int rank, char* string)
{
fprintf(stderr, "Process %d: Error %d in %s\n", rank, error, string);
MPI_Finalize();
exit(-1);
}
main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
int start, end;
int length;
int error;
char* buffer;
int nprocs;
int myrank;
MPI_Status    status;
MPI_File      fh;
MPI_Offset    filesize;
if (argc != 3)
{
fprintf(stderr, "Usage: %s FileToRead FileToWrite\n", argv[0]);
exit(-1);
}
/* Initialize MPI */
MPI_Init(&argc, &argv);
MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &nprocs);
MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &myrank);
/* Open file to read */
error = MPI_File_open(MPI_COMM_WORLD, argv[1],
MPI_MODE_RDONLY, MPI_INFO_NULL, &fh);
if(error != MPI_SUCCESS) ErrorMessage(error, myrank, "MPI_File_open");
/* Get the size of file */
error = MPI_File_get_size(fh, &filesize);
if(error != MPI_SUCCESS) ErrorMessage(error, myrank, "MPI_File_get_size");
/* calculate the range for each process to read */
length = filesize / nprocs;
start = length * myrank;
if (myrank == nprocs-1)
end = filesize;
else
end = start + length;
fprintf(stdout, "Proc %d: range = [%d, %d)\n", myrank, start, end);
/* Allocate space */
buffer = (char *)malloc((end - start) * sizeof(char));
if (buffer == NULL) ErrorMessage(-1, myrank, "malloc");
/* Each process read in data from the file */
MPI_File_seek(fh, start, MPI_SEEK_SET);
error = MPI_File_read(fh, buffer, end-start, MPI_BYTE, &status);
if(error != MPI_SUCCESS) ErrorMessage(error, myrank, "MPI_File_read");
/* close the file */
MPI_File_close(&fh);
/* Open file to write */
error = MPI_File_open(MPI_COMM_WORLD, argv[2],
MPI_MODE_WRONLY | MPI_MODE_CREATE, MPI_INFO_NULL, amp;fh);
if(error != MPI_SUCCESS) ErrorMessage(error, myrank, "MPI_File_open");
error = MPI_File_write_at(fh, start, buffer, end-start, MPI_BYTE, amp;status);
if(error != MPI_SUCCESS) ErrorMessage(error, myrank, "MPI_File_write");
/* close the file */
MPI_File_close(amp;fh);
/* Finalize MPI */
MPI_Finalize();
}
In the above example:
The first step is to establish the MPI environment, so the
MPI_Init(C version)
is required, and must be the first call in every MPI program.
The
MPI_File_open
function opens a file on all processes. Several access modes are supported. The one used in the example (
MPI_MODE_RDONLY
) is for read only.
The
MPI_File_get_size
function gives the file size, which is used later to determine the offset for each process.
The
MPI_File_seek
function points to the position in the file where each process will start reading data.
The
MPI_File_read
function reads data into the buffer specified in the second parameter. The size to be read is defined in the third parameter.
The
MPI_File_write_at
function will write data from the buffer (the third parameter) into a specific position in the file given by the second parameter.
The
MPI_File_close
function closes the file opened by
MPI_File_open
.
The MPI environment in every process must be terminated by the
MPI_Finalize
function. No MPI calls may be made after
MPI_Finalize
.
Fortran examples
Following are two Fortran examples:
Example 1:
!^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
program  create_file
!**************************************************************************
!  This is a Fortran 90 program to write data directly to a file by each
!  member of an MPI group.  It is suitable for large jobs which will not
!  fit into core memory (such as "out of core" solvers)
!
!  Copyright by the Trustees of Indiana University 2005
***************************************************************************
USE MPI
integer, parameter :: kind_val = 4
integer, parameter  :: filesize = 40
integer :: realsize = 4
integer ::  rank, ierr, fh, nprocs, num_reals
integer ::  i, region
real (kind = kind_val) :: datum
integer, dimension (MPI_STATUS_SIZE) :: status
integer (kind = MPI_OFFSET_KIND) :: offset, empty
!  Set filename to output datafile
character (len = *), parameter :: filename = "/u/ac/rays/new_data.dat"
real (kind = kind_val), dimension ( : ), allocatable  :: bucket
!  Basic MPI set-up
call MPI_INIT(ierr)
call MPI_COMM_RANK(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
call MPI_COMM_SIZE(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)
!  Sanity print
print*, "myid is ", rank
!  Carve out a piece of the output file and create a data bucket
empty = 0
region = filesize / (nprocs )
offset = ( region * rank )
allocate (bucket(region))
!  There is no guarantee that an old file will be clobbered,  so wipe out any previous output file
if (rank .eq. 0) then
call MPI_File_delete(filename, MPI_INFO_NULL, ierr)
endif
!  Set the file handle to an initial value (this should not be required)
fh = 0
!  Open the output file
call MPI_FILE_OPEN(MPI_COMM_WORLD, filename, MPI_MODE_CREATE+MPI_MODE_RDWR, MPI_INFO_NULL, fh, ierr)
!  Wait on everyone to catch up.
call MPI_BARRIER(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
!  Do some work and fill up the data bucket
call random_seed()
do i = 1, region
call random_number(datum)
bucket(i) = datum * 1000000. * (rank + 1)
print *, " bucket  ",i ,"= ", bucket(i)
enddo
!  Basic "belt and suspenders insurance that everyone's file pointer is at the beginning of the output file.
call MPI_FILE_SET_VIEW(fh, empty, MPI_REAL4, MPI_REAL4, 'native', MPI_INFO_NULL, ierr)
!  Send the data bucket to the output file in the proper place
call MPI_FILE_WRITE_AT(fh, offset, bucket, region, MPI_REAL4, status, ierr)
!  Wait on everyone to finish and close up shop
call MPI_BARRIER(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
call MPI_FILE_CLOSE(fh, ierr)
call MPI_FINALIZE(ierr)
end  program  create_file
Example 2:
!^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
program  read_file
!**************************************************************************
!  This is a Fortran 90 program to read data directly from a file by each
!  member of an MPI group.  It is suitable for large jobs which will not
!  fit into core memory (such as "out of core" solvers)
!
!  Copyright by the Trustees of Indiana University 2005
***************************************************************************
USE MPI
integer, parameter :: kind_val = 4
integer,  parameter  :: filesize = 40
integer :: realsize = 4
integer ::  rank, ierr, fh, nprocs, num_reals
integer ::  i, region
integer, dimension (MPI_STATUS_SIZE) :: status
integer (kind = MPI_OFFSET_KIND) :: offset, empty
!  Set filename to output datafile
character (len = *), parameter :: filename = "/u/ac/rays/new_data.dat"
real (kind = kind_val), dimension ( : ), allocatable  :: bucket
!  Basic MPI set-up
call MPI_INIT(ierr)
call MPI_COMM_RANK(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
call MPI_COMM_SIZE(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)
!  Carve out a piece of the output file and create a data bucket
empty = 0
region = filesize / (nprocs )
offset = (region * rank )
allocate (bucket(region))
!  Sanity print
print*, "myid is ", rank
!  Set the file handle to an initial value (this should not be required)
fh = 0
!  Open the output file
call MPI_FILE_OPEN(MPI_COMM_WORLD, filename, MPI_MODE_RDONLY, MPI_INFO_NULL, fh, ierr)
!  Wait on everyone to catch up.
call MPI_BARRIER(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
!  Basic "belt and suspenders insurance that everyone's file pointer is at the beginning of the output file.
call MPI_FILE_SET_VIEW(fh, 0, MPI_REAL4, MPI_REAL4, 'native', MPI_INFO_NULL, ierr)
!  Read only the section of the data file each process needs and put data in the data bucket.
call MPI_FILE_READ_AT(fh, offset, bucket, region, MPI_REAL4, status, ierr)
!  We could check the values received in the bucket (debug hint)
!
!      do i = 1, region
!         print *, "my id is ", rank, " and my ", i, "number is ", bucket(i)
!      enddo
!  Wait on everyone to finish and close up shop
call MPI_BARRIER(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
call MPI_FILE_CLOSE(fh, ierr)
call MPI_FINALIZE(ierr)
end  program  read_file

title: IU internal server co-location agreement
content:
This document represents an agreement between a
client
and UITS for server co-location in Indiana University Data Centers. The responsibilities and services provided are outlined, which include equipment installations, data center access, and operational procedures.
Definitions
Data Centers:
Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Facility (the IU Data Centers at IU Bloomington and IU Indianapolis)
UITS:
The party providing service within the Data Centers
Client
:
The IU party receiving service through UITS
Overview
This document describes the server co-location services that University Information Technology Services will provide. Departments can use physical space in the Data Centers for their servers as a transition strategy to standard options provided by UITS that improve efficiency and reduce environmental impact:
Virtualization:
Intelligent Infrastructure (II) is the recommended path for departmental web, application, and database servers. Moving to IU's virtual environment achieves benefits of hardware efficiencies, reduced environmental impact, and increased flexibility to respond quickly to changing service needs. For more, see
About IU Intelligent Infrastructure
.
Consolidation:
A
co-location service provided by IU's
Research Technologies
consolidates physical servers and components into fewer physical entities, achieving economies of scale and allowing greater flexibility for shifting resources from one application area to another.
Environmental
Machine Room environmental services and security in the Data Centers will be provided by UITS as follows:
Power backup:
UPS service and generator backup are provided as a secondary source of power in the event of utility power failure. UPS service is designed to provide power for seamless transition to an emergency generator. In the event of a lengthy power failure, the generator can be refueled as necessary and run indefinitely until power is restored. UITS may determine that it is not in the university's best interest to run the generator for extended periods if power has not been restored, and every effort to inform the
client
will be made.
Fire protection:
Fire suppression is provided via dry pipe, pre-action sprinkler system, in accordance with university risk management policy.  All other fire protection is provided in accordance with university policy and procedure and Indiana state code.
Cooling:
Air conditioning is provided via chilled water coils in computer room air conditioner (CRAC) units:
Indianapolis Data Center:
Primary source of chilled water is campus (CTE) water, with a dedicated backup chiller in case of a loss of primary supply
Bloomington Data Center:
Dedicated chilled water plant with redundant chillers and cooling towers
Client
will follow shipping/receiving and storage (equipment, supplies, boxes) guidelines set forth and provided by UITS.
Client
will coordinate their installation activities, including any temporary need for secure storage, with UITS.
Client
is responsible for removing debris, supplies, etc., from the area after installation. Only the equipment can be stored in the rack.
Security/access provisions
Security system:
Video cameras digitally record activity at each machine room entrance door. Access to the Data Centers is provided to only those individuals who are authorized. For non-regular visitor access, the procedures outlined in the
Data Center access control policy
document should be followed.
Client
s agree to operate within the security and access policies and procedures of the Data Centers.  This includes access limitations and sign-in procedures.  A copy of these procedures will be provided by UITS and updated on a periodic basis.
Client
s will provide UITS with a list of personnel who are authorized for access.
Upon termination of this agreement or the resignation/termination of staff, it is the
client
's responsibility to notify UITS of staff changes. UITS will immediately deactivate card access privileges.
Client
s that occupy an entire rack and/or require isolation from shared rack space may install additional physical rack security measures at their own cost, provided these measures have been reviewed and approved by UITS in advance. Examples of such measures include cameras, locked racks, and rack door sensors. If the
client
chooses additional methods, UITS must also have access on-site (keys for locked racks in case of an emergency).
Data network provisions
All cabinets will have network switches installed at the top of the cabinet to provide 10/100/1000 Mbps Ethernet connections into the Data Center switching infrastructure (10000 Mbps available and priced on an individual request). All public and private Ethernet connections are provided by UITS unless very special circumstances are reviewed and approved by Network Engineering and Campus Network Infrastructure.
Client
will not deploy switching gear or other networking devices in their rack unless some specific exception is requested, documented, and granted by UITS.
All servers will be place behind the Data Center firewall.
Equipment
Server rack space will be assigned and all servers will be installed in the standard cabinets provided by UITS unless the server manufacturer specifically dictates the equipment must be housed in their proprietary cabinets. Proof of vendor requirements for proprietary cabinets must be submitted to UITS. Such cabinets should have front, back, and side panels. Doors on the cabinet must be closed when no one is working in the unit. Server racks should not exceed 5 kW per rack (additional cost to be applied based on power consumption).
Client
s will provide a space plan to UITS.  The space plan will include the number of servers, equipment, storage devices, and other devices having space and power considerations. UITS will approve these plans before
Client
s begin installing equipment.
Client
s will be responsible for delivery arrangements of equipment to the Data Centers and notifying UITS of the delivery date.
Client
s are responsible for all costs associated with this process and are liable for any equipment damaged during transportation.
Client
s are responsible for the installation of the equipment in the racks, and retain responsibility for the equipment and liability for any damages to that equipment during the installation and through to the initial power-up process.  After installation, UITS assumes responsibilities as outlined in this agreement.
Client
s will adhere to the "
Data Center standards
" document.
All servers in the Data Centers are expected to be administered in a secure manner using industry best practices (
Security of Information Technology Resources (IT-12)
), including employment of host based firewalls and to be operated behind the Data Center firewall.
Client
s agree to provide UITS with firewall rules that restrict incoming traffic to include only those protocols, ports, and properly sourced packets as needed for operation of each server.
Client
s will not store cardholder data on equipment without compliance to Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards (PCI DSS). The PCI DSS security requirements apply to all system components. In the context of PCI DSS, system components are defined as any network component, server, or application that is included in or connected to the cardholder data environment. System components also include any virtualization components, such as virtual machines, virtual switches/routers, virtual appliances, virtual applications/desktops, and hypervisors. The cardholder data environment is comprised of people, processes, and technology that store, process, or transmit cardholder data or sensitive authentication data.
If there is an exception to process cardholder data, you must be compliant with the PCI DSS. This will require review and approval from UISO and the IU Office of the Treasurer.
Disaster recovery
The current UITS disaster recovery plan for the Data Centers does not include replacement of co-located systems. Systems in the Data Centers are not insured by UITS. In the unlikely event that the Data Centers are substantially damaged or destroyed, UITS will make a best effort to restore services starting with those systems critical to the business needs of the university. Co-located systems remain the responsibility of their owners. Should the Data Centers be disabled, but owners' systems remain undamaged, UITS will attempt to find an acceptable alternate site or return the systems temporarily to their owners. UITS may be able to assist owners with disaster recovery planning.
UITS cannot be responsible for system owner's business continuity or any losses directly or indirectly associated with use of UITS co-location services.
Operational support
UITS will provide contact information to
Client
s for use in requesting "eyes and hands" assistance with
Client
s' equipment when problems arise.  System monitoring and failure notification will be provided by UITS operations staff on site 24x7x365. There are no service-level guarantees for the availability of such resources.
Client
s will provide contact information to UITS for use in notifications.
UITS will provide timely notification to
Client
s for planned and unplanned outages of power and/or cooling.
UITS will make a good faith effort to provide workstation space to
Client
s.  However, the amount of space available to
Client
s may be minimal.
Client
s should plan accordingly.
Client
s will provide timely notification to UITS for all activities and agrees to coordinate with UITS Data Center Operations for any rack space changes.
Client
s will not sublet rack space or resale the functional equivalent of the service to another project, department, or third party.
Client
s may incur one-time setup charges if their requirements are beyond standards for rack(s) and/or power.
Data Center Operations contact information
Visit the
DCOPS Request Form
or email
dcops@iu.edu
.
Rack definitions
Rack space:
The rack space is assigned for the server co-location. The rack space may not be contiguous and could possibly be shared with other co-location customers.

Create, edit, or delete Access Control Management (ACM) groups

October 14, 2025
When using the Microsoft Teams web app, full-featured calling is not available.
Difficulty using the Teams web app with off-campus calls and calling

Signing into a Teams CCX500, MP54, or MP56 desk phone

REFRESH CODE
(as prompted on the phone screen) does not work.
On the phone screen, touch
Sign In On This Device
; when prompted, enter the username and passphrase. Respond to the Duo prompt; when prompted touch
Register
. Follow any other standard prompts.
May 20, 2025
Accounts with an A1 license are unable to set meetings to automatically record
The
Record and Transcribe automatically
button is not present for A1 accounts. A1 accounts will need to manually start meeting recordings and transcription. This is true for personal meetings or channel meetings.

June 12, 2024
New Teams calls muted when selecting hyperlinks

New Teams Mutes Mic When Clicking Hyperlinks

MP50 phone not fully compatible with new Teams client

When trying to choose options on a phone menu, the dial pad of MP50 and touch display may not work; use dial pad on client instead. UITS is waiting on a firmware update from the vendor.
UITS is checking with the vendor for a solution.
April 1, 2024
Inability to dial or end a call using the Yealink MP50 phone

Skype
for Business
app is running on your computer, the phone may not respond when using the dial pad, when the handset is replaced, or when choosing the End Call screen option.
Completely exit the
Skype
for Business
app. You may also need to disable
Skype
for Business
in your list of startup apps to prevent it from launching automatically when Windows launches.
March 29, 2023
Linux client unsupported
Users are unable to download Microsoft's Teams client for Linux; previous downloads no longer work.
Linux users can use the web version of Teams to receive incoming calls or make PC-to-PC calls. If you use Linux and need to dial outbound calls by number, use a mobile app, or request an IP phone from your department.
March 3, 2023
Yealink MP50 missing user info, dial tone, dialing issues
Windows users may not hear dial tone, or see or be able to use the dial pad. They may not see their name or number appear on the screen.
Windows users should sign into the phone using
Hot Desking mode
.
March 3, 2023
Yealink MP50 does not work with macOS.

Choose another
USB phone or headset equipment
.
March 3, 2023
Loud or persistent dial tone after
Skype
for Business
call or meeting is completed.
Interaction between Teams and Skype for Business may cause Skype for Business users to hear a persistent dial tone or off-hook sound even after their call or meeting is completed. Microsoft is working on a Teams update which will likely solve this problem.

Teams Calls

February 17, 2023
Features missing in some web browsers
When using the web version of
Microsoft Teams
, not all web browsers are fully supported. See
Limits and specifications for Microsoft Teams
.
Use the web app in a fully supported browser, or download the desktop app.
February 16, 2023

Teams Calls
on Windows

with newer Dell Latitude laptops and CX300 phones may experience the following:
No dial tone
Dial pad on the CX300 phone does not work
Answering and ending calls with the phone does not work (these must be done from the Teams app)

Run Windows updates.
In the Device manager, choose
Sound, video and game controllers
.
Right-click
Intell Smart Sound Technology/Intel SST
, and choose
Disable device
.
Unplug the phone, and restart the computer.
Plug the phone back in.

For some steps, admin permissions may be necessary.

title: Access Esri maps and data at IU
content:
The
Esri Data
collection contains many types of map data at many scales of geography. The data are useful for general purpose basemaps and for more specific uses. For each geographic scale included, the significant basemap layers are boundaries, cities, rivers, and roads. Where possible, demographic data are provided for states, counties, and their equivalents. Vector datasets include the United States, Europe, Canada, Mexico, and the world. Image and elevation data are available for North America and the world.
Esri also offers the
ArcGIS Data & Maps
group via ArcGIS Online, providing access to data layers from the Esri Data & Maps DVDs.
IU's license agreement with Esri allows students, faculty, and staff to access GIS datasets for educational use. Datasets include census and market data, and are updated annually. Some additional datasets are available through the UITS GIS OneDrive; to request access,
complete the GIS Help form
. For information about how you may use the data, read the documentation included with the files.

Overview
For Apple computers, the IU Common Build provides central management for a great number of endpoint management functions. This includes Global Configuration Profiles for common applications, automatic FileVault key escrow, macOS LAPS, and a high security standard based off of the CIS Benchmarks.
IU Common Build structure and naming
Computer naming convention
Computers will use the naming convention
IU-
SerialNumber
, to stay in alignment with our Windows counterparts.
IU Common Build and Active Directory
Binding is supported only for devices that will be on campus full time. UITS
Endpoint Management Services
(EMS) does not recommend attempting to bind any device that will be used off campus for any length of time. If the device cannot maintain an always-on connection to the IU ADS, the client's passphrase can become out of sync and prevent login to the device.
To set up the AD binding option, contact EMS via the
Ticket Submission form
. Provide an AD admin group, and specify which systems will be bound.
For more, see
AD binding macOS on the IU Common Build
.
Build process
For instructions on the IU Common Build process, see
Build information for Apple computers under the IU Common Build
.
Manage computers on the Common Build
Local UITS support person access to Jamf
Local UITS support people will retain
audit-level
(that is, read-only) access to their new site within the IU Common Build, which includes all policies and configuration profiles. The site url is
adm01.iu.edu:8443
. The access level is determined by
ACM
group, which will be set up by EMS; if access needs to change, managers will be able to edit the members of the ACM group. EMS requires that any administrative accounts be group accounts.
Clients will retain the rights to view LAPS password rotations and FileVault encryption keys as well as the ability to create, edit, and save searches and groups.
Local UITS support person tools
Some policies on the IU Common Build have been placed into the IU Self Service store for use by local UITS support people. All of these policies are hidden by default in IU Self Service and require local UITS support people to sign into IU Self Service using their IU Jamf admin group account. After login, local UITS support person-specific tools will be available under "Admin".
Access to these policies is granted by the iu-entlmt-iu-uems-apple-itpros AD group. Membership is nested from your IT unit's local UITS support admin group, via ACM. IT managers have access to edit their unit's ACM group, using their admin group account. Contact EMS if you need to change or check access.
FileVault
As part of IT-12, all laptops in the IU Common Build receive a configuration profile on enrollment to enable FileVault. The keys are automatically escrowed to Jamf for the entry of the device. You can view these keys with audit access to the Jamf site.
Software
To enable standard build software, use the Setup Your Mac policy in IU Self Service; see
Build information for Apple computers under the IU Common Build
.
Submit all requests for new applications via the EMS
Ticket Submission form
.
Updates
To ensure software stays as up to date as possible, application updates are automatically installed for all supported applications daily, outside of business hours.
macOS security updates will be deployed as soon as they become available, with the option to defer for up to one week. After one week, the device will be put into a new update group and notifications will be sent. A week after the notifications are sent, an update will be forcibly applied to the device outside of business hours.
By default, the EMS team will not restrict any major macOS or iPadOS releases. For macOS operating system changes, the upgrade will be blocked until an evaluation of the new operating system and security compliances can be updated.
Retire assets
EMS relies on on-site local UITS support people and the UITS Asset Management team in order to properly facilitate the retirement of university assets. Any time a device is being sent to Surplus, follow the instructions in
Decommissioning procedure
in
About Apple ADE (Automated Device Enrollment) and decommissioning
to ensure the device is properly removed from endpoint management. For more about disposing of unneeded equipment, see
Departmental disposal of equipment at IU
.
Note:
Once every six months, EMS will run an inventory of devices that have not been in communication with Jamf. Any that have not checked into the service in over six months may be subject to lockdown until the client can be contacted.

Use the
Ticket Submission form
for Common Build requests.

Scope:
Rather than having a single team for an entire organization, it is usually better to have multiple teams, each with a more focused group of people. For example, if a group is working on a project, that could be its own team. Other examples include student clubs, research labs, internal or interdepartmental committees, and teammates within an organization. If a team becomes unwieldy, with too many members or tasks, create new ones to help maintain focus and security.
Institutional data:

title: About cloud computing
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Service models
Software as a Service (SaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Types of clouds
Private clouds
Public clouds
Hybrid clouds
Overview
Cloud computing is the delivery of shared, on-demand computing services over the internet ("the cloud") to offer faster innovation, flexible resources, and economies of scale.
Cloud services include servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, intelligence, and more. You typically pay only for what you use, helping lower your operating costs, run your infrastructure more efficiently, and scale as your business needs change. This lets people access and share information at any time from multiple devices, rapidly deploy computing services without purchasing hardware, temporarily leverage massive computing power, and more.
Cloud computing allows both consumers and IT providers to use technology as a utility, which makes IT nimbler and more cost-effective. Cloud computing includes familiar examples of cloud storage, such as storing pictures on
Flickr
, videos on
YouTube
, or files on
Google Drive at IU
, but also encompasses services such as
Amazon Web Services (AWS)
,
Google Cloud
, and
Microsoft Azure
, which allow online services (for example, servers delivering a website) to rapidly scale up or down based on sudden fluctuations in traffic.
Service models
Cloud computing has three main service models, commonly referred to as Software as a Service (SaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).
Software as a Service (SaaS)
Software as a Service lets you access a provider's services running on the provider's infrastructure, typically from multiple devices. Examples of commonly used SaaS applications are
OneDrive
, Canvas,
Facebook
, and Snapchat.
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Platform as a Service removes the need for organizations to manage the underlying infrastructure (usually servers and operating systems) and allows them to focus on the deployment and management of their applications. Examples of PaaS include AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Microsoft Azure Web Apps, Salesforce, and the Google App Engine.
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Infrastructure as a Service contains the basic building blocks for cloud IT and typically provides access to networking features, computers (virtual or on dedicated hardware), and data storage space. Some examples are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.
Types of clouds
There are three deployment models for cloud computing: private, public, and hybrid clouds.
Private clouds
Private clouds involve a distinct and secure cloud-based environment in which only the specified client can operate.
Public clouds
Public clouds are cloud-based computing environments provided by a commercial provider, accessed via the internet. Their infrastructure is built to leverage massive scale and is shared with multiple clients. IU currently has contracts with two public cloud computing vendors, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure. To get an account, see
Get an AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure account at IU
.
Hybrid clouds
Hybrid clouds use elements from both private and public clouds. For example, a hybrid cloud may use a public cloud for all non-sensitive information and only use a private cloud for more sensitive or confidential data.

title: About Varonis at IU
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Varonis at IU
Impact on users
Guidance and resources
Overview
Varonis is an enterprise data security and governance platform that helps Indiana University protect institutional data across supported storage and collaboration services. It provides visibility into where data resides, how it is accessed, and how it is shared, supporting alignment with university policy and information security expectations. Varonis helps safeguard institutional data while enabling appropriate collaboration and access for faculty, staff, students, and affiliates.
Varonis at IU
At IU, University Information Technology Services (UITS) uses Varonis to proactively identify and mitigate data risks within IU-managed environments, including Microsoft Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and file servers. This includes:
Data classification and labeling:
Varonis works in concert with
Microsoft Information Protection
(MIP) sensitivity labels to help classify and label data according to IU's
institutional data standards
. This ensures shared files and folders are appropriately marked based on their sensitivity and regulatory requirements.
Risk detection and exposure reduction:
Varonis continuously scans IU-managed storage environments to identify sensitive or regulated data that may be at risk due to misconfigured sharing or permissions. The system flags files and folders that are accessible to the public or broadly within IU, and highlights instances of excessive or unnecessary access.
Remediation of overexposed data:
When Varonis detects that sensitive data has been over-shared (for example, via links that allow anonymous access to the public or with anyone who has an IU username), UITS Varonis administrators take action to mitigate risk. This may involve removing public or anonymous sharing links, tightening permissions, or contacting data owners to confirm appropriate access levels. Remediation focuses on correcting sharing and access configurations, not altering or deleting the underlying data.
Incident response and compliance support:
If regulated data, such as Social Security Numbers, financial records, or health information, is found to be exposed, IU's incident response protocols are activated. Designated staff review findings, coordinate with data owners, and ensure that remediation aligns with university policies, including
Privacy of Electronic Information and Information Technology Resources (IT-07)
. All actions are conducted in accordance with IU privacy policies, and access to data is limited to authorized personnel only as needed.
Impact on users
Most data owners will not notice Varonis in daily operations. If Varonis identifies a potential risk, such as over-shared sensitive data or misconfigured permissions, data owners may be contacted to help resolve the issue or clarify sharing needs. In some cases, automated system changes may occur to protect institutional data, after which data owners will be notified.
Remediation actions focus on correcting access and sharing configurations, not modifying or deleting the data itself. All actions are performed with respect for user privacy in accordance with IU policies, and only authorized personnel are involved.
Guidance and resources
Use of Varonis at IU aligns with existing university policies and standards related to data privacy, classification, and information security.
Users storing and sharing institutional data are encouraged to follow IU guidance, including the data classification and handling resources provided by
IU Data Management
, and to consult relevant Knowledge Base articles for additional information. IU encourages all data owners to stay informed about institutional guidance for
storing and sharing data
, and to regularly review access permissions for files and folders.
If you have questions about secure data practices and policies at IU, contact the
University Information Security Office
(
uiso@iu.edu
).

Overview
Microsoft Power BI is a suite of business analytics tools for analyzing data and sharing insights with reports and dashboards. At Indiana University, authorized users can access interactive reports and dashboards using a standard web browser.
Power BI consists of several elements that work together, starting with these two basics:

Version control
Version control, also known as source control or revision control, is the practice of tracking and managing changes to software code, documents, or other collections of information.
UITS strongly recommends that your source files (PBIX reports as well as templates and themes) be stored somewhere that implements version control. The most important reason for this is to be able to roll back to a previous version if some change produces unwanted results.
There is currently no standardized process at IU for how you should store these files, but here are some options that range from simple to complex:
Microsoft OneDrive at IU
,
SharePoint Online
,
Microsoft Teams at IU
:
These three options are related, and if your department is already using one of them, it may be the easiest to choose to save your PBIX files in a folder inside of one of these systems. This is a very good, simple option, as the data are not hosted on premises, and you get version history by default every time a file is saved.
File servers:
If your department uses an on-premises file server, that may also be a good place to store your files
if
that server has Shadow Copies (also known as Previous Versions) enabled. Check with your
local UITS support person
to determine if and how Shadow Copies are implemented on the file server. You may want to use one of the MS options above, since Shadow Copies usually makes one or two copies per day (for example, at noon and midnight). If you made multiple versions within a single day (for example, at 8am, 9am, 10am, and 11am), you would miss some of the versions that were created between the scheduled times.
GitHub, Azure DevOps, etc.:
While these are full-featured source control platforms, you're still a bit limited, since PBIX files are binary, not text. This means that while you do have version control, you still lack the ability to compare what changed between versions. Additionally, they will be much more complicated to configure. Configuration of these platforms is beyond the scope of this document; however, if your team already uses one of these tools, it may be worth investigating further. Additionally, when on Power BI Premium capacity, you can use Azure DevOps or GitHub to integrate with Power BI Deployment pipelines for additional automation.

The Palisade Suite in IUanyWare has an expired license. This includes the following applications:
AtRisk 7
BigPicture 7
Evolver 7
NeuralTools 7
Ptree 7
StatTools 7
TopRank 7
IUanyWare admins have contacted the application owners. The Palisade license may not be renewed for all users in IUanyWare. This issue is still being investigated.
Workspace app or Receiver with scaled or high resolution displays
In Windows, you may experience display issues when using multiple displays with different resolutions or scaling.
Use the latest version of
Citrix Workspace app
to enable the app to scale the session for high resolution. If you are still using the Citrix Receiver for special use cases or for the LTSR client, this feature is available in Receiver 4.9 and above.
In the system tray, right-click the
Workspace
icon and select
Advanced Preferences
>
High DPI
>
Yes
>
Save
. Disconnect from your sessions and reconnect to them for the changes to take effect.
Note:
This setting locks the application to a single monitor if the scaling of any monitor is different (it cannot be stretched across multiple displays).
Workspace or Receiver problems
If you experience problems with IUanyWare which you have not encountered before, check to make sure you have the latest version of Citrix Workspace app.
Before you begin, be sure to uninstall your current Citrix Workspace app or Citrix Receiver.
Visit
Download Citrix Workspace app
from the device experiencing the problem. This site will automatically install the proper version of Citrix Workspace app. Otherwise, it may direct you to the app store for your particular device to search for the latest version of the app.
Invalid root certificate
You see this message:
"This server has an invalid root certificate, so this may be a malicious server. Connection dropped."
Strictly speaking, this is not an issue with IUanyWare.
See
Fixing an invalid root certificate in IUanyWare
.
Duo
Citrix Workspace app lacks a Duo interface to let you choose your preferred Duo option. The Workspace app sends Duo Push notifications to your mobile device by default.
Best practice: From a browser, log into
https://iuanyware.cloud.com
. Use the Duo interface to choose your preferred Duo option. From the browser's store of apps, you can run applications and desktops from the browser or through the Workspace app on your client.
If you prefer to use the Workspace app directly, and you want to use a token key for your second authentication method, see
Logging In With the Citrix Receiver Client
.
Audio
Audio is enabled on all applications, but some applications (for example, Adobe Audition) will not work through a standard IUanyWare virtual machine.
There is no workaround for this issue.
Mathematica
When you access Mathematica from the Receiver on an iPad, the
Return
key does not evaluate an expression the way pressing
Enter
on a Windows keyboard or
Shift-Return
on a Mac keyboard does.
Tap and hold
Return
to access the right-click menu, and select
Evaluate
.
MATLAB
Students cannot set the path in MATLAB because they cannot write to the restricted server drive where the application is hosted.
Have a faculty or staff member add the path by adding the path command to a
startup.m
file in
c:\users\
username
\My Documents\MATLAB
.
R
Packages cannot be installed in R because you cannot write to the restricted server drive where the application is hosted.
Request any additional packages using the
Software Request Form
.
Cloud Storage
For best results, use a Cloud Storage File Share. Always use a cloud storage location when working in IUanyWare. To set up your File Shares for use with IUanyWare, use the
Cloud Storage utility
.
Virtual Private Network (VPN)
If while off campus you make a
VPN
connection via the SSL VPN tool available on IUware, you may have difficulty connecting or reconnecting to IUanyWare.
To connect to VPN before starting IUanyWare, browse to
https://vpn.iu.edu
and follow the prompts.
If you are already in IUanyWare when you browse to
https://vpn.iu.edu
, you will temporarily lose your IUanyWare connection; reconnect to IUanyWare through the browser at
https://iuanyware.cloud.com
.
Note:
While off campus, VPN is not required to access IUanyWare.
Passphrases longer than 48 characters
Users with passphrases longer than 48 characters will sometimes see their application launches fail. This has been reported to Citrix, and it is a Citrix issue. UITS has started a ticket asking them to increase this character limit to allow users to use IU's maximum of 127 characters.
To use IUanyWare, reduce passphrase to 48 characters or less.
HTML5 Receiver
When printing, the HTML5 Receiver will not inherit the default printer of the local machine.
Choose a printer available in IUanyWare, or save the file to cloud storage or to the local machine to print elsewhere.
When saving, the HTML5 Receiver will not establish read/write access to your local hard drive.
Use a cloud storage or file share option to save your files.
In most cases, when you save a backup of the file, you'll also have an option in the "Save" dialog box to select
Save to My Device
. When you make this selection, the session will send a copy of the file to the default download folder used by the browser in which you're working.
When using the HTML5 Receiver via Firefox on Windows 10, you will not be able to type the
\
(backslash) character in applications or desktops.
Use another browser to access the HTML5 Receiver if you need to be able to type
\
. Alternatively, you can copy the
\
character from within the open IUanyWare application and paste it where desired.
Citrix Workspace App for Linux
Users are experiencing issues configuring the Citrix Workspace App/Receiver with the URL
https://iuanyware.cloud.com
.
The IUanyWare Team is investigating the issue. All Linux users should access IUanyWare via the web; see the first two sections of
Use IUanyWare in Linux
and
Access and use IUanyWare with Citrix Workspace app for Web
.
UITS staff:
First launch fails
We believe this is because items like the icon cache and some unnecessary files are actually being captured in the user profiles. This is causing the profile to take just long enough to load that it causes the application to fail on first launch.
We have done some preliminary testing, and so far it's positive and resolving the issue. After we perform a couple more tests, we hope to roll it out into production.
Error Message "The User Profile Service service failed the logon.  User profile cannot be loaded"
This error may result if the write cache of the XenApp server becomes full from user files, page files, etc. We are working to expand the write cache by an additional 20 GB. We were able to isolate a server, fill the write cache to almost full, and replicate the error message. In the IUanyWare environment, the cache is continually fluctuating as users log on and off, open large files, and engage in activities that increase the page file.
We are hoping the expansion of the drive and possibly setting a limit on the page file will help to resolve this issue.
This error has also occasionally appeared when a user selects an option multiple times, causing the service to attempt to log the user onto several servers at the same time. The profile is being downloaded by one server and then immediately requested by another server. We have not been able to consistently reproduce this.
Error message "The task you are trying to do can't be completed because Remote Desktop Services is currently busy. Please try again in a few minutes. Other users should still be able to log on."
This could be a Microsoft issue, but we need to make sure we are not using all our licenses.
See
Remote Desktop Services Client Access License (RDS CAL) Availability
.
Printer queues not populating in a timely manner
This is because we are mapping multiple printer queues. The mapping process can take 45 seconds to a minute. Users should be able to see their locally installed default printer immediately. The locally installed printers are not guaranteed to work with IUanyWare. Our universal print driver should work with about 90% of the printers out there, but there are going to be printers that will not work properly with IUanyWare.

title: Security tips for international travel
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Purpose
Considerations
Getting assistance
Export and import restrictions
Data security safeguards
Before your trip
During your trip
After your trip
Overview
For members of the campus community, a trip to a foreign country presents unique data security challenges.  The nature of international travel requires you to use your device (laptop, tablet or smartphone) in various unfamiliar places that may expose your data and device to malicious people and software.
Staying digitally connected often means connecting devices to public networks in hotels, airports, train stations, and conference halls, which may employ minimal security measures.  Public networks can harbor malware from cybercriminals looking to steal your data for identity fraud, as well as nation-state actors and government agencies targeting academic and business travelers for intellectual property and data theft.
Purpose
To help you protect institutional data throughout your trip, add the following data security safeguards, presented below by phase of trip, to your travel checklists:
Before your trip
During your trip
After your trip
This guide attempts to make safeguarding institutional data more approachable for all members of the campus community. Supplemental links and contact information for supporting units are provided, where possible.
Considerations
Getting assistance
Securing institutional data is a team sport. IT staff are available to assist you. If you are not comfortable performing any of the following security tips and considerations, or would like someone to assist you, contact IT support:
Your unit’s or department’s local IT staff member
Unit-specific contact information
Campus IT Support Center
Executive and Internal Technology Support (EITS)
Client Technology Support (Academic, Health, and UA Technology Support)
Export and import restrictions
In addition to data security safeguards outlined below, international travelers need to consider export and import restrictions imposed by the United States and destination countries. IU’s Research Security Office (RSO) specializes in this area and can assist you if you are unsure about your responsibilities.
Resources for complying with U.S. export laws and regulations
General concerns, email
rsohelp@iu.edu
Export control laws may require you to obtain a license or license exception under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) prior to traveling overseas. Additionally, IU's encryption software is subject to export control for certain countries.
For the most recent list of approved countries, see
Supplement No. 3 To Part 740
in the EAR document.
For help determining whether your university-issued electronic components, information, and software on your device can be safely and legally transported to another country, email IU Research Compliance (
orcinfo@iu.edu
).
Data security safeguards
Each international trip is unique, and not all safeguards may apply in your travel scenario. Be sure to review each data security safeguard and act, where appropriate. See
Getting assistance
if you are unsure.
Before your trip
In the weeks before your scheduled travel date, add the following data security safeguards to your travel checklist:
Leave your data and/or device at home.  The best way to safeguard your data or device is to not bring them on the trip.  If you don't need to access data stored on your computer, leave your computer in a secure location at home.
Register your trip and sign up for travel alerts. We recommend you sign up for the free US Department of State
STEP program
to register your travel and sign up for alerts on political unrest, natural disasters, and other health warnings.
Review
travel advisories
.  Travel advisories are official warnings from the U.S. Department of State that provide information about the safety of traveling to a specific destination.
Should you need a device and traveling to a Travel Advisory Level 2 through Level 4 destination, consult your local IT Staff to see if there’s an option to borrow a computer (i.e. a loaner computer) for your trip.
For destination-level information, item #3 above.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
Back up your data.  Whether you are traveling with a borrowed computer (that is, a loaner), your regular computer, tablet, or smartphone, you should always back up your data. Availability and integrity of your data are the primary reasons to do so. In the event of device loss or compromise, your data can be recovered.
Note:
For data stored on IU servers or in IU cloud storage services (for example, Teams, OneDrive), backup is not required.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
Install and configure disk encryption software.  In the unfortunate scenario where your device is lost or stolen, disk encryption software can help encode your data such that only you and people you authorized can decode and read the encrypted data.  Full disk encryption software, which is freely bundled with recent Microsoft Windows (BitLocker) and Mac OS X (File Vault) operating systems, is easy to use and setup.
For assistance specific to full disk encryption, see:
Bitlocker
File Vault
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
Install and configure campus VPN software.  To protect against eavesdroppers on networks during your trip, install and configure VPN Software to secure all internet traffic.
Download and install Avanti Secure from
IUware
.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
Implement multifactor authentication (MFA). As a member of the IU community, your IU account is protected with Duo, and you already have an authenticator app, like Duo, installed. In some destinations, the use of Duo is restricted. If your destination is one of these, see
About international Two-Step Login (Duo) access and restrictions to some services
.
Note:
If you will not have access to your personal cell number while traveling and you use SMS (that is, text messages) as a MFA form at sites such as banking institutions, reconfigure those accounts to use authentication apps (for example, Duo, Google Authenticator, etc.) instead of SMS, if possible.
Ensure the following computing security state before departure:
Update operating system and application software to the latest versions, where possible
Install and update anti-malware (virus) software
Strong credentials (that is,, passphrases) established on user accounts
Establish at least two computing accounts
; one privileged account (for example, root, administrator) that have elevated privileges, and one user account (for example, non-root, non-administrator) used for day-to-day computing.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
During your trip
Do NOT leave your device unattended. Physically having control of your device is the easiest way for someone to access your data.  Do not leave your device unattended, lend it to untrusted individuals, or leave it in your checked bag on your flight. When you leave your computer, turn it off instead of putting it to sleep.
Do NOT plug in untrusted accessories. Accessories that come from untrusted sources can be infected with malware (i.e., virus) intended to steal your data.  Avoid plugging in any questionable accessories (e.g., flash drive, charging cable, SD cards, USB drive/stick, etc.) to your device.  Take all the necessary accessories with you, but if you must purchase an accessory abroad, make sure it is from a reputable source.
Do NOT enter your credentials into public computers.  Public computers such as hotel business center workstations and internet cafe computers are often poorly managed and provide minimal security protection for their users.  If you need to use a public computer during your travel, avoid entering your credentials in the computer.
Note:
If you cannot avoid entering credentials in an untrusted computer (i.e., a travel emergency), consider changing your used password as soon as possible thereafter.
Connect only to known, trusted wireless (WiFi) and wired networks. Anyone can create a network and give the network a legitimate sounding name, hoping to lure unsuspecting travelers to connect so they can capture personal information transmitted through the network. This is especially prevalent at public cafes, hotel lobbies and airports.  When connecting to a network, verify the correct network name with establishment staff.
Note:
Establish a connection to the IU VPN service when connected to a public network.
Allow only trusted Bluetooth hardware to connect to devices. Limiting Bluetooth connectivity to only trusted hardware will help limit the attack vectors for your devices. If possible, do not leave your device in "discoverable" mode; this prevents unsolicited nearby connections to your device.
Enable security settings to protect data on your mobile device. Set a PIN or passcode, set the device to time out (and require a password) when idle, and depending on the data classification of stored data, consider setting the device to auto-wipe its contents after several incorrect login attempts.
Note:
Auto-wipe is a disruptive measure that should only be implemented with due care and under advisory of IT Staff to ensure appropriate recovery measures are in place.
If your
mobile device
is lost or stolen, immediately contact the
Campus IT Support Center
; see
If your computer or other device is stolen
.
Consider implementing privacy best practices such as:
Use a webcam cover to protect against unknown monitoring
Install a privacy screen that prevent others from shoulder surfing
Comply with any request from a border official to log into your laptop or mobile device.
If your device is seized by a foreign agency:
Obtain a contact name, phone number, and written documentation that the device was seized.
Contact the local US embassy or consulate for advice on resolution in the local country.
Note:
If the incident involves the US government, report it to your department’s IT staff and contact
IU Compliance: Export Control
.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.
After your trip
If you have traveled to a Travel Advisory Level 2 through Level 4 destination, reset credentials (that is, passwords) you used during the trip.  As noted above, consider credentials you used during the journey to be compromised.  Use a trusted computer, whether it's your own or one provided by your IT support staff, to reset credentials that were used during the trip.
If you have traveled to a Travel Advisory Level 3 or Level 4 destination, consult your local IT Staff to have your computing devices' security state assessed.
For IT help, see
Getting assistance
.

Overview
Below is a list of external tools (also called LTI tools, LTI apps, or external apps) that have been reviewed and approved for use at Indiana University. Most are available in all Canvas courses, but some are restricted by campus, school, or department to comply with licensing agreements or other constraints.
Most of the tools integrated with Canvas are available for use by students, faculty, and staff without fee because IU or a sponsoring unit is covering the licensing costs. Exceptions (noted below) include online textbooks and digital courseware and learning tools offered by textbook publishers.
A few of the tools on this page are either included in your course navigation menu, or appear in other parts of the Canvas user interface. Most, however, are hidden, which means you'll need to expose them if you want to use them. For more about installing and exposing external tools, see
Add an external app to your course in Canvas
.
Important:
As an instructor, if you use an application managed by a supplier with whom IU does not have a contract, and it collects protected student data, you may be subject to sanctions, according to university policy
Disclosing Institutional Information to Third Parties (DM-02)
. If your intended use will collect any
FERPA

content:

Overview
Geode-Project
is a
Research Technologies
service providing disk-based persistent storage allocations to research projects using Indiana University's
research supercomputers
.
Geode-Project
allocations are hosted on
Geode
, which is co-located at the IU data centers in Bloomington and Indianapolis, and are managed through the
RT Projects
portal. Files stored in
Geode-Project
space are replicated, by default, at each data center. Project space users can access
Geode-Project
directly from all IU
research supercomputers
and remotely from personal workstations connected to the IU campus network.
To request a
Geode-Project
allocation, you must complete a memo of understanding (MOU) with
UITS
Research Technologies
; see
Request a project space allocation on Geode-Project
.
Once space on
Geode-Project
is allocated, UITS
Research Technologies
will work with the project owner's
local UITS support person
to set up
ADS
security groups for controlling access permissions for the project space (as explained in the next section).
Set up AD groups for administrator and user access
The local UITS support person will create two security groups in IU
ADS
for controlling the administrator and user roles for the project space:
The "admin" group (for example,
BL-BIO-GEODE-LAB1-ADMINS
) should be populated with only the local UITS support people who are responsible for administering the project space. Users added to this group are granted full permissions to the project space.
The "user" group (for example,
BL-BIO-GEODE-LAB1-USERS
) should be populated with the individuals and groups using the project space. Users added to this group are granted modify permissions.
Note:
If your IT unit provides support for many organizations, leveraging a single group for each
Geode-Project
allocation is acceptable and encouraged.
The local UITS support person will share the group names with UITS Research Storage, which uses them to populate corresponding AD groups for managing administrator and user roles in
Geode-Project
.
Once this step is complete, the local UITS support person may add users and groups to the allocation by adding them to the appropriate AD group. Changes take approximately 15 minutes before they become available for use on
Geode-Project
.
Research Storage staff will provide a share path or mount point for your allocation.
Mount your allocation. Allocation names should follow the IU ADS naming conventions; see
Map or mount a drive to your home directory space or a Geode-Project space
.
Set up a sub-allocation within a project space
The local UITS support person may also create a sub-allocation and restrict it to a single AD group:
Create an AD group that contains the users you want to limit to the sub-allocation (for example,
BL-BIO-GEODE-LAB1-PROJECT1-USERS
), and then add it to the main "user" group set up for the project space (for example,
BL-BIO-GEODE-LAB1-USERS
). Changes take approximately 15 minutes before they become available for use on
Geode-Project
.
In Windows,
map a drive to the appropriate project space
, and then, immediately below the root level of the project space, create a new directory for the sub-allocation.
Right-click the new folder, select
Properties
, and then, on the
Security
tab, select
Edit
.
Select
Add
, enter the sub-allocation group name (for example,
BL-BIO-GEODE-LAB1-PROJECT1-USERS
), and then select
OK
.
Select the appropriate "Allow" permission (typically,
Modify
), select
Apply
, and then select
OK
twice.
Users may need to log out and then log back in again for this change to take effect.
Note:
To set a quota on a sub-allocation to limit the amount of storage available to a group of users, the local UITS support person should email the UITS Research Storage team (
store-admin@iu.edu
) for help.

content:

Overview

Overview
RT Projects
allows you to request new
Geode-Project
allocations, request modifications to allocations, and manage collaborators in each allocation. An RT Project can contain a single Geode-Project allocation per principal investigator (PI). Geode-Project allocations must be linked to a single RT Project. All Geode-Project allocations are subject to an annual renewal in order to keep the storage active.
Important:
Only the RT Project's principal investigator (PI) can make changes to an existing allocation.
Request a Geode-Project allocation
When the PI is viewing the "Allocations" section of a project, selecting
Request Resource Allocation
will display a list of resources. At the bottom of this list, under "Storages", is a request form to create a new Geode-Project allocation. This form will ask for a secondary contact, the storage size needed,
Active Directory security groups
for the users and admins of the project, the purpose of the storage allocation, and some general questions about project lifetime, generation and protection of the data, and how long the data will be computed against. The owner of the RT Project will be the owner of the Geode-Project allocation.
Request a change to a Geode-Project allocation
Within your RT Project, under "Allocations", in the "Actions" column, select the folder icon to view the details of the project.
Within the details of the project, you may view the Geode-Project allocation's attributes, and request a change or removal of a project.
Requesting a change results in a form that allows you to request a new quota for the project. The quota change is subject to an approval process and other technical limits. For example, it would not be suitable to reduce an allocation from 4 TB to 1 TB if 3 TB of data still exists in the project. All quota increase requests must provide a demonstrated need for the increased quota.
Request removal of a Geode-Project allocation
To request removal of a Geode-Project allocation, use the
Removal
button next to the
Change
button. Make sure you have selected the correct allocation before proceeding at the confirmation screen.
Manage user access for a Geode-Project allocation
Anyone with an active IU account can be given access to the Geode-Project allocation's storage space. The RT Project's PI does this by adding usernames to either of the
Active Directory security groups
provided when the allocation was requested. Granular file storage access is also managed by the project's PI via
NFSv4 ACLs
within the Geode-Project.
Two Active Directory security groups are used to manage access in a Geode-Project: Admins and Users.
Admins:
Users in the Admins group have read/write access to the top-level directory in the Geode-Project storage allocation and have access to edit the NFSv4 ACLs within the directory structure.
Users:
Users in the Users group have basic read/write access to all directories below the top-level directory or as permitted by the NFSv4 ACLs set by the project's PI.
These groups are set upon the creation of the Geode-Project, and only the members of the groups should be modified over time.

content:

Overview

Examine the data lineage

Overview
When using
Denodo
for data virtualization and integration, you may be able to improve the performance of Denodo views. For potential options, see below.
Use caching
In Denodo at IU, caching is not performed at the server level. Instead, each virtual database (VDB) is configured with an exclusive Oracle tablespace for caching. Developers have sufficient permissions to manage partial caching at the view level.
Note:
Denodo caching is used to enhance query performance. Caching is resource intensive, so you should implement it only after detecting query performance issues (not by default). Run cache jobs as infrequently as possible. Do not refresh your cache more than once an hour. Cache necessary data only, and do not cache excessively large database columns, such as CLOBs or LOBs.
Note:
UITS recommends setting TIMETOLIVEINCACHE to
NOEXPIRE
.
Examine the data lineage
You can examine your data lineage for a derived view by using
Tree View
. If you are combining data that you don't need, consider redesigning your derived view.
Change the execution plan
You can change how Denodo executes complex joins by modifying the execution plan. For details, see the Denodo
Virtual DataPort Administration Guide
. If you wish to try
data movement
, your cache tablespace is exclusive to your VDB and available for your use.

content:

Accounts

Accounts
The Indiana University
Research Database Complex
(
RDC
) supports research-related MySQL and PostgreSQL databases and data-intensive applications that require databases. The
RDC
is strictly devoted to supporting research, and is not an instructional, classroom environment.
Access to the RDC is available to all IU graduate students, faculty, and staff. Undergraduate students and non-IU collaborators need IU faculty sponsors to get access.
To create a database on the RDC, submit the
RDC Database Account Application
.
When your database login has been created, you will receive a confirmation message in email with your login and information about connecting to your database. You will need to renew your database account annually.
By submitting the RDC Database Account Application, you will be affirming that:
You understand the database is to be used only for research purposes.
You agree to not store
Critical data
(except for ePHI data) on RDC databases.
You will acknowledge use of IU's high performance computing systems in publications resulting from your research.
You will provide periodic listings of citations of those publications upon request.
You agree to annually renew your RDC account.
Database group accounts are used on the RDC. Although you are not allowed to use a group account for regular data access, group accounts are often the best process for administering a database that is used by a project or team. The RDC Database Account Application lets you specify a database group account. When you request a database group account:
You must first have an
IU username
for your group.
You will be considered the responsible party for the group database account.
You must create additional logins for all access to data, and you must ensure that the database group account is never used for data access. It should only be used to administer user logins, schemas, and permissions.
For more, see
About group and departmental accounts
.
Database security
HIPAA
This system or service meets certain requirements established in the
HIPAA Security Rule
thereby enabling its use for work involving data that contain protected health information (
PHI
). However, using this system or service does not fulfill your legal responsibilities for protecting the privacy and security of data that contain PHI. You may use this system or service for work involving data that contain PHI only if you institute additional
administrative
,
physical
, and
technical
safeguards that complement those UITS already has in place.
For more, see
Your legal responsibilities for protecting data containing protected health information (PHI) when using UITS Research Technologies systems and services
.
Note:
In accordance with standards for access control mandated by the
HIPAA
Security
Rule
, you are not permitted to access data containing protected health information (
PHI
) using a group (or departmental) account. To ensure accountability and maintain appropriate levels of access control, all users must use an individual login for all work involving PHI.
If you have questions about securing HIPAA-regulated research data at IU, email
securemyresearch@iu.edu
.
SecureMyResearch
provides self-service resources and one-on-one consulting to help IU researchers, faculty, and staff meet cybersecurity and compliance requirements for processing, storing, and sharing regulated and unregulated research data; for more, see
About SecureMyResearch
. To learn more about properly ensuring the safe handling of
PHI
on UITS systems, see the UITS IT Training video
Securing HIPAA Workflows on UITS Systems
. To learn about division of responsibilities for securing PHI, see
Shared responsibility model for securing PHI on UITS systems
.
Passwords
Once your RDC Database Account Application is processed, you will receive a confirmation email message that describes how to access your database. Your initial database password will be sent under separate cover as a second email message.
For security reasons, when using a command-line client to connect to your MySQL database, do not enter your database password on the MySQL command line. Follow the instructions in
Access your MySQL database at IU RDC
.
Responsibilities
You are responsible for:
Creating and managing your schemas and schema objects (for example, tables, views, procedures, triggers, and schema privileges)
Creating and managing user logins for your databases (see the previous
Database security note
about maintaining appropriate access for sensitive data, including PHI)
Changing datatypes
Any data processes, such as data imports, deletes, modifications, transformations, and retrievals
Creating and maintaining copies of scripts
Emailing the RDC Administration team (
rdcadmin@iu.edu
) about changes in space or database administration, or if you no longer need access to the research database
Adapting your schema and data as required during system and database upgrades
Adapting client applications and tools to system and database versions
RDC database administrators are responsible for:
Managing space allocation
Monitoring and reporting database performance
Monitoring and reporting invalid schema objects
Installing database and system upgrades and
patches
If you have questions or need help, email the RDC Administration team (
rdcadmin@iu.edu
).
Acknowledging grant support
The Indiana University cyberinfrastructure, managed by the
Research Technologies
division of
UITS
, is supported by funding from several grants, each of which requires you to acknowledge its support in all presentations and published works stemming from research it has helped to fund. Conscientious acknowledgment of support from past grants also enhances the chances of IU's research community securing funding from grants in the future. For the acknowledgment statement(s) required for scholarly printed works, web pages, talks, online publications, and other presentations that make use of this and/or other grant-funded systems at IU, see
Sources of funding to acknowledge in published work if you use IU's research cyberinfrastructure
.
Database backup and recovery
Backups for MySQL database servers on the RDC are the responsibility of the user. UITS recommends using MySQL's
mysqldump
command; for more, see
mysqldump - A Database Backup Program
in the MySQL documentation.
Scheduled downtime
The RDC's maintenance window is the third Sunday of each month, 12am-6am. Make sure to plan for this downtime each month. Notice of any emergency downtime will be posted at
Status.IU
.
Disk space for data loading and other applications
If you need space on the RDC for staging data, or for data-related packages and applications, email the RDC Administration team (
rdcadmin@iu.edu
), which will evaluate requests on a case-by-case basis.
Mail usage
Production mail service is not provided on the RDC.
Reporting problems
To report a problem with the RDC, email the RDC Administration team (
rdcadmin@iu.edu
) with the following information:
The name of the database server to which you were connecting
A description of what you were trying to do
A description of the problem
The name and version of the tool you were using to connect to the database server
Your computer's operating system
The error message number and text, if applicable
The time the problem occurred
Support staff are available from approximately 8am-5pm Monday-Friday.
Questions and comments
UITS established the policies described in this document with the goal of providing a stable, powerful, and efficient research database environment for IU graduate students, faculty, and staff. If you have a question or comment about these policies, email the RDC Administration team (
rdcadmin@iu.edu
).

title: Why SiteKube and AppKube are separate
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Different use cases have different security needs
Minimizing security risk for sites
Providing flexibility where needed
Protecting IU's data and systems
Supporting security compliance and auditing
Enabling better resource optimization
Common questions
Overview
IU has intentionally separated hosting into two environments:
SiteKube
(for
WCMS
sites) and
AppKube
(for dynamic applications).
This approach improves security, simplifies management, and ensures each environment is optimized for its purpose.
This article summarizes why the environments are separated and what benefits this architecture provides.
Different use cases have different security needs
SiteKube
is designed for WCMS-managed sites with minimal dynamic content or server-side code.
AppKube
is designed for custom applications that need databases, APIs, or dynamic server-side code.
Minimizing security risk for sites
Static sites rely on fewer technologies (like databases), making them well-suited for a more restricted environment that maximizes security and stability.
Centralized publishing through WCMS limits who can make changes on the server. It also helps ensure sites use IU's most secure, accessible content management tools (such as the IU Web Framework).
Providing flexibility where needed
AppKube allows more complex functionality (databases, APIs, cron jobs) that SiteKube sites often don't need.
Developers can use server-side PHP, database connections, and custom logic.
This extra flexibility requires a hosting environment with stricter security controls, monitoring, and management.
Protecting IU's data and systems
Segregating environments reduces the risk of cross-site vulnerabilities.
SiteKube content stays isolated from more complex, potentially risky code.
Sensitive data (for example, database credentials) can be better secured with environment-specific secrets management.
Supporting security compliance and auditing
Having a tightly managed environment makes it easier to prove security compliance for most public-facing IU websites.
Dynamic applications and web services in AppKube follow approved workflows, security reviews, and DevOps practices.
Enabling better resource optimization
SiteKube can scale more efficiently for the management of thousands of WCMS sites.
AppKube dedicates more advanced resources to applications that need them without compromising the performance and management of simpler sites.
Common questions
Why can't everything just go on one system?
Different types of sites have different security and technical needs. Separating static sites from dynamic applications lets administrators optimize the security, performance, and management of each.
Isn't the static environment too restrictive?
The restrictions are intentional. Static sites often don’t need server-side code or databases (or use them minimally), so keeping them tightly controlled reduces risk without limiting necessary features.
Why do I have to use the WCMS for my static site?
Restricting publishing to the WCMS ensures that only authorized users can write to the server. It also helps ensure that content managers are using IU's most security and accessibility focused tools for content management, such as the IU Web Framework.
Why can't I just use PHP includes or database calls like before?
Allowing cross-site includes, database calls, or filesystem code on all sites increases security risk. SiteKube is designed for safer, more static content, while AppKube allows common developer
customization options
.
Can I move my old Sitehost site exactly as-is?
Static content can often be migrated with minimal changes. Dynamic functionality will need to be reviewed to see if it belongs in SiteKube or AppKube. For more, see
