title: SQL example statements for retrieving data from a table
content:
Overview
SELECT statements
Examples
Learning more about SQL
Overview
Structured Query Language (SQL) is a specialized language for updating, deleting, and requesting information from
databases
. SQL is an
ANSI
and
ISO
standard, and is the de facto standard database query language. A variety of established database products support SQL, including products from Oracle and Microsoft SQL Server. It is widely used in both industry and academia, often for enormous, complex databases.
In a distributed database system, a program often referred to as the database's "back end" runs constantly on a server, interpreting data files on the server as a standard relational database. Programs on client computers allow users to manipulate that data, using tables, columns, rows, and fields. To do this, client programs send SQL statements to the server. The server then processes these statements and returns result sets to the client program.
SELECT statements
An SQL
SELECT
statement retrieves records from a database table according to clauses (for example,
FROM
and
WHERE
) that specify criteria. The syntax is:
SELECT column1, column2 FROM table1, table2 WHERE column2='value';
In the above SQL statement:
The
SELECT
clause specifies one or more columns to be retrieved; to specify multiple columns, use a comma and a space between column names. To retrieve all columns, use the wild card
*
(an asterisk).
The
FROM
clause specifies one or more tables to be queried. Use a comma and space between table names when specifying multiple tables.
The
WHERE
clause selects only the rows in which the specified column contains the specified value. The value is enclosed in single quotes (for example,
WHERE last_name='Vader'
).
The semicolon (
;
) is the statement terminator. Technically, if you're sending only one statement to the back end, you don't need the statement terminator; if you're sending more than one, you need it. It's best practice to include it.
Note:
SQL is not case sensitive (for example,
SELECT
is the same as
select
). For better readability, some programmers use uppercase for commands and clauses, and lowercase for everything else.
Examples
Following are examples of SQL
SELECT
statements:
To select all columns from a table (
Customers
) for rows where the
Last_Name
column has
Smith
for its value, you would send this
SELECT
statement to the server back end:
SELECT * FROM Customers WHERE Last_Name='Smith';
The server back end would reply with a result set similar to this:
+---------+-----------+------------+
| Cust_No | Last_Name | First_Name |
+---------+-----------+------------+
| 1001    | Smith     | John       |
| 2039    | Smith     | David      |
| 2098    | Smith     | Matthew    |
+---------+-----------+------------+
3 rows in set (0.05 sec)
To return only the
Cust_No
and
First_Name
columns, based on the same criteria as above, use this statement:
SELECT Cust_No, First_Name FROM Customers WHERE Last_Name='Smith';
The subsequent result set might look like:
+---------+------------+
| Cust_No | First_Name |
+---------+------------+
| 1001    | John       |
| 2039    | David      |
| 2098    | Matthew    |
+---------+------------+
3 rows in set (0.05 sec)
To make a
WHERE
clause find inexact matches, add the pattern-matching operator
LIKE
. The
LIKE
operator uses the
%
(percent symbol) wild card to match zero or more characters, and the underscore (
_
) wild card to match exactly one character. For example:
To select the
First_Name
and
Nickname
columns from the
Friends
table for rows in which the
Nickname
column contains the string "brain", use this statement:
SELECT First_Name, Nickname FROM Friends WHERE Nickname LIKE '%brain%';
The subsequent result set might look like:
+------------+------------+
| First_Name | Nickname   |
+------------+------------+
| Ben        | Brainiac   |
| Glen       | Peabrain   |
| Steven     | Nobrainer  |
+------------+------------+
3 rows in set (0.03 sec)
To query the same table, retrieving all columns for rows in which the
First_Name
column's value begins with any letter and ends with "en", use this statement:
SELECT * FROM Friends WHERE First_Name LIKE '_en';
The result set might look like:
+------------+------------+-----------+
| First_Name | Last_Name  | Nickname  |
+------------+------------+-----------+
| Ben        | Smith      | Brainiac  |
| Jen        | Peters     | Sweetpea  |
+------------+------------+-----------+
2 rows in set (0.03 sec)
If you used the
%
wild card instead (for example,
'%en'
) in the example above, the result set might look like:
+------------+------------+-----------+
| First_Name | Last_Name  | Nickname  |
+------------+------------+-----------+
| Ben        | Smith      | Brainiac  |
| Glen       | Jones      | Peabrain  |
| Jen        | Peters     | Sweetpea  |
| Steven     | Griffin    | Nobrainer |
+------------+------------+-----------+
4 rows in set (0.05 sec)
Learning more about SQL
To learn more about SQL programming, Indiana University students, faculty, and staff can
download materials for self-study from IT Training.
For the general public, various online tutorials are available, such as the
w3schools.com SQL Tutorial
.

title: Migrate from Sitehost to SiteKube
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Publish your site to SiteKube
Handling remaining Sitehost content
Sitehost.iu.edu URL retirement
Sitehost vs. SiteKube feature comparison
Troubleshoot your SiteKube migration
What can I NOT do on SiteKube?
Check for broken images and links
Fix PHP include errors
Blank or white pages
Restore missing CSS or JavaScript
External forms or integrations not working
General tips
How do I know if my site is ready for production?
What do I do about old Sitehost URLs?
Can I get my old files and data from Sitehost, MachForm, or MySQL?
Overview
This article explains the process for moving from Sitehost to SiteKube. For more about SiteKube's capabilities, see
About SiteKube
.
Initial migration to test environment
UITS will publish WCMS content to the SiteKube test environment.
Test sites will be accessible at:
https://
<accountname>
.sites-test.iu.edu
Sites will need to be reviewed by site administrators and stakeholders.
Site review and QA
Site managers must review their test sites for functionality and completeness.
Many WCMS sites currently have external dependencies and may not function fully.
Site administrators must work within the WCMS to bring their sites to a production-ready state.
Approval and publish to production
UITS is finalizing the production SiteKube environment. Once it is available, you will be notified and can publish your site to production directly through the WCMS.
If a site uses only WCMS content, it may be ready for production after minimal QA.
Resources
Request a WCMS site
Transition your Machform to enterprise tools
Publish your site to SiteKube
In order to publish to SiteKube, you will need to update your
.htaccess
file. For instructions, see
Update .htaccess when moving from Sitehost to SiteKube
(requires IU login).
Handling remaining Sitehost content
For remaining content on Sitehost (apps, databases, files), you may either:
Transfer to
WCMS
Move to
AppKube
Sitehost.iu.edu URL retirement
Note:
If your site previously used a production URL in the format
username
.sitehost.iu.edu
, it will need to be transitioned to a new URL.
We are in the process of identifying appropriate replacement domains, and site stewards will be contacted directly with a recommended new URL for their site.
Sitehost vs. SiteKube feature comparison
Compare Sitehost and SiteKube features
Feature
Sitehost compatibility
SiteKube compatibility
PHP version
PHP 8.1, 8.2 (default), 8.3
8.2, 8.3
Apache version
2.4
2.4
Virtual host required
No
Yes
.htaccess file management
On Sitehost server
Published from WCMS
CMS compatibility
No limitations
WCMS (Cascade) only
Web apps allowed
Yes
No
Server-side integrations with other accounts, databases, and servers
Yes
No
Troubleshoot your SiteKube migration
When you review your test site on SiteKube, you might find that some pages or features aren't working the way they did on Sitehost. Below are some common issues you can check and fix yourself.
What can I NOT do on SiteKube?
SSH/SFTP into the server
Connect to external databases or APIs directly from PHP
Include PHP files from other IU group accounts or sites
Use symlinks to other sites' content
Run cron jobs
Use certain PHP functions
(IU Login required to view article).
Check for broken images and links
Problem:
Images or links don't load or show errors.
Steps to fix:
Make sure all images and pages were published to SiteKube from the WCMS. Republish missing images and pages to SiteKube.
Check that links use relative paths (
/images/my-image.webp
) instead of hard-coded URLs (
https://mysite.iu.edu/images/my-image.webp
).
If you see old URLs (like
username.sitehost.iu.edu
), update them to use relative paths (if linking to image or page on your site) or the virtual host (if linking to image or page on another IU site).
Check all external link assets in the WCMS to ensure URLs have been updated to the correct domains (or pointed to temporary alternative URLs if the original link hasn’t been migrated to SiteKube).
If links in a shared/attached section are pointing to the wrong URLs or leading to 404 pages, make sure that shared section’s link rewriting behavior is set to
Site-relative
under the
Edit
>
Configure
tab.
Fix PHP include errors
Problem:
You see errors like
"Failed to open stream"
or blank areas where includes should load.
Why:
The PHP include path has changed in SiteKube. In addition, SiteKube blocks PHP includes from one account into another.
Steps to fix:
Make sure your
.htaccess
file has been correctly updated; see
Update .htaccess when moving from Sitehost to SiteKube
(requires IU login).
Update any includes that used
/groups/accountname/web/
to use
/var/www/html/
.
If you have PHP files that are shared across multiple sites, move copies of those PHP files into each individual site and include those instead.
Check that your included PHP files are present in your site's
/_php
folder in WCMS. Be sure to publish those PHP files to SiteKube.
Check that your PHP files aren’t using any of the PHP functions that have been disabled on SiteKube; see
PHP functions disabled on SiteKube
(requires IU login).
Blank or white pages
Problem:
Entire page is blank or partially missing content.
Why:
PHP errors can stop pages from rendering.
Steps to fix:
Check that all PHP includes are updated to use the correct paths (see previous section).
Remove any includes that try to load files from other IU accounts or old systems—cross-site includes are blocked (see previous section).
Make sure your page doesn't depend on any databases or external server connections (which SiteKube now blocks).
If the PHP script was fetching information from a database, consider replacing it with static content, a folder of page assets in the WCMS with an index block, or FireForm.
For complex integrations, plan to move the server-side code to AppKube (IU’s environment for more advanced apps).
Information about AppKube is forthcoming.
Restore missing CSS or JavaScript
Problem:
Styles look broken or interactive elements (like menus, accordions) don't work.
Why:
Your site might be linking to CSS or JS files that weren’t copied over.
Steps to fix:
Open your browser’s Developer Tools (usually by right-clicking and selecting
Inspect
) and go to the
Network
tab.
Refresh the page and look for any 404 errors for CSS or JS files.
Upload the missing CSS files to your site's
/css
folder in the WCMS and publish them.
Upload missing JS files to your
/js
folder in the WCMS and publish them.
Update your HTML or Velocity includes to use the local copies.
Make sure "Brand Version" in the "Settings" block is set to
3.3.x
(Framework sites only).
External forms or integrations not working
Problem:
Forms or tools that used to connect to databases or other systems don’t work.
Why:
SiteKube doesn’t allow server-side connections to external systems or databases.
Steps to fix:
If the form or integration was pulling live data, consider replacing it with static content, a folder of page assets in the WCMS with an index block, or FireForm; see
Transition your MachForm to enterprise tools
.
For complex integrations, plan to move the server-side code to AppKube (IU's environment for more advanced apps).
Information about AppKube is forthcoming.
General tips
Make sure your site is correctly set up for
publishing to SiteKube for the first time
.
Always republish your page or folder in WCMS after making changes.
Keep all required assets (images, CSS, JS, PHP includes) in your site's WCMS folders.
Remember that SiteKube only supports WCMS-managed sites—no direct server access or database connections.
How do I know if my site is ready for production?
Make sure:
All images, CSS, JavaScript, and PHP includes are present in WCMS.
Pages display correctly in the SiteKube test URL.
Navigation works with no broken links.
Forms or integrations are replaced or updated for SiteKube compatibility.
If you're not sure, involve your site's stakeholders to help with review and testing. You can also
contact the Support Center
.
What do I do about old Sitehost URLs?
Any hard-coded links to
accountname.sitehost.iu.edu
need to be updated. (In general, hard-coded links to sitehost.iu.edu were discouraged, so there should not be many of these links.)
Use relative paths when possible so your site works in test and production. If you need to link to images or pages on another site, use their virtual host URL (the URL
without
sitehost in it).
Can I get my old files and data from Sitehost, MachForm, or MySQL?
Yes—learn more about
requesting files and data from your old site or database
.

content:

Overview and definitions
The
Windows Hosting Environment
(
WHE
) enables clients to use desired technologies not available in any other hosting environment provided by University Information Technology Services (UITS), for as low a cost as possible, while maintaining an acceptable level of performance, reliability, and security. Applications requiring other levels of performance, reliability, or security must be hosted elsewhere.
The unique features of this hosting environment are a Microsoft IIS Web Server with the ability to serve dynamic web pages written using Adobe ColdFusion, Microsoft .NET Framework 4.8+, and Microsoft .NET 8 programming languages.
WHE
also provides a Microsoft SQL Server database environment. The web pages and database servers can be used with resources outside of this environment.
The
Windows Hosting Environment
is available to departments and affiliates on all campuses of Indiana University and student organizations with a full-time faculty or staff sponsor. The clients develop and maintain the applications, and University Information Technology Services provides the hardware, software, and systems administration.
This environment is provided by the UITS Enterprise Windows and Azure Administration group. The remainder of this document describes the environment, and the relationship between the service provider and the service clients.
Terminology:
"Client" refers to the consumer of the services provided by this environment. A client is the organizational unit and all associated individuals served.
"Provider" or "Service Provider" refers to the University Information Technology Services groups and personnel responsible for providing some aspect of this environment.
"Workspace" refers to the total scope of a client's use of this environment. A workspace is comprised of all file and database space provided to a client.
"Project" refers to a sub-grouping of resources within a workspace. A "Workspace" can have one or more "Projects". File and database space are associated with a "Project". The primary reason for multiple "Projects" is security–to compartmentalize access to files and data to different groups of people.
WHE
:
Windows Hosting Environment
Changes as of 2026
Upgrades and migrations
ColdFusion 2023 is available.
Maintenance windows
ColdFusion and .NET environments:
Windows security updates will be applied to non-production systems on the Wednesday prior to the third Sunday of the month between 6pm and midnight. For production server environments, updates will occur on the third Sunday between midnight and 8am.
Production environments:
Maintenance windows will be scheduled on Thursdays between 7-9am or Sundays between midnight and 8am.
Non-production environments:
Maintenance windows may occur at any time; WebTech will post a notice on
webhost.iu.edu
if these maintenance periods are likely to affect availability of the stage servers.
Important information at a glance
Fees
The
Windows Hosting Environment
is a baseline service. There are no fees for internal departments to use the shared hosting environment. However, there may be fees for additional services such as file restorations and resources such as disk space. For more information, see the
Fees section
.
Site and application requirements
The client is required to maintain a developer for each project. Code and databases that cannot be maintained to respond to environmental changes will be removed.
Web applications and sites cannot create or upload files to the project content directories. If a web application needs a location to create and write files, the client must request a Storage Share location from the
WHE
administrators.
All websites should include a privacy notice. The notice needs to be updated or reviewed at least every two years. For more information, see
Privacy Notice Generator
.
UITS
WHE
reserves the right to end service to any application that:
Violates any IU policy or this service agreement
Fails to match environmental upgrade deadlines
Adversely affects the performance of other users
Compliance and data requirements
To host
Critical or Restricted data
and protected data types in the
Windows Hosting Environment
, the owner of the data and UITS
WHE
needs to grant approval.
Critical data
will require the approval of the IU
Data Stewards
before hosting in
WHE
. Owners of
WHE
-hosted sites and databases with
Critical data
,
Restricted data
, or protected data will be required to sign the service agreement annually.
If your site has HIPAA requirements, notify
WHE
administrators and describe your use case. The
Windows Hosting Environment
satisfies certain requirements of the HIPAA security rule, but can only be used with protected health information (PHI) if you have the complementary safeguards in place. For more information, review
Shared responsibility model for securing PHI on UITS systems
. If the PHI is part of research and you have questions how best to secure it, email
securemyresearch@iu.edu
.
WHE
does
not
meet compliance for Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards (PCI DSS) 0 SAQ A-EP. Merchant questionnaires submitted with the assistance of
WHE
will note areas where policy is not met.
Outages
If you have a problem with the
WHE
that is not covered by any of the notices on
Status.IU
, refer to the
Emergency communications section
.
All system-wide
WHE
outages will be posted to the Webhost Admin Portal at
https://webhost.iu.edu
. We will follow up by sending email to all developers listed in the contacts section of your project. It is up to our clients to make certain this list is up to date for efficient communications. If the
Webhost Admin Portal
is not available, see
Status.IU
.
Agreements
Service provider agreements
The service provider agrees to:
Provide a
Windows Hosting Environment
24 hours a day, 7 days a week, except for maintenance and emergencies. See the
Guidelines
section for further information about scheduled and emergency maintenance.
Provide a full range of support resources. The service provider responsibilities are divided between the Enterprise Web Technical Services (WebTech)
Windows Hosting Environment
(
WHE
) team, Enterprise Windows and Azure Administration Enterprise Server Administration (EWA), Storage and Virtualization (SAV), and Support Center (SC) groups within University Information Technology Services (UITS).
Additionally:
UITS
WHE
is the service owner and primary contact for all clients. UITS
WHE
will introduce new clients to the environment and provide general information to existing clients.
The EWA group is the database administrator for this environment. The EWA group will install, configure, and maintain the stage and production database software.
The SAV group will provide virtual servers and allocate additional virtual resources as needed.
Client agreements
The client agrees to:
Secure projects and workspace data:
From the
WHE
Admin portal, the client must ensure Contact and Active Directory membership lists are up to date.
Inform UITS
WHE
before you use the environment for
Critical data
,
Restricted data
, or protected data. For information about data classifications, see
Classification levels of institutional data
and
About sensitive data at IU
. Sites that access or store HIPAA data require additional security measures. PCI DSS compliance is not met on the
WHE
.
Maintain project workspace in accordance with the terms of this agreement:
The
Windows Hosting Environment
(
WHE
) is shared by many clients. The configuration of all applications is standardized to provide a maintainable and acceptable level of performance, reliability, and security. The client may request deviations from the standard, but the provider reserves the right to deny any request for customization.
All client applications must not adversely affect other client applications.
If a client application adversely affects other client applications, the provider may remove the offending client application from the service.
Maintain project workspace to be compatible with environment upgrades:
The client is responsible for implementing any changes necessary to make their application function in the patched, updated, or upgraded environment.
The client is required to maintain a developer for each project
. Projects that cannot be maintained to respond to environmental changes will be removed.
The client is required to patch, modify, and edit code to bring it to a working state.
In some cases, environmental changes will make previously working code fail to execute or display properly. The
WHE
administrators may be able to assist with additional logs, error codes, etc.
If an environmental upgrade or policy change forces a change of hostname, server operating system, database version, or programming language, the service provider will give a timeline for this change. The timeline will be reasonable but nonnegotiable.
Use the following procedures to make changes:
UITS
WHE
is composed of stage and production environments. Best practice is to develop and adequately test in the staging environments before moving changes to the production area. Only tested code should be applied to the production area.
For timely production deployments for web applications and databases,
WHE
administrators must be given ample notice by sending email to
webhost@iu.edu
. Failure to plan a new deployment could result in a delayed launch date.
Each time a new site is deployed or code is updated, the client must perform a web application security scan in the stage environment before the application will be placed into production. For instructions on how to request a scan, see
About vulnerability scanners
Significant changes to the production environment (database or file content) should be preempted by an additional web application vulnerability scan against modified test data.
Other changes can be made by submitting a request to
webhost@iu.edu
. Requests must clearly specify the changes desired. The actual completion date and time will be determined upon review of each individual request.
The client must notify the
WHE
administrators of any anticipated "significant" changes in usage, such as a dramatic user base increase or the need for a dramatic increase in disk space, in order to ensure the environment has the resources to accommodate the changes.
Important:
Failure to meet these expectations will result in actions necessary to eliminate the resulting problem or risk. In most cases this will result in a site or database being taken offline until security concerns are met, or until an alternative hosting location is identified.
Guidelines
Initiate service
For projects that include a web presence, you must submit the
Website Request form
before sending a request to WebTech. Submissions to this form will return a ServiceNow ticket number; include this number in your request to WebTech. For database-only projects, you don't need to submit this form.
Submit all new requests to
WHE
by sending mail to
webhost@iu.edu
or filling out the
New Site Request form
.
Include a proposed name for the client, project, and the Network ID and email address for the primary contact.
Additional information that you can share, such as your additional contacts, your programming language, a description of the project function, and the project's
data classification
will speed up the initial process.
Development workspaces are available within a week.
End service
The client may end their use of the service at any time.
UITS
WHE
reserves the right to end service to any application that violates any IU policy or this service agreement, fails to match environmental upgrade deadlines, or adversely affects the performance of other users.
When a client ends their use of the service, the provider will archive all files on the production file share and a complete backup of the production database; a copy of the archive will be made available to the client upon request. The provider will keep a copy of the archived project for one year.
Emergency communications
The current status of UITS systems and services is available at
Status.IU
. If a client is having a problem with a
WHE
application that is not covered by any notices on
Status.IU
or the
WHE
Admin Portal, follow the guidelines below:
In case of an emergency, the client must first consult their developer to resolve the problem.
If the problem cannot be resolved by the client's developer, then the client may contact
webhost@iu.edu
for assistance. The problem will be investigated during normal business hours; if the problem is reported outside of normal business hours, it will be investigated the next business day.
If a problem with production is identified outside of business hours, then clients or users may contact their campus
Support Center
. If immediate elevation is required, developers may report the problem to
DC Operations
. The Support Center or Operations will report the problem to the system administrators, who will only be able to perform high level functions such as restarting a problematic server. Do not contact the Support Center or Operations for problems with a stage environment outside of business hours; instead, email
webhost@iu.edu
and the problem will be addressed the next business day.
When clients or users report a problem to
webhost@iu.edu
, Operations, or the Support Center, the following information will be needed:
That the application is part of the
Windows Hosting Environment
The name of the application
The name, email address, and phone number of whom to contact during troubleshooting
A description of the problem, including details such as:
The complete URL to the problem page
The UNC path to the share containing the file with the problem
The server and database name (if the problem is a database connection)
A description of the aberrant behaviors
Refer your users to
Report a problem in the Windows Hosting Environment
for instructions for user problem reporting for the
Windows Hosting Environment
.
All system-wide
WHE
outages will be posted to
Status.IU
. UITS
WHE
will follow up with an email to all developers listed in the contacts section of your project as soon as possible. It is up to our clients to make certain this list is up to date for efficient communications.
Virus protection
Clients are responsible for ensuring their files do not contain viruses, malware, or other code insecurities.
The service provider can provide a log of file share access failures.
The service provider may periodically scan files for viruses.
Data backup
UITS SAV's CommVault service is used for backups and restores.
Files are backed up as detailed in
Virtual Server Hosting Services (Intelligent Infrastructure): Service Level Expectations
). Content/storage file share backups are kept for 30 days.
"AllDisk" backups will be performed on Virtual Machines (VMs) as defined in
Data Protection Services (DPS) backups and VM disk tagging
.
Clients with backup needs beyond what SAV and EWA provide are responsible for ensuring those needs are met.
Database backups
A full backup of each SQL database is performed daily and written to a file server.
A transaction log database backup of each SQL Server database is performed every 10 minutes for production databases and every hour for non-production databases. Log backups are written to a file server.
Production backups are kept for 30 days. Non-production backups are kept for 14 days. All backups are stored on an EWA file server. Additionally, two days' worth of backups are kept locally on the database server.
Clients with backup needs beyond what default SQL Server backups offer are responsible for ensuring those needs are met. Additional backup and retention accommodations may result in additional fees.
Database requests
To restore a backup of a client database, send a request to
webhost@iu.edu
with the source database server name, the date of the backup to be used, and the target database server of the backup. A database restore will replace the target database.
Due to the complexity of some database designs, it may not always be possible to move individual objects from one
WHE
database to another (for example, if a table has multiple dependencies) as these moves are extremely time-consuming and can place the client's data at risk. In these cases, the client is required to provide a script for reassigning any special attributes the object may possess (most commonly identity, foreign keys, triggers, and/or primary keys).
WHE
administrators will work with EWA to perform all backups and restores.
Data restoration
Send requests to restore files and databases to
webhost@iu.edu
. Provide the server name, database name, or file name and path. Include the last "known good" date.
Scheduled jobs
All client scheduled job requests in Windows and ColdFusion must be reviewed, accepted, and set up by the
WHE
administrators. All jobs will need to be scheduled to provide optimal server performance. The client and
WHE
administrators will agree on job times.
This also applies to SQL Server Integration Services (SSIS). If a resource-intensive SSIS package running on a weekday after 8am is negatively impacting the
WHE
environment, it may be terminated at the service provider's discretion. The service provider will make every effort to contact the affected client before or immediately after the SSIS package has been terminated.
SQL jobs and SSIS packages in
WHE
must adhere to a naming convention specific to the environment. To learn more about setting up SSIS packages and SQL jobs, contact
webhost@iu.edu
.
Scheduled maintenance
ColdFusion and .NET environments: Windows security updates to non-production server environments will occur on the Wednesday prior to the third Sunday of the month between 6pm and midnight ET. For production server environments, updates will occur on the third Sunday between midnight and 8am. Exceptions in timing may occur if UISO identifies a vulnerability requiring expedited patching. The servers or affected services will be down for only the amount of time necessary for the updates.
Other maintenance to production environments will occur on Thursdays between 7am and 9am ET, or Sundays between midnight and 8am ET.
Other maintenance to non-production environments may occur at any time. Whenever possible,
WHE
will announce these maintenance periods in advance if they are likely to affect availability of the stage servers.
Non-Windows updates will be announced at least three days in advance to affected
WHE
clients. Any maintenance likely to affect the availability of production servers will be performed outside of normal business hours if possible. Whenever possible, these updates will be applied in advance to stage environments to allow time for testing.
Non-scheduled production maintenance activity will be listed at
Status.IU
and the Webhost Admin Portal, and in some instances will be presented at UITS Change Management.
Emergency maintenance
Emergency maintenance will occur as needed. The first priority is preventing service loss or restoring service. Consequently, emergency maintenance may be performed without advance notice to clients. Clients will be notified of the emergency maintenance as soon as possible, before or after as the situation allows.
A system administrator is on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for production environments. During an emergency, the system administrator will give their best effort to restore service. However, there is no guaranteed response or recovery time during an emergency.
Problems and emergency maintenance activity will be listed at
Status.IU
.
Virtual host names and data encryption
Virtual host names and SSL certificates are available upon request. The client is responsible for obtaining approval for domain names. For the DNS policies, see
DNS policies at IU
.
By default, all volumes at rest and network communications between servers are encrypted.
Web application vulnerability scans
Windows Hosting Environment
websites must be scanned by the UISO web vulnerability scanner. A scan must also be done to any new sites or major revisions, or annually. Clients will be responsible for requesting the scan and working with UISO to resolve any vulnerabilities. For instructions to request a scan, see
About vulnerability scanners
.
Important:
UITS recommends doing all security scans in a stage environment outside of business hours and pre-coordinating with UITS
WHE
. If a database refresh is needed before or after a scan, send the request to
webhost@iu.edu
.
Fees
There is no fee for shared web hosting.
Additional disk space fees:
All workspaces include 10 GB of disk space. The space includes:
Script, image, and data files on file share
Database data and log files
Development, test, and production
For a list of costs for additional disk space, see the "Disk Storage" and "Data Backup" sections in
UITS Rates for Direct-Bill Services
.
Charges for additional file spaces are based on average monthly usage during the previous fiscal year.
Access control
Contacts and client access to the environment
The client must designate at least one individual as a contact for all matters related to use of this service. The provider will only act on requests made or approved by a designated contact.
The client must provide a developer contact for all projects.
The client is completely responsible for controlling access to their workspace.
The client is responsible for ensuring anyone with access to their workspace understands their responsibilities stated in this service agreement.
The client is responsible for developing and maintaining their content for the entire application lifecycle.
The client is responsible for adapting their application to changes to the environment, such as software and hardware updates and upgrades.
NTFS and database access is controlled by Active Directory (ADS) domain groups. The groups have the following naming convention:
ADS\IU-WH-Clientname-ProjectName_Developers
The Project ADS group has modify permission on the file content and storage (NTFS) directories.
Web applications and sites cannot create or upload files to the code content directories. If a web application needs a location to create and write files, the client must request a Storage Share location from
WHE
administrators. Space requirements will be discussed at the time of the request.
Critical data
may not be stored on the
WHE
Storage Shares without prior approval from the provider. This is nonnegotiable; shares that violate this rule will be terminated.
The Project ADS group has
db_owner
role permissions on development and non-critical production database environments.
The Project ADS group has
db_datareader
and
db_datawriter
roles on the critical production database servers. Production databases with a
Critical data
classification can only have permissions elevated for four hours.
The project
-Owner
local SQL login will have
db_datareader
and
db_datawriter
permissions only in all environments.
The client may request other groups, permissions, or database server logins as needed.
Website and virtual directory settings
Each web application will have its own application pool running as a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) managed by UITS
WHE
.
You may request other website and virtual directory settings as needed.
IU Login
UITS
WHE
supports IU Login and CAS or SAML protocols for limiting access to web pages. See
Integrate IU Login with a web application
.
UITS
WHE
may be able to provide code samples for popular security procedures upon request.

Overview
You can use Denodo to create simple APIs based off nearly any data source. Instead of architecting an application around a difficult data source, you can build a Denodo API to suit an application. See below for potential use cases and details about creating an API with Denodo.
Potential use cases for Denodo APIs
Denodo APIs can be useful if:
An app needs a simpler RESTful interface to data, instead of a JDBC or ODBC connection.
An app needs to combine data from multiple sources.
An app needs data from sources that are difficult to access or parse, such as cloud sources (for example, AWS or Azure), cubes, Hadoop, LDAP, SFTP, Excel files, flat files, or other APIs.
Existing application APIs do not meet application specifications because of inflexible output format, inability to accept filters or criteria, missing data, or data format issues.
Following are suggested use cases for an API with Denodo:
Use an API to circumvent native APIs, so data are provided with the proper filter and in the required format.
Use an API to expose tables as a RESTful API, cutting down on the overhead and complexity of direct database calls while providing a filter and output that meet specifications.
Use an API to seamlessly union or join an Excel file on NPM or GitHub with relational databases.
Use an API to query the ADS through LDAP, and return the members of a group or an individual's groups.
Use an API as a proxy for SFTP transactions.
Default RESTful web service
All Denodo views are automatically and securely exposed through a default API. Before creating a new RESTful web service, access the default Denodo web service to check whether it is adequate.

https://ebidvt.uits.iu.edu/denodo-restfulws/iu_edss/views/ims_translate_i

title: Avoid phishing scams
content:
Note:
To learn how to spot fake email messages and social engineering scams, visit
Phishing Education & Training
. For online courses on phishing and email security, see
Email Security Fundamentals
.
Table of contents
Phishing explained
Specific types of phishing
Avoid scams
Warnings
Report phishing attempts
If you've fallen for a phishing scam
Example of a phishing scam
Phishing explained
Phishing scams are typically fraudulent email messages appearing to come from legitimate enterprises (for example, your university, your
internet service provider
, your bank). These messages usually direct you to a spoofed website or otherwise get you to divulge private information (for example, passphrase, credit card, or other account updates). The perpetrators then use this private information to commit identity theft.
One type of phishing attempt is an email message stating that you are receiving it due to fraudulent activity on your account, and asking you to "click here" to verify your information.
See an example below.
Phishing scams are crude social engineering tools designed to induce panic in the reader. These scams attempt to trick recipients into responding or clicking immediately, by claiming they will lose something (for example, email, bank account). Such a claim is always indicative of a phishing scam, as responsible companies and organizations will never take these types of actions via email.
Specific types of phishing
Phishing scams vary widely in terms of their complexity, the quality of the forgery, and the attacker's objective. Several distinct types of phishing have emerged.
Spear phishing
Phishing attacks directed at specific individuals, roles, or organizations are referred to as "spear phishing". Since these attacks are so pointed, attackers may go to great lengths to gather specific personal or institutional information in the hope of making the attack more believable and increasing the likelihood of its success.
The best defense against spear phishing is to carefully, securely discard information (that is, using a cross-cut shredder) that could be used in such an attack. Further, be aware of data that may be relatively easily obtainable (for example, your title at work, your favorite places, or where you bank), and think before acting on seemingly random requests via email or phone.
Whaling
The term "whaling" is used to describe phishing attacks (usually spear phishing) directed specifically at executive officers or other high-profile targets within a business, government, or other organization.
Avoid scams
To guard against phishing scams, consider the following:
Indiana University and other reputable organizations will never use email to request that you reply with your password, full Social Security number, or confidential personal information.
Be suspicious of any email message that asks you to enter or verify personal information, through a website or by replying to the message itself.   Never reply to or click the links in such a message. If you think the message may be legitimate, go directly to the company's website (that is, type the real
URL
into your
browser
) or contact the company to see if you really do need to take the action described in the email message.
Read your email as plain text.
Phishing messages often contain clickable images that look legitimate; by reading messages in plain text, you can see the URLs that any images point to. Additionally, when you allow your
mail client
to read
HTML
or other non-text-only formatting, attackers can take advantage of your mail client's ability to execute code, which leaves your computer vulnerable to
viruses
, worms, and Trojans.
If you choose to read your email in HTML format:
Hover your mouse over the links in each email message to display the actual URL. Check whether the hover-text link matches what's in the text, and whether the link looks like a site with which you would normally do business.
On an iOS device, tap and hold your finger over a link to display the URL. Unfortunately, Android does not currently support this.
When you recognize a phishing message, first
report it as noted below
, and then delete the email message from your Inbox, and then empty it from the deleted items folder to avoid accidentally accessing the websites it points to.
To learn more about guarding against phishing scams, see:
Phishing Education & Training
Tips to Protect Yourself Against Phishing Scams
(video)
Warnings
Reading email as plain text is a general best practice that, while avoiding some phishing attempts, won't avoid them all. Some legitimate sites use redirect scripts that don't check the redirects. Consequently, phishing perpetrators can use these scripts to redirect from legitimate sites to their fake sites.
Another tactic is to use a homograph attack, which, due to International Domain Name (IDN) support in modern browsers, allows attackers to use different language
character sets
to produce URLs that look remarkably like the authentic ones. See
Don't Trust Your Eyes or URLs
.
Report phishing attempts
If the phishing attempt targets IU in any way (for example, it asks for those using IU
Exchange
to "verify their accounts", includes a malicious PDF directed to university human resources, or impersonates IU or UITS), you have two options for reporting it:
Use the
Outlook Report Message add-in
.
Forward it with
full headers
to
phishing@iu.edu
.
For instructions on displaying and sending full headers, see
Display and send the full headers of an email message
.
Note:
The
UISO
(University Information Security Office) can take action only if the message asks for IU account credentials or originated from within IU. All other spam should be reported to the appropriate authority below. If the message did originate from within IU, see
If you receive spam
.
You can report a phishing scam attempt to the company that is being spoofed.
You can also
send reports to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
.
Depending on where you live, some local authorities also accept phishing scam reports.
Finally, you can send details to the
Anti-Phishing Working Group
, which is building a database of common scams to which people can refer.
For more about phishing scams, see
Email and Phishing Scams
.
If you've fallen for a phishing scam
For specifics about what to do if you're a victim of a phishing scam, see
Email and Phishing Scams
.
Example of a phishing scam
The following phishing scam was targeted at the IU community:

details to enable us know if you are still making use of your

are as follows:

title: About Microsoft Power Platform licenses
content:
Overview
There are many licensing options for Microsoft Power Platform products. The information here can help you choose the best option for your needs. To purchase licenses or learn more, see
Purchase and activate licenses for Microsoft Select Plus titles
.
If you have questions, contact
Enterprise Windows & Azure Administration
(
EWA
) at
ewahelp@iu.edu
.
Power BI
For Power BI, you may already have the license you need. Below are the licenses for students, faculty, and staff, as well as other licensing options.
Power BI Free license for students
Students have the Power BI Free license, which allows them to publish (but not share) content in "My Workspace". To view content that is published to a workspace, students can use the
Premium Capacity license
.
Power BI Pro license for faculty and staff
Faculty and staff have a Power BI Pro license that grants access to most features, including publishing to a workspace and sharing content.
Other Power BI license options
If the Power BI licenses for students, faculty, or staff will not meet your needs, other licensing options are available:
NK5-00001 - Power BI Pro:
Students may want this license if they need to publish content to a workspace or view content in a non-premium workspace.
B1B-00007 - Power BI Premium Per User (PPU):
You might use the PPU license if you have a small group of people who need to access premium features (such as paginated reports, XMLA endpoints, and AI capabilities), and you don't want to use a
Premium Capacity license
. Note that anyone who needs to
view
these reports also needs a PPU license. A Premium Capacity license is generally better than a PPU license.
Power BI Premium Capacity:
This license has all the premium features and allows large datasets.
Many SKUs
have various RAM and CPU offerings, two of which are:
GTT-00001 Premium Capacity EM2
GST-00001 Premium Capacity P1
Power Platform
Power Automate:
Faculty and staff already have the Power Automate license, which lets them connect to basic Microsoft apps such as
Outlook
(
Microsoft 365
Exchange
) and SharePoint.
Power Automate licensing can be complex, but here are some notes to help:
SFQ-00001 - Per User license:
This license allows "cloud flows" to use premium connections, such as connections to databases (for example, SQL and Oracle) and Microsoft Dataverse; it also enables more functionality.
1SM-00001 - Per User license with RPA (attended):
This license is the same as the
SFQ-00001 license
, except it does robotic process automation (RPA), also known as a Desktop Flow. You only need RPA if you have a line-of-business app that requires UI automation (that is, you have to automate the app through actions such as clicking a mouse button or typing in text boxes). These flows are "attended", which means they require a human to trigger them.
1SO-00001 - Unattended RPA:
This license is the same as the
1SM-00001 attended license
, except it allows an app to run from an agent on its own server that can be fully automated based on other triggers (for example, a schedule, an incoming email, an update to a SharePoint list, etc.). This instance will need to run on a server in the Data Center, and you will also need an attended license while you're developing the solution.
SFK-00001 - Power Automate Per Flow plan:
This license is for cloud flows, not RPA, and it allows specific flows for everyone at IU. If you have a couple of flows with premium connectors, and you need a large number of people to execute them, it may make more sense to buy this license instead of a license for each person.
Copilot Studio:
Formerly known as Power Virtual Agents, this is a low-code tool for creating bots. A limited version is included with Microsoft 365 Copilot app licenses, but to take full advantage of this product and publish them for public use, you need the following two SKUs:
YGB-00001 - Copilot Studio Messages:
This subscription gives you 25,000 messages per month. This can be split up between multiple Power Platform Environments; for example, you may want 5,000 assigned to your development environment and 20,000 assigned to your production environment. A billable message is a message sent to the bot triggering an action and/or response. A response using Generative AI consumes two messages, while all other responses consume one.
SYT-00001 - Copilot Studio User:
This license is a $0 license that is required for all developers. When you order the Messages license, you'll need to make sure each developer also has one of these licenses to be able to use Copilot Studio to create your bot.
Power Apps:
I21-00001 - Power Apps Per User license:
This license allows you to create or execute a Power App that uses premium connections, such as connections to databases (for example, SQL and Oracle) and Microsoft Dataverse. (This special SKU replaced SEK-00001.)
SER-00001 - Power Apps Per App plan:

retired

title: Stellic quick start guide for students
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Landing dashboard
Track progress
Progress symbol overview
Plan your path
Schedule term
Overview
Important:
IU Columbus, IU East, IU Fort Wayne, IU Kokomo, IU Northwest, IU South Bend, and IU Southeast:
Use
Stellic
to register for spring and summer 2026 classes.
IU Bloomington and IU Indianapolis:
Continue to
use the SIS Student Center
to register for your spring and summer 2026 classes.
Stellic
provides a fast, easy way to see your full academic plan for your remaining terms, organize your upcoming courses, and arrange your schedule. This article serves as a quick guide to some of the primary features; a
more detailed student guide
is also available.
You will still want to work closely with your advisor. Preparing with Stellic beforehand will make reviewing your plan with your advisor quicker and more effective.
Landing dashboard
After logging into Stellic, you will land on a dashboard that provides a quick view of your current programs, schedule, and academic progress. It also shows recent messages and a quick view of your academic calendar.
Track progress
In the
Track Progress
tab, hover over your degree progress bar to see the number of courses you have taken, the number of courses remaining, the number of courses for which you are registered, and the number of courses that do not count toward your degree.
To view the list of requirements for your program, scroll down and select
Progress
, and then select either
Official
(to see classes you have taken or officially registered for) or
Planned
(to see everything you have planned out with Stellic, including any unofficial programs you have added to your plan). Additionally, choose
Full Audit
to see your full audit,
Compact
to see a compact version of your audit, or
Remaining
to see only the requirements you have remaining.
Progress symbol overview
The following symbols are used in the audit to indicate whether or not you have completed a requirement, are currently taking it, or have yet to complete it:
Symbol
Description
Green checkmark:
The course/requirement has been completed. These are already taken and passed classes, or requirements that are completely fulfilled. These will remain the same in the official and planned audit.
Red box:
The course/requirement still needs to be completed. In your official audit, any section not taken or registered will show as red; in your planned audit, any section that is not yet in your plan will be red.
Yellow single checkmark:
The course/requirement is in the plan and will be satisfied once completed. In your official audit, only classes registered for the current semester will be yellow; in your planned audit, all the classes you already have planned out with Stellic, even years ahead, will be yellow.
Yellow double checkmarks:
The course is currently being taken.
Red number in a red box:
This is the number of remaining courses for a requirement. Non-course requirements are not included in this total.
Green chain link:
The course is double counting with a requirement in another program. Hover over the link symbol for details on where the class is double counting.
Green circular arrow:
The course has been taken more than once. This appears only if the course has been taken more than once and cannot be counted for more than one requirement.
Red circle with an exclamation point:
The course is taken/registered but not counting for the requirement (for example, a course with a grade too low to fill the requirement, or a course that is counting for a different requirement). These courses are listed at the bottom of the audit, under "Unmatched Courses".
Double-headed arrow:
The requirement is being filled by a course that your institution has designated as equivalent with the course noted in the audit. (Not all schools use this, so you may not see it in your audit.)
Plan your path
In the
Plan Your Path
tab, you can view and plan out each of your terms individually. You can easily see only the courses you have left to plan out and add them to the term you choose. Stellic will let you know if you need a prerequisite for a course or if a course is not available in that term.
On the right, the
Tentative List
shows only courses that still need to be planned. Select a course from the
Remaining Requirements
column and drag it to the chosen semester.
Search for specific classes by selecting
Add to [Term]
in the planner, or select
Search Courses
on the right.
Enter a course subject keyword in the search box and filter the results by desired qualifiers. When you find a course, drag it to the planner. Classes linked as pre-requisites or co-requisites will be highlighted.
Alternatively, on the right, select
Progress
, and then drag and drop classes between terms to find your ideal schedule. Any transfer courses and advanced placement credits are listed at the bottom of this view.
To add additional programs to your plan, select
+ Add program to plan
near the top of the page.
Schedule term
In the
Schedule Term
tab, you can plan course sections and times for the upcoming term (as long as the course schedule has been released for that term).
In the
Schedule Term
tab, select a time slot in the weekly calendar view to see courses available for that time slot that are still needed for your plan. Select a course and hover over the
+
(plus sign) to see how each section fits into your weekly plan. Select the
+
(plus sign) to add the section to your plan.
To change or modify sections already showing in your weekly view, in the
Schedule Term
tab, on the sidebar, select the drop-down arrow for a course to see its alternate sections. Hover over each section to see it on your weekly view, and then select the desired new section.

How to customize your settings
Refer to
Customize your settings in Stellic
.
Add or remove programs
To add a program, navigate to the top of your profile in the
Plan your Path
tab. Select
+ Add program to plan
, and then search for and select other programs to add.
To remove a program, select
x
next to the program name at the top of your profile. You will see a "not declared" tag until you've officially declared a new program with the university; if you remove a declared program, the program name will still appear, but it will have a "not in plan" tag. You can add the program again by selecting
add to plan
.
How individual courses count towards specific requirements
Students don't have the ability to choose where a course will populate within an audit. Generally, a class will always fill in the highest-level category first. Classes that are already completed (with grades) are prioritized first, then registered classes, and finally planned classes last.
Rules (constraints) about which class can fill a category, grade requirements, and double counting are set by your school.
About courses counting double
Double counting rules are set for each degree program by your school. Reach out to your advisor if you think there's an issue with a class double counting or not, but it isn't something that Stellic support can change or update.
Courses you've taken that don't count
When a course you've taken doesn't count toward a requirement, a red exclamation point will display next to it. Reasons for this can vary. More information will be available soon.
View a list of courses that will fufill a requirement
You have several options for viewing courses that will fulfill a requirement.
Track Progress tab
In the
Track Progress
tab, find the requirement/category.
Hover over the requirement, and select
Search Qualifying Courses
(the magnifying glass icon).
A right-side panel will open. To more easily see courses you can take right away, refine your list further by selecting
Only with cleared prerequisites
.
Plan your Path tab
In the
Plan your Path
tab, the default view shows the "Tentative List" in the right-side panel, which lists all the requirements that you haven't taken or added to your plan. Any course that appears with a dotted outline is a placeholder, which is a requirement that has several course options.
To bring up a list of courses that will count for that requirement, select the placeholder either directly from the tentative list, or add it to your plan to narrow the search by term.
Course search
From the left navigation menu's
Explore Courses
tab, select the
Counts for
filter to search by requirement. You can search for requirements for any program that you have in your Stellic plan, including any majors, minors, or other programs that you have added to your planner.
From the search results, select a course. In the right-side panel, to add the course to a specific term, select
Add to Another Semester
; alternatively, select
Add to Tentative List
.
If you thought a course would count and it doesn't
Stellic gets information for degree plans and audits from IU. Stellic staff cannot manually change course information or audits. Reach out to your advisor or instructor if something doesn't seem right.
What-if scenario: Remove a registered course from your planner
Note:
This process is hypothetical. Dropping a course in Stellic does not remove it from your IU registration.
To see what happens if you drop a registered course from your Stellic planner, from the
Plan Your Path
tab, hover over the course in your plan, and select the
x
that appears in the course's upper right corner.
A warning message will appear at the top of the screen reminding you that this will not drop the course in the Student Information System (SIS) until it is removed there also. To dismiss the message, select
OK
.
Two versions of your progress view are available. The Official view shows all courses you have taken and for which you've registered. The Planned view incorporates future planned courses from your planner. Select either option to toggle between them.
In the Official view, the course you removed appears in the requirements since it is still registered in SIS. In the Planned view, the course no longer appears in the requirement, but instead appears in "Unmatched courses". In certain scenarios, you may see that another course will count for the requirement if you drop this one.
Confirm that your requirements are met and you're ready to graduate
To see how many classes you've taken or have left, check the top bar in your profile on the
Plan your Path
tab.
You'll want to see 0 (zero) remaining in "Unplanned" to know that you have all of your audit requirements in your plan.
You also can check the
Track Progress
tab (the
Official
option shows only classes officially taken or registered with the university) to see what classes are remaining. A red box next to any requirement means there are classes remaining to fill that category.
Stellic support cannot give you an official all-clear for graduation. Always work with your advisor who knows your program well and can warn you of any pitfalls.

IU Bloomington and IU Indianapolis:
Continue to
use the SIS Student Center

Students will not be able register for classes in
Stellic
until the enrollment period for the term is open. You will know if an enrollment period is open if you see the "Registration Open" message displayed at the top of your Home page or dashboard view. You will also see a "Registration Opens" message displayed under "Quick Access" in the "Schedule Your Courses" area on the Home page.
If the enrollment period for your selected term is not open, you will see a "Registration hasn't yet been enabled for this term" message.
Get started
Landing dashboard
After logging into Stellic, you will land on your default Home page or dashboard view. This page gives you a quick glance at your current programs, schedule, and academic progress. It also includes any recent messages and a quick view of your academic calendar.
From the menu on the left, select
Plan your Path
.
Plan your Path tab
On the
Plan your Path
tab, you can view and plan out each of your terms individually. If you do not see the term for which you are planning course sections and times, you can add the term to your plan; from the
Select Semester To Add
drop-down, select the semester you wish to add.
The selected semester will appear in your plan.
Selecting
Tentative List
on the right side of the page will display courses that still need to be planned. Select a required course from the "Remaining Requirements" column.
Courses that fulfill the selected requirement will be listed at the bottom of the right sidebar. These courses cover all semesters.
Under "Filters", select
Semesters
, and then use the "Planning for" drop-down or the "Semester" selections to choose the semester you are currently planning.
The list of courses is filtered to show only those available during your chosen semester. To select the course you wish to add to your plan for this semester, select the course name.
Review the course information and select the semester you would like to complete the course.
Scroll down to display the class sections available during your chosen semester.
Choose your desired class section by selecting the blue plus sign (
+
) to the left of the class section number.
The blue plus sign (
+
) changes to a green checkmark to indicate your choice. The class is added to your plan for this semester.
Continue adding your desired classes to the plan for this semester. When you have finished, you will be ready to schedule your classes.
Schedule Term tab
On the
Plan your Path
tab, select
Go to schedule
in the "Registration" information block located in your plan for this semester.
On the
Schedule Term
tab, a class you selected appears in the weekly calendar view if a day and time period is assigned to it (such as an in-person class).
If the class you selected is an online class, it will not appear in the calendar view. You will need to check the semester on the
Plan your Path
tab to verify that you are enrolled in the class.
Register for your courses
When you are ready to register your courses for the semester, select
Confirm Courses For Registration
at the top of the calendar view on the
Schedule Term
tab.
The Registration Cart pop-up window should display. Check the entries in the cart to determine that you are cleared to register for your selected courses.
Select
Complete Registration
at the bottom of the Registration Cart window.
The registration process may take several minutes to complete. If you receive a "Failed to register" message, make note the failure messages and course information. Common reasons that registration might fail include incomplete prerequisites for a class, instructor permission is needed to enroll in a class, and a hold exists on your account. Select
Back to schedule

Schedule Term
tab and select
Confirm Courses for Registration

Select
Complete Registration

Back to schedule

Schedule Term
tab.
You should receive an email from the Stellic system indicating that you have successfully registered for classes, and that you are required to process and pay in your Student Information System (SIS) to complete your registration.
