title: KB contributor style guide
content:
Table of contents About this style guide Content Structure Titles and headings Tables of contents Lists Order of information Voice and tone Grammar Style specifics Elements of technology Capitalization Punctuation Emphasis Acronyms Pronouns Links Numbers Campus locations Images Tables About this style guide This style guide is intended to guide those who contribute new content or edits to the Knowledge Base as part of the Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) initiative.  KCS contributors should adhere as closely as possible to these guidelines.  However, everyone who sends content to the Knowledge Management team using any method is encouraged to use this style guide to make rough drafts match KB style.  The more closely your draft follows KB style, the more quickly it can be published. During the first stage of the KCS rollout, the Knowledge Management team will take care of editing anything that requires working directly in markup; thus, those style guidelines are not covered here.  These items include: Panels (that is, “Note:” or “Important:” panels or blocks with visibility that's more restricted than the surrounding article) Blockquotes In a future iteration of the KCS model, we may make changes to make it easier to edit from the rich-text editor in ServiceNow. Check back for updates. For now, you can simply include the text you want to include for blockquotes or panels, and we'll mark it up. (If you are comfortable working in markup, you are welcome to do so.  Ask the KM team for guidance on how to use markup options to match KB style.) UITS style generally follows conventions outlined in the Chicago Manual of Style , with exceptions specific to IU Brand Guidelines (which includes the Editorial Style Guide ).  This style guide covers situations specific to technical writing for the KB. Note: The KM team has made some style changes with the migration to ServiceNow Knowledge and subsequent adoption of KCS; thus, existing articles will often not match the style listed here. Use this style for changes and new content going forward. Content Only create content that's needed Don't create a KB article unless there's a clear need for it.  The KCS philosophy encourages creating documentation in response to support needs, rather than creating documentation in advance just in case it's needed. Give clients all the information they need to solve or avoid common problems, but don’t include details most people won’t need to know.  Stick to the minimum. Don’t include background information unless it’s necessary to prevent confusion, or to help people understand whether they need to take action or not. Don't duplicate information Be sure to check whether the KB already includes the information, or similar information that could be edited to meet the need. If the information exists and is publicly available elsewhere, link to it rather than duplicating it.  Don’t reproduce vendor instructions unless there is a clear need to do so, such as: Vendor instructions that will cause client confusion because of IU-specific details Vendor instructions that aren’t accessible to people with disabilities Make content stand alone Some KB content may appear in other websites and applications, and instructions may be shared in email messages to clients or used in other ways.  Make the content clear no matter how clients access it. Make the scope clear Be sure that the information is as general as the way you're presenting it. For example, if something works only on the Windows version or the Mac version of a program, make that clear. Information should apply to all IU campuses unless you specify otherwise. Structure In general, make the organization of new content as similar to existing content as possible.  However, don’t include a section that’s not needed just because it’s in a template, or in a similar document.  Avoiding unnecessary content is more important than following a pattern. Titles and headings If you're editing in ServiceNow Knowledge directly, be sure to designate headings with the appropriate selection from the Paragraph drop-down menu (or the equivalent tag in markup).  Use Heading 2 for the top level within the body; level 1 is reserved for the title. Heading 3 and (sometimes) Heading 4 are appropriate for sub-sections, but if you need more than that, you should probably rethink the organization of your article.  Do not simply use bold font to mark a heading. Titles and headings should be clear, concise, and descriptive. Capitalize only the first word and proper nouns. If the content gives instructions for a task, the title or heading should be what you would say if you were telling a person to do that task.  Don’t use gerunds (-ing verbs used as nouns) in titles or headings.  For example: Use: Change your passphrase Avoid: Changing your passphrase Avoid: How do I change my passphrase? Avoid: How to change your passphrase Avoid: Passphrase change procedures Where applicable, use the following standardized headings: Overview: The intro about a topic; not always needed Before you begin: If you need to do things before doing the actual task Troubleshoot: For troubleshooting info or tips Learn more: Information such as resources and other documentation Get help: Support resources and/or contact information Sometimes we combine the last two into "Learn more and get help". Note: KB style does not typically use an FAQ format; the industry experts we’ve read suggest that FAQs are usually not the most efficient way for people to get the information they need. They often include redundant or unneeded information conveyed in more words than necessary. Instead of using questions as section headings, use the shortest, clearest way to indicate the content of each section, and make sure all the information people need is present (only once) in a clear logical format. If there is some specific reason why an article should include real questions that are actually being frequently asked, consult with the KM team about whether an FAQ would make sense for a particular circumstance. Tables of contents If an article has any headings, it should have a matching table of contents.  ServiceNow Knowledge has an option you can select that will automatically generate a table of contents based on the headings present in an article.  If you change the headings at all (whether adding, removing, or rewording), be sure to revise the table of contents to match; you can do this with a single button, as well. With rare exceptions, if there is a table of contents, don’t include any text outside of a relevant heading.  Add an “Overview” section if necessary. Make sure everything under a heading belongs in that section.  For example, a sentence at the end of the document that says “Contact someunit@iu.edu with questions” should only be in the last section of the document if it is specific to that section.  Otherwise, it should be under a separate heading such as “Get help”. Lists For all but the briefest instructions, use numbered lists. Use numbers only for steps one must follow in order. Use lowercase letters for sub-lists of ordered steps, and lowercase Roman numerals for third-level ordered lists, if applicable. As a general rule, each step in an ordered list should be an action you take.  If you need to include a description of something that isn’t an active step (such as “A dialog box will open”), you can usually combine that either with the step before or the step after, whichever it’s more closely related to.  It’s typically not necessary to include a step such as “This process is now complete,” but if there is important information about the completion state that readers need to know, it may make more sense as a paragraph following the end of the ordered list. Use unordered (bulleted) lists for everything other than steps one must follow in order, such as: People, places, or things that might create differences in user experience (for example, university roles, types of accounts, operating systems, campuses, etc.) Options or form fields that are all presented in the same page or window Different paths the user could follow To introduce lists: If you have a paragraph introducing the list, you’ll usually end it with a colon.  If the point of the list is obvious without an introduction, you don’t need to include one. Omit needless words.  For example: Instead of: To convert the database, follow these steps: Use: To convert the database: Instead of: For more information, consult the following KB articles: Use: For more, see: (unless there’s a specific reason to highlight the kind of information) Begin list items with a capital letter (unless the word is a proper name that is correctly spelled with a lowercase letter, such as “macOS”). If a list consists of items followed by a colon and information about the items, use bold text for the introductory words and the colon, and capitalize the word after the colon, thus: Windows: Download and install WinSCP. macOS: Download and install Cyberduck. Put a period at the end of a list item if it’s a complete sentence.  Omit the period if it isn’t. Do not use commas, semi-colons, or conjunctions such as “and” or “or” at the end of a list item.  Make the relationship between the list items clear from the introduction to the list, if it isn’t already obvious based on context.  For example, you can say “do one of the following:” to communicate an “or” relationship between the bullets of a sub-list. As much as possible, try to make items within the same list logically and grammatically parallel. For example: Instead of: There are several requirements for using Unicorn Maker: Start with a horse. Two pints of pixy dust You should already have passed your magical qualifying exams and obtained your license before you begin. Try: To use Unicorn Maker, you will need: A current, valid magical license One horse Two pints of pixy dust Order of information Put software versions in order from newest to oldest.  This applies to the organization of sections within an article, bullets in a list, and mentions in running text. When possible, keep the language generic, such as “In Windows 10 and earlier . . .” When dealing with a slight variation between versions, combine them if possible; for example, use "Select Save or Save file " rather than "In Windows 8.x, select Save ; in Windows 7, select Save file ". When giving instructions, present information in the order users will need it.  For example, "From the Toppings menu, select Anchovies " helps the user know what to look for first. See below for the order for IU campuses. Always list "students, faculty, and staff" or "students, faculty, staff, and affiliates" in that order. Voice and tone Use a style that’s simple, natural, practical, and concise Avoid being wordy or overly descriptive. Be as clear and simple as possible, and no more technical-sounding than necessary for the audience. For public articles, use the words most people will be familiar with. For example, refer to a person's computer, not their machine. Don't use a fancier word if a simpler one will work. Consider replacements such as: Instead of Try Assist, assistance Aid, help Finalize Complete, finish Implement Carry out, finish Require Need Utilize Use It's fine to use contractions, and will typically sound more natural than avoiding them (for example, “Log out when you’re finished” rather than “Log out when you are finished”). You can usually omit words like “the . . . button” or “the . . . link”; instead, say "Select OK" or "Select Turn on maximum security " without extra words. Don't be too casual. Use standard language, without slang or jargon. Readers shouldn’t notice the style; let them focus on the meaning. Avoid using words such as "simply" or "just" (for example, "Simply complete and submit the form" or "Just download the software"); in addition to being wordier, this trivializes any difficulties readers may have. In most cases, omit “please” in KB articles. Focus on telling people how to do things; don’t use extra words to try to persuade them. (In most cases, it’s something they’re trying to do anyway!) Address readers directly Address readers as "you" in most cases (whether the "you" is stated or implied). For example: Rather than: The user should clear their browser's cache. Say: Clear your browser's cache. You may need to clarify who should take action in some articles. For example, if both students and instructors will be using an app, you may sometimes need to say something like "The instructor will need to enable the Direct submission option to allow students to submit their papers." However, if there's no risk of confusion, address the reader directly. Prefer active voice Most instructions should state directly, clearly, and concisely who does what with verbs in the active voice, thus: Rather than: Security settings will need to be configured to block automatic application changes. Use one of these: Configure the security settings to block automatic application changes. An administrator will need to configure the security settings to block automatic application changes. (Use if, for example, the intended reader doesn't have permission to do this themselves.) Passive voice may be better when saying who does something calls attention to a detail that doesn't matter. For example: UITS will disable your accounts after two semesters of non-enrollment. (This focuses on UITS unnecessarily.) Your accounts will be disabled after two semesters of non-enrollment. (This focuses on the impact on the student, which is more important if they're worried about keeping their stuff.) Grammar Avoid common grammatical errors, such as: Using a comma to join two sentences. Instead of: Open a new document, start composing your proposed article. Use one of these: Open a new document.  Start composing your proposed article. Open a new document; start composing your proposed article. Open a new document, and start composing your proposed article. Using an apostrophe to make a plural. Instead of: Students use smartphone’s to access Top Hat. Use: Students use smartphones to access Top Hat. Note: Omit the apostrophe for plurals of abbreviations and dates as well. For example: CPUs 2020s Style specifics For specific words and phrases to use or avoid, and how to spell them, consult the KB standard terms list . Do not change the font, size, or color of text manually. For consistency, let the KB's style sheet control these details. When pasting in content from Word or Google Docs, choose Remove formatting to prevent font information from being pasted into ServiceNow Knowledge. (This will remove details like font size and color, but keep basic formatting such as lists.) Elements of technology Use the following conventions for designating certain parts of technical instructions: Things people select: Use bold font for anything a user will select, such as: Names of buttons, tabs, icons, and radio buttons, for example: At the top of the page, select Publish . Note that informal descriptions of an icon's appearance don't get tags.  Make sure you have the official name by which a screenreader will announce the icon somewhere as well; for example: Select the Settings (gear) icon. Select the Edit icon (looks like a pencil). Names of menus and the options within them, for example: From the Month drop-down menu, select May . Typographic representations of selectable items (for example, a plus sign when it means a control used to expand a list, or the letter X when it means a control that closes a window) Names of ServiceNow assignment groups Names of folders or directories only when most users in the target audience will select them (for example, folders within Microsoft Outlook).  If users will navigate to a directory or folder at the command line, treat the name as text users type, as described below. You can designate a path of options people select with greater-than signs, particularly in articles aimed at more technically savvy users, like so: Navigate to Control Panel > System > Display . However, in articles aimed at beginning users, or anytime things are less obvious, it may be better to spell things out: Choose Control Panel , select System , and then, in the left pane, choose Display . Short commands, keystrokes, and text users type: Use tags for commands, keystrokes, or any kind of text that users enter, when it makes sense to keep the text inline. You can apply this formatting by first selecting the text in the rich-text editor, and then choosing the Insert/edit code sample icon ( ) from the editing bar.  (Don't choose the icon before typing the text; doing so will open an editing window for a code block, as described below.) Note: Avoid using inline tags immediately before a punctuation mark. Because the pink background may not be visible to everyone, doing so may create confusion about where the command ends. When in doubt between inline tags and a code block, it's generally better to use a code block. Use tags for items such as: Commands, including flags or options Named keys (such as Ctrl or Shift ), except for the Spacebar and arrow keys (which are untagged) Keystroke combinations; use hyphens to connect these: Ctrl-x Representations of prompts of any kind Names of Unix programs/commands that go by their filenames, as well as Unix shell names, for example: less more cat Exceptions: vi gets no tags. Do not use tags around names that are capped, such as Python or Emacs. Do not use tags around environment variables, such as PATH, PYTHONPATH, X509_USER_PROXY, etc. Filenames and file extensions Exception: For common file types, you may use all caps, no tags, and no dot ("a ZIP file", "a PDF file", "a CSV file"). When referencing a specific filename, then use code tags, thus: filename.zip . Certain elements of internet addresses: Usernames, when used alone Example email addresses, such as dvader@iu.edu ; for real, active email addresses, instead use a mailto: link. Fully qualified machine names HTML tags and attributes Longer commands or code blocks: Use the Insert/edit code sample button ( ) in the ServiceNow rich-text editor for commands and blocks of code. This will set the text off in a gray box with a fixed-width font and all line breaks and whitespace preserved, allowing you to represent a block of code where line breaks or spacing matters, like this: age = 20 if age >= 18: print("You are an adult.") else: print("You are a minor.") Selecting the button will open a dialog with a drop-down menu and a text box for the code. From the drop-down, you must select one of the following language options: HTML/XML JavaScript CSS PHP Ruby Python Java C C# C++ If your code block is not one of these, consult with the KM team.  Although the language you select will not appear visibly in the KB portal, there is a class specifying the language within the markup, so it would be semantically incorrect to choose a language that's inaccurate. Note: Although the Preformatted option from the Paragraph drop-down menu renders the same visually in the KB portal view, it doesn't insert tags within the 
tags, so it's better to use
Insert/edit code sample
instead.
Things people read:
Use quotation marks for text that appears on the screen that people don't directly interact with, such as headings, names of fields, and names of dialog boxes, windows, or pages within apps such as Canvas when using the exact name as it appears on the screen.  (Don't use quotation marks if you're simply indicating the general purpose rather than quoting the name.) See below for examples.
KB style uses British quotes, in which ending punctuation marks are placed
outside
quotation marks. This allows our documentation to represent the text on the screen clearly and accurately; if a punctuation mark appears within the user interface, put it inside the quotes, and if it doesn't, put it outside the quotation marks.
For example:
In the "Search domains:" field, enter your desired search domains.
Under "Quick actions", select
Edit your quick actions
.
On the "Gradebook Items" page, choose
+ New Gradebook Item
.
Longer quotations:
Use quotation marks for short snippets of text presented within a sentence, such as in the examples above.  For longer segments of text, such as error messages (except very short ones), exact text of automated mailings, and postal addresses, use a blockquote. Since this option is currently unavailable from the editing bar, you can leave it to the KM team to apply the markup.  Don't use quotation marks within blockquote tags (unless they appear on the screen as part of the message), and don't resume a sentence after a blockquote.  For example:
In the "Destroy planet?" dialog box, choose
No
. If you accidentally select
Yes
, you will see the following message:
You have chosen to destroy your planet to make room for a hyperspace expressway. Your cooperation is appreciated. A Vogon fleet will arrive shortly to fulfill your request. Allow up to two business days for planetary destruction.
If you see this message, contact your campus Support Center to avert global catastrophe.
Capitalization
Capitalize proper names using the correct form for each product or service.
For vended products, follow the vendor’s usage.  This includes spacing.  Check the vendor’s website if you’re not sure.
For example:
macOS, Honorlock, PowerPoint, Top Hat
For IU systems, refer to the standard terms list.  (The standard terms list also includes some vended products with unusual capitalization, but it isn’t comprehensive.)
For example:
IUware, IUanyWare, IU eTexts
Follow the capitalization on the screen exactly when referring to part of the user interface.
For example:
Under "User Settings", select
Show All Courses
.
Avoid over-capitalization. Other than at the beginning of a sentence, title, list item, etc., only capitalize proper names and as needed to match the user interface.
Capitalize titles only when they're specific.
For example:
"Call the Support Center Manager" is correct, as is "All managers must fill out the following form."
Punctuation
Commas:
Use a comma before a conjunction that joins the last two elements in a series:
The Knowledge Base contains information for IU students, faculty, staff, and affiliates.
You'll need to clear your browser’s cache, change your passphrase, and restart your computer.
To help guide readers through the sentence, put a comma at the end of an introductory phrase that gives context, for example:
Instead of:
In the "Snacks" window that appears select the checkbox for
Twinkies
.
Use:
In the "Snacks" window that appears, select the checkbox for
Twinkies
.
Quotation marks:
We use British quotes, wherein ending punctuation marks are placed outside quotation marks. This also applies to commas or any other punctuation mark within the sentence: only the text and punctuation marks that appear on the screen go within the quotation marks (or tags); any that belong to the sentence rather than the quoted material go outside the quotation marks.
Hyphens:
We mostly follow
The Chicago Manual of Style
, which tends to dehyphenate. Generally,
A compound noun gets compressed into one word (checkbox).
Hyphenate verb-preposition combinations (pull-down).
Hyphenate pairs of words that work together to modify a noun when they come before the noun; don’t hyphenate them when they’re not immediately before a noun.  Thus:
. . . a third-party vendor
Do not share your IU passphrase with a third party.
Many common hyphenation issues are covered in the
KB standard terms list
.
Slashes:
As a general rule, avoid using the slash symbol (/) as a substitute for “and” or “or”.
Emphasis
Use bold text to emphasize important words or phrases.
Do not use italics or all caps for emphasis. Italics have several specific purposes in the KB, which the KM team will apply with specific tags. You should never use all caps except for acronyms or as needed to match the user interface.
Don't overuse bold text. Most of the time, bolding only the most important words (such as "not") should be enough.  Putting a longer phrase or an entire sentence in bold may be appropriate in some cases, but use this judiciously.
Acronyms
To keep titles concise, use only the acronym in the title, unless the acronym is not commonly known.
The first time an acronym (including "Indiana University") is used in the body of an article, spell it out; follow it with the acronym in parentheses (except in the case of IU). In later instances, use only the acronym. Follow this style whether or not you spell out the acronym in the title.
Don't use acronyms for IU campuses (see
below
).
Pronouns
When a pronoun refers to a non-specific person, use "they", "them", or "their".
Often, it sounds better to recast the sentence in the plural, thus:
Instead of:
An employee should lock their workstation when leaving.
Try:
All employees should lock their workstations when leaving.
However, if the plural version of the sentence will cause confusion, use the plural pronoun with a singular noun rather than using "his or her", etc.
Don't use "we" in public Knowledge Base documents. Readers may not know who that is. In most cases, say "UITS recommends . . .", etc., but referring to a more specific team is okay if that will be clearer.
Links
When quoting information that may change, list a URL for the original document so that readers can find the most recent copy. It is not adequate to just provide the information without an up-to-date link.
For most links, use one of the following as the link text:
The title of the page; match the spelling and capitalization of the site you’re linking to
A short phrase indicating the purpose of the link, for example:
If your computer is compromised, you’ll need to
change your passphrase
.
Make sure that the link text indicates what readers will get, even if they don’t read the surrounding context.  Do not use general phrases like “click here” for link text.  For details, see
Write link text for accessibility
.
You may use the URL for the link text in rare cases when it is short and memorable, so that you might reasonably expect that users will type it directly into their browser’s address bar in the future without looking up the instructions again (for example,
status.iu.edu
).
If a sentence ends in a link that includes a question mark as part of the link text, the question mark serves as the final punctuation for the sentence; don’t add a period after the question mark.  For example:
To add a hidden tool to your course navigation menu, see
How do I manage Course Navigation links?
Use as few words as possible to introduce links, for example:
For more, see
Wireless networks for IU departments
.
UITS recommends using a separate course site; see
Create a new course site in Canvas
.
For links to other KB articles, use this format for the URL:
/kb?id=kb_article_view&sysparm_article=KB0012345
Do not include a link to a more-restricted article within public or less-restricted content.  If you need to include a link to more-restricted content, it should typically be within a knowledge block that is restricted to the same Can Read criteria as the link, so that readers don't see a link they can’t use.  There will be
no
visual indication of links to restricted content, so you must pay careful attention to the Can Read criteria of articles you link to.
Alternatively, if you're linking from a public article to an article in the iu-all audience, you may simply put "(requires IU Knowledge Base login)" after the link text to alert readers that they will be prompted to log in, since all of the primary audience for the IU KB will be able to access the content if they log in.
For email addresses, use links with
mailto:username@iu.edu
as the URL and the email address as the link text.
Numbers
Spell out zero through nine; use numerals for 10 and up.
We generally say "24 hours a day, 7 days a week"; "24/7" or "24/7/365" are acceptable in internal docs, and in a few public docs under special circumstances.
When referring to a step in an ordered list, use a numeral rather than spelling out the number ("If your widget is already installed, skip to step 5 below").
Any other time the number is serving as a designator rather than indicating how many of a thing there are, use a numeral (for example, "roll 3" to indicate a specific roll of paper on a plotter).
Units of measurement
File sizes, speeds, etc. should appear in the format "300 MB" (with a space between the number and the unit of measure).
Money
Don’t use decimals unless the amount includes cents.
Phone numbers
Use the format 812-123-4567.
Dates and times
Use "am" and "pm" without periods, and without spaces between them and the time they modify (for example, 9am).
Omit the colon and zeroes for on-the-hour times (9am and 9:30am).
For ranges of time, use a single hyphen.
When listing a range of days and times, use the format "Day-day time-time", with no comma between (Saturday-Sunday 8am-5pm).
Instead of "12pm" and "12am", use "noon" and "midnight".
If you need to specify a time zone, use “Eastern Time” or “Central Time”; do not use “Eastern Standard Time” or “EST”.  Eastern Standard Time refers to the time most of Indiana follows in the winter months (as opposed to Eastern Daylight Time).
Don't capitalize the names of semesters (for example, spring semester and fall semester).
Spell out months and days of the week.
Do not use ordinal suffixes (May 2, not May 2nd).
Use numerals for years.
Include the year in any reference to a specific (rather than recurring) date, except for short-term modifications that you know will be removed promptly (for example, temporary hours for spring break)
Do
not
use relative time references such as "this year" or "next month".  For example, use “spring 2026” rather than “next spring”.
When listing the time, day, and date together, place the time at the beginning or end of the sequence. For example:
Changes are scheduled to go live 6am Sunday, July 17, 2022.
The office will close Monday, July 25 at 4pm.
Thus, proper KB style would be as follows:
The office is open Monday-Thursday 8am-midnight, Friday 8am-9pm, Saturday noon-5pm, and Sunday noon-midnight. However, on August 30, 2030, it is closed.
Campus locations
Campuses
Refer to Indiana University campuses as follows; spell out the full name the first time in the body of the article (at least in public content), and use the shorter version with just "IU" for later references.  It's also fine in some contexts to say things like "the Bloomington campus", etc.  Always use the order below when naming more than one campus.
Indiana University Bloomington, IU Bloomington
Indiana University Indianapolis, IU Indianapolis
Indiana University Columbus, IU Columbus
Indiana University East, IU East
Indiana University Fort Wayne, IU Fort Wayne
Indiana University Kokomo, IU Kokomo
Indiana University Northwest, IU Northwest
Indiana University South Bend, IU South Bend
Indiana University Southeast, IU Southeast
Buildings and rooms
Use full building names rather than the two-letter abbreviations used on campus maps (although the abbreviations may be added in parentheses if needed for clarity).
Use abbreviations when the full name is already present (for example, in a column of a table with room numbers when the full name of the building is elsewhere in the table)
For the Indiana Memorial Union on the Bloomington campus, use the full name for the first appearance, and if necessary add "(IMU)" after the first appearance; you may then abbreviate to IMU thereafter.
After the first spelled-out appearance, abbreviate "Learning Commons" as "LC".
For rooms in the ICTC, use "IT". Since it is commonly known as "the IT Building" on campus, refer to it that way when giving directions.
Put a space between the building name or abbreviation and the room number, thus:
Hayes Hall 109
IT 126
Images
Images often help users follow a task, but they add to the work needed to maintain an article (for example, if a software update changes the look of a button, but not the name or the way it works).  Only include images in KB articles where they add value.
Don’t rely on images alone to convey information; this is critical for accessibility.  Put the information people need to do the task in the text of the article, and use images if they help people follow the directions more easily.  For example:
Use a screenshot with an arrow or circle to help users locate something in a dense user interface.
Use a small image of an icon when the link between its name and its appearance isn’t obvious.
Use a screenshot with sample data to help users picture how a step will work.
All images need alt text that makes sense in context. For general guidelines, see
Alternative text for images
.
When using screenshots, redact sensitive or personal information, such as the names or usernames of real people.
For more, see
Images in the IU Knowledge Base
.
Tables
Don’t use tables unless the data fits a table format logically.  (Don’t use a table just for layout, for example.)
Make sure tables aren’t too wide to render properly.  If they are, the table should be broken up or presented in nested list format, or something of that sort.
All tables need a caption.
For more, see
Tables in the IU Knowledge Base
.

title: Make course changes during the first week of classes
content:
Important:
IU Columbus, IU East, and IU Fort Wayne, IU Kokomo, IU Northwest, IU South Bend, and IU Southeast:
For spring and summer 2026 registration, use
Stellic
rather than the instructions here. Stellic is a new easy-to-use tool to help students plan their path, track their progress toward graduation, and register in one location. See
Stellic quick start guide for students
.
IU Bloomington and IU Indianapolis:
For spring and summer 2026 registration, continue to use the SIS Student Center to register for your classes.
Table of contents
Overview
Add a new course to your schedule
Swap courses in your schedule
Overview
Continuous drop/add is available from the beginning of early registration through the Sunday following the first week of classes; check your campus academic calendar for the exact timing. If you drop a class during this time, the class won't appear on your transcript or grade reports, and you will not be billed for it. If you need to adjust your class schedule and want to avoid a W ("Withdrawn") grade, make sure to drop by this deadline.
You can make changes to your schedule either directly from your iGPS plan, or with the
Schedule Builder
. For help making changes from your iGPS plan, follow the instructions below.
Note:
The examples below are from the fall 2020 semester, but the process is the same for each semester.
Add a new course to your schedule
To add a new course to your schedule:
Log into your iGPS Plan from
One.IU
.
Once your full plan is displayed, find the semester tile for the term for which you would like to make changes. You will see the courses for which you are currently registered, as well as any courses you may have left in your shopping cart or that you considered for enrollment but did not use (planned items). At the top, select
Continue planning
to begin adjusting your schedule:
From the single-term view of iGPS, check your weekly calendar to see available slots for scheduling. Use the search tools to find all the classes in which you want to enroll and add them to your shopping cart; start by selecting
Add from Course Search
.
In the new window that opens, you can search for courses by entering a keyword. You can also choose a subject area, level (for example, 100, 200, 300, etc.), or number of units. In the example below, courses are filtered by the subject "Integrated New Media Studies".
For more filters, select
Class Filters
. You can select
Hide Closed Classes
, specify the days and times you want, or choose a particular mode of instruction. The filters will help limit your search results.
If you find a course that looks interesting, select the link below to view available sections (in the example above,
View FA20 classes/add to Shopping Cart
). Check your calendar to confirm it will fit into your schedule, and then select
Add to cart
:
Return to the single-term view and select
Enroll
. You will be returned to the enrollment shopping cart.
Select the class, select
Validate
, and then
Enroll
:
Swap courses in your schedule
To swap courses in your schedule:
Follow steps 1-5
above
to identify the course you'd like to swap with one for which you are already registered.
If you are swapping classes, don't worry if you have already registered for a course that conflicts with the new course's time; you can still add it to your shopping cart.
From either the Full Plan view or within the Single Term view, select
Enroll
. You will be returned to your enrollment shopping cart.
From the menu on the left, under "Enrollment", select
Swap Classes
.
All classes you are currently enrolled in will appear in the list with a
Swap This Class
button to the right. Select
Swap This Class
for the course you wish to swap out of.
You will see the following swap options:
With class from Search
With class from shopping cart
with class from Class Number
Since you would have put your new class into your shopping cart when in iGPS Plan, select that option.
The window that appears will show you all classes in your shopping car. Select the class you want by selecting
Swap
.
Review your swap confirmation information and select
Confirm
.

title: About the Student Center Dashboard
content:
Important:
IU Columbus, IU East, and IU Fort Wayne, IU Kokomo, IU Northwest, IU South Bend, and IU Southeast:
For spring and summer 2026 registration, use
Stellic
rather than the instructions here. Stellic is a new easy-to-use tool to help students plan their path, track their progress toward graduation, and register in one location. See
Stellic quick start guide for students
.
IU Bloomington and IU Indianapolis:
For spring and summer 2026 registration, continue to use the SIS Student Center to register for your classes.
Table of contents
Overview
Dashboard navigation and layout
Change your campus/institution
Learn more or submit feedback
Edit your widgets
Overview
As part of the Student Information System (SIS), the Student Center applications provide access to many services for students. In the Student Center, students can view course offerings, register for classes, view class schedules and grades, change contact information, view financial aid information, and other such tasks.
When you navigate to the
Student Center
, you'll be on the
Dashboard
, and your preferred name will be displayed. In the navigation on the left side, you'll see the following sections:
Dashboard
,
Change Campus/Institution
,
Class Search
,
Schedule
,
Enrollment
,
Academics
,
Financial
,
My Information
, and
My Profile
.
The Dashboard includes a
General
section and an
Academics
section.
Dashboard navigation and layout
General section
When you arrive on the Dashboard, the
General
section is displayed, showing holds on your record, to do items, shopping cart information, and waitlisted classes.
To expand the navigation on the left, select the three stacked horizontal lines at the top of the blue bar.
Academics section
At the top of the Dashboard, select
Academics
to change to the Academics section, where you can view your class schedule and grades.
Change your campus/institution
After you've expanded the navigation on the left, your campus's logo will display above the menu. By default, the campus displayed is the campus at which you are admitted, currently enrolled, or last enrolled.
To view information for another IU campus:
At the top left, in the navigation menu, select
Change Campus/Institution
(or select the gear icon):
Select the campus or institution you'd like to view. Note that the campus you are currently viewing will be selected.
Select
Change Campus/Institution
.

title: Read an OME-encrypted message
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Scenarios
IU Exchange to IU Exchange - same tenant
IU Exchange to non-IU Exchange - different tenant
IU Exchange to non-Exchange - self-validating provider (Gmail or Yahoo)
IU Exchange to non-Exchange - other providers
Open an attachment
Mailing lists
Forwarding
Overview
UITS
has enabled
Office Message Encryption
(OME) as a replacement for CSESS (Cisco Secure Email Encryption Service) formerly CRES (Cisco Registered Envelope Service). The method for reading an OME message depends on the recipient email system; for the highest compatibility, the sender and recipient should both use the "click to run" version of
Outlook
(often referred to as the "Microsoft 365 version of Office"), or use
Outlook on the web
(OWA). However, other versions of
Outlook
2016 or higher should perform similarly.
To check your version of
Outlook
, select
File
, then choose
Office Account
, and look under "About Outlook".
Note:
To learn how to force the encryption of a message, see
Ensure that mail sent from your Exchange account to an outside address is encrypted
.
Even if the sender does not force encryption, all outbound messages from IU mail servers to external recipients are scanned for certain potentially sensitive information; if the scan determines that the message is likely to contain sensitive data, it is encrypted.
Scenarios
In any of the scenarios below, if you select
Read the message
and get the following error message, "User account
user@external.com
from identity provider "mail" does not exist in tenant "Indiana University" and cannot access the application...", copy the link and open it in a browser that is not already authenticated to your credentials.
IU Exchange to IU Exchange - same tenant
In this scenario, there should be no difference from any other standard send/receive scenario. You may see some text saying that the email is encrypted, but the encryption will be seamless and should not impact message operations.
IU Exchange to non-IU Exchange - different tenant
If the external tenant's settings are configured in the same way as IU's tenant (usually they are not), there should be no difference from any other standard send/receive scenario. The
.rpmsg
attachment is not intended to be opened, and should be ignored.
If the external tenant's settings are not configured in the same way as IU's tenant:
Open the notification email, and select
Read the message
.
A dialog box may prompt you for the intended recipient's email address (this might not be you), if it isn't automatically applied from the link.
Request a temporary code that will be sent to the intended recipient's email address, and then use it to access the message.
IU Exchange to non-Exchange - self-validating provider (Gmail or Yahoo)
The
.rpmsg
attachment is not intended to be opened, and should be ignored.
Note:
Other high volume email vendors may offer account self-validation, but Gmail and Yahoo are the only ones known currently.
Open the notification email, and select
Read the message
.
A web page will open with the option to either access the message with the intended recipient's Gmail login, or to receive an access code.
If you choose to use the intended recipient's Gmail login,  enter the intended recipient's Gmail credentials to access the message.
If you choose to receive an access code, it will be sent to the intended recipient's Gmail account; use it to access the message.
IU Exchange to non-Exchange - other providers
The
.rpmsg
attachment is not intended to be opened, and should be ignored.
Open the notification email, and select
Read the message
.
A dialog box may prompt you for the intended recipient's email address (this might not be you), if it isn't automatically applied from the link.
A web page will open with the option to receive an access code.
The code will be sent to the intended recipient's email address; use it to access the message.
Open an attachment
If the attachment is a file that was sent with the email, then you can open it like a standard attachment. If the attachment is a
OneDrive
link, when you attempt to open it you may be prompted to receive and then enter a temporary code that is specific to
OneDrive
. The code will be sent to the intended recipient's email address; use it to access the attachment.
Note:
As a Data Loss Prevention function, automatic encryption cannot be disabled. If you believe your message was incorrectly encrypted, contact
it-incident@iu.edu
; if possible send the message as an attachment, or include the text of the message in your email. Make sure to include the following:
Sender email address
Recipient email address
Date and time of the message
Subject of the message
Mailing lists
As a best practice sensitive data should not be sent via listserv. If you send data that could be considered sensitive, you may need to use a different service, or send the message from the
IU List interface
.
Forwarding
Since encrypted messages are intended for a specific recipient, forwarding an encrypted message is not considered best practice.

title: SEO best practices for IU websites
content:
Table of contents
Digital Strategy Initiative and search engine optimization (SEO)
Site structure and SEO
Subfolders vs. subdomains
Other resources
Digital Strategy Initiative and search engine optimization (SEO)
Indiana University has launched the
Digital Strategy Initiative
(DSI), working towards a more user-friendly web experience to improve IU's reputation and brand recognition as well as aid in student recruitment and retention.
A site audit in the summer of 2023 found nearly one-third of IU's web presence to be unmaintained or dead, with issues that have a direct impact on web traffic and visibility on search engine results pages.
Website owners can check their sites in
Siteimprove
, a tool that identifies issues to address to improve search engine optimization (SEO). Some of the most important issues for SEO include:
Broken links:
Once found, these should be removed or replaced quickly because they negatively affect user experience and search authority.
Canonical URLs:
Search engines like Google consider a page's canonical URL the "one true source" of information about the content. The canonical version of a page's URL should include the full filename (that is,
bloomington.iu.edu/research/index.html
instead of
bloomington.iu.edu/research/
).
Redirects:
Redirects should link to the final canonical version of the new page. Uncorrected redirect chains slow page loading and create a negative user experience, resulting in reduced search authority.
Image file size:
Images over 1 MB should be replaced with something smaller (see the IU Web Style Guide for information about
compressing images
); when replacing images, use the
WebP
format for better performance.
Autoplay videos:
Videos should not be set to autoplay or appear in the hero section of a webpage; the large file size creates slower page load speed.
Sitemaps:
sitemap.xml
files should update nightly (WCMS sites update sitemaps automatically). Make sure to update sitemaps when large sections of sites have changes in folder structure, content changes, or redirects; search engines use sitemaps as guideposts for indexing pages. Large sites should break the sitemap into multiple sitemaps, linked together; for more, see
Google Search Central Documentation on sitemap management
.
Virtual tours:
Search engines will read virtual tours on higher education websites, so be sure to include equivalent text descriptions and present that version first, before any interactive or 3D tour. Well-crafted text within the tour, along with alt text and text transitions, can be effective SEO indicators; the
IU Brand
website has more
best practices for creating virtual tours
.
Accordions:
While content in closed accordion panels is readable by search engines, it may not be considered as important as top-level content; for best results, use a maximum of 5-7 accordions on a page, be sure headers clearly summarize the body content, and avoid including critical content in closed panels.
Site structure and SEO
In order to improve IU's search engine results, custom subdomains will only be approved in special circumstances. Subfolders (or subdirectories) are the recommended practice for IU websites.
A website's structure has a significant impact on search performance, so it's important to create a structure that drives traffic in a way that brings the best possible results.
Subfolders vs. subdomains
Search engines consider subdomains separate from the main domain (
president.iu.edu
is considered a subdomain of iu.edu), so they rank the content and assets within each subdomain separately, leading to reduced traffic.
Because subfolders organize content and assets within an individual site's domain (as in
iu.edu/president/
), search engines consider them part of the main site. This boosts the site's domain ranking and can drive more traffic. When building sites, it's recommended to use subfolders for better SEO performance.
Other resources

Domain and virtual host request form

title: Differences between development and production projects in IU REDCap
content:
In
IU REDCap
, your new project has "Development" status while you're building and testing it. When you're ready to enter real data, you change the project status to "Production" from the "Control Panel" page (accessed via the menu on the left). When you're finished collecting data, or if you wish to stop collection, you can set the status to "Inactive". You can change the status back to "Production" whenever you're ready to resume data collection.
Changes you make to a project with "Development" status take effect immediately. Once your project's status has changed to "Production", you can no longer edit its database fields in real time. To modify a project with "Production" status, you must enter Draft Mode to make your changes, and then pass them for approval to a REDCap administrator. For more, see
Make changes to an IU REDCap project that is currently in production
.
If you have questions about IU
REDCap
, or need help setting up or managing an IU
REDCap
project, email IU
REDCap
Support at
redcap@iu.edu
.

title: Use cron jobs in AppKube
content:
Note:
The following information is technical and intended for web application developers.
Table of contents
About cron jobs
Enable cron job functionality in AppKube
Define cron jobs
Cron job name character limits
How the naming works
Examples
Reference information
Get help
About cron jobs
A cron job is a command that runs on a fixed schedule or interval. These are typically used to automate maintenance tasks or other background processes that support the operation of an application. Within
AppKube
, you can schedule one or more cron jobs that will have access to your application's code, your secrets, and any persistent storage that you may be using. They are defined within your application's code and are deployed alongside your application.
Enable cron job functionality in AppKube
To enable cron job functionality in AppKube, you need to ensure that the
Requires Cronjob
option is selected for your application. If you did not enable cron jobs when you originally requested your application, you can go to
https://webapps.iu.edu
and request to add the feature. Once the option is enabled, you can define and deploy cron jobs through your application's deployment process as outlined below.
Define cron jobs
To define one or more cron jobs in AppKube, you must first create a directory named
.appkube
in the root directory of your application's source code in GitHub. Then, within the
.appkube
directory, create a file named
cronjobs.yaml
. This file can define zero or more cron jobs for your application.
Following is an example
cronjobs.yaml
file:
cronjobs:
- name: daily-task
schedule: "0 21 * * *"
timeZone: "US/Eastern"
command: "php"
script: "scripts/my-daily-task.php"
arguments: [ "$STORAGE_DIR/my-output-file.txt" ]
environments: [ "test", "prod" ]
enabled: true
- name: monthly-task
schedule: "30 2 L * *"
command: "php"
script: "scripts/my-monthly-task.php"
The above example schedules two cron jobs:
The first cron job runs daily at 9pm (ET) and executes the PHP script in the
scripts
directory of the project named
my-daily-task.php
. It passes two arguments to the script. The first argument is a command line option named
--output
; the second argument references the $STORAGE_DIR environment variable, which points to the location of persistent storage (for apps that are using it). This cron job is configured to execute in the test and production environments.
The second cron job executes a script on the last day of each month at 2:30am (ET) in the test and production environments. It takes no arguments.
When your application is deployed to test and/or production, the
cronjobs.yaml
specification will be read, and the requested cron jobs will be installed within AppKube's infrastructure. You can update these later by changing the file and redeploying. If you remove any cron jobs from the list, those cron jobs will be shut down and removed; if you add any new ones, they will be newly installed for you.
Important:
If you have existing cron jobs configured for your application and want to completely remove them from all environments, modify your
cronjobs.yaml
file to look like the following, and then deploy it to your test and production environments:
cronjobs: []
If you only remove the
.appkube/cronjobs.yaml
file from your project, the AppKube build process will skip the cron job deployment workflow step, and as a result will not remove any existing cron jobs. If you want to remove the file completely from your project, deploy a file with an empty set of cron jobs (as shown above) before removing the
cronjobs.yaml
file.
Cron job name character limits
AppKube cron jobs are subject to Kubernetes' 52-character limit for cron job names. The system automatically maximizes the available characters for your cron job names and validates this limit during deployment.
How the naming works
Full CronJob name format: {group-account}-{app-code}-{cronjob-name}
Total name length limit: 52 characters
Available characters for cronjob name = 52 - (group-account length) - (app-code length) - 2 (for hyphens)
Examples
Example 1
Group account:
infotern
(8 characters)
App code:
internship-app
(14 characters)
Cron name:
very-long-cronjob-name-that-exceeds-limit
(41 characters)
Full name:
infotern-internship-app-very-long-cronjob-name-that-exceeds-limit
(65 characters)
Too long (exceeds 52-character limit)
Example 2
Group account:
infotern
(8 characters)
App code:
internship-app
(14 characters)
Cron name:
daily-cleanup
(13 characters)
Full name:
infotern-internship-app-daily-cleanup
(37 characters)
Okay (within 52-character limit)
The system will automatically validate cron job names during deployment and provide clear error messages if the limit is exceeded, preventing deployment failures.
Reference information
Reference for
cronjobs.yaml
fields
Field
Required?
Description
name
Yes
This is a unique, human-readable identifier for the job. It is limited in size and may be truncated if too long; see
Cron job name character limits
for details. Each of your application's cron jobs
must
have a unique name.
schedule
Yes
Standard 5-field cron schedule; for example,
"*/5****"
(see note below)
timeZone
No
IANA time zone (for example,
"America/New_York"
); if omitted,
"US/Eastern"
is the default
command
Yes
Execution command; currently restricted to
php
(see note below)
script
Yes
This is the path to the script you want to execute. If you provide a relative path, it will be relative to the root of your application's deployment directory.
arguments
No
Zero or more command-line arguments passed to the script
environments
No
This is used to specifiy the environments where the job should run. The only options are
"test"
and
"prod"
(if not present, it defaults to both
"test"
and
"prod"
).
enabled
No
Toggles job activation; enabled by default
Note:
For more about the
schedule
field, see the
FreeBSD crontab manual page
and the
go.dev cron manual page
.
Currently, only
"php"
is supported as the execution command for cron jobs. The majority of cron functionality can be implemented using PHP code within your application project. The system is configured this way to avoid arbitrary code execution within the container in which your application runs. This is partially for security reasons and partially to avoid dependencies on the binaries installed within AppKube that could lead to compatibility issues as the environment continues to evolve. To share feedback about any limitations you may experience, email
apphelp@iu.edu
.
Get help
For help using your AppKube cron jobs, email
apphelp@iu.edu
.

title: Set appointment availability in the Student Appointment Scheduler
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Set up your calendar
View and manage your appointments
Scheduling notice to redirect students
Email messages to students
Overview
The Student Appointment Scheduler (SAS) lets staff, faculty, tutors, and other users create and manage blocks of available time in an online calendar. Students may access this calendar to view, schedule, and cancel appointment slots.
Set up your calendar
When setting up your calendar, you can view an individual day or week by using the
Day
and
Week
buttons. Note that appointment blocks cannot be set from the month view.
To navigate between months, use the arrows in the upper corners of the inset calendar or the arrows to the left of the
Day
,
Week
, and
Month
buttons.
Appointment restrictions
Appointment restrictions let you select parameters for which students can view and schedule appointment slots restricted to student populations you specify. To create a restriction:
From your main calendar view, select
Manage Restrictions
, and then
Create New Slot Restriction
.
Enter a name for your restriction, and then select one of the options below:
Include assigned advisees
, along with any additional criteria from the drop-down menus. If you are interested in having only your assigned advisees able to see your appointment slots, check this box only and save with the name of the group; any other criteria could create a much smaller number of students who could see your availability.
Any/all of the parameters you would like associated with that restriction from the drop-down menus
One of your Caseload Groups from
AdRx
If you are creating a campaign for a group of your students, select the name of the campaign as the only criteria and save it along with a restriction name.
Note:
Within a restriction, all criteria are set up with "AND" logic; that is, students have to meet
all
selected criteria in order to schedule an appointment at the time you specify. The best practice is to make each restriction as clear and simple as possible.
As you save restrictions, they will display on the left. Select a restriction to view its details, as well as to access the
Delete
button to remove it. You cannot edit a saved restriction. If there is a restriction that does not work for what you need, you can delete the existing restriction and create a new one with adjusted details.
Create appointment slots
To set an appointment slot:
Important:
Make sure you can see your calendar in full (that is, the left, center, and right panels). The following appointment options will appear in the right panel.
Choose a date and time:
Select any 30-minute interval on the calendar. The details for the appointment will appear in the right sidebar:
Appointment Date:
Confirm the correct date of the appointment slot.
Time:
Adjust an appointment's start and/or end times. Remember to:
Put a zero (
0
) before all single digits
Leave no spaces before am/pm (for example, use
09:00am
, not
9:00 am
)
Select a meeting type:
From the
Meeting Type
menu, select
Appointment
,
Group
, or
Drop-in
. For each meeting type, select one to three meeting modes:
in-person
,
online
, or
phone
. When you select a meeting mode, the appointment details will expand to include specific information for the students about each mode. This information will be included in the confirmation and reminder emails to the student.
Drop-In
shows students that they may drop in to see you, but they cannot reserve that time.
Group appointments require that you enter both the number of students who may meet with you during that appointment slot and a name for the group slot. The group slot name is displayed in SAS for students searching your calendar. Students will see the group meeting only if spots are still available.
If the appointment is recurring, selecting
Yes
will display the frequency of the appointment slots and the start and end dates for the reoccurrence.
Important:
To account for server load issues and improve performance, the maximum length for which you can set a recurring series is 31 calendar days, regardless of how frequently the series repeats (weekly, every weekday, every day). You can set up recurring series multiple months in advance, but you must make a new recurring series for each month. OCSS recommends setting up appointments only three to four months into the future.
Choose a profile:
If you have more than one profile, select the appropriate profile for the appointment slot. If you have only one profile, your default will be this profile.
Set restrictions
:
Apply any restrictions by checking the boxes next to them. If you add more than one restriction within an appointment slot, the limitation is an "OR".  For example, students who meet
either
restriction A or restriction B could view and schedule this appointment slot.
Set location details:
For in-person, select the building and enter the room number. The default selection is from your profile, in your user settings managed by your
AdRx
administrator. If your building is not listed, there is a
Building Not Listed
option at the bottom of the "Building" list; you would then enter both your building and room location in the specified field.
For online, you can enter your Zoom link, but you are required to provide details on how to connect with you online.
For phone, you can enter your office phone, but you are required to describe who initiates the call and how. Remember that if the student has a US-based telephone number, they will enter it when scheduling an appointment and that is the number you would call.
Finalize the appointment:
To finish creating the appointment slot, select
Create Slot
or
Schedule
for a specific student.
View and manage your appointments
You can view appointments by day, week, or month. With day and week views, you see times allotted for each appointment, an icon showing the type of appointment, and restrictions on the appointment block.
View student details
If a student has scheduled to meet with you during an appointment block, the student's name will appear in the box and will change to a black font color. Select the student's name to see more details, including the student ID and purpose for the appointment.
You can also view student details from the "Appointments" area in
AdRx
.
Change an appointment
From the calendar, you can delete an appointment, change the appointment type (for example, change from an in-person to a phone appointment), update the reasons for the appointment, or change the profile assigned to the appointment.
To change the appointment time, you must delete the appointment or appointment series and re-create it where desired.
Important:
Users cannot add new modes to existing flexible appointments. If a new mode is needed, you will have to delete the appointment and make a new appointment. For instance, if you have an in-person or Zoom appointment and a student scheduled for Zoom, but would like to change to in-person, you will be able to edit the existing appointment for the alternate mode.
If you have an in-person or Zoom appointment and a student scheduled for Zoom, but would like to change to phone, you will need to delete the old appointment and make a new appointment with phone as the mode.
Best practice:
Offer as many modes as are reasonable when you first make appointments to minimize difficulty in editing. (If you are working in your office, for instance, we recommend offering all three modes on any appointment.)
View all appointment blocks
In the month view, you will see the calendar for the month with a listing of how many open appointment slots you have and how many scheduled appointments you have for each day. Selecting a specific day will take you to the daily view.
During peak advising times and course registration times, it's possible that all appointment slots are filled and new students will have no times to select unless you add more appointment slots, or make more slots available based on your maximum future time setting in "
AdRx
- My Profile - SAS Student Appointment Scheduler - Calendar Settings".
Note:
Because SAS is integrated into Outlook, student names will display in the subject of the Outlook calendar item. Any related scheduling history (for example, students who canceled that spot, making it available) will be in the notes area.
Scheduling notice to redirect students
Advisors may sometimes have no available appointments for weeks or months due to employment status, extended leave, or job requirements such as orientation programming. A scheduling notice gives students this information in SAS and directs them to another advising source while their assigned advisor is unavailable.
You might use scheduling notices for the following cases:
Summer New Student Orientation means you are largely meeting with new students; a scheduling notice informs continuing students and provides directions on how to get help and whom to contact.
A faculty advisor is on a 10-month contract, so for two months the advisor will not be meeting with students; a scheduling notice lets students know whom they can contact for advising until the faculty advisor's return.
An advising office only takes drop-in appointments the week prior to a new semester and the first week of classes; a scheduling notice would inform students of that and direct them to the hours the office is taking drop-ins.
An advisor will be unavailable for an extended period (such as FMLA) and needs to remind students whom they can see for advising in the interim.
Note:
Scheduling notices are not "out of office" messages or constant reminders ("this is a busy time of year") that replace calendar and caseload management. In most cases, such as PTO, training, or busy advising seasons, students can still make future appointments on your SAS, so you should not use a scheduling notice.
Example scheduling notices
Scenario 1: Faculty who are not available over the summer need to refer students to an advising office for assistance
Subject: No appointments until fall semester
Message: During the summer, from (date) to (date), I won't have advising appointments available; please contact the Undergrad Advising Center for advising questions  and help at 123-4567.
Scenario 2: An advisor is largely working in orientation for the summer and needs to refer students to others for assistance
Subject: Summer Orientation Advising
Message: I will be working with New Student Orientation this summer and most or all of my appointments will be taken up with new student advising meetings. If you need advising help or an advising appointment, please contact the advising office at 123-4567 to meet with an academic advisor.
Scenario 3: An advisor is on FMLA for an extended leave and needs to refer students to colleagues for assistance
Subject: On extended leave, contact Sally or Anne
Message: I will be away on extended leave from (date) to (date). Please contact Sally Supervisor at 456-7891 or Anne Advisor at 123-4567 for academic advising during this time. They have access to all of the notes, plans, and advising emails from our appointments and are happy to help you with registration.
Email messages to students
Example confirmation email
Below is an example of an email message sent to students after they schedule an appointment. The appointment details are filled in automatically. The personalized message was created by the advisor in the "SAS Student Appointment Scheduler – Advisor Messaging – Appointment Confirmation Message to Students" setting in My Profile.
Appointment Confirmation with Ima Advisor-Coach on Wed Feb 08 2020, 09:00 AM
Hello [Student Name]
Your appointment is confirmed with Ima Advisor-Coach.
Appointment Details
Date : Wed Feb 08 2020
Time : 09:00 AM- 09:30 AM
Reason : I need to discuss graduation
Location : Dunes Med/Prof Bldg 3104
Details: Please check in at the front reception desk so they can let me know you have arrived.
Hello! I am looking forward to meeting with you. Please prepare for our meeting by bringing your questions, possible course selections and your academic plan. Thank you for using the calendar.
Ima Advisor-Coach
Cancellation email
If either the advisor or the schedule manager cancels an existing appointment, the student is automatically notified from the advisor's email. The message includes the reason entered by whoever canceled the appointment.
How to direct students to SAS
Direct students to visit
One.IU
and search for
Student Appointment Scheduler
.
You can also send basic directions, such as:
You can access my calendar online to find the time that best fits with your schedule:
SAS One.IU direct URL:
https://one.iu.edu/task/iu/student-appointment-scheduler
snippet: to redirect students Email messages to students Overview The Student Appointment Scheduler (SAS Appointment Scheduler - Calendar Settings". Note: Because SAS is integrated into Outlook, student due to employment status, extended leave, or job requirements such as orientation programming

title: PDQ reports in the Data Delivery PDQ application
content:
Table of contents
Overview
IUIE PDQ report migration to the Data Delivery PDQ system
Changes to IUIE PDQ report terms and concepts
Run reports
View completed report output
Joblog
Saved parameters
Create saved parameters
Manage saved parameters
Share saved parameters
Schedule jobs using saved parameters
Overview
The IUIE PDQ report system has been rewritten and moved out of the IUIE. PDQ reports that have been migrated from the IUIE are available in this system. Access it at
https://pdq.dd.iu.edu
.
IUIE PDQ report migration to the Data Delivery PDQ system
PDQ report developers will migrate reports from the IUIE to DD PDQ as they are ready. Until that happens, you may continue to use the report in the IUIE. After the report is migrated, you will still be able to look up the report in the IUIE, but it will be changed into a link pointing to the migrated report in the new system.
Note:
When a report is migrated, your shortcuts and scheduled jobs for that report will also be migrated.
Changes to IUIE PDQ report terms and concepts
Some terms and concepts have changed in the redesign:
Master and Test Catalogs have become main and develop contexts
In the IUIE, the "Test Catalog" was for reports that were being developed and the "Master Catalog" was for reports that were finished and ready for production use. The Data Delivery PDQ system has two contexts that fulfill the same roles as those catalogs, "develop" for reports that are still under revision, and "main" for reports that are ready for wide use. Each report appears on the home page
https://pdq.dd.iu.edu
with each context it is published to.
Shortcuts have become saved parameters
The functionality of shortcuts (saving the values entered in a report form in order to rerun the report with the same values) is now saved parameters. Any report with saved parameters will show them in a selectable drop-down menu at the top of the form. For more, see
Saved parameters
below.
Run reports
To run a report:
On
https://pdq.dd.iu.edu
, select the report name to open the report run form.
Enter values for each of the form parameters.
Under "Output format", if the report developer has enabled multiple formats, select the format you want the output to be delivered in.
Under "Output destination", select
Wait
to wait for the report to run and the output to be displayed in the browser, or
Send to Completed Reports
to have the report run in the background and be notified when it has finished. You will receive an email from the Central Notification Service when the report finishes.
Note:
If you don't have the option to send the report to Completed Reports, it's because the report has been classified as sensitive. You may only run it and wait for output.
If you want to save the values you have entered for form parameters, select
Save Parameters
. For more, see
Saved parameters
below.
Choose
Run
.
Note:
By default, PDQ reports in the develop context will execute queries to DSS against DSS1TST, while reports in the main context will execute DSS queries against DSS1PRD. To override this and have the report run against the other DSS instance, instead of
Run
, select
Run against Prod
for reports in the develop context, or
Run against Test
for reports in the main context.
View completed report output
To view reports you selected to go to completed reports, visit
Completed reports
. Under the "Action" drop-down menu, choose
Details
to view the joblog entry for that report run.
Joblog
The joblog entry has links to the report output and to logs from the report execution, as well as metadata about the run.
Note:
Report output is retained for 30 days before deletion. You can choose
remove now
to delete output immediately, or extend the retention period to 60 days by choosing
extend 30 days
.
While the report output is avilable, you can run the report again using the parameters from the run that generated this joblog; to do so, at the bottom of the page, choose
Replicate
. This will take you to the report run form with all form parameters that were entered for this run filled in. To save these parameters separately from the joblog, see
Create saved parameters
below.
Saved parameters
Create saved parameters
As you enter values into a PDQ report form, you may save them to be loaded back into the form later. To do so, after entering values for fields in a report form, at the bottom select
Save Parameters
. You will be prompted to enter a unique name to save them with.
To have your saved parameters populate the form fields, at the top of the form, select the name from the "Populate with saved parameters" selector.
To update existing saved parameters that you have loaded previously, when saving leave the name unchanged and check the "Overwrite existing saved parameters?" box before choosing
Save
.
To manage saved parameters, next to the "Populate with saved parameters" selector, choose
Manage
to go to the
Saved parameters page
.
Manage saved parameters
The
Saved parameters page
displays the saved parameters you have access to in two sections. The top section shows saved parameters you have created. The bottom section shows saved parameters created by other users that they have shared with an ACM group you are a member of. For shared parameters you have created, the "Actions" drop-down allows you to take several actions:
Details
takes you to the detail page for the saved parameters where you can view their metadata, manage sharing them, and create scheduled jobs using them.
run
allows you to run a report using the saved parameters.
delete
allows you to delete the saved parameters.
rename
allows you to change the name under which the saved parameters are stored.
Share saved parameters
The saved parameters that have been shared with you will appear in the saved parameters drop-down selector in the form of the report they were created for. You cannot modify saved parameters shared with you; you can only load them in report forms. If you would like to give saved parameters shared with you a personal name distinct from the name given by the creator, under the "Actions" drop-down, choose
Change Personal Name
and enter a name. This name will only appear for you.
To share saved parameters you have created, on the "Details" page, choose
Share
. In the "Select Sharing Group" popup, enter the name of an ACM group to share them with, and then choose
Save
. To stop sharing, on the "Details" page, select
Stop Sharing
.
Schedule jobs using saved parameters
To run a report on a schedule, create a scheduled job using saved parameters. To do so:
On the saved parameters "Details" page, choose
Schedule Job
.
Fill out the form to configure how you want the schedule to function.
To have the job run on the schedule you entered, choose
Save
. Alternatively, to keep a scheduled job but prevent it from running, select the
Disable this schedule
checkbox and then choose
Save
.
To see all your scheduled jobs, go to
Scheduled jobs
.

title: Request a new AppKube application
content:
Note:
The following information is technical and intended for web application developers. AppKube is still under active development and this information may change. Subscribe to this article to get updates.
Table of contents
Request form
After you submit your request
While awaiting approval
When your AppKube repository is ready
Support
Request form
To request a new AppKube application, go to
https://webapps.iu.edu/
, select
Request New Application
, and then provide the following in the request form:
Group account name:
Must be a valid IU group account
You'll need to
create a new group account for use with your application
if you don’t already have one.
Your application will be owned by this group.
Application name:
Must be lowercase, alphanumeric, with dashes only (for example,
my-iu-app
)
Determines default test and production URLs on
*.webapps-test.iu.edu
and
*.webapps.iu.edu
For example, if your application name is
my-iu-app
, your default test and production URLs would be
my-iu-app.webapps-test.iu.edu
and
my-iu-app.webapps.iu.edu
, respectively.
You can point your
custom virtual hostname
to the production URL later.
Determines the name of the GitHub repository that will be generated for you
Try to limit application names to fewer than 15 characters, as many other features such as
cron jobs
can also add characters that ultimately can exhaust Kubernetes' system-imposed character limit of 52.
Application type:
Choose from these options:
Static
An application that only includes static files (no server-side PHP)
PHP 8.2/8.3
Choose the latest version of PHP unless your application needs to run on an earlier version for compatibility reasons.
Laravel with PHP 8.2/8.3
Same as PHP 8.2/8.3 but mounts in a writable storage​ folder which is required for Laravel to function
Note:
AppKube does not currently support other server-side programming languages (Python, PERL, etc.).
