title: Apply and customize the IU Course Template for your Canvas course
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Apply the template to your course
Adapt the template to your course
Create additional modules
Delete the template from your course
Overview
The IU Course Template is a collection of instructional assets to help you get started with developing your face-to-face, hybrid, or fully online course in Canvas. Created by the UITS Teaching and Learning Technologies team, this fully accessible template includes a home page, a syllabus, a "Getting Started" module for students, and a sample module with a module overview page, interactive lecture placeholder, discussion topic, and an assignment. To review the template structure and content before copying it to your course, visit the
preview course in Canvas
.
Apply the template to your course
Important:
When you apply a template to your Canvas course, the settings and navigation in your course will be replaced with those in the template. Apply the template
before
you start creating or importing course content. If you apply it afterward:
You may overwrite your course syllabus or other content in your course. If you already created content in your course site, consider making a copy of the course before applying the template.
If you made customizations to the settings or navigation of the course, you may need to reset them.
If your course uses an
eText
, you will need to re-add the IU eTexts (Unizin Engage) tool to your course navigation. For help with course navigation, see
How do I manage Course Navigation links?
To apply the IU Course Template to your Canvas course:
Navigate to your course and select
Settings
.
In the settings sidebar at the right or bottom, choose
Apply Course Template
. You'll see a pop-up with information and instructions.
Note:
The
Apply Course Template
button is only visible in unpublished courses.
Select
Indiana University
to expose the templates available to the entire institution.
Look for the template named "IU Course Template". To preview the template, select the template name. To apply the template to your course, select
Apply Template
. An informational pop-up will appear. Choose
Apply
to proceed with applying the template.
The template will be copied to your course immediately, but it may take a few minutes for the template to be fully imported. To check the import status, open the Settings tool. In the sidebar, choose
Import Course Content
, and review the status of the first item under "Current Jobs".
Adapt the template to your course
The template is a starting point for your course. You can keep the elements you like and remove or modify the ones that don't quite fit. You can also add tools, materials, and activities as needed.
Begin by reading and following the instructions on the course home page to customize it. Carefully review and customize each element in the template to reflect the particulars of your course. As your review each item, look for and follow the instructions that appear in boldface surrounded by brackets. For example:
[Note to instructors: Replace the bullet points below with the information that pertains to this assignment.]
If you plan to use the Canvas Modules tool for organizing the materials and activities in your course, continue with the
next section
. If not, delete the "Week 1" module from the Modules tool, but leave the tool enabled so students can access the "Getting Started" module.
Create additional modules
There are two options for creating modules from the sample module and content in the template:
Option 1: Duplicate modules manually
The template includes one sample module. If you'd like to create additional modules, you can duplicate the sample. Duplicating a module also creates copies of the module's items, that is, the pages, assignments, and discussions that make up the module.
Before duplicating the sample module, review the structure and content to make sure it works for your class. Add, remove, or modify the module items as needed. Once you are satisfied with the content and structure of the module, begin making copies.
Important:
Modules containing one or more quizzes cannot be duplicated unless the quizzes were created with the New Quizzes tool. If you want to include classic quizzes in your modules, you'll need to add them to your modules after duplication.
From your course navigation, select
Modules
.
At the upper right of the "Week 1" module, open the
Options
menu (
...
) and select
Duplicate
. A copy of the module and its items will be added to the Modules tool. The word "copy" (or "copy 1", "copy 2", etc.) will be added to the name of the module and each item.
Repeat the previous step to create as many modules as you'll need for your course.
After your modules are created, customize the title and instructions or instructional content in each module item with material appropriate for your course.
Option 2: Duplicate modules with the Multi-Tool
The Module Builder utility in the DesignPlus Multi-Tool, an external app from Cidi Labs, allows you to quickly create a complete set of modules for your course. Also, unlike the manual method described above, the Multi-Tool offers support for duplicating classic quizzes. To use the Multi-Tool to generate course modules from the IU Course Template:
Open the Settings tool in your course and from the settings sidebar, select
Multi-Tool
.
On the Multi-Tool home page, select
Module Builder
. Under the "Existing Modules" heading, Module Builder displays the two modules that are part of the template.
Scroll down to the "New Modules" heading.
Use the "Module Prefix" dropdown to select the prefix that should be applied to the beginning of each module and item name (for example,
Module
,
Lesson
,
Week
, etc.). You can even designate your own custom prefix.
For "Number of Modules to Create", enter the number of modules that will be needed to cover all of your instructional content in the course.
For "Starting Number", leave the value at
1
. You will eventually delete the sample module that was included in the template.
Next, you'll create the Module Pattern. The module pattern is the sequence of content and activities that should appear in most or all mod ules.
Since each module will begin with an overview page, under "Add Items" select
Page
to add a page to the pattern as the first item. A page row is added to the module pattern:
Use the "[Blank Page]" dropdown to the select the sample module overview page,
Week 1: Overview
, as the page template.
In the "Page Name [Optional]" box, enter
Overview
,
Introduction
, or something similar. When Module Builder creates your module, the page name will be preceded by the prefix and module number. For example, "Lesson 1: Overview", "Lesson 2: Overview", and so on.
Use the item options under "Add Items" to add the other items to your module pattern. The number, type, and order of items in the module pattern is up to you. For each item, you will enter a name, and select the template in the template dropdown. Where appropriate, use the items provided in the sample module as template files. For quizzes, select
[Blank Quiz]
since the sample module does not include a sample quiz. Additional considerations:
For assignments added to the pattern, enter the submission type, the point value, and the "[Display grade as]" value.
For graded discussion topics added to the pattern, enter the point value and the "[Display grade as]" value.
To move any item in the pattern, select the handle to the left of its icon and drag to the desired location.
Review the module pattern to make sure you've added all the necessary items and the requested parameters for each. Your module pattern should look similar to the example below:

title: Build information for Linux computers on the IU Common Build
content:
Important:
Read the documentation and installation guide in their entirety before attempting to build the device. While the new installation and configuration processes are automated, they require the builder to take a fresh approach and discard any previous experience with Ubuntu.
Table of contents
Overview
IU Common Build notable standards
Computer naming convention
Entra login
Build process
Prepare a device
LUKS and full-disk encryption
Build experience
Build a device

LUKS recovery key
Software

Overview
For Linux computers, the IU Common Build provides a widely used, enterprise-friendly desktop operating system and central management solution. This includes automated full-disk encryption, system configuration, and a high security standard based on CIS Benchmarks. Device sign-in is managed with Microsoft Entra. The goal isn't to enforce a "one size fits all" solution, but to provide a "one size fits most" option.
Endpoint Management Services (EMS) selected Ubuntu Linux for the IU Common Build based in large part on Ubuntu's popularity with university constituents and enterprise organizations.
IU Common Build notable standards
Computer naming convention
To align with the IU Common Build naming standard for macOS and Windows, Linux computers use the naming convention
IU-
SerialNumber
.
Entra login
Due to technical limitations and potential security risks, the UITS recommends logging into your Linux system using the format
username
@iu.edu
.
Important:
The system expects authorized users to log in by defining the actual
IU email address
. Windows and macOS mask the
@iu.edu
portion of the domain name, but Linux requires the whole name.
Failing to explicitly include
@iu.edu
in your login as recommended above will result in degraded performance.
Build process
Make sure to review the PDF installation guide before proceeding. The installation guide is comprehensive and provides a large amount of detail.
See the
Build media
section below for download links to each ISO and its respective installation and configuration guide(s). These items can be used to build a virtual or bare-metal machine.
If you are building a virtual machine, make sure to assign a serial number to your VM's BIOS before installing the operating system. For example, if you are building a VM in VirtualBox:
To set the serial number for the PC BIOS, use the command:
$ VBoxManage setextradata "My VM 1" "VBoxInternal/Devices/pcbios/0/Config/DmiSystemSerial" "string:VM
[your_initials]
001"
To set the serial number for the EFI firmware, use the command:
$ VBoxManage setextradata "My VM 2" "VBoxInternal/Devices/efi/0/Config/DmiSystemSerial" "string:VM
[your_initials]
002"
In the above examples, replace
[your_initials]
with your initials; for example,
vmjqp001
or
vmjqp002
.
Prepare a device
There are currently no data preservation options; the operating system installation is fully automated. Make sure you have a full backup of the system's data before proceeding with the build process. Any pre-existing data will be lost.
If you encounter any issues booting the ISO or installed system, first try disabling Secure Boot for your Boot Device within your UEFI firmware settings. Due to technical limitations, TPM devices and the Secure Boot setting currently are not fully supported.
LUKS and full-disk encryption
Full-disk encryption (FDE) is enforced and cannot be disabled. Be aware that LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) requires the encryption key to be provided at boot time. The system will fail to boot if the disk cannot be unlocked. Local UITS support people may use the
uems.py
application to cycle through encryption keys, after initially re-keying the device.
Build experience
Make sure to fully review the PDF installation guide before attempting to build a device. The build experience can be categorized as follows:
Phase 1
Operating system installation
Phase 2
System configuration
Phase 3
During system configuration, you'll be asked to provide the IU network username of the client receiving the computer. This doesn't require knowledge of their passphrase, but the client needs to be present when the device is delivered because their login is required to complete the re-keying process (as the default key should not be left as the active key, and the default installation credentials and keys should not be provided to clients).
Build a device
Make sure to read the build documentation before starting to build a device.
ISO:
ubuntu-24.04.2-IU-LCBv2-GA1-desktop-amd64.iso
MD5:
ubuntu-24.04.2-IU-LCBv2-GA1-desktop-amd64.md5
Installation guide:
UEMS Ubuntu 24.04 Install Guide - LCBv2-GA1.pdf
Post-installation and configuration notes
LUKS recovery key
Per
Security of Information Technology Resources (IT-12)
, FDE is automatically enabled for all IU Common Build systems. Due to current technical limitations, the system owner is responsible for remembering the encryption key. If you forget your encryption key, you will have no way to access or recover data from the device.
Software
While
apt
is available for installing software packages, UITS recommends using
snap
instead. These packages are designed to automatically update and do not conflict with system software or configurations. Installing software with
apt
may result in unintended negative effects.
System updates
Security patches are automatically installed. You should only update the system under advisement, as critical configurations could be overwritten, resulting in degraded performance.
Get help
Use the
Linux Support Request
for Linux Common Build requests.

Before you begin
Before adding an image to a Knowledge Base article, consider the following:
Is the image needed?
If a written step is easy to understand, the image may not be needed. For example, a step that says to select
OK
rarely needs an image. However, if a step tells you to find a drop-down menu in a busy or confusing interface, an image may be helpful.
Important:
For accessibility reasons, images should always support rather than replace written instructions.
Is the image clear and easy to read?
If the image is so blurry or small that the text is unreadable, it won't add value.
Does the image focus on the right details?
Crop large images to show only what's needed, or add annotation (arrows, circles, etc.) to highlight buttons, menus, or other details.
Has alt text been prepared for the image?
For accessibility reasons, all images must have meaningful alt text. To learn more, see
Alternative text for images
.
Is the image the right size?
Small images used within sentences should measure somewhere between 14 x 14 pixels and 22 x 22 pixels.
Large images should be cropped or resized as necessary.
Does the image contain information that should be redacted, such as a username or personal phone number?
If so, either edit the image to remove this information, or create a new image.
Does the image only show text on a screen?
For accessibility reasons, error messages and code snippets should be actual text. Text in images can't be read by assistive technology.

title: About KB workflow
content:
Note:
This information is intended for contributors to the Knowledge Base who are part of the Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) initiative.
Knowledge Base articles may move through any of the following workflow states:
Draft:
An article is in the Draft state whenever there is an unpublished version of it, whether it's the initial draft (0.01) or a revision that someone with editing privileges is working on (1.01, 2.01, etc.) As a KCS contributor, you'll be able to see in-progress drafts in the KB portal, regardless of who initiated them.
Draft revisions (version 1.01, etc.) have "(Draft)" immediately after the article number in the portal.
Initial drafts (version 0.01) do not have a visible draft designation in the portal.
For either type of draft, if someone else began it, you won't see the
Edit Article
option from the
Actions
drop-down menu in the portal.
Initial drafts won't be returned in KB searches. You won't see them in the portal unless you view them from a direct link using the article number.
Only people with editing privileges in ServiceNow Knowledge can see drafts.
Review:
After someone chooses
Publish
from the editing screen, an article moves to the Review state, and stays there until a member of the Knowledge Management team approves it. The version number (visible within ServiceNow) will change from
N
.01 to
N
.02.
For revisions (version 1.02, etc.), you'll see "(Review)" after the article number in the portal.
Like version 0.01, version 0.02 lacks the indication of the state in parentheses.
For either type of revision in a Review state, you won't see the
Edit Article
option from the
Actions
drop-down menu in the portal.
Version 0.02 won't be returned in KB searches.
Scheduled for publish:
The KM team can schedule revisions or drafts for future publication, but we don't do this extensively, because the live version of the article can't be updated in the meantime, since only one draft of a given article can exist at any given moment. If you'd like to submit a revision to go live at a future date, consult with the KM team, and avoid beginning your edit too far in advance of the publication date.
Published:
When an article is in a Published state (that is, there is no current draft of it), you won't see anything following the article number in the portal,
and
you'll have the
Edit Article
option from the
Actions
drop-down menu.  (However, this may also be true of an initial draft that you began.)
Pending retirement:
As contributors, you won't see an option to retire KB articles; the KM team will still do that.  Send us a ticket requesting the retirement of an article by the usual methods.  As we move through the process of approving our own actions in the system, it's possible (though not very likely) that you may see an article marked "(Pending retirement)".
Retired:
When an article is retired, no one except the KM team can view it.  Anyone else will see the same message that appears when you try to view an internal article that you don't have permission to see.
When updating articles, be sure not to link to anything that's retired. This is unlikely, of course, if you're looking at the current live content in the KB portal when working on content, which is always the best practice. Avoid working from old drafts, as content may have changed in the meantime.

title: Determine whether high performance computing can help your research
content:
Those new to high performance computing (HPC) often have a difficult time understanding if or when HPC can help their research. The information here offers a starting point, though it does not answer the question comprehensively. The staff of Indiana University's
Research Technologies
division of University Information Technology Services are happy to answer any additional questions. See
Research and high performance computing
for more information.
HPC systems provided by
Research Technologies
offer significant advantages over personal computers for unique or demanding computational tasks. However, for many day-to-day tasks, running programs on local personal computers may be more convenient and/or faster than using an HPC system. For example, depending on the specific situation, an HPC system may take longer to load a given application than a personal computer, but provides an advantage in terms of huge throughput for processing a large job.
You may benefit from HPC systems if you are working with one of the following:
You have computationally intensive programs that can be divided into multiple tasks, taking advantage of parallel processing with multiple processors. For example, if your program takes only an hour to run but you need to run it a thousand times, or your program can be scaled up to run across multiple processors, HPC systems may be beneficial.
Your programs require more CPUs, GPUs, or memory than your personal computer can handle.
Your projects involve working with massive data sets that exceed the storage capacity of your personal computer.
You estimate that you cannot complete your research tasks in a reasonable amount of time with your personal computing resources.
However, HPC systems may not provide an advantage if:
Your tasks are simple or small in scale; for smaller tasks that cannot be scaled up, personal computing devices will likely perform better (for example, office-type tasks, spreadsheets, word processing, etc.).
You are working with smaller data sets that can be processed effectively on your personal computer.
The increased parallel processing, expanded memory capacity, ample disk space, and efficient file system access offered by HPC systems make them indispensable for computationally demanding projects. On the other hand, do not use HPC systems for simple CPU jobs and smaller data sets, as these systems might not perform any better than your personal computing devices.
If you need help evaluating whether HPC is right for you,
contact the UITS
Research Applications and Deep Learning
team
.

Overview
Note:
This information is intended for contributors to the Knowledge Base who are part of the Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) initiative.
Much of the content in the IU Knowledge Base is available publicly, but a significant amount is restricted to one or more internal audiences.  Some of the most important audiences are:
iu-all:
All IU students, faculty, staff, and affiliates
uits:
UITS staff
local-support:
Local UITS support people; content in this audience is usually in the UITS audience as well
In ServiceNow Knowledge, the audience metadata is set by Can Read criteria.  These appear with "km-aud" before the specific audience name, such as "km-aud-iu-all".
When working with any KB content, it's very important to keep in mind who can access it.
Note:
For Phase 1 of the KCS initiative, please don't modify Can Read criteria. If you believe Can Read criteria need to be set, removed, or modified, let the KM team know. In future phases, this guidance may change; consult with the KM team if you have questions or concerns.

Below the article number, between the number of views and the

Near the bottom of the metadata fields, above the Meta Description field

At the bottom of the entry for each article

Put the link inside a

For more, see

Overview
Note:

Following is a list of metadata fields for articles in the IU Knowledge Base. Metadata refers to structured information about the article, which includes creation date, who last updated the article, etc.
All articles in the KB use the KM_T1 template, which includes custom fields meant to preserve information about content migrated from the old system.
Important:

do not
change the fields listed below. Consult the KM team first.
Metadata fields
Custom fields
Docid:
For the four-letter docids of migrated content. These are used for old URLs that redirect to ServiceNow (for example, kb.iu.edu/d/abxl).
Stakeholder:
The stakeholder/owner group responsible for the content. Plain text field.
Original Author:
For the original creator of migrated content. Leave blank in new articles.
Birth Date:
For the original creation date of migrated content. Leave blank in new articles.
Last Verified:
The date when the article was last approved by the stakeholder/content owner. We update this date manually.
Default fields
Number:
ServiceNow generates numbers for articles automatically.
Version:
ServiceNow generates version numbers for articles automatically.
Created:
The date when the article was created in ServiceNow; not the same as the custom "Birth Date" field, which refers to a creation date in the old system.
Helpful count:
Not currently used.
Published:
The date when the article was published.
Knowledge base:
Make sure this field shows "Indiana University Knowledge Base".
Category:
Not currently used; leave blank for now.
Ownership group:
Not currently used; leave blank for now.
Updated by:
The person who last updated the article, including any field.
Revised By:
The person who last checked out the article and published.
Meta:
A place to enter keywords to improve the article's searchability. For more, see
Boost articles in Knowledge Base portal search results using meta tags
.
Meta Description:
This field is what Google and other search engines crawl; the text in this field should appear in Google search results. To edit this field, deselect
Custom Meta Description
if it's selected, add your text, select the custom checkbox again, and save your changes to the article.
Scheduled publish date:
This is where we can select a date and time to publish an article in the future. There can only be one scheduled version of an article at a time, and we cannot publish other changes to the article in the meantime; thus, we'd use this sparingly and only when something will go live in the very near future.
Valid to:
The date when the article will no longer be valid and will be unavailable to users. To prevent this from happening, all KB articles are automatically created with a "valid to" date of 2100-01-01. Avoid changing this field.
Can Read/Cannot Read:
These fields determine which groups can and can't view articles. If an article is to be public, leave the "Can Read" field blank. If it's to be internal, use the "Can Read" drop-down to choose the audience(s)s in the form km-aud-kbstaff, for example. Currently we don't use the "Cannot Read" field.

and

title: Reasons your network connection may have been blocked
content:
Individual computers (not you as the user) may be prevented from accessing the Indiana University network for a variety of reasons:
Viruses:
Certain viruses reside on the computers they infect and use those computers to attack other users' computers over the network. The user of the infected machine will usually not be aware of the attacks leaving the computer. In these cases, the computer is blocked to protect other computers on the IU network and on the internet.
For more about viruses and protecting your computer, see:
About viruses, worms, and Trojan horses
Tips for staying safe online
Why you should reformat your hard drive and reinstall Windows after your computer is infected with a virus
Bots:
Often put in place on the blocked computer by a virus, Internet Relay Chat (
IRC
) bots are scripts or independent programs that perform special functions on IRC. Bots can be used to launch denial of service attacks against other computers, to log and transmit keystrokes (including passwords and credit card numbers), and to facilitate transmission of copyrighted material. In these cases, the infected computer is blocked both to protect other computers on the network, and to prevent the loss of users' sensitive personal information.
Unauthorized device or service on network:
The blocked computer is connected to the IU network through a router or other network-extending device, or is running as a server without authorization and/or of a possibly dangerous type on the IU network. In these cases, the computer or unauthorized device can be used as a less-secure point of entry for threats to the IU network, or in some cases can cause direct disruption to the operation of other computers on the network.
For more about routers and servers, see:
About rogue DHCP servers on the IU network
About wireless access points in IU campus housing, classrooms, or offices
Illegal file sharing:
The computer has been observed running file sharing services online that degrade network services on the IU network, or, more often, IU has received a complaint from the copyright holder or his or her appointed agent. In these cases, according to law, IU must take certain actions to remove the material from the IU network.
For more about file sharing and protecting yourself, see:
About the Digital Millennium Copyright Act
Peer-to-peer (P2P) file sharing and copyright safety
Spamming:
Multiple reports indicate that the computer is sending unsolicited email, or spam. The cause of spam is most often a compromised computer. An attacker sends spam from a compromised computer (rather than from his or her own computer) in the hopes that the spam will more easily get through mail filters.
FTP servers on non-standard ports:
File Transfer Protocol (FTP) servers are file depositories. Users can connect to an FTP client and download or upload files. FTP servers are typically on TCP port 21; when an FTP server is found on a non-standard port, it usually means that an attacker set it up and is trying to hide it. An attacker may use this server to store his own files (often unauthorized copyrighted material) or to copy off files that were present on the machine.
For more about FTP, including how to use it safely, see
Use FTP to transfer files
.
SSH brute-forcing:
The computer has been observed attempting to make a large number of SSH connections. This activity typically means that someone is trying to guess account names and passwords. It also usually means that the computer is compromised, and that this activity is being performed by an attacker.
Check your email for a block message from the University Information Security Office (UISO).

title: Use knowledge blocks as a KB contributor
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Common use cases for blocks
Limitations of blocks
Components of a knowledge block
View a knowledge block
Edit an existing knowledge block
Add a knowledge block to an article
Create a knowledge block
Overview
Note:
This information is intended for contributors to the Knowledge Base who are part of the Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) initiative.
In ServiceNow Knowledge, a knowledge block is a smaller unit of content intended to appear within one or more Knowledge Base articles.  Knowledge blocks serve two purposes:
Reuse:
When the same content should appear in multiple articles, a knowledge block allows you to update it in one place and have the change automatically appear everywhere the block is used.  In IU's legacy system, this type of block was called a "boiler" (short for "boilerplate").  Reusing (in other words, single-sourcing) content can help keep information consistent; when the same information lives in multiple places, it tends to get out of sync as changes occur.
Audience restrictions:
A knowledge block can have Can Read criteria, which display the content to only those who belong to the relevant group and are logged into the Knowledge Base.  You can thus include more restricted information (for example, a note about how support staff should address issues related to what the article describes) within a public or less restricted article.
For Phase 1 of the KCS initiative, contact the Knowledge Management team if you need an internal block, or if you believe the Can Read criteria of an existing block should be changed.
A block can serve both purposes (that is, internal as well as public blocks can appear in multiple articles).
Common use cases for blocks
Blocks are useful when you can reasonably expect a piece of information to apply equally to a set of articles for its useful lifespan.  For example:
To alert users to an upcoming retirement of or significant change to a service
To provide support information for a given service or unit
To warn users of about something they should or should not do, whether because of policy or technical risk
To present a common set of instructions that applies to multiple tasks or contexts
However, in some cases, even if you need the same wording in more than one article, it may be more trouble than it's worth to use a block.  You should be reasonably confident that if the information changes in the future, the change will apply to every article in which the block is used, so be cautious about using the same block to apply to different services or systems.  Also, too much repetition can clutter articles and dilute search results.  In some cases, it may be better to link to an existing article rather than including reused information in more than one place.
When in doubt about whether using a block makes sense, consult the Knowledge Management team.
Limitations of blocks
Note the following restrictions:
Blocks cannot be renamed.
Knowledge blocks display on a block level only and can't be used inline. For example, a knowledge block that consists of a name or a single word can't be used in a sentence. By default, blocks have paragraph tags around them that can't be modified.
Blocks can't be nested.  This also means that a block created to restrict content to a smaller group can't contain a block of reused content, and vice versa.
Components of a knowledge block
A knowledge block consists of the following:
Metadata:
Blocks have some of the same metadata as articles, but they do not have the stakeholder field or "Last verified:" field. The most relevant metadata fields are:
Number:
Block numbers begin with "KBB" rather than "KB", for example: KBB0014392.
Version:
Version numbers work the same for blocks and articles.
Can Read:
Blocks without "Can Read" criteria will be visible to anyone who can see the articles in which they appear. If a block should not be visible to the public, be sure to set "Can Read" criteria on the block itself, so that it isn't accidentally placed in a public article.
Workflow:
Blocks can have the same workflow values as articles. When a block is no longer used in any live articles, the KM team recommends retiring it to reduce clutter, unless it's likely to be used again in the future.  Contact the KM team for help with this process.
Short description:
The title for the block will not appear in the articles in which the block is used, which means that end users of the KB will never see it. Think of it as a code to help you and other people who work on the KB find the content and know what it's about. The Knowledge Management team has historically used a series of words separated by hyphens for block names. For example:
kcs-contributor-documentation
is the name of the block that appears in the overview section of this article. Notice that it's fine to use shorthand like acronyms in block titles.
ems-linux-support
is the name of KBB0014391, which contains a link to Endpoint Management Services' request form for Linux users.
honorlock-tech-reqs
is the name of KBB0014370, which contains a list of technical requirements for Honorlock.
For boilers and internal notes migrated from the legacy Knowledge Management System (KMS), you'll see short descriptions that begin with "PUB" (for public reused boilers), "INT" (for internal reused boilers), and "WHO" (for internal notes that were previously maintained directly in one document).  In the case of "WHO" blocks, which didn't have boiler names in the KMS, the migration process automatically generated short descriptions based on the (legacy) document ID. Since Can Read criteria is visible in a block when you view it, the Knowledge Management team does not intend to maintain the "PUB", "INT", and "WHO" naming convention going forward.
Body:
The body of a block can contain any combination of elements that can stand alone within the body of an article, such as paragraphs, lists, or tables.
Blocks can also consist of, or contain, panels such as those headed by "Note:" or "Important:". Since you need to work in the markup of an article to create a panel, for KCS Phase 1, the KM team will take care of formatting panels; just include the content in some way that makes your intention clear.
For internal sections, the KM team has historically used the following style in order to alert those who can see the information that it is internal:
Audience:
The body of the internal content goes here. Note that the designations we use for the audience are not the technical names of the "Can Read" criteria, but a human-friendly description such as
IU community:
or
UITS staff and local support:
, etc.
Since you need to work in the markup of an article to edit a panel, the KM team may be evaluating alternatives to simplify our style in the future. For now, ask the KM team for help with editing or creating an internal block.
View a knowledge block
When you're editing an article in ServiceNow, you won't see the content of knowledge blocks within the article.  Instead, you'll see a rectangle with the number and short description (name) of the block, like this:
You can view the content of this block in any of the following ways:
View the block in the context of the article:
View the entire article in the KB portal using the permalink for the article number; the KM team recommends having the portal view of an article you're editing open in another tab or window so that you can see the content of blocks in context.
Below the editing window, under "Related Links", select
View Article
.  This takes you out of editing mode to the agent view of the article.  Note that the formatting of some content will be different from the way it will appear in the live KB.  To resume editing from this view, at the top of the page, choose
Edit
.
View the block alone:
View the content of the block itself in the KB portal using a URL of the same format as an article permalink.  For example, if you replace the article number
KB
XXXXXXX
in the permalink of any KB page with
KBB0014405
, you can see the sn-next-experience block alone at
https://servicenow.iu.edu/kb?id=kb_article_view&sysparm_article=KBB0014405
.  The KM team recommends previewing knowledge blocks in the portal when you're editing them, just as you do for articles.  Note, however, that you can't find knowledge blocks by searching in the KB portal; you can only get to one by the direct URL.
Tip:
In Chrome and Firefox, you can set up a shortcut to go directly to any block or article by its number.  For instructions, see
Create browser shortcuts to view Knowledge Base content by number
.
View the block in the editing view in ServiceNow.  From the
All
menu in ServiceNow, type
block
, and then, under "Knowledge Blocks", select
Published
to see a list of all published blocks.  (If you don't see the
All
menu, turn on the Next Experience, as described in the knowledge block under discussion.)  You can then filter by any field visible on the screen.  When you find the block, select its number to view it.
Edit an existing knowledge block
If the content you want to edit is within a knowledge block, the block needs to be checked out and edited separately.
Note:
If a block is used in more than one article, it's important to determine whether the changes will make sense and be accurate in all the contexts where the block is used before proceeding. If you're reasonably confident that your changes will apply everywhere (for example, the information in the block is specific to a service you own, it's true in all contexts without exception, etc.), go ahead and submit the changes according to the process described below. If you're not sure whether the changes will make any other articles inaccurate, contact the KM team for help with analyzing the impact of the change.
Tip:
Take care if you're adding a link to a KB article within a block; if the block appears in that article, you'll create a circular reference that goes nowhere.  Watch out also for adding a block to an article that it links to.
For KCS Phase 1, although you may submit edits to blocks with a relatively limited impact (as indicated above), feel free to ask the KM team for help with edits to blocks.
View the block using one of the methods listed above under "View the block alone".
If you're starting from the KB portal, from the
Actions
menu, select
Edit Article
.
At the top of the editing view of the block, choose
Checkout
.
Edit the block just as you would edit an article.
When you're done, choose
Publish
to route it to the Knowledge Management team for action.  The revised language will appear in all the articles containing the block when the KM team publishes it.  If it's important that the changes to the block and other changes to your article go live at the same time, contact the KM to specify that.
Add a knowledge block to an article
To add an existing knowledge block to an article:
While editing an article in the agent view of ServiceNow, make sure your cursor is positioned where you want to add a knowledge block. Either at the top of the editing window or just below the editing pane, select
Add Blocks
.
Important:
Do
not
select the
Insert
or
Insert and Stay
button.  Doing so will create a copy of the article.
In the "Add Blocks" sidebar, search for the knowledge block, or enter the block's ID number if you have it, and then select
Insert
.
If the basic search doesn't work, select
Advanced search
. Select the checkbox for the block you want and then, at the top, select
Insert to article
.
Important:
If you open a knowledge block to view it,
do not try to insert it into the article from that window
. When you're viewing a block, the
Insert
and
Insert and Stay
buttons above and below the body are the same as those above and below an article in editing view, meaning that they create a
copy
of the block instead of inserting it into an article.
Create a knowledge block
For KCS Phase 1, the KM team recommends that contributors not create new knowledge blocks.  This guidance may change in future phases; contact the KM team if you have questions or concerns.

title: Data Cookbook definition workflow cheat sheet
content:
Table of contents
About workflows
IU standard definition approval
Underlying assumptions
Stages of standard definition approval
Rejected definitions
About workflows
Workflow definition
In Data Cookbook, a workflow is a predefined process for approving an object or a request for information. Data Cookbook includes a customizable workflow engine. Custom workflows specific to Indiana University were created and tested for adoption by the IU Data Cookbook community during the first quarter of 2017.
Workflow types
Data Cookbook includes three basic workflow types: definition approval, specification approval, and information request resolution. At IU, Data Cookbook only uses workflow for definitions and specifications.
Workflow stages and steps
Stages
Each workflow has several stages that represent a point in the process that requires specified action from one or more users or groups of users.
Happy path
In Data Cookbook, "happy path" is a term that describes the most common approval process. In project management terminology, this would be the critical path. Steps with green-colored transition action buttons are the happy path for the stage.
Steps
In a stage, steps represent available tasks and/or groups of actions. Steps can be required or optional and may be assigned to specific users or user groups based on the workflow object's attributes.
Transition actions
Transition actions are associated with steps within stages and represent what a user does to move an object from one stage to another. These actions appear as buttons on the definition or specification. The transition actions available to a user will depend on both the user's role and the workflow stage that contains the object.
In the following example, two transition actions are available; you can send the definition to QA or reject it:
Conditions
Conditions function as "where" clauses for workflows. Conditions let you specify appropriate workflows or steps based on criteria such as functional area, data system, or classification code.
Note:
IU Data Cookbook currently doesn't use conditional criteria. For ease of understanding and maintenance, the current implementation defines a flexible standard approach to workflow. Direct experience and business requirements will dictate future revisions to workflows or the creation of conditional workflows.
Workflow permissions
Workflow stages, steps, and transition actions are governed by permissions handled by interactions between user groups, assignment mappings, and named roles.
User groups
User groups are the primary means for granting permissions within Data Cookbook, especially in the absence of workflow integration. You can grant user groups permissions for definitions, specifications, and technical information based on functional area. For specifications and definitions, these permissions are manager, editor, and viewer. For technical information, these permissions are editor, view, and hidden. Any user assigned to the group will have the permissions associated with the group.
Note:
Workflow stages and steps can override user group permissions both positively and negatively. For example, during the quality assurance stages of workflows, only staff associated with QA functions are allowed to make modifications. Conversely, data stewards or data managers may sometimes delegate authority to user groups to edit or approve definitions.
User groups of moderators and editors are associated with definitions; user groups of specification managers and specification developers are associated with specifications.
Assignment mappings
Assignment mappings are a way to create "super groups" of users for assigning steps in a workflow. They allow workflow standardization and let you create correlations between attributes such as functional areas, data systems, or specification types so that you can assign user groups to specific steps in workflow stages.
As mentioned in the
Conditions
section, the current implementation of Data Cookbook defines a standardized workflow that uses assignment mappings based on functional area. Direct experience and business requirements will dictate future revisions to this approach.
Named roles
Named roles allow you to define a "pool" of users who may be added to a workflow step when the step is initiated. These users are assigned by another defined "pool" of users who receive notification to make an assignment. If you are tasked with managing an assignment, named roles let you assign an individual user to a step in a workflow stage.
Note:
At this time, named roles can't be mapped to functional areas and are not being used. Instead, IU Data Cookbook uses assignment mappings and user groups to associate specification managers and developers to workflow stages and steps in the appropriate functional areas.
IU standard definition approval
Underlying assumptions
The stages of the IU standard definition approval workflow were created using the following assumptions:
The fewer the variations that exist, the more understandable and maintainable the workflows will be.
Data managers and data stewards should be involved as appropriate for reviewing, editing, and applying classification codes.
Data managers should not be solely responsible for the creation of all definitions. Initial creation should take place as gaps are identified during the creation of specifications/reports by developers and functional experts.
Quality assurance is necessary for good governance to ensure a solid body of consistent standardized information; however, QA should not adversely affect the workflow.
All stages will have explicit steps that allow designated workflow administrative users to intervene and "unstick" the workflow as needed. This step will not be included in subsequent documentation.
Stages of standard definition approval
At IU, approval of a standard definition proceeds through the following stages; see
below
for a visual representation of these stages:
Create/Revise
QA Initial Review
DM Review/Edit
DM Apply Classification (optional)
QA Final Review
Approved
1. Create/Revise
During this stage, definitions are created and revised. This stage is made up of two primary steps, "Create/Revise Definition" and "Edit Draft as a Moderator".
a. Create/Revise Definition
Access to the "Create/Revise Definition" step is available to definition editors associated with each functional area. These editors can create definitions and submit them for QA initial review, or they can reject definitions. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): Create/Revise Definition", select
QA Initial Review
or
Reject
:
b. Edit Draft as Moderator
Access to the "Edit Draft as a Moderator" step is available to definition moderators; "moderator" is Data Cookbook's term for data managers or their delegates. Moderators fulfill an oversight role with regard to definition content, and in many cases also with regard to definition classification. Moderators have the ability not only to create definitions but also to submit them to multiple stages. In this stage, moderators can choose to approve definitions and submit them for final QA, if they believe the definitions are both accurate and complete. To take a transition action on the item, under "Step(s): Edit Draft as a Moderator", select
QA Initial Review
,
Approve/QA
,
Reject
, or
Request Classification
:
2. QA Initial Review
During the QA initial review stage, definitions are checked for compliance with naming conventions and adherence to IU's Data Cookbook standards. Only administrators are able to edit a definition in the QA initial review stage, to ensure that QA is not being done on a moving target. In general, standards and formatting are overseen by the QA role, while the actual definition content and classification of the data are overseen by the moderator or data manager role. The EBI team within UITS is the service owner for Data Cookbook, and staff from the EBI team are currently responsible for QA. A definition that passes QA is submitted for DM review; if it does not pass QA, it will be returned to the previous stage for further revision.
The QA initial review stage is made up of the primary "QA Initial Review" step and an optional "QA Return for Revision" step.
a. QA Initial Review
QA occurs during the "QA Initial Review" step. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): QA Initial Review", select
DM Review
or
Return for Revision
:
3. DM Review/Edit
In the DM review/edit stage, the moderator reviews, edits, or rewrites the definition. This stage is made up of two steps, the primary "DM Review/Edit" step and the optional "Revise Definition" step.
a. DM Review/Edit
In the "DM Review/Edit" step, the moderators, who are the designated primary subject matter experts for the corresponding functional area, review the content of the definition. Moderators can choose to approve, modify, or rewrite the definition; return the definition to the initial stage for revision; or request that the classification be assigned. This step is at the heart of the data governance process. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): DM Review/Edit", select
Approve/QA
,
Reject
,
Request Classification
, or
Return for Revision
:
Revise Definition:
The optional "Revise Definition" step allows the initial definition creator or editor group to retrieve a definition from data manager review for further editing or revision. The creator or editor can retrieve the definition without intervention on the part of either the moderator or administrators. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): Revise Definition", select
Reject
or
Return for Revision
:
4. DM Apply Classification (optional)
Apply classification is an optional stage where you can apply the security classification to the definition. In most cases, it is expected that the group responsible for the DM review/edit stage will supply the classification, but there are functional areas in which this will not be the case (for example, in student records, the Data Steward has delegated responsibility for the DM review/edit stage to UIRR, but the Student Data Management & Access group supplies the classification); for that reason, this step is optional. The original "Moderators by Functional Area" assignment mapping is used for the DM review/edit stage, while a new "Data Managers by Functional Area" assignment mapping is used for the apply classification stage.
The apply classification stage is made up of the primary "Apply Classification" step, and the optional "Request DM Revision" step.
a. Apply Classification
During the "Apply Classification" step, if there is a separation of duties for managing definition content and managing security, the classification is supplied. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): DM Apply Classification", select
Approve/QA
,
Reject
,
Return for DM Revision
, or
Return for Revision
:
Request DM Revision:
In the "Request DM Revision" step, the data manager associated with the previous stage can retrieve a definition from the current stage for further editing. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): Request DM Revision", select
Reject
,
Return for DM Revision
, or
Return for Revision
:
5. QA Final Review
During the QA final review stage, the definition gets a final check for completeness and adherence to IU's Data Cookbook standards. Only administrators are able to edit a definition in the QA final review stage, to ensure that QA is not being done on a moving target. The EBI team within UITS is the service owner for Data Cookbook, and staff from the EBI team are currently responsible for QA. A definition that passes final QA is approved and becomes the current official version.
The QA final review stage is made up of the primary "QA Final Approval" step and an optional "Request DM Revision" step.
a. QA Final Approval
Final QA occurs during the QA final approval step. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): QA Final Approval", select
QA Final Approval
,
Return for DM Revision
, or
Return for Revision
:
Request DM Revision:
In the "Request DM Revision" step, the data manager associated with the DM review/edit stage can retrieve a definition from the current stage for further editing. To take a transition action on the definition, under "Step(s): Request DM Revision", select
Reject
,

title: Data Cookbook specification workflow cheat sheet
content:
Table of contents
About workflows
IU standard specification approval
Underlying assumptions
Stages of standard specification approval
Canceled specifications
About workflows
Workflow definition
In Data Cookbook, a workflow is a predefined process for approving an object or a request for information. Data Cookbook includes a customizable workflow engine. Custom workflows specific to Indiana University were created and tested for adoption by the IU Data Cookbook community during the first quarter of 2017.
Workflow types
Data Cookbook includes three basic workflow types: definition approval, specification approval, and information request resolution. At IU, Data Cookbook only uses workflow for definitions and specifications.
Workflow stages and steps
Stages
Each workflow has several stages that represent a point in the process that requires specified action from one or more users or groups of users.
Happy path
In Data Cookbook, "happy path" is a term that describes the most common approval process. In project management terminology, this would be the critical path. Steps with green-colored transition action buttons are the happy path for the stage.
Steps
In a stage, steps represent available tasks and/or groups of actions. Steps can be required or optional and may be assigned to specific users or user groups based on the workflow object's attributes.
Transition actions
Transition actions are associated with steps within stages and represent what a user does to move an object from one stage to another. These actions appear as buttons on the definition or specification. The transition actions available to a user will depend on both the user's role and the workflow stage that contains the object.
In the following example, two transition actions are available; you can send the definition to QA or reject it:
Conditions
Conditions function as "where" clauses for workflows. Conditions let you specify appropriate workflows or steps based on criteria such as functional area, data system, or classification code.
Note:
IU Data Cookbook currently doesn't use conditional criteria. For ease of understanding and maintenance, the current implementation defines a flexible standard approach to workflow. Direct experience and business requirements will dictate future revisions to workflows or the creation of conditional workflows.
Workflow permissions
Workflow stages, steps, and transition actions are governed by permissions handled by interactions between user groups, assignment mappings, and named roles.
User groups
User groups are the primary means for granting permissions within Data Cookbook, especially in the absence of workflow integration. You can grant user groups permissions for definitions, specifications, and technical information based on functional area. For specifications and definitions, these permissions are manager, editor, and viewer. For technical information, these permissions are editor, view, and hidden. Any user assigned to the group will have the permissions associated with the group.
Note:
Workflow stages and steps can override user group permissions both positively and negatively. For example, during the quality assurance stages of workflows, only staff associated with QA functions are allowed to make modifications. Conversely, data stewards or data managers may sometimes delegate authority to user groups to edit or approve definitions.
User groups of moderators and editors are associated with definitions; user groups of specification managers and specification developers are associated with specifications.
Assignment mappings
Assignment mappings are a way to create "super groups" of users for assigning steps in a workflow. They allow workflow standardization and let you create correlations between attributes such as functional areas, data systems, or specification types so that you can assign user groups to specific steps in workflow stages.
As mentioned in the
Conditions
section, the current implementation of Data Cookbook defines a standardized workflow that uses assignment mappings based on functional area. Direct experience and business requirements will dictate future revisions to this approach.
Named roles
Named roles allow you to define a "pool" of users who may be added to a workflow step when the step is initiated. These users are assigned by another defined "pool" of users who receive notification to make an assignment. If you are tasked with managing an assignment, named roles let you assign an individual user to a step in a workflow stage.
Note:
At this time, named roles can't be mapped to functional areas and are not being used. Instead, IU Data Cookbook uses assignment mappings and user groups to associate specification managers and developers to workflow stages and steps in the appropriate functional areas.
IU standard specification approval
Underlying assumptions
The stages of the IU standard specification approval workflow were created using the following assumptions:
The fewer the variations that exist, the more understandable and maintainable the workflows will be.
Data managers and data stewards are not necessarily directly involved in the workflow unless they have requested or are overseeing the specification under development.
Product owners, functional managers, and business analysts will be responsible for initial drafts and/or approval as appropriate.
Quality assurance is necessary for good governance to ensure a solid body of consistent standardized information; however, QA should not adversely affect the workflow.
All stages will have explicit steps that allow designated workflow administrative users to intervene and "unstick" the workflow as needed. This step will not be included in subsequent documentation.
Data stewards grant approval of security classification at the specification level outside Data Cookbook via existing systems and channels (for example, ACM).
Stages of standard specification approval
At IU, approval of a standard specification proceeds through the following stages; see
below
for a visual representation of these stages:
Initial Draft
Development
QA Initial Review
Approval Requested
QA Final Review
Approved
Note:
To see the transition action buttons for a particular specification, to the far right and near the top of the specification, select the
Workflow
tab:
1. Initial Draft
Specifications are created and revised during the initial draft stage. In this stage, you'll create a request for a report and flesh out its business requirements. This stage's primary step is draft specification.
a. Draft Specification
Access to the "Draft Specification" step is available to members of the "Spec Drafters by Functional Area" assignment mapping. By default, this step is mapped to the moderator user groups; note, however, that it is not assumed that this step is the responsibility of the moderator or data manager. In areas where EBI has ongoing or anticipated future development, the EBI business analysts and the EBI AM360 product owner are also mapped to this step. Additionally, for the financial and budget areas, the EBI KPI product owner is mapped to this step. Mapping of user groups to this step will be updated appropriately based on adoption and need. As user groups for specification managers by functional area are incrementally built, they will also be mapped to this step.
After you've completed the initial draft stage, move the report to the development stage for potential assignment to a specific person for development. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Draft Specification", select
Submit
or
Cancel
:
2. Development
Once you've made your request and added the initial requirements to the specification, the development stage begins. The development stage is made up of the primary "Initial Development" step, as well as two optional steps, "Edit Specification - Manager" and "Edit Specification - Drafter".
a. Initial Development
Access to the "Initial Development" step is available to members of the "Specification Developers by Functional Area" assignment mapping. Once the specification is under development, any developer in this group can edit the specification to reflect the iterative development and refinement of requirements. When complete, select
Request QA
to submit the specification for QA:
During the development stage, the manager and the specification drafter have the option to edit the specification:
Edit Specification - Manager:
Access to the "Edit Specification - Manager" step is available to members of the "Specification Managers by Functional Area" assignment mapping. The specification manager can edit and take various transition actions on the specification in this step. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Edit Specification - Manager", select
Request QA
,
Back to drafting
,
Cancel
, or
QA Final Review
:
Edit Specification - Drafter:
Access to the "Edit Specification - Drafter" step is available to members of the "Specification Drafters by Functional Area" assignment mapping. The user group that drafted the specification can edit and take various transition actions on the specification in this step. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Edit Specification - Drafter", select
Request QA
,
Back to drafting
, or
Cancel
:
3. QA Initial Review
During the QA initial review stage, specifications are checked for compliance with naming conventions and adherence to IU's Data Cookbook standards. Only administrators are able to edit a specification in the QA initial review stage, to ensure that QA is not being done on a moving target. In general, standards and formatting are overseen by the QA role, while the actual specification content is overseen by the product owner or specification manager role. The EBI team within UITS is the service owner for Data Cookbook, and staff from the EBI team are currently responsible for QA. A specification that passes QA is submitted for approval; if it does not pass QA, it will be returned to the previous stage for further revision.
The QA initial review stage is made up of the primary "QA Initial Review" step, with an optional "QA Return for Revision" step.
a. QA Initial Review
QA occurs during the "QA Initial Review" step. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Request Approval", select
Request Approval
or
Return for Revision
:
QA Return for Revision:
The "QA Return for Revision" step is an optional step allowing members of the "Specification Managers by Functional Area" assignment mapping to intervene and return the specification for further development or refinement. To take this transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): QA Return for Revision", select
Return for Revision
:
4. Approval Requested
During the approval requested stage, members of the "Specification Manager by Functional Area" assignment mapping review the specification and then either approve it or return it (and, by extension, return the associated report/object) to development. Note that this step represents approval of the specification itself, not data manager security approval for the report/object, which is handled via regular processes.
The approval requested stage is made up of the primary "Approve Specification" step (associated with the specification manager), and the optional "AC Return for Revision", "Spec Drafter Delegation" and "Cancel" steps. Only the original report requester has the option to cancel at this point.
a. Approve Specification Step
In the "Approve Specification" step, the specification manager reviews work to date on the specification and the associated report/object, and then either approves it or sends it back to development for modifications. For DSI-related specifications, this approval is associated with the product owner. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Approve Specification", select
Approve
,
Cancel
, or
Return for Revision
:
AC Return for Revision:
In the "AC Return for Revision" step, agile coaches can return the specification to the development stage, allowing them to correct issues they or the product owner have identified without the PO having to take action. To take this transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): AC Return for Revision", select
Return for Revision
.
Spec Drafter Delegation:
In the "Spec Drafter Delegation" step, the user group associated with drafting specifications for the associated functional area can choose to return the specification for revision or to cancel it. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Spec Drafter Delegation", select
Cancel
or
Return for Revision
:
5. QA Final Review
During the QA final review stage, the specification gets a final check for compliance with naming conventions, adherence to IU's Data Cookbook standards, and completeness. Only administrators are able to edit a specification in the QA final review stage, to ensure that QA is not being done on a moving target. In general, standards and formatting are overseen by the QA role, while the actual specification content is overseen by the product owner or specification manager role. The EBI team within UITS is the service owner for Data Cookbook, and staff from the EBI team are currently responsible for QA. A specification that passes final QA is approved and becomes the current official version.
The QA final review stage is made up of the primary "QA Final Approval" step, with optional "Return to Spec Manager" and "QA Return for Revision" steps.
a. QA Final Approval
Final QA occurs during the QA final approval step. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): QA Final Approval", select
QA Final Approval
,
Return for Revision
, or
Return to Approval
:
Return to Spec Manager:
In the "Return to Spec Manager" step, the product owner can return the specification to the previous stage, in order to correct any identified issues or perform any other actions available in the "Approve Specification" step. Note that the user in this step may be a member of both the specification managers and the specification drafters groups; this will not be uncommon. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Return to Spec Manager, Return for Revision", select
Return for Revision
or
Return to Approval
:
Return for Revision:
In the "Return for Revision" step, the user group associated with managing specifications for the associated functional area can choose to return the specification for revision or, where there is an assigned product owner, to act on behalf of the PO. To take a transition action on the specification, under "Step(s): Return for Revision", select
Return for Revision
or
Return to Approval
:
6. Approved
The approved stage is the final stage of the specification workflow. A specification that reaches this point has received approval for both content and format, and is the current official version for the IU Data Cookbook community. Any subsequent revision to an approved specification requires a new version of the specification to be created, and those new versions must go through the above workflow and be approved in their turn.
Canceled specifications
At various stages and steps in the workflow, appropriate users can choose to cancel a specification for any reason (for example, duplication of specifications, discovery that the specification is not required).

Overview
Important:
This information is intended for web developers, providing a holistic process for performing an initial pass of evaluating your website for accessibility. This is not a substitute for performing a complete
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1
AA site evaluation, but following this full process will capture most of the WCAG 2.1 AA Guidelines more efficiently.
It is impossible to meet Indiana University's digital accessibility standard and related accessibility policies using only automated tools.
Automated tools can be useful for identifying certain types of web accessibility issues. There are many tools you can use, each with different strengths and weaknesses. Be aware that automated tools can find only about 30% of accessibility problems; the rest must be located using manual methods.
Automated tools can detect programmatic accessibility issues based on the code. For this reason, the tools will produce more accurate results if the code is valid. If you have not already validated your code, running the
HTML Nu
checker before using automated accessibility tools will improve the quality of the results.
There are many automated tools available for use.
Recommended tools
aXe
aXe
is an accessibility rules library from
Deque
that is also available as a browser extension in Chrome or Firefox. The aXe library will only flag as errors the things that can be reliably programmatically checked. aXe strives to report zero false positives. The aXe extension is run on each web page individually, and exists in the browser's Developer tools.
Add aXe to Chrome
Add aXe to Firefox
Add aXe to Edge
aXe is a very useful tool for developers.
Accessibility Insights for Web
Accessibility Insights for Web
from Microsoft is available as a browser extension in Chrome or Microsoft Edge. Powered by Deque Systems' aXe library, Accessibility Insights for Web offers a quick FastPass check to get you started and a full Assessment that includes step-by-step instructions for manually performing tests. Accessibility Insights for Web is run on each web page individually.
Add Accessibility Insights for Web in Chrome
Add Accessibility Insights for Web in Microsoft Edge
A Windows application version,
Accessibility Insights for Windows
, is available to test Windows applications.
Accessibility Insights is useful for developers.
WAVE
WAVE
, from
WebAIM
, is available as either a browser extension or as a web service, which requires web pages to be public, rather than behind authentication. WAVE will flag errors which can be programmatically checked, and will also flag issues for further manual review. WAVE is run on each web page individually.
Add WAVE in Chrome
Add WAVE in Firefox
WAVE web service
WAVE assesses the whole page after it has been rendered in the browser, which means that it will look at objects that are visually on the screen and objects that are hidden.
WAVE is a good tool for checking color contrast and headings automatically. Because WAVE checks the hidden content, some headings that are normally hidden may be shown.
WAVE is easy for anyone to use.
For tips on using this tool, see
WAVE Help
.
ARC Toolkit
ARC Toolkit
, available as a browser extension in Chrome, will flag errors that can be programmatically checked, and will also flag potential errors for further manual review. ARC Toolkit is run on each web page individually and is accessed in the Chrome Developer tools.
Add ARC Toolkit in Chrome
ARC Toolkit is useful for developers.
ARC Toolkit also includes easy tests for focus order and new WCAG 2.1 success criteria Reflow and Text spacing as well as buttons to validate the code through the W3C Nu HTML validator.
AInspector
AInspector is a Firefox browser extension developed by the
University of Illinois Division of Disability Resources & Educational Services
. AInspector is run on each web page individually.
Add AInspector in Firefox
AInspector is most useful for developers. It will go deeper into explaining the issues and label a lot more manual checks than any other tool.
Helpful user guides are available in the
AInspector Sidebar documentation
.
Siteimprove
Siteimprove
is a cloud-based web governance tool enabling IU's web professionals to continuously and efficiently improve their unit's web presence. Siteimprove will scan, analyze, and suggest ways to grow engagement; boost search engine rankings; and improve the accessibility, performance, and usability of your website.
IU units can learn more at
About the Siteimprove service at IU
.
Bookmarklets
Many bookmarklets are available that will highlight roles, states, and properties of various elements on a web page. Bookmarklets are JavaScript programs stored as bookmarks in your browser. They are easy to use: select the bookmark and the JavaScript program will run on the current page.
To install a bookmarklet, open one of the bookmarklet resource links below. Choose the bookmarklet you want to install. Drag and drop the bookmarklet to your bookmarks bar.
In some browsers, you may need to manually add the bookmarklet. Copy the link address of the bookmarklet. Open the bookmark manager in your browser. Add a new bookmark. Enter a name for the bookmark and paste the link address as the URL.
The
Javascript Bookmarklets for Accessibility Testing
from Paul J. Adam are easy to use and highlight many important features of a web page.
Disability Resources and Educational Services (DRES) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and Pixo have also created easy to use,
open source accessibility bookmarklets
.
A11y audit bookmarklets
includes several useful tools, such as Are Ya Hidden? and List images.
Bookmarklets are useful for developers and designers.
Types of content issues that automated tools can find
Links
Most tools will identify common link issues such as:
Links with no link text
Links with the same link text but different
href
attributes
Links with different link text but the same
href
attributes
Tools may or may not identify:
Anchors with missing
href
attributes
Links with the wrong
href
attribute
Links with invalid
href
attributes
Suspicious link text such as "click here", "here", "more", "more details", or "click the red button"
Links to PDFs and other file types
That links are uniquely styled to differentiate from page text
Headings
Tools usually identify the programmatic
heading structure
of a web page. Some tools, such as WAVE, will present the headings as an outline of the page. Tools will catch:
Skipped heading levels
Missing
h1
headings
Headings of the same level with the same text
Headings with no text content
Compare the HTML headings to the visual headings:
Visual headings should match HTML headings.
Things that appear to be headings should be HTML headings.
Things that are HTML headings should appear to be headings.
Headings should follow a hierarchical order, creating an outline for the page.
Headings should not skip heading levels.
The headings should describe the topic of the section.
Images
Tools will identify:
Images missing
alt
attributes
Images where the alt text is similar to nearby text
Instances where multiple images have the same alt text
A manual check is still necessary to verify that the alt text for each image is appropriate. For a more in-depth discussion of alternative text, see
Alternative text for images
.
Tables
Automated tools will find the most common table issues:
Data tables need accessible names. An accessible name may not be visible onscreen but is used by assistive technology to identify the table.
Data tables should have header rows and/or columns.
Layout tables should have the ARIA attribute
role="presentation"
.
Tables should not have empty rows, columns, or cells.
Landmarks
Tools are useful for identifying
landmarks
and checking that the landmarks follow landmark rules:
All content should be contained in a landmark, including skip-links.
Every web page should have at least
main
and
navigation
landmarks.
Each page should have only one
main
,
banner
, and
contentinfo
landmark.
banner
,
main
,
contentinfo
, and
complementary
landmarks must be top-level, not nested in other landmarks.
Landmarks of the same type, such as two
navigation
landmarks, must have unique names so they may be easily differentiated from each other.
ARIA
Automated tools will help identify common problems with
Accessible Rich Internet Applications (ARIA)
. Many tools will identify:
Incorrect ARIA roles
Incorrect ARIA labeling
Invalid ARIA properties
Invalid ARIA attributes
Invalid ARIA values
Forms
Automated tools excel at checking certain aspects of forms. They will identify if:
Form elements are correctly labeled
Form labels are unique
Radio buttons are grouped in fieldsets
Fieldsets have legends
ID attributes are unique
Some automated tools may also verify that the
accessible name
matches or starts with the visible label.
Beyond the programmatic checks that automated tools carry out, forms will always require additional manual checking with keyboard and screen readers, and to explore their error handling.
Page language
Automated tools will check if the human language used on the page (for example, English) has been set using the
lang
attribute on the
<html>
element. Automated tools are not good at finding language changes within a page. If the language used on the page changes, you will need to manually check that the
lang
attribute has been used correctly.
Language of Page: Understanding Success Criterion 3.1.1
Language of Parts: Understanding Success Criterion 3.1.2

title: Check zoom and magnification for web accessibility
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Font size
Zooming
