Log into the self-service portal; see
Access the Intelligent Infrastructure self-service portal
.
If prompted, select
Service Broker
,
Catalog
, and then
Request
within the "Create New VM" dialog box.
Fill out the required fields for the VM request. Any field marked with a red "*" is required. Select
Submit
when finished.
Notes:
Do not use hard returns on any fields on the request.
Use custom fields 1-5 if you wish to record any additional information with this virtual machine. These fields will populate custom attributes on the VM in vCenter.
The "Pool Utilization" field will populate once you select the pool this VM is to bill against. Current and maximum CPU usage, memory (in GB), and Disk (in GB) are displayed on the form for reference.
Important:
Application tier:
Within II, the virtual server system administrator has the ability to align system criticality with a tier rating. University Information Technology Services (UITS) services delivered with II leverages the tier to prioritize recovery operations in the event of a disaster recovery. All system administration teams are encouraged to utilize the tier settings to align with service criticality. It is understood this tier rating could change based upon the University calendar, and the tier rating can be modified at any time based upon University business requirements. Office of Vice President for Information Technology (OVPIT) division leadership manages the assignment of tier for UITS services.
Application tier [0-3] definitions:
Tier 0 is the highest level of services, to be deployed geographically independently and able to deliver services without operational impact. Examples of these services would be Active Directory, IU Login, and Domain Name Services (DNS). If all computing services experience an interruption of services, ensuring Tier 0 services are operational will be prioritized over other service tiers.
Tier 1 represents services that are critically important to the end user community to deliver business functions to operate university. Example services Human Resource applications, Student Systems applications, and Finance applications. Priority of recovery order of these services would follow Tier 0.
Tier 2 represents services whose primary role is to assist in the support and management of Tier 0 and Tier 1 services. Priority of recovery would follow Tier 0 and Tier 1.
Tier 3 is the default tier rating when creating a new server within II. It represents the lowest priority service for recovery operations.
You may view the current status of your requests in the
Consume
tab under "Deployments".
You can also search VM requests by using the search field, or by selecting the blue filter icon and using various filters.
Once the VM has been created, it will appear in the
Consume
tab under "Virtual Machines".
Use the search field toward the top to search for a VM.
To refresh the view, use the refresh icon in the upper right of the page.
If there are any errors, read and attempt to correct.
For questions or issues with your VM deployment,
contact the Storage and Virtualization team
.

Overview
UITS has created a fund to pay for UA-VPIT FTE (employees whose salaries are funded out of a 19-XXX-XX account number) to lifecycle their computers over a four-year term. E
ligible people may have one primary computer at a time, unless a documented business or instructional need requires otherwise.
This article describes the terms and conditions for the use of these funds.
Computer lifecycle
The lifecycle fund should be used primarily to purchase one of the following computers:
Dell Pro 14 Plus laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor, 16 GB memory, 512 GB SSD
Dell Pro 16 Plus laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor, 16 GB memory, 512 GB SSD
Dell Pro Plus Slim desktop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor, 16 GB memory, 512 GB SSD
Dell Pro 24 All-in-One desktop with an Intel Core Ultra 5 processor, 16 GB memory, 512 GB SSD
MacBook Air 15" laptop with a 10‑core CPU, 10‑core GPU Apple M4 chip, 16 GB memory, 512 GB SSD
Non-standard computer options and requirements
A selection of non-standard computers is available to those who have computing needs beyond those of standard office applications, PDFs, and web browsing. For those with a legitimate job function (software development, business analytics, video editing, etc.), UITS provides the following computer options:
Dell Pro 14 Plus laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 32 GB memory, 1 TB SSD
MacBook Air 15" laptop a 10‑core CPU, 10‑core GPU Apple M4 chip, 24 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD

If a non-standard computer is selected, an automated approval process will be triggered and will require the approval from the director (or director level equivalent) of the person for whom this computer is being requested. A bona fide business need for the device will be required.

The UITS Lifecycle Fund will pay for computer accessories at any time, except at the end of a computer's lifecycle. The following items are eligible for purchase with the UITS Lifecycle Fund. Shipping and return of computer equipment
The UITS Lifecycle Fund will not pay for the shipping of computers and related equipment to an employee working fully remote (from home). The department that employs a person working fully remote is responsible for the payment for shipping computers and computer equipment to the employee's home.
The UITS Lifecycle Fund does not pay for computers to be returned from fully remote employees when those employees separate from IU. Payment for shipping equipment back is the responsibility of the employee's department.

content:

Request Kubernetes access
Indiana University's Enterprise Kubernetes Environment is a multi-tenant system where multiple teams' workloads run on shared infrastructure. These workloads are logically separated through a Kubernetes construct called a
namespace
. To request a new namespace, submit the
Request Kubernetes Access
form. On the form, you'll need to:
Provide the name of the cluster on which you'd like your team created; see the list of
Available Kubernetes clusters
.
Provide the department, division (optional), and name of your team. These are combined to form a unique identifier for your namespace.
Provide an
ACM group
containing the users who will be granted access to the resources in your namespace. The ACM group must be
provisioned as an ADS security group
with membership requiring at least the completion of the
Acceptable Use Agreement
. If your workloads require additional compliance requirements (FERPA and/or HRMS Data Use), those requirements should be enforced on the group also.
Indicate whether you want a Kubernetes service account that can be used in your continuous delivery pipelines. See
Configure delivery pipelines
for information on how to use a deployer service account.
Indicate the total amount of
CPU and memory resources
required to run your applications. See
Configure container CPU and memory resources in a namespace with quotas enabled
for help choosing the appropriate values.
Provide a group email address for your team. This will be added to relevant mailing lists to keep you informed about updates and changes. This is necessary only when first requesting access.
Indicate the highest
data classification
your workloads will be processing or storing. If you are working with
Restricted data
or
Critical data
, review the guidelines in
Guidelines for Kubernetes workloads that interact with sensitive data
.
The information above will be used to create a Kubernetes namespace in the specified cluster(s), and set up access to the Harbor image registry and the LogInsight logging appliance where all application logs are aggregated.
Access to Harbor
Harbor
is a Docker image registry and
Helm chart
repository. Access to Harbor is required to use IU's Kubernetes environment, but you do not need to use Kubernetes to use the Harbor repository. When you request access to the Kubernetes environment, you will be set up with access to Harbor as well. To get access to Harbor without using Kubernetes, create a pull request in the
helm-rbac project
and set the property
registryOnly: true
in your values file; alternatively, email
docker@iu.edu
with the following details:
An identifier for your team (this must be globally unique; indicate what you want to use and UITS will inform you whether it is available)
The name of an
ACM group
containing the users who will be granted access to your artifacts in Harbor. The ACM group must be
provisioned as an ADS security group
with membership requiring at least the completion of the
Acceptable Use Agreement
.
Bot access
For pushing images, IU's Harbor image registry supports
robot accounts
that serve the same purpose. This allows you to create one or more accounts (that are not directly tied to ADS) for managing resources in Harbor. Harbor requires mutli-factor authentication, so setting up a robot account is equivalent to using a Harbor CLI secret for a group account.
For accessing Kubernetes, UITS recommends using a set of dedicated
service accounts
. These service accounts can interact with the Kubernetes API and are easier to manage compared to group accounts. Access to the Kubernetes API requires multi-factor authentication, so service accounts are a simpler solution for automated deployments.

title: Funding for Intelligent Infrastructure resources used by UITS services
content:
Due to technology advances that significantly reduced rates for
Intelligent Infrastructure
(II), UITS no longer bills UITS teams for use of II resources (exceptions noted below). This approach, in operational practice since January 2017, eliminates the administrative burden of budgeting and billing for II resources within UITS.
All II virtual machines (VMs) have a funding source, including those used by UITS services (there are no free VMs within II). Enterprise Systems provided existing funding from the ES budget. No additional funding was used.
II resources used by UITS services are funded from existing Enterprise Systems budgets with the following exceptions:
Costs billed to a third-party (external to UITS) client for II resources that support a service will continue to be charged. Example scenarios may include but are not limited to:
UA Technology Support
funding II costs through revenue from client departments.
II costs funded through grant money for a specific project.
II costs funded through student technology fees.
II resources funded from chargeback accounts (typically chargeback accounts start with a 6) will continue to be billed within UITS unless specific exceptions are evaluated.
Additional II resources for UITS services were allocated based on December 2016 resource levels, plus an additional 10% to enable growth. Growth rate maximums were calculated and maintained within each manager's portfolio, and allow for 10% growth in CPU, memory, and storage needs. Growth beyond 10% requires review by divisional leadership and a new funding source.
Self-service provisioning was introduced as part of this process; for more, see
Self-service provisioning in Intelligent Infrastructure (II)
.
System administrators can review available capacity by following the instructions in
Determine remaining resources in an Intelligent Infrastructure (II) resource pool
.

title: Perform document separation in the OnBase Unity Client
content:
When you scan documents from a multi-function device (MFD) directly into OnBase, all the pages are stored as a single document. Document separation allows you to store a large batch of scanned pages as several separate documents. The following explains how to perform document separation within the OnBase Unity Client.
Log into the OnBase Unity Client and scan your documents into OnBase from your MFD.
In the task ribbon, select
Batch Processing
. Under
Scan Queues
>
Document Separation
, a batch should appear in the
Awaiting Document Separation
queue.
Select the
Awaiting Document Separation
queue once to enter it, and select the batch you would like to work on. Then right-click and select
Perform Document Separation
.
A screen showing an unindexed document will appear.
Check the document you want to separate. It will be easiest to separate each page into its own document and then append pages together (if necessary) during the indexing phase. To do so, from the ribbon, select
Split
. Select
Break into Documents
, and then
Every Page
.
The "Document Separation" screen should now display a list of unindexed documents.
When you are finished separating the document, select
Save and Close All
. In the confirmation box that appears, select
Yes
.
The batch will move to the
Awaiting Index
queue. From there, you can index the documents as normal.

tab. Here, you'll see all of your assigned advisees in one group at the top of the list. All the other groups listed on the tab are organized by academic program plan. The expectation is that every student has at least one advising assignment (individual advisor or advising office) while they are active in an academic degree plan. Assigned advisees can be added individually or in a batch process within the Student Information System (SIS).
Note:
Advisor assignments are visible to students in the Student Online Advising Record (SOAR) system, in the Student Appointment Scheduler (SAS), and in the Student Center. The advisor/office email address and phone number are displayed.
If you wish to create an ad hoc group, select the
Ad Hoc Caseload Group
tab. Here, you'll see an alphabetical list of all of the ad hoc Caseload groups that you've created. Ad hoc Caseload groups are static lists of students created and maintained by individual users, and your groups will remain visible to you as long as you have permission to access this feature.
Create a new ad hoc Caseload group
To create a new ad hoc Caseload group:
From the
AdRx
Dashboard, select
Caseload
, and then select the
Ad Hoc Caseload Groups
tab.
At the top of the list, select
Create New Caseload Group
.
In the pop-up window, enter a name for the new group.
Under "Caseload Group Members", paste or type a list of student usernames or University IDs, with entries separated by a space, comma, or new line. If you want to create an empty ad hoc group, leave the "Caseload Group Members" box blank.
Select
Find Students
to import the student names and confirm your list has no errors.
To remove any student that should not be in the group, select the
x
to the right of the student's information.
Once you've established that the list is complete and does not include any students that don't belong, select
Create Group
to add this group to your other ad hoc groups.
Note:
Ad hoc Caseload groups have a size limit of 10,000 students in a single group. You can create an ad hoc Caseload group with over 10,000 students, but you won't be able to open it. In such cases, you'll need to either delete the group or remove all members from it; see
Rename, delete, or remove all members from an ad hoc Caseload group
.
Add students to an existing ad hoc Caseload group
There are several methods to add students to an existing ad hoc Caseload group:
Option 1:
From the list view of an ad hoc group, at the top of the list, select
Add Students
.
In the "Add Students" dialogue box, paste or type a list of student usernames or University IDs, with entries separated by a space, comma, or new line.
Select
Find Students
.
Verify that the students listed are correct, and then select
Add Students
.
Option 2:
From the list of students for a particular Caseload group, select at least one student, and select
Add to a Caseload Group
.
In the dialog box that appears, you'll have the option to add the student(s) to a new ad hoc group, or to add the student(s) to an existing group selected from a drop-down list of your groups.
Rename, delete, or remove all members from an ad hoc Caseload group
To modify an ad hoc Caseload group, navigate to the
Adhoc Caseload Groups
tab. To the right of the group you want to change, select the three vertical dots, and then, as appropriate, select
Rename Group
,
Remove All Members
, or
Delete Group
.
Remove members of an ad hoc Caseload group
To remove specific members of an ad hoc Caseload group, navigate to the group, select the member(s) you want to remove, and select
Remove Members
. This button will become active once you've selected at least one student.
Set Caseload filters
You can use Caseload's filter options to help you find students that have common characteristics within your assigned advisees group or an ad hoc group.
The filters pane is displayed to the left of any group, and always contains the same options to start:
Campus
Career
Action Items
Admit Term
Alerts
Area of Study
Class Standing
Course Grades
Course Registration
Enrollment
GPA
Graduation Review Status
Hours
Service Indicators
Student Engagement Roster
Student Groups
Transfer Students
To apply filters to a group:
Select and set filter values as desired, either one at a time or all at once; a summary of all the filters you have selected will display as you go.
If you wish to delete a filter before it's applied, select the
x
next to it. To remove all filters and start again, select
Clear All
.
Once you've selected at least one filter value, it will be displayed above the selections. At that point, you can either apply that filter, or you can return to the larger list to add more. In other words, you can continuously filter the list one parameter at a time, or you can add multiple filters at once; the results will be the same.
If you are applying multiple filters at once, you will see limited options in some categories for filtering based on the values you've already chosen.
Once you've selected all the filters you want, select
Apply to Results
.
Once a filter is applied, it will be displayed at the top of the page under "Selected Filters". All available filters will also continue to be displayed on the left side of the page.
Your results will be displayed. The number of students in the filtered group as compared to the number in the entire group will appear next to the group name.
Note:
If you choose to
export your list
, the exported file will only include the students in the filtered list (as opposed to all students in the Caseload group). The file will display an addition column for each filtered value.
Navigate to, from, and between student records
When you select the name of a student in the list, you'll be taken to the "Student Summary" page, and a secondary header will display. The secondary header provides two navigation options:
To return to the Caseload group, select the group's name at the upper left of the secondary header; any filters you selected will still be applied when you return to the group.
To page through the list of students without returning to the overall Caseload group, use the arrows on the right side of the secondary header; these arrows work on entire Caseload groups or on filtered lists.
Export Caseload lists
You can use Caseload to generate and export a comma-delimited (
.csv
) file containing a Caseload group page. Such files store data as plain text and are viewable in Excel.
To export a Caseload list:
On the Caseload landing page, select the group you want to export from either the
Assigned Advisees
tab or the
Adhoc Caseload Groups
tab.
Select
Export
in the upper right corner.
Note:
The exported list will contain all members of the chosen group, regardless of whether any students were selected or not. For each student, the list will include a standard set of student data along with the values of any filters you may have used.
If you wish to save the list as an Excel file, open the
.csv
file in Excel, select
Save As
, and save the file as an Excel file type (such as
.xlsx
or
.xls
).
Send messages or add an advising note via Caseload
For details about sending messages and adding advising notes with Caseload, see
Email a group of students using Caseload in AdRx
.

title: Set up a Google Custom Search Engine for your IU website
content:
On this page:
Overview
Request a Google Custom Search Engine
Set up your Custom Search Engine
Add your Custom Search Engine to your website
Edit your Custom Search Engine
Delete a Custom Search Engine
Overview
At Indiana University, you can use Google Custom Search to help people find the information they need on your website(s). You can add a Google Custom Search Engine to your web page(s) by copying and pasting a few lines of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. You can configure your Custom Search Engine to search whatever site(s) you want, even sites you don't own. People who use the Google Custom Search box on your website will see search results from only the site(s) you choose.
At IU, you can use Google Custom Search on your website without fee as part of the
Google at IU
service.
Request a Google Custom Search Engine
Note:
To create and administer your department's Google Custom Search Engine(s), UITS recommends using one of your department's
group accounts
to create a shared
Google at IU
account. Using a single shared
Google at IU
account to create, own, and manage your department's Custom Search Engine(s) saves you the inconvenience of managing multiple Google accounts, and simplifies the reassignment of search engine duties whenever staff and roles change within your department.
To request a Google Custom Search Engine for use with your IU website, fill out and submit the
Google@IU Custom Search Engine Request
form.
On the form, you must provide the following information:
Name:
Enter your full name (first and last name).
Email address:
Enter the IU group account email address used to create your department's shared
Google at IU
account.
Phone number:
Enter the phone number of a contact person whom the
Google at IU
administrator can call if any questions or problems arise.
Username(s) of CSE administrator(s):
Enter the
IU username
(or usernames, comma-separated) of the individual(s) to whom you want to grant administrative rights to your Custom Search Engine.
"Friendly" name for CSE:
Enter a name to identify this search engine (for example,
Deathstar.org search
) from others your department has created or may create in the future.
URL of search site:
Enter the URL of an initial website to add to the Custom Search Engine (you can add more websites later).
When you're finished, enter your name in the
SIGN HERE
box, and then select
Submit
. The
Google at IU
administrator will notify you when your Custom Search Engine is ready.
Set up your Custom Search Engine
Go to
Google Custom Search Engine
. If you're not already logged into
Google at IU
with your department's shared Google account, select
Sign in To Custom Search Engine
, and then log in through
IU Login
and
Two-Step Login (Duo)
using the group account credentials associated with your department's shared Google account.
Under "Edit search engines", find the search engine you created, and select its name.
On the
Setup
page, on the
Basics
tab, you can change the name of your search engine, add a description and keywords, and list the URLs of the websites you want the search engine to search. When you're finished making changes, at the bottom of the page, select
Update
.
From the menu on the left, choose
Look and feel
and use the provided tabs to customize your search engine's appearance:
On the
Themes
tab, you can select one of the provided design themes.
On the
Customize
tab, you can choose the fonts and colors that are used in search engine elements (for example, search box, search button, and search results).
On the
Layout
tab, you can choose one of several layouts that display the search box and search results on the same web page, or choose the layout for displaying the search box and search results on separate pages.
When you're finished with
Look and feel
changes, select
Save & Get Code
.
Important:
Once you add your Custom Search Engine to your website, you can apply your site's CSS rules to customize it further. However, to comply with the university's agreement with Google, do not use CSS to remove/hide Google branding from your search results. The light gray "powered by Google Custom Search" text is a standard component that cannot be altered in the search engine's control panel. Although the text can be hidden using CSS, UITS requests that you honor its agreement with Google and refrain from doing so. Also, UITS recommends not using a gray background for your search pages (most IU-affiliated search pages have white backgrounds). The Google logo is an image, and its appearance cannot be changed.
Add your Custom Search Engine to your website
The process of embedding Custom Search components (your search box and search results) in your web page(s) involves copying the code you generated by selecting
Save & Get Code
at the end of the previous section, and pasting it into the HTML of your web page(s). The exact steps you take will depend on the layout you choose. Following are instructions for one of the one-page layouts and the two-page layout.
Overlay:
Choosing the
Overlay
layout and selecting
Save & Get Code
generates code for displaying the search results as an overlay on the same page as the search box. The generated code will look similar to this (the value for
cx
will be a unique ID specific to your search engine):
<script>
(function() {
var cx = 'your_search_engine_ID';
var gcse = document.createElement('script');
gcse.type = 'text/javascript';
gcse.async = true;
gcse.src = 'https://cse.google.com/cse.js?cx=' + cx;
var s = document.getElementsByTagName('script')[0];
s.parentNode.insertBefore(gcse, s);
})();
</script>
<gcse:search></gcse:search>
Copy the generated code, and then paste it into a single <div> element in the body of your web page(s).
Two page:
Choosing the
Two page
layout and selecting
Save & Get Code
generates code for displaying your search box and search results on separate pages. The generated search box code will look similar to this (the value for
cx
will be a unique ID specific to your search engine):
<script>
(function() {
var cx = 'your_search_engine_ID';
var gcse = document.createElement('script');
gcse.type = 'text/javascript';
gcse.async = true;
gcse.src = 'https://cse.google.com/cse.js?cx=' + cx;
var s = document.getElementsByTagName('script')[0];
s.parentNode.insertBefore(gcse, s);
})();
</script>
<gcse:searchbox-only></gcse:searchbox-only>
Copy the generated code and paste it into a <div> element in the body of the web page(s) where you want your search box to be displayed. To specify the URL of your search results page, add the resultsUrl argument to the <gcse:searchbox-only> element; for example:
<gcse:searchbox-only resultsUrl="search_results_url"></gcse:searchbox-only>
Back on the "Get code for search box" page, select
Next: Get code for search results
(beneath the text/code box). On the resulting "Get code for search results" page, copy the generated code and paste it into a <div> element in the body of your search results page.
Note:
Alternatively, you can specify the URL of your search results page without manually adding it to your search box code:
On either the "Get code for search box" or "Get code for search results" page, select
Search Results Details
(above the text/code box).
In the resulting window, enter the complete URL of your search results page. (In the "Specify the query parameter name embedded in the URL" field, either leave the default
q
or, optionally, change it to
query
.)
Select
Save
.
For more about Custom Search elements, see Google's
Custom Search Element Control API
page.
Note:
Google Custom Search also has a JSON/Atom API you can use to develop websites and applications that query your Custom Search Engine and retrieve search results in JSON or Atom format. Use of the JSON/Atom Custom Search API is free for up to 100 queries per day, but any usage beyond the free quota will result in charges being assessed. For this reason, UITS recommends using the JavaScript API.
Edit your Custom Search Engine
To edit the name, description, websites to search, and/or the look and feel options of your Custom Search Engine, return to
Google Custom Search Engine
and follow the steps (as needed) from the
Set up your Custom Search Engine
section, above.
To add or remove search engine administrators, email the Google at IU administrator at
tlthelp@iu.edu
.
Delete a Custom Search Engine
To delete a Google Custom Search Engine, email the Google at IU administrator at
tlthelp@iu.edu
.

title: About Google Course Tools
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Set up and manage Google Course Tools (instructors only)
Enable Google Course Tools
Select desired features and permissions
Sync the roster with Google Course Tools
Grant or remove access to IU guests
Access and use course folders
Access course folders from Google Course Tools
Access course folders from
Google at IU
My Drive
Access course folders as an IU guest
Share and collaborate on content in course folders
Course folder permissions
Permissions inheritance
Upload files or folders
Create new Google content
Share existing
Google Drive
content that you own
Use the course mailing list/discussion forum in
Google Groups
Overview
Google Course Tools is an external app that integrates Canvas with the
Google at IU
service. Currently this tool facilitates sharing and collaboration among class members by creating a collection of folders for the course in
Google Drive
and
Google Groups
for managing permissions on the folders. Instructors can also create a mailing list and web-based discussion board for the course in
Google Groups
.
Important:
Files that you add to folders created by Google Course Tools count toward your
5 GB quota
. To keep your
Google Drive
account under the quota, you may need to remove files in folders for courses from prior terms. To retrieve a list of Google files that have been shared with other users or groups, including files shared in Google Course Tools folders, run the
Google at IU "My Drive" Shared Files Report
.
Set up and manage Google Course Tools (instructors only)
Enable Google Course Tools
The Google Course Tools app is hidden by default. To add a hidden tool to your course navigation menu, see
How do I manage Course Navigation links?
Select desired features and permissions
Using the "Google Course Tools setup" screen, you can decide which features to enable and determine whether TAs and Designers should have instructor-level access or not. To set up Google Course Tools:
From the course navigation menu, select
Google Course Tools
. The first time you launch the tool, the setup screen will display immediately. After that, you can access the setup screen from the main menu by selecting
Set up Google Course Tools
.
Read the folder/feature descriptions and check the boxes for the folders/features you wish to enable.
By default, TAs and Designers will have the same permissions to access the folder content as students. To give one or both roles instructor-level access, under "Which additional roles should have instructor-level access?", check the boxes for the desired roles.
When you are satisfied with your selections, select
Submit
. You can revisit the setup screen later to enable additional folders/features or change TA or Designer permissions.
After a few seconds, the main menu will appear with a success message at the top of the page. You'll also receive a Canvas notification of the groups and folders created.
The setup program enables the folders/features you selected and changes TA and designer permissions if requested. It also creates two Google groups, one for instructors only and one for all members of the class.
Sync the roster with Google Course Tools
Access to the resources created by Google Course Tools is controlled by membership in two Google groups, one for instructors only and the other containing all members of the course. When course members launch the tool for the first time, they are automatically added to the appropriate groups. In addition, a nightly sync updates the membership of the groups based on the current course roster. You can also run the roster sync at any time by selecting
Sync course roster
from the Google Course Tools main menu.
The roster sync job makes the following changes to the course groups and folders:
Removes users who have dropped or been removed from the course
Adds users who are added to the course manually or via SIS enrollment updates
Creates student drop boxes for students who were added after drop boxes were enabled
Removes drop box editor permissions for students who dropped or were removed
Adds or removes TAs and/or Designers from the instructors-only group to reflect current permissions chosen on the setup screen
Grant or remove access for IU guests
Course members with an IU Guest account do not have permission to use the Canvas Course Tools app. Guests who attempt to launch the app will receive an error. Instructors can, however, give guests access to the Google resources created by the app. You can do so by manually adding the guests in your course to the appropriate Google groups.
Important:
In order to add guests to your course groups, you'll need the Google username for each guest. Ask each guest to provide you with this information.
The roster sync option will not remove guests who have been removed from the course. You must remove them from the Google groups manually.
Personal drop box folders are not created for guests, and instructors do not have permission to create them manually.
To manually add guests:
From the course navigation menu, select
Google Course Tools
.
From the Google Course Tools main menu, select
Course information
.
The two Google groups created for the course are listed at the top of the page. Select the group for the entire class. You will be taken directly to the selected Google group.
In the menu for the group at the lower left, under "People", select
Members
.
On the "Members" page, select
Add members
.
In the "Add members" pop-up, under "Group Members", enter the Google username for each guest into the text box.
Select
Add members
. In the "Group Members" list, guests will be flagged as "external".
To also give a guest instructor-level access to course resources, repeat steps 1-7 above, but on step 3, select the link for the "Teachers only" group.
Send the guest a message letting them know they've been added.
To remove a guest :
Repeat steps 1 through 4 above.
Locate the guest in the member list for the group and check the box for the guest's name.
Select the
Remove Member
icon (
).
In the confirmation window, select
OK
.
Access and use course folders (all roles)
You can access the folders created by Google Course Tools from the main menu of the Canvas app or directly in Google. However, you must launch the app in Canvas at least once in your course before the folders will appear in your
Google at IU
My Drive
.
Access course folders from Google Course Tools
To access a folder from the Google Course Tools app:
From the course navigation menu, select
Google Course Tools
.
Links to the folders you have permission to access appear under "Course folders (open in
Google Drive
)". Select the name of the folder you wish to open. The folders are:
COURSE FILES
: For course materials shared with the entire class
INSTRUCTOR FILES
: For files and folders shared by and accessible to instructors only
DROP BOXES
: Container for individual student drop boxes
MY DROP BOX
: Personal drop box for the current user
FILE REPOSITORY
: For files and folders shared by any class member
GROUP FILES
: Container for folders created for Canvas groups; a separate folder is created for each group
If you are not already logged into
Google at IU
, you will be prompted to do so. At the
IU Login
prompt, enter your username and password. You may also be prompted to complete a
Two-Step Login
.
You will be taken directly to the selected folder in
Google at IU
My Drive
.
Access course folders from
Google at IU
My Drive
The folders created by Google Course Tools are owned by an administrative account and shared with the Google groups created for each class. The individually shared folders are listed under the
Shared with me
tab in
Google Drive
.
All course folders are also organized under a folder shortcut named
Google Course Tools (
your_username
)
in your
Google My Drive
. Beneath this folder is a separate folder for each course in which the Google Course Tools app has been enabled. Beneath the top-level folder for each course are the special purpose folders (
COURSE FILES
,
INSTRUCTOR FILES
,
DROP BOXES
,
FILE REPOSITORY
,
GROUP FILES
) created for the course.
Most folder names begin with the course title followed by the Canvas internal ID for the course in parentheses, for example,
SP21: ECOTOURISM: 25256 (1559999)
. The only exception are student drop box folders, which begin with the student's name and username followed by the course title and ID, for example:
Doe, Jane (jdoe): SU15: ECOTOURISM: 25256 (1559999)
.
Your role in the corresponding Canvas course will determine your permissions for each folder. For more about the folder permissions, see
Course folder permissions
.
Access course folders as an IU guest
Users with IU Guest accounts cannot use the Google Course Tools app in Canvas. In order to access the Google resources created by the app, you'll need to ask your instructor to manually add your Google account to the appropriate Google groups for the course as described above in
Grant or remove access for IU guests
. After the instructor has added you, launch Google Course Tools and select the link to the top-level course folder to access the folder for the first time. To add a shortcut to your
Google My Drive
, right-click the folder link in the
Google Drive
breadcrumb trail and select
Add shortcut to Drive
.
Important:
Do not attempt to send a request for access in
Google Drive
. The folder owner will not receive your request and you will not be added.
If you want to be removed from the course groups and folders, ask the instructor to remove you. You cannot unsubscribe on your own.
Share and collaborate on content in course folders
You can add content to the folders created by Google Course Tools in the following ways:
Upload files and folders from your computer or mobile device.
Create new Google content (such as Docs, Sheets, Slides, Forms, Sites).
Share existing content that you own in
Google Drive
.
This section covers all three options. However, before you start sharing content, it's important to understand how permissions work in the folders created by Google Course Tools.
Course folder permissions
The default permissions for each course folder determine which course roles can add, view, edit, or comment on content in the folder. Editors can open, view, add, delete, and edit the content in the folder. Viewers can open and view content, but cannot make changes. The table below gives the default permissions for each folder.
Folder and permission
Folder
Instructors
1
Everyone else
TOP-LEVEL COURSE FOLDER
Viewer
Viewer
COURSE FILES
Editor
Viewer
INSTRUCTOR FILES
Editor
No access
DROP BOXES
2
(container for individual student drop boxes)
Viewer
Viewer
MY DROP BOX
(individual student drop boxes)
Editor
Students can see and edit their own drop box; otherwise no access.
FILE REPOSITORY
Editor
Editor
GROUP FILES
(container for individual group folders)
Editor
Viewer
[
Canvas Group Folders
]
3
(container for Canvas group folders)

Students can see and edit folders for their own Canvas groups; otherwise no access
Notes:
1
TAs and/or Designers can be given instructor-level access via the Google Course Tools setup menu.
2
All course members can see and open the
DROP BOXES
container folder. However, student drop boxes are only accessible to instructors and the student for whom the folder was created.
3
All course members can see and open the
GROUP FILES
container folder. However, the folders created for each Canvas group are only accessible to instructors and the student members of the group.
When Google Course Tools is initialized, two Google groups are created for each course, one for instructors only and one containing all course members. Access to the course folders is managed by sharing them with one or both groups. This keeps the "
Google Drive
sharing" screen uncluttered and makes it much easier to manage permissions on content added to each folder. The screenshot below shows the group permissions for a sample
COURSE FILES
folder.
The naming convention for the groups created by Google course tools is "Course Title - Canvas Course ID" (the number following the word "courses" in the Canvas course URL), followed by the word "All" (for the group with all course members) or "Teachers" (for the instructor-only group). For example:
FA20: AMERICAN SUPERNATURAL: 35157 - 1942004 All
FA20: AMERICAN SUPERNATURAL: 35157 - 1942004 Teachers
To see the names and Google ID for the groups in your course, from the course navigation menu, select
Google Course Tools
, and then, on the main menu, select
Course Information
. When sharing individual files and folders via the
Google Drive
interface, you can add specific course groups as collaborators just as you can add specific users.
Permissions inheritance
When files or folders are added to a course folder, they inherit the permissions of their parent folder. The owner of the added items can either leave the inherited permissions or modify them as desired.
Permissions for course groups can be changed or removed entirely. The owner can also add specific course members by name in order to grant them greater access than the permissions granted to the groups to which they belong.
For more about sharing files and folders in
Google Drive
, see
Share files from
Google Drive
and
Share folders in
Google Drive
.
Upload files or folders
Users with folder editor permissions can upload files or folders from their desktop or mobile device to a course folder using the drag-and-drop method, or by browsing and selecting the items:
Open the course folder where you want the files or folders to go.
Follow the instructions in
Upload files and folders to
Google Drive
.
To change the permissions on any of the uploaded items, see
Share files from
Google Drive
and
Share folders in
Google Drive
.
Create new Google content
Users with editor permissions can add new Google files and folders to a course folder. Most Google file formats support real-time and asynchronous editing and collaboration, which can be very powerful in teaching and learning contexts. Available file formats include:
Docs (word processing documents)
Sheets (spreadsheets)
Slides (presentations)
Forms (for surveys, data collection, self-assessments, etc.)
Sites (for building web sites)
Maps
Drawings
A variety of third-party apps integrated with
Google Drive
To add a Google file or folder to a course folder:
Navigate to the course folder where you want to add the item.
Select
+ New
in your web browser, or select
+
>
Create new
in the
Google Drive
mobile app.
From the new item menu, select the item type you wish to create.
If you created a folder, you'll be prompted to enter the folder name. If you created a file, you'll be directed to a new file of the specified format. Give the item a file name before you attempt to share it.
To modify the permissions on the item, see
Share files from
Google Drive
and
Share folders in
Google Drive
.
Share existing
Google Drive
content that you own
Although there are several ways to share existing
Google Drive
content with members of your course, the "Share Google Files and Folders" option in the Google Course Tools main menu is safer and more flexible than manipulating items directly in Google. When you use this feature:
The shared file or folder remains in its original location. Rather than moving the file, a shortcut to the file is added to the destination course folder.
The original permissions on the file or folder (whether inherited from the parent folder or added manually) remain intact, ensuring that users who already have access to the items don't lose it. You'll be prompted to specify the permissions for the two Google groups for your course.
The same files or folders can be shared with multiple courses at the same time. You don't need to make copies in order to share content with multiple sections of the same class.
To use the "Share Google Files and Folders" feature:
From the course navigation menu, select
Google Course Tools
.
On the Google Course Tools main menu, select
Share Google files and folders
. If a pop-up appears reminding you to use your

title: About Google Gemini at IU
content:
Table of contents
Overview

Use Google Gemini with your Google at IU account
Learn more and get help
Overview
Google Gemini is a generative artificial intelligence chatbot tool available to all Indiana University students, faculty, and staff. Along with
Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat
, Google Gemini is one of IU's recommended tools for interacting with generative AI. Like other generative AI platforms, Gemini can be used to create new content, including text and images, and to help brainstorm ideas, draft or summarize writing, explore complex topics, and assist with research and creative work.
IU accounts provide access to the base Gemini chatbot, including its ability to create and use Gems, custom AI agents designed to perform specific tasks. Gemini is powered by Google's Gemini model family and offers enterprise-grade data protections, making it a flexible and creative tool for learning and productivity.
Limitations on Gemini accounts at IU
Under IU's license agreement, Google sets daily quotas of some advanced-level Gemini features. Such feature add-ons may be called AI Pro, Ultra AI, or other names. As of summer 2025, there is no a pathway for IU users to upgrade their institutional Google accounts to increase these quotas or add capabilities. If the vendor offers such individual licenses in the future, the Knowledge Base will be updated.
Use Google Gemini with your Google at IU account
Google Gemini is approved to interact with
Restricted data
except for research data with contract restrictions related to AI (see
Acceptable use of AI tools with IU research data
); you must be logged in with your
@iu.edu
email address and
IU passphrase
to ensure you're using
Google at IU
rather than the consumer-based Google service.
There are two ways to access Google Gemini:
Browser:
Navigate directly to
https://gemini.google.com
in your preferred web browser (for example, Firefox, Chrome).
Apps:
Google Gemini mobile apps
are available for iOS and Android devices.
Important:
Always use your IU account for Indiana University business. Personal (free) non-IU Google accounts are not approved for institutional data. Gemini users' chats and uploaded files are not reviewed by human reviewers or otherwise used to improve generative AI models only if used with your
Google at IU
account. Also, your interactions and generated content within Gemini in Google at IU remain in IU's domain and are not shared externally. Any public Google account will not have such protections.
Be aware of how to
navigate between your IU Google account and non-IU Google accounts
, or consider creating a
Google Chrome profile
to manage multiple Google accounts.
The following are general use cases for Google Gemini at IU:
Answer questions:
If you need a quick fact, a detailed explanation, or information on a complex topic, Gemini can provide answers and summaries across a vast range of subjects.
Generate images:
You can use Gemini to generate original images for general use, such as presentations.
Research and brainstorming:
The Gemini app can help you research and brainstorm new ideas (for example, for lesson plans or IT security policies), and can speed up time-consuming tasks.
Double-check feature:
Gemini includes a feature that uses Google Search to help you verify the accuracy of its responses.
Even if you use generative AI tools for activities that do not share personal or institutional data, you should still check the tool's output for accuracy. Since these tools have been known to produce inaccurate content (sometimes called "hallucinations"), verify any factual information generated by an AI tool, and make sure to reference the tool as you would any other source.
If you have any privacy-related concerns related to Google Gemini, or if you have questions about the type of data that can be shared with it, email
privacy@iu.edu
.
Learn more and get help
To learn more about Google Gemini and discover ways it can help boost your productivity and accelerate learning, see
Get Started with Google AI in Higher Education
.
For technical assistance or concerns, contact the Google at IU Administration team at
tlthelp@iu.edu

title: About disk quota in Unix
content:
A disk quota is the amount of space allotted to each user for file storage on a given computer.
On shared systems such as
Unix
, every user has a maximum disk quota. This prevents any individual from using more than his or her fair share of disk space. In order to keep from going over your quota, you must be sure to periodically clean out old, unused, and unneeded files.
Two commands are very helpful in bringing your disk space back under control:
The
ls -al
command shows you the contents of your directory.
The
rm
command removes any unnecessary files.
To use the
rm
command (which stands for "remove"), enter:
rm filename
Replace
filename
with the name of the file you want to remove.
You can also enter:
rm -i filename
The
-i
flag tells Unix to inquire for confirmation before removing.
Always be careful when you remove files, because there is no command to retrieve the file. You may create an alias that will move files to a trash can rather than removing them from the system completely, but this is generally not an accepted practice.
If you are unsure of the content of a file, enter:
cat filename
Replace
filename
with the name of your file. If it is a text file, the
cat
command will print the contents of the file to the screen. If it is a
binary file
,
cat
will print screen after screen of garbage characters. If you are unsure of the type of file, you may prefer to use the
more
command, which will show only one screen of the file at a time and will allow you to cancel the command easily. To use the
more
command, enter:
more filename
Replace
filename
with the name of your file.
The following items can usually be discarded:
Any file named
core
, which is a file created when certain programs crash
Temporary files which have names that begin and end with
#
Backup files which have names that end with
~
Backup files which have names that end with
%
Also, discard any personal files that are obsolete or no longer needed.
Don't forget to check all of your directories and subdirectories. Directories are the items that begin with "d" in the first column when you issue the
ls -al
command.
For example, to check the subdirectory
galactica
, enter the following commands:
cd galactica ls -al rm filename1 filename2 filename3 cd
At Indiana University, for personal or departmental Linux or Unix systems support, see
Get help for Linux or Unix at IU
.

title: Data Protection Services (DPS): Known limitations
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Backup limitations
Recovery limitations
Overview
Known limitations within the
Data Protection Services (DPS)
environment can cause issues when backing up or recovering a VM.
Backup limitations
Limitation:
VMs with client snapshots that have existed for an extended period of time, or snapshots that have grown beyond the recommended safe size limit, or snapshots that were created with the "Snapshot the virtual machine's memory" (
or equivalent
) option selected, could present problems when performing a backup.
Result:
The backup will fail and leave the VM in an unprotected state. This occurs due to fragmentation within the VM's
vmdk
files when any of the above conditions are true. The fragmentation means DPS will not be able to properly collect the client data in time, causing a timeout.
Workaround:
Ensure VM snapshots are deleted in a timely fashion. VMware's
Best practices for using snapshots in the vSphere environment
suggest that snapshots remain for a maximum of 72 hours.
Ensure that snapshots do not grow beyond a safe limit. IU's ESXi Admins suggest that snapshots should be deleted once they have grown beyond 10 GB in size.
Ensure that snapshots do not include memory:
Snapshots created from vRA:
"include memory?"
Recovery limitations
VM configurations
Limitation:
There are certain VM configurations that limit the ability to perform self-service recovery operations within DPS. Depending on the configuration, this could mean that either no volumes or only some of the volumes will appear when browsing the backup history for your VM. These limitations are presented below:
Volumes affected:
All VMs (regardless of OS):
Volumes using full disk encryption (for example, BitLocker)
Volumes that have been configured in a software raid or have data striping enabled within the operating system
Volumes using deduplication software within the operating system
Windows VMs:
Volumes that are configured using Windows Storage Pools or Storage Spaces
Linux VMs:
Volumes formatted with the Oracle ASM file system type
Result:
When browsing from the web console, volumes for the VM will not be displayed properly. Granular file recovery is not available for these configurations.
Workaround:
VMs should be built in a way that does not limit the use of granular file recovery.
Max session file limit
Limitation:
For VMs that do not have the
Data Protection Services (DPS) Restore Only Agent (ROA)
installed, the maximum number of files that can be restored in a single session is one million. Once the session hits the max number of files, the session will stop and will report back that it completed successfully.
Result:
The restore process reports that it has completed successfully, but not all client data was restored.
Workaround:
Install the Data Protection Services (DPS) Restore Only Agent (ROA)
on any VM that you want to be able to restore from and to without restrictions.
For VMs without the ROA installed, break up restores into multiple jobs to limit the number of files restored in any one session to under one million. If you cannot easily break up the restore into multiple jobs, the SAV team will need to perform an assisted restore to ensure that all data is recovered. SAV works with the application vendor to notify our team when this issue occurs.
Max browse file limit
Limitation:
For all VMs, regardless of OS, the maximum number of files that can be browsed in a single folder/directory is one million. Once the session hits the max number of files, the browse window will stop and report back that no files could be found.
Result:
No files are available to view for restoration.
Workaround:
Limit the maximum number of files for a single folder or directory to a value under one million files.
Down level ROA versions
Limitation:
For VMs with a down level version of the ROA installed, you may encounter issues when attempting to browse or restore operations.
Result:
Not all data is shown when attempting to browse the backup. You may be able to successfully browse the backup data for the VM, but not the file structure of the target destination. The restore process may also fail, reporting communication errors between the ROA and the DPS environment.
Workaround:
Update the ROA version by downloading the current published version from
IUware
. See
Install the Data Protection Services (DPS) Restore Only Agent (ROA)
.
Filesystem Compression
Limitation:
For VMs that have filesystem compression set, clients will encounter longer than normal windows for recovery processing.
Result:
The window to complete the restoration will take on average, four times longer to process when compared to processing the same uncompressed data recovery.
Workaround:
Refrain from enabling compression at the filesystem level on VMs that require Commvault Data Protection Services.

title: About the II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service at IU
content:
On this page:
Overview
Namespaces and tenants
Data protection
Size limits
Multi-part uploads
Multi-threading support
Object versioning support
Billing
Differences between II Enterprise S3 Object Storage and Amazon's S3 offering
Bucket-level IP address restrictions
Request a new tenant or additional namespaces
Connect to a namespace
Overview
At Indiana University, the Intelligent Infrastructure (II) Enterprise S3 Object Storage service is an S3-compatible, on-premise object storage service provided by the
UITS
Storage and Virtualization (SAV) team. Serviced from two distinct Hitachi Content Platform (HCP) clusters, the S3 Object Storage service provides high availability and durability through a combination of object replication and hash verification. The II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service is available to enterprise systems at UITS.
The list
sav-hcp-l@list.iu.edu
is used for communicating updates and patch schedules to HCP end users. If you're using the II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service, UITS highly recommends subscribing to this list.
Note:
Although the SAV team does not prohibit it, you should not use S3 for another application that resembles a file system. Overlaying a file system on an object store is not recommended, as the emulation of the file system is slow and does not scale well.
Namespaces and tenants
Namespaces are the term Hitachi uses to refer to a bucket. You will see both terms used interchangeably while working with the II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service.
A tenant is a collection of namespaces, users, and permissions. Tenants are generally created for a department or a particular project that requires specific object isolation. Charge-back is calculated at the tenant level; objects within a tenant will be charged to a single account.
Data protection
Objects are continuously replicated in near-realtime to the HCP cluster in the opposing data center.
As objects are ingested into the cluster, a SHA-256 hash is generated and stored as metadata with the object. Automated object health checks compare hashes, and healing is performed if needed.
Storage quotas
Each bucket (namespace) is assigned a quota for space consumption. Quotas are used to keep bucket consumption from growing unchecked. Quotas can be adjusted by the SAV team upon request (contact the SAV team at
sav-request@iu.edu
).
Access to the II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service is limited to addresses within the IU Data Center IP space. External access to objects must be provided by your application.
Size limits
The maximum object size supported is 5 TB, using multi-part upload.
Multi-part uploads
Multi-part uploads are supported for objects with up to 10,000 parts. Attempts to upload objects with more than 10,000 parts will fail.
Multi-threading support
Multi-threading is supported and recommended to achieve high throughput.
Object versioning support
Object versioning can be configured on a per-bucket (per-namespace) basis and will be retained by the configured duration (0 days - several years). Each object version will count toward the bucket's quota. Expired versions are pruned from the object store periodically throughout the day.
Billing
Billing is calculated by the total amount stored at the end of the billing cycle. There is no charge for reads, writes, deletes, or network transfers.
Differences between II Enterprise S3 Object Storage and Amazon's S3 offering
The II Enterprise S3 Object Storage service does not have a "region" setting. Some applications are required to have this configuration. Using the tenant name as the region may be a possible workaround in some instances.
Example:
The region name is the same as your tenant name. If your tenant name is ABC, you would also use ABC for region aligning with your URL:
https://ABC.s3b.uits.iu.edu/bucket
Bucket-level IP address restrictions
All buckets (namespaces) are required to have IP access restrictions applied. These can be applied per IP address or over an IP range.
Request a new tenant or additional namespaces
To request a new tenant or additional namespaces, email
sav-request@iu.edu
with the following information:
Tenant name
Contact email (group email only)
Billing account number
Initial space requirement
Initial namespaces (buckets) to create
Quota on each namespace
IP ranges for access (CIDR notation preferred)
Whether versioning is required for each bucket
Connect to a namespace
To connect to a namespace, see
Tools for use with II Enterprise S3 Object Storage
.

title: Use file systems and persistent storage in AppKube
content:
Note:
The following information is technical and intended for web application developers.
Table of contents
About file systems in AppKube
Use cases for writable storage
Temporary storage
Persistent storage
Persistent storage outside the web root
Use symlinks for persistent storage inside your application's deployment root or web root
Upload files to persistent storage
Quotas
Backup
Other storage options
Get help
About file systems in AppKube
The file system where AppKube deploys your code is loaded into your application’s execution environment in read-only mode. This means that once your application is deployed, the files within the deployment directory cannot be modified, and you cannot create new files or directories within the location that your application is deployed. In general, this is a best practice that improves the overall security of the AppKube environment. That said, there are still valid use cases where writable storage is required.
Use cases for writable storage
Your application might need writable persistent storage for certain use cases, such as:
Writing compiled files or temporary caches
Storing and serving files uploaded by a user of your application
Dynamic generation of web content or other files that will be served on the web
Temporary storage
You can write files to temporary storage within your AppKube environment if you wish. The best way to do this is to reference the
TMPDIR
environment variable to determine where to write these files to.
Important:
Temporary storage in AppKube is volatile and will disappear as soon as your application gets restarted, which can happen at any time. Use it only for things which are truly temporary and can be regenerated again, such as caches or compiled templates.
AppKube runs multiple instances of your application (at least two) and balances load between them. Each of these instances has its own independent temporary storage.
Do not use temporary storage for large files or large numbers of files; aim to use less than a few megabytes per app. Space in the AppKube environment for this type of storage is limited.
Do not write to log files in the AppKube environment if you can avoid it. You will not have access to these files, so collecting log output there just consumes space. Instead, configure your application to log to
stdout
and
stderr
. These output streams will be automatically collected by AppKube’s logging sub-system. More information on logging and log retrieval in AppKube is coming soon.
If your use cases don't fit well into temporary storage given the caveats noted above, consider using persistent storage instead.
Persistent storage
AppKube can deliver persistent storage to your application's environment. Unlike temporary storage, persistent storage will be writable, readable, and consistent across all instances of your application which may be running at the same time.
This storage is mounted into your application's runtime environment
outside
of the path where your application's code is deployed. However, you can include persistent storage paths
within
your application's deployment using symbolic links (symlinks), which will be described later in this document.
When you
request an application
, you will be able to request your desired amount of persistent storage (in gigabytes) . You can request a maximum of 100 GB. If you have a valid use case which requires more storage than that, email
apphelp@iu.edu
to submit your request and justification.
Persistent storage outside the web root
Maintaining persistent storage outside of your application's web root is preferred because it prevents anything unexpected from being exposed onto the web. You can still read and write from this storage inside of your application's code. You should use the
STORAGE_DIR
environment variable to retrieve the location of your persistent storage. This environment variable will automatically be available within your application's environment. UITS recommends always using this environment variable instead of hardcoding the absolute path.
This type of persistent storage is ideal for storing and retrieving user-supplied file upload data, or any other file-based data you will manage from your application's code.
Use symlinks for persistent storage inside your application's deployment root or web root
You can use symlinks in AppKube to create links from within your application's deployment directories to locations within your persistent storage. This includes creating symlinks within your application's web root, which is the
public
subdirectory by default. To use symlinks:
Within your application's source code in GitHub, create a folder named
.appkube
.
In this folder, create a file named
storage.yaml
.
In this file, you will define one or more storage links that will define which symlinks are created when your application is deployed into the AppKube environment.
Below is an example
storage.yaml
file with comments:
storageLinks:
- webPath: /public/example-webpath
storagePath: /example-storagepath
- webPath: /storage
storagePath: /laravel-storage
In this example, we are creating two symlinks. The
webPath
is relative to the root of your application’s deployment. The
storagePath
is relative to the location of your
STORAGE_DIR
.
The first entry will create a symlink named
example-webpath
inside the
public
directory of your deployed application code, pointing to a directory named
example-storagepath
within the root of your
STORAGE_DIR
. This means that whatever files are in
example-webpath
will be available on the web and served from your application.
Use this very carefully!
It is crucial that you don't expose anything under your web root that you don't want to be available to those interacting with your web application. This approach is useful for larger sets of static or generated assets (files, images, etc.) that you want to serve directly to the web.
The second symlink is an example of how to create a storage location for Laravel. Laravel requires a special writable directory named
storage
to be mounted in the same location as its application code. Since the file system that AppKube deploys is read-only, by default Laravel will be unable to write to this directory. Instead, any Laravel app should request storage and set up a symlink in this manner from the
storage
location within the application directory to a location (like
laravel-storage
) within your persistent storage.
Note:
The
storage.yaml
file uses the YAML format. Within YAML, indentation is semantic and must be done correctly and consistently in order for the file to be successfully parsed. By convention, two spaces are used for indentation within YAML, and the indentation must be consistent throughout. Do
not
use tabs.
Upload files to persistent storage
Since your persistent file storage is made available in writable mode to your AppKube application, you can always interact with it from your application's code. If you need to interact with it through SFTP, the AppKube team can give you access to do this. Access will generally be granted on a temporary basis and is meant to be used for storage maintenance or initial loading or migration of files, but the AppKube team will consider use cases that require longer-term access when requested.
To request SFTP access to your persistent storage, email
apphelp@iu.edu
.
Quotas
The amount you select when requesting your storage will define your quota. The system will enforce this quota, and the technical contact for your application will be notified at certain points as your quota nears exhaustion. You can request additional quota when needed through
https://webapps.iu.edu
(up to the maximum of 100 GB), subject to review and approval by AppKube administrators.
Backup
Your application's storage is automatically backed up twice a day (at noon and midnight Eastern Time). If you need a restore, contact
apphelp@iu.edu

title: Make better use of your disk space in Unix
content:
On this page:
Delete backup and temporary files
Store temporary files elsewhere
Compress files
Store unused files elsewhere
To effectively manage your disk space at Indiana University, you need first to determine the size of your disk space and how much of it you have used. On a
Unix
computer, to see how much disk space you are using and how much you are allowed to use, from the Unix
shell
prompt, enter:
quota
To see how much space each file on your account takes, enter:
ls -alR ~/
The command above shows a listing of all files in your account, including those in subdirectories. If you have many files and subdirectories, the output may be very long. To read it in page-sized chunks, use the
pipe
command to format it:
ls -alR ~/ | more
See the following examples for ways to maximize storage on your Unix account without a space increase.
Delete backup and temporary files
Delete backup and temporary files of the form
filename~
and
#filename#
by entering:
rm *~ rm \#*
Note:
With some
shells
, you need to escape the
#
(pound sign) character with a
\
(backslash) character, since otherwise the shell would treat the rest of the line as a comment.
Store temporary files elsewhere
Put temporary files in the directories
/tmp
,
/scratch/username/
, or
/scr/username/
while you are using them (where
username
is your username).
Some systems may not have
/scr
or
/scratch
directories, or you may have to create your own subdirectory in
/scr
or
/scratch
. Files in these directories are periodically erased and are not counted against your space. For information about scratch space on IU's research systems, see
Available access to allocated and short-term storage capacity on IU's research systems
.
Compress files
Compress files using one of several Unix compression programs. To compress a file named
bigstuff
with the Unix
gzip
command, at the Unix prompt, enter:
gzip bigstuff
The file will be replaced in your directory with a compressed file that has a
.gz
extension. You can't read files or run programs while they are in compressed format, so this command is most useful for storing things you want to keep but won't need to use soon. To expand the file back to its original state, enter:
gzip -d bigstuff.gz
For more information about Unix compression utilities, see the online manual pages. At the Unix prompt, enter any of the following:
man gzip man tar man zip man compress
Store unused files elsewhere
Download some of the files you are not using to a Windows or Macintosh computer and save them on the hard drive or a removable disk.

Get help for Linux or Unix at IU
.

content:
Table of contents
Overview
Differences between Red Hat and CentOS
Choice to upgrade or build new servers
Build process
Issues ELA encountered during the migration
Differences between Red Hat 6 and 7
How ELA patches Red Hat and CentOS servers
Overview
The following provides details on Enterprise Linux Administration's migration from Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) to CentOS.
Differences between Red Hat and CentOS
ELA encountered the following differences going from Red Hat to CentOS:
Most CentOS package updates are available within a day or two of becoming available for Red Hat.
CentOS point releases (for example, 7.2 to 7.3) are often a month or two after the same release in Red Hat.
For more, see Wikipedia's
CentOS Version 7
.
Choice to upgrade or build new servers
ELA built new servers for the migration. Although an upgrade-in-place function is available, it wasn't compatible with ELA's standard build.
Red Hat provides a pre-upgrade check application, but it doesn't check all necessary points; you need to pay careful attention to the notes.
For more, see
Red Hat Migration Planning Guide
.
Build process
ELA began with the CD-ROM images available in
Intelligent Infrastructure
.
ELA then implemented a variety of hardening recommendations (such as the
CIS Benchmarks
) and customizations/scripts as required by the ELA environments.
Finally, ELA cloned remaining servers from the initial servers (the "Golden Masters").
Issues ELA encountered during the migration
Even though CentOS is basically identical to Red Hat, some vendors would not support their applications when running on CentOS.
Differences between Red Hat 6 and 7
ELA encountered the following differences between Red Hat 6 and 7:
grub2
has a different emergency/rescue boot process
Apache httpd 2.4
systemd
versus
init
Firewall management through
firewalld
versus
iptables
NetworkManager by default
The default filesystem is xfs rather than ext4
/bin
changed to
/usr/bin
(
/bin
is now a link to
/usr/bin
)
Other differences are listed in
Red Hat's Migration Guide
.
How ELA patches Red Hat and CentOS servers
Red Hat:
ELA syncs local repositories (Red Hat 6 and 7) against the IU Red Hat Satellite server.
In the future, ELA will re-register servers, as described in an earlier CBRI presentation.
CentOS:
ELA uses the CBRI Open Source Mirror. See:
Index of /linux/epel/7/x86_64
Index of /linux/centos/7
ELA updates production servers from a local repository that is synced to spout when test patches are applied. This prevents the application of any updates to production that haven't been verified in the test environment.

Dependent policies
The
Exchange
service at Indiana University is bound by all applicable existing
Information and IT policies
.
Account policies
All IU students, faculty, staff, and affiliates are eligible for Exchange accounts.
Note:
Any mail sent to
username
@exchange.
campus
.edu

username
@iu.edu

Account generation:
Create your Exchange account by following the instructions in
About Exchange Online at IU

Disk space policies:
Primary user accounts in a paid status at IU are allotted 100 GB of storage capacity, while affiliates and group accounts are allotted 50 GB. There is no provision for expansion.
To determine how much data you have saved in your Exchange mailbox (that is, Inbox and folders), see
Check the storage space of your IU Exchange account

Data restoration policies:
UITS
will restore Exchange data
only
due to a system failure.
UITS will not restore single messages or single mailboxes.
Take care when deleting items.
Deleted messages are moved to the
Deleted Items
folder, where you may recover them.
To use the
Deleted Items
folder as an effective recovery mechanism, turn off Microsoft Outlook's
Empty Deleted Items at exit
option.
For a certain number of days, you can undo deletions after they have left the
Deleted Items
folder. See

.
Object removal policies:
If someone has left the university and the department requires an "Out of Office" notification to redirect mail to another account, contact
it-incident@iu.edu

Institutional data
IU Exchange accounts are appropriate for storing
institutional
data
elements classified as
University-internal
.
Official classifications for institutional data at IU are defined in
Management of Institutional Data (DM-01)
. If you have questions about the classifications of institutional data at IU, see
Classification levels of institutional data
, use the
Data Sharing and Handling (DSH) tool

Data Stewards
. To determine the most sensitive classification of institutional data you can store on any given UITS service, see
Choose an appropriate storage solution

Critical or Restricted data
via email unless it is required by your role within the university. Instead of email, use

University-Internal data
(for example, names, University IDs, student addresses, etc.) via
Exchange
mail, best practice is to limit the data set to 100 or fewer individuals; to share larger data sets, use Secure Share. If you are unsure whether email is appropriate for a particular situation, consult with the appropriate
Data Stewards
and the
UIPO
. Always
force encryption for messages that contain Restricted or Critical data

About confidential information in email
.
Address book

LastName, FirstName Initial
Resources:

)

@indiana
namespace
Departmental identifiers that adhere to the IU given code will take precedence over unofficial departmental or workgroup codes.

Status.IU
and

Protection

IU
Exchange
account
s to opt out of these security settings, individually or in total.
IU community:

About Microsoft 365 security
.
Log requests
To request logs or activity reports from this system, contact the

Overview
When people leave IU, their
Google at IU

Google at IU

About changes to storage in Google at IU
. The information here outlines the process for removing these accounts, as well as the process for transferring ownership of data in Google to another person's account before deletion.
Process to remove separated people
On August 15, 2022, the quota for all separated accounts was set to zero bytes of data. After this date, any newly separated accounts continue to be transferred to separated status and also have their data quota set to zero. On November 1, 2022, all data from those who have been separated from IU for 30 days or longer were deleted.
This process will continue into the future;
all separated accounts will be deleted from
Google at IU
after 30 days of separation has passed
.
Identify data owned by those who've left IU
Below are two possible ways to determine whether data you routinely use is owned by a separated person:
You may open a file in Google and see this banner:
This file is view-only. No edits can be made to this file. Contact file owner for details.
This means the owner has a quota set on their files in Google. Select
Share
on the file to confirm who the owner is. If that person is separated from IU, follow the process below to transfer ownership and unlock the file.
Some files may not be part of your regular work process, but are owned by a separated account. To ensure that files you haven't accessed recently are not deleted:
Log into
Google at IU
My Drive
via
https://drive.google.com/drive/my-drive
.
Hover over the toggle icon in the search bar that says "Search options" and select it.
Select the owner drop-down menu and choose
Specific person

Next to "Specific person", enter the name or email address of the separated person. On the lower right, select
Search
.
You will then see a list of all files you have access to that are owned by that separated person.
For data that is shared with the internet or that is internal to everyone at IU, but not specific individuals, follow the non-collaboration process of transferring ownership outlined below.
Transfer ownership of data
Note:
Taking ownership of a separated individual's files includes all of them. As owner, you can then handle them as seems best.

Requests will be processed at the end of business day every Friday on a weekly basis
