Indiana University's enterprise license for VoiceThread, a multimedia presentation and discussion app that plugs into Canvas, has changed as of January 1, 2025. As part of a regular review of actual tool usage, Teaching and Learning Technologies in UITS determined that the level of use did not justify maintaining a university-wide site license.
Instructors who wish to continue to use VoiceThread in their Canvas courses can order it as a digital learning tool under the
IU eTexts program
. Under this program, the heavily discounted licensing costs are charged directly to students as part of regular bursar billing processes. To learn more about IU eTexts, see the
IU eTexts: A Faculty and Staff Introduction
Canvas resource site.
Beginning January 1, 2025:
The VoiceThread tool will be available only in Canvas courses in which VoiceThread has been licensed through the IU eText program.
Faculty and students who aren't enrolled in a course with VoiceThread will be able to access their accounts at
https://voicethread.com/
. For more, see
Access VoiceThread outside of Canvas
.
The rest of this article is intended for instructors who aren't planning to use VoiceThread through IU eTexts.
Export VoiceThread content
You don't need to export your content unless you want a video output of your threads to use in a different platform. Otherwise, all of your content is available in VoiceThread format to view and share from within your account.  You can export individual threads (with or without comments and annotations) and download them to a local hard drive or a cloud storage account. Exported threads are saved as
.mov
files, a common video format compatible with
Kaltura
.
To export an entire VoiceThread, including all audio, video, text comments, and annotations, see the VoiceThread support article,
How to export
. Then download the
.mov
file as described in
Downloading an exported VoiceThread
.
To export a VoiceThread without the comments and annotations or with only your own comments, first create a copy and select the desired setting for copying comments as described in
Copying a VoiceThread
. Then follow the instructions above to export and download the copied VoiceThread.
Notes:
Students with free accounts will be charged $2.99 for each export.
Short VoiceThreads take just a few minutes to export, but longer threads can take over an hour. You’ll be notified by email when the export is complete. To view the status of any export, see
Viewing the status of an export
.
Exported VoiceThreads will be available to download for 90 days.
Moderated (hidden) comments are never included in exports.
By default, anyone with whom you have shared a VoiceThread can export it. If you do not want others to export your threads,
edit the settings
for each VoiceThread.
Alternatives to VoiceThread
No other tool available at Indiana University offers the unique combination of presentation and interaction capabilities afforded by VoiceThread. If your courses rely heavily on VoiceThread to facilitate graded or ungraded activities in your course, your best option is ordering VoiceThread through IU eTexts.
If you don’t use VoiceThread intensively enough to justify the additional cost to your students, you can combine other supported technologies to acheive a similar result. Your technology choices will depend on how you use VoiceThread in your course. Below are some of the common ways in which VoiceThread is used and alternative technologies that can achieve a similar result. If you need advice on which options would work best for your classes, contact your
campus teaching and learning center
.
Alternatives for creating multimedia presentations
The focus and centerpiece of all discussion in VoiceThread is a multimedia presentation consisting of any combination of slides, photos, video and audio clips, and documents. In VoiceThread, a

requires the student to watch or listen to a presentation without making comments. The following technologies can facilitate a similar workflow:
PlayPosit

without any interactions. If the bulb is graded, students will receive full points upon viewing the complete presentation. If the bulb is ungraded, use the bulb analytics to track completion.

content:
Table of contents
Overview
Math formats
LaTeX
AsciiMath

Converters

Additional tools
Mathpix Snipping Tool
Overview
A variety of resources are available to help you understand the features of and libraries used by the
math converter tool
. This document includes an overview of math formats, grammar rules (speech styles) for verbalizing math, format converters, and rendering tools.
Math formats
LaTeX
LaTeX is a high-quality typesetting system commonly used for producing scientific and technical documents. Because of its exceptional and well-known support for mathematical notation and complex formulas, its math syntax is widely used in other contexts, such as web pages, markdown documents, and equation editors.
Format:
Expressions start and end with delimiters such as
$…$
,
\(…\)
,
$$…$$
, and
\[…\]
. For example, the Canvas LMS uses
\(…\)
for inline expressions and
$$…$$
for displayed (block) expressions.
Expressions then consist of math terms, operators, and commands, starting with backslashes and using braces for grouping; for example,
\[\frac{a}{b+c}\]
.
Advantages:
Familiar to academics and authors, it's easier to author by hand than MathML. It's supported by MathJax, KaTeX, many markdown processors, equation editors, and to some extent by Microsoft Word.
Accessibility notes:
LaTeX needs to be rendered to MathML for full screen reader support. It's not inherently accessible on its own. Raw LaTeX is typically not meaningfully interpreted by assistive technologies unless first converted into MathML.
Documentation:
Overleaf is an online collaborative writing and publishing platform designed for researchers, students, and professionals.
The Mathematical Expression section
offers a variety of math expressions, templates and examples that are translated into LaTeX formatting.
AsciiMath
AsciiMath is a more human-readable alternative to LaTeX and was designed to be easier to type quickly.
Format:
Some systems (for example, MathJax) use the backtick character as delimiters for AsciiMath expressions:
`…`
. Expressions are generally simpler and shorter than the equivalent LaTeX. Here is the equivalent AsciiMath for the expression used in the LaTeX example above:
`a/(b+c)`
.
Advantages:
AsciiMath is designed to be easier to type quickly.
Accessibility notes:
AsciiMath needs to be rendered to MathML for full screen reader support. It's not inherently accessible on its own.
Documentation:
See
asciimath.org
for details on the syntax and how to use it in web pages with MathJax or the AsciiMath JavaScript file.
MathML
Mathematical Markup Language (MathML) is an XML-based markup language for describing mathematical and scientific content on the web. It's a W3C recommendation and an ISO standard.
When authoring mathematical content for the web, EPUBs, and other digital formats, it's important to understand the distinction between the full MathML specification and
MathML Core
. MathML Core is a focused subset of the larger MathML specification specifically designed for web browser implementation. Unlike the complete MathML3 specification, which was extensive but lacked detailed rendering guidelines, MathML Core prioritizes consistent visual presentation across browsers through clear implementation rules and integration with modern web technologies, such as HTML, SVG, CSS, and DOM.
Limit your mathematical markup to MathML Core features to ensure the widest compatibility for your content across web browsers, e-readers, and other digital platforms that process mathematical expressions.
Format:
MathML is the internal format for representing math expressions in many systems. While MathML is powerful for an internal purpose, it can be difficult to create manually. It's rarely written by hand and most often is generated by conversion tools. It can be recognized by its beginning and ending
<math>
tags; for example:
<math><mfrac><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>
Advantages:
MathML is designed for machine-readability and accessibility.
Accessibility notes:
MathML is directly understood by many assistive technologies, such as screen readers (when supported).
Many libraries and tools exist for converting MathML into other formats such as rendered expressions, speech text, and braille.
MathML is the preferred format for accessible math.
Documentation:
See
www.w3.org/Math
for a comprehensive overview of MathML, its standards, supporting software, and future implementations.
See the
MathML Core
specification for details on authoring MathML that is suitable for browser implementation.
Converters
MathJax
MathJax
is an open-source JavaScript library that processes TeX, LaTeX, AsciiMath, and MathML to render mathematical notation using CommonHTML mode with web fonts, plain HTML-CSS, SVG, and native MathML.
Accessibility notes:
MathJax converts input formats to MathML behind the scenes and applies various heuristics to given MathML to correct for bad practices commonly found from MathML producers.
MathJax can be configured to supply hidden "assistive" MathML for assistive technologies.
MathJax can be configured to enlarge (zoom) math expressions upon a given trigger. Some versions (MathJax 4+) are "self-voicing" and can provide built-in speech access for the print-impaired.
MathJax uses the Speech Rule Engine (SRE) for speech text, braille, and expression navigation features.
The MathJax menu varies across versions and can be difficult for a screen reader user to operate. When manually adding MathJax to a web page, make sure the MathJax configuration provides accessibility support by default.
The MathJax menu allows users to copy equations for use in other applications, such as Microsoft 365 applications, LaTeX, wikis, and other software.
Speech Rule Engine (SRE)
The
Speech Rule Engine
(SRE) is a JavaScript/TypeScript library for generating speech and braille output for mathematical expressions. It can be used in the web browser, as a standalone tool, or as a node module for Node.js. SRE provides extensive browser support not only for translating mathematics into text or braille but also for voicing, navigating, highlighting, and semantically restructuring expressions.
Accessibility notes:
SRE is used internally by MathJax.
SRE provides speech text in the MathSpeak™, ClearSpeak, and ChromeVox styles.
SRE provides braille output using the Nemeth braille and Euro braille codes.
MathCAT
Math Capable Assistive Technology (
MathCAT
) is a library designed to convert MathML notation into speech text and braille, and to provide multiple ways to navigate math for use with assistive technologies. It is intended for use in screen readers, such as JAWS and NVDA, and is under active development.
Accessibility notes:
MathCAT was designed as an open-source replacement for Design Science's MathPlayer. It provides high-quality speech and/or braille output and intuitive yet powerful expression navigation features.
MathCAT provides speech text in the ClearSpeak and SimpleSpeak styles.
MathCAT provides braille output using the Nemeth and UEB braille codes.
MathCAT can provide unambiguous intuitive math speech tailored to user needs.
MathCAT works with content created in MathML, so ensuring that your content is available in MathML format (either directly or through conversion) will make it compatible.
MathCAT provides some support for speaking chemical expressions for MathML generated using the LaTeX
mhchem
package.
Math speech grammars (styles)
A math speech style is a standardized approach to verbalizing mathematical notation through synthesized speech. It's a set of rules and conventions that defines how mathematical expressions are translated from their written form (like MathML or other formats) into spoken words.
Each speech style must address several fundamental challenges:
Structure representation:
How to convey the hierarchical structure of expressions (such as fraction numerators and denominators, exponents, and nested functions)
Ambiguity avoidance:
How to avoid ambiguities (such as announcing where fractions begin and end)
Verbosity control:
Finding the right balance between providing enough information and avoiding overwhelming the listener
Specialized notation:
How to handle specialized mathematical symbols and notations consistently
Prosody:
How pausing, timing, and speech emphasis can be used to aid understanding
The choice of math speech style for users depends on multiple factors, including the user's needs, background, and preferences.
ClearSpeak
ClearSpeak was originally developed through collaboration between Educational Testing Service (ETS) and Design Science (creators of MathPlayer). It aims to make mathematical expressions sound more natural and classroom-like. ClearSpeak was created because the MathSpeak™ speech style did not meet the requirement for classroom-like speech, a major goal being the creation of a new automated synthetic speech style that would better reflect how math is spoken in educational settings.
Accessibility notes:
The implementation of ClearSpeak is not consistent between MathCAT and MathJax.
ClearSpeak does not always produce unambiguous speech for expressions.
The listener must understand how prosody (mainly pauses) is used to communicate structural information and be practiced in interpreting it.
The ClearSpeak style comes in three verbosity levels: Verbose, Medium, and Terse.
The least ambiguous option of the ClearSpeak style is the Verbose implementation provided in MathCAT.
Documentation:
No detailed treatment of the ClearSpeak speech style is available online.
See the MathCAT, MathJax, and Speech Rule Engine documentation for settings information.
MathSpeak™
MathSpeak™ was developed by Abraham Nemeth (creator of the Nemeth Braille Code) and is maintained by SeeWriteHear. It's designed as a standardized way to verbalize mathematical expressions with a focus on precision and unambiguity. It's particularly notable for its relationship to Nemeth Braille, as it was optimized for real-time Nemeth Code transcription by creating a one-to-one mapping of speech to Nemeth Code symbols.
Accessibility notes:
MathSpeak™ may be preferred by users who need precise structural information about complex expressions, especially those who are familiar with Nemeth Braille.
MathSpeak™ is available in MathJax via its use of the Speech Rule Engine.
MathSpeak™ is not currently available in MathCAT (but is planned).
Documentation:
MathSpeak™ Grammar Rules
(SeeWriteHear)
Quick MathSpeak™ Tutorial
(SeeWriteHear)
MathSpeak™ Settings Tutorial
(SeeWriteHear)
SimpleSpeak
SimpleSpeak follows the principle of speaking simple expressions as simply and briefly as possible while using begin/end markers to disambiguate more complicated expressions. It does not attempt to map directly to Nemeth Code or to any other braille system, nor does it attempt to replicate how math is spoken in the classroom.
Accessibility notes:
SimpleSpeak is not recommended for non-visual learners who are beginning to learn math or just learning how to listen to math.
This style is unambiguous for listeners who understand its rules and are competent in interpreting the speech combined with the rules.
SimpleSpeak is available in MathCAT.
This style may be preferred by experienced users who want to listen to math spoken with the fewest words possible.
The listener benefits from understanding how prosody (mainly pauses) is used by SimpleSpeak to help communicate structural information.
Documentation:
No detailed treatment of the SimpleSpeak speech style is available online.
See the MathCAT documentation for settings information.
ChromeVox
ChromeVox refers to the speech rule set originally developed for the ChromeVox screen reader extension for Chrome. This style became the foundation for the Speech Rule Engine (SRE) that is now used with MathJax.
Documentation:
No detailed treatment of the ChromeVox speech style is available online.
See the MathJax and Speech Rule Engine documentation for settings information.

Braille codes
Nemeth Braille Code for Mathematics and Science Notation
The Nemeth Braille Code is a specialized 6-dot braille system developed by Dr. Abraham Nemeth in the 1950s for encoding mathematical and scientific notation. It's primarily used in the United States and other English-speaking countries. It provides a comprehensive system for representing complex mathematical expressions, including algebraic equations, geometric formulas, calculus notation, and scientific symbols, all while maintaining structural clarity. The code uses special indicators and context-sensitive symbols to represent different mathematical operations and structures, making it particularly effective for advanced mathematics.
Documentation:
Nemeth Tutorial
(APH)
Nemeth Code
(Braille Authority of North America)
Unified English Braille (UEB)
Unified English Braille (UEB) is an internationally adopted standard for English-speaking countries that unifies literary and technical braille within a single system. Unlike Nemeth, which is specialized for math and science, UEB handles both general text and technical material consistently. It uses a 6-dot system with specific symbols and indicators for mathematical expressions. UEB Technical outlines how to represent complex math, though its methods differ from Nemeth. UEB was developed to eliminate the need to switch between braille codes when reading text that includes math.
Documentation:
UEB Math Tutorial
(APH)
Unified English Braille
(Braille Authority of North America)
Terminology - UEB Math/Science and UEB with Nemeth
(Braille Authority of North America)
Euro Braille
The Euro Braille output option in the MathJax 4.0+ beta uses a braille mode provided by the Speech Rule Engine (SRE) and is not yet fully documented. Euro Braille might not be a formal braille code standard recognized by international authorities, and instead is a naming convention used uniquely by MathJax and the SRE. Based on analysis of the Unicode braille strings MathJax produces, for Euro Braille it appears to encode parts of the LaTeX source directly into 8-dot braille using ASCII-style mappings. Using 8-dot braille allows for representation of a full ASCII character set, including symbols, and upper and lowercase letters, without ambiguity.
Additional tools
Mathpix Snipping Tool
The
Mathpix Snipping Tool
is a Windows and macOS app that allows rubber-banding any content/image displayed on the screen. It uses AI-powered OCR to process handwritten or typeset math and chemistry. It can output various flavors of LaTeX and MathML that are compatible with the Math Converter tool, Microsoft Word, Canvas, and markdown environments.

Overview
The BitLocker Drive Encryption security feature in Windows protects files on your computer in the event that anyone tampers with the computer's startup process. BitLocker can leverage the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) security hardware to guard data and system files in the Windows operating system directory, and also protects early boot component integrity. Encrypting the entire Windows volume with BitLocker can help prevent others from seeing your files, even if your computer is stolen or a hard disk removed. At Indiana University, BitLocker may provide a useful tool for meeting the requirements for protecting confidential data described in
Protecting Data & Privacy
.
For more about BitLocker, see Microsoft's
BitLocker Drive Encryption Overview
.
When to encrypt
BitLocker Drive Encryption is a Windows security feature that protects your data. BitLocker works best when used with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) version 1.2. A TPM is a chip built into most modern computers. For more about BitLocker, see Microsoft TechNet's
BitLocker Overview
.
Before you set up BitLocker in your department, test the processes you will use first.
Tier 2 Desktop, Server, and Mobility (DSM)
suggests you encrypt a few machines using the guidelines below. To help you become comfortable with BitLocker's processes and settings, the machines should have your most common build.
In all cases, you should follow the institutional, federal, or state guidelines governing the data that may be hosted on the systems or application. See
Classification levels of institutional data
.
For more data protection resources, see
Data Encryption
.
According to
Mobile Device Security Standard (IT-12.1)
, any laptop or notebook computer used by faculty, staff, affiliates, or student employees to access, store, or manipulate institutional data must have full disk encryption.
Although IT-12.1 does not specifically address desktop machines, you should encrypt the drives on desktops when possible.
Cyber Risk Mitigation Responsibilities (IT-28)
and
Security of Information Technology Resources (IT-12)
cover topics specific to servers; for more, see
Protecting Data & Privacy
.
Note:
You can use BitLocker on a bare metal server with a TPM version 1.2 or later. UITS is currently investigating BitLocker support in the II environment.
Tools needed
To effectively manage BitLocker in an Active Directory environment, you will need to download the Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT) package from Microsoft. Specifically, you will need the Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) and Group Policy Management (GPM) tools.
Be sure to include the BitLocker Recovery Password Viewer after installing RSAT. To do so:
Open the Control Panel.
Choose
Turn Windows features on or off
.
Expand
Remote Server Administration Tools
, then
Feature Administration Tools
, and then
BitLocker Drive Encryption Administration Utilities
.
Select
BitLocker Recovery Password Viewer
.
Choose
OK
or
Next
(depending on the OS) to start the installation.
Supported configuration
Operating Systems:
Windows 10
/
Windows 8.1
Ultimate and Enterprise editions, /
Windows Server 2012
Trusted Platform Module (TPM):
1.2 or higher
BIOS/UEFI:
Must be compatible with TPM
Partitions:
Must be two hard drive partitions; Windows desktop standard installation will automatically set this configuration.
To use BitLocker on the Windows Surface tablet, see
Encrypt your Surface tablet using BitLocker
.
Turn on a TPM
Before you can manage BitLocker with a TPM, you must enable the TPM in the BIOS/UEFI:
Windows 11
The TPM is enabled automatically and cannot be disabled. To clear the TPM:
From the
Start
menu, type
tpm.msc
and press
Enter
.
In the right pane, choose
Clear TPM...
and follow the instructions to have it reset. This will result in a restart.

Enter
.
In the right pane, choose
Prepare the TPM
, which will require restarting and agreeing to modify the BIOS/UEFI settings during boot. If that option is unavailable, choose
Clear TPM...
and follow the instructions to have it reset. This will result in more than one restart.
After returning to the desktop, you will receive a message that the TPM is ready for use. If you wish, you can save the TPM owner password by selecting
Remember my TPM owner password
and saving the
.tpm
file to a secure location; see the
Save recovery keys
section below.
For cmdlets for enabling a TPM via PowerShell command line, see
TrustedPlatformModule
.
TPM recovery information is different than the BitLocker recovery information. TPM recovery information can be backed up when you:
Set the TPM owner password during TPM initialization
Change the TPM owner password
When to use a PIN as two-factor authorization
As a local UITS support person, you should follow the institutional, federal, or state guidelines governing the data that may be hosted on your systems or application. See
Classification levels of institutional data
.
Machines storing any data above the IU data classification of Public should use a PIN with TPM in addition to encrypting the drive with BitLocker. This can provide a two-factor option for your system.
You may also use a PIN if you do not have TPM; see
Enable BitLocker without a TPM
.
If you are not using Folder Redirection, Offline Files, or running third-party backup software on your clients, consider investigating these options before encrypting your data. It is always wise to back up the data before you encrypt the drive.
Manage BitLocker using Group Policy (PIN optional)
Note:
Tier 2 DSM
recommends
enabling the TPM
before you apply the GPO changes below.
These are the standard settings for domain-joined machines that are using a TPM. Also listed are optional settings to allow two-factor authentication or devices that do not support TPM.
Changing the encryption method and cipher strength will not harm machines that are already encrypted or are in the process of encrypting.
Open the Group Policy Management Console tree and navigate to:
Computer Configuration > Local Computer Policy > Administrative Templates >
Windows Components > BitLocker Drive Encryption
The following options need to be enabled and modified in their respective folders:
Root folder of BitLocker Drive Encryption
Enable
Choose drive encryption method and cipher strength (Windows...)
and select AES 256-bit.
Enable
Choose drive encryption method and cipher strength
and select AES 256-bit.
Enable
Store BitLocker recovery information in Active Directory Domain Services (Windows Server 2008...)
.
Enable
Choose how users can recover BitLocker-protected drives (Windows Server 2008..)
.
Fixed data drives
Enable
Enforce drive encryption type on fixed data drives
and set the encryption type to
Full
.
Enable
Choose how BitLocker-protected fixed drives can be recovered
and ensure
Save BitLocker recovery information to AD DS
is checked.
Operating system drives
Enable
Enforce drive encryption type on operating system drives
and set the encryption type to
Full
.
Enable
Choose how BitLocker-protected operating system drives can be recovered
and ensure
Save BitLocker recovery information to AD DS
is checked.
Optional:
If you wish to use two-factor authentication, or the device does not have a TPM, enable
Require additional authentication at startup
for both entries, and configure the settings as necessary.
Removable data drives (optional)
If you decide to use or allow BitLocker encrypted removable drives, it's a good idea to enable
Choose how BitLocker-protected removable drives can be recovered
so that the keys are also stored in Active Directory.
Finally, select the
Scope
tab on the GPO itself. Under
Security Filtering
, you will want to make sure that the device (or security group the device belongs to) is listed.
Important:
If you don't complete these steps before encrypting the laptop, the recovery key will not appear in the Active Directory.
Enable BitLocker with a TPM
Requiring a PIN (optional)
If Group Policy was configured to require a PIN, you will need to run a few commands on the client to finalize the process. These commands will work on
Windows 11
,
Windows 10
, and
Windows 8.1
.
Open an elevated command prompt.
Run the following command:
manage-bde -protectors -add c: -TPMAndPIN.
To ensure the TPMAndPin protector has been added, run the following command:
manage-bde -status
Under
Key Protectors
, you will see
TPM and PIN
.
Windows 11
/
Windows 10
/
Windows 8.1
From the
Start
menu, type
Manage BitLocker
and select the top result.
In the new window, choose
Turn on BitLocker
. You can now determine if a PIN is necessary; otherwise, select
Let BitLocker automatically unlock my drive
.
On the following screen, you will want to print the recovery key, or store the
.txt
file in a secure location; see the
Saving recovery keys
section below.
On the next screen, UISO recommends encrypting the entire disk (not just the used space) for added security measures.
On the next screen, choose
New encryption mode
unless
the drive is removable and may need to be accessed using
Windows 8.1
or
Windows 10
version 1507. In that case, choose
Compatible mode
.
On the final screen, BitLocker will run a final system check. A restart will be required, and the encryption process will begin. This process could take several hours to complete, but it will run in the background so work can continue.
To enable BitLocker with TPM via Windows command line, see Microsoft TechNet's
BitLocker: Use BitLocker Drive Encryption Tools to manage BitLocker
(for
Windows 11
,
Windows 10
, and
Windows 8.1
).
You cannot enable BitLocker via Group Policy. The BitLocker settings you can apply to systems via GPO simply dictate the options BitLocker will use or allow when it is enabled.
Enable BitLocker without a TPM
If your computer was not manufactured with TPM version 1.2 or later, you can create a BitLocker startup key using a USB flash drive to store the encryption and decryption keys. You will have to insert the flash drive each time you start the computer.
You also have the option of creating a startup personal identification number (PIN) of four to 20 digits. You can create either the startup key or the startup PIN, but not both. The PIN is stored on your computer. You will have to type the PIN each time you start the computer.
To enable:
From the
Start
menu, type
Manage BitLocker
and select the top result.
From the management window, select
Turn On BitLocker
. This will only appear with the operating system volume.
On the following screen, choose
Require Startup USB Key at every startup
. This is the only option available for non-TPM configurations. This key must be inserted each time before you start the computer.
Insert your USB flash drive in the computer, if it is not already there.
Choose the location of your USB flash drive, and then select
Save
.
On the next screen, you will be able to save or print the key. Be sure to do so in a secure location (see the
Saving recovery keys
section below).
After continuing, you will be required to restart. Upon returning to the desktop, BitLocker will begin encrypting the drive.
Enable BitLocker (non-domain joined with TPM)
For machines that are external to the IU network or cannot be joined to the Active Directory domain, you can still use BitLocker to encrypt the drive.
Back up the key manually
The commands listed below are compatible with
Windows 11
,
Windows 10
, and
Windows 8.1
.
Backup key
To generate a key file, which can be placed on a USB drive to bypass the manual entry of the key, run the following command in an administrative command prompt (replacing
c
with your drive letter):
manage-bde -protectors -add c: -recoverykey c:
This command will generate a
.bek
file to the root directory of the chosen driven (in the example it was
c:\
).
Back up BitLocker recovery information manually to Active Directory
Run the following commands in an administrative command prompt to manually add the recovery information to the computer object in AD:
manage-bde -protectors -get c:
manage-bde -protectors -adbackup c: -id {numerical password ID from step 1}
Encrypt hard disk and external drives
Encryption of removable media is possible with BitLocker. The recovery key can be stored inside the computer object in Active Directory that was responsible for the encryption; see the
Manage BitLocker using Group Policy
section above.
From the
Start
menu, type
Manage BitLocker
and select the top result.
If a removable drive is connected, it should appear under "BitLocker To Go", with a
Turn On BitLocker
link. After selecting the link, you have two options (depending on any restrictions that may have been applied with Group Policy):
Use a password to unlock the drive
is the most commonly used (and recommended) method. After choosing a password, you can save the recovery key to a file, or print it.
Use my smart card to unlock the drive
requires the PC smart card to decrypt the drive. This option requires an additional piece of hardware.
View the recovery keys
View the key in Active Directory
IU's Active Directory allows the storage of BitLocker recovery information for your BitLocker encrypted devices, including the required schema updates.
Tier 2 DSM
recommends storing the keys in Active Directory as a disaster recovery option. The recovery password is stored with the computer object as a confidential attribute viewable only to the OU administrators, UISO, and the domain administrators.
Note:
For this to work, you must first follow the directions in the
Manage BitLocker using Group Policy
section above.
The AD object containing the key that can recover a BitLocker-encrypted volume in Active Directory is
m-RecoveryInformation
; this is attached to the computer object. To view the AD object:
Open Active Directory Users and Computers.
Choose
View
and select
Users, Groups, and Computers as containers
.
Browse through the Active Directory tree until you find your computer object.
Select your computer object; you will see
msFVE-RecoveryInformation
.
In the right pane, right-click the object type
msFVE-RecoveryInformation
.
Security groups with full control to
msFVE-RecoveryInformation
can see the recovery key in the BitLocker recovery tab in Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC). By default, this is the OU Admins group. You can delegate full control to the object on your sub-OU to a group to allow help desk access to the recovery passwords.
If the computer is moved to a new OU,
msFVE-RecoveryInformation
is moved with the computer object.
Note:
If you join the machine to ADS and forget to pre-create the machine account, the recovery key is not visible to others within the Computers OU. However, all local UITS support people can move the object to their OU, and they would receive the ability to view the key. Moving the machine to your departmental OU is best practice.
To view the key on the local machine, open an administrative command prompt and run the following command:
manage-bde -protectors c: -get
Replace
c:
with the encrypted drive letter.
You will see output in this format:
BitLocker Drive Encryption: Configuration Tool version 6.2.9200
Copyright (C) 2012 Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
Volume C: [OSDisk]
All Key Protectors
TPM:      ID: {37CE71B7-8FE4-4CA9-9637-42516F599C02}
Numerical Password:    ID: {31514A2F-147C-478C-B6A2-618CD6F66653}
Password:
249238-002442-716694-646503-010879-234894-155485-185372
Note:
There is a top-level BitLocker policy that is applied to all machines (unless Block Inheritance is enabled) that will allow UISO to potentially recover the drive data if no other option exists (for example, if no one in your department has the rights to see the BitLocker key). However, the BitLocker key must have been previously escrowed. That policy in and of itself does not escrow the BitLocker key. Drives encrypted before April 26, 2015, will not inherit the policy. For drives encrypted before this date, you'll need to back up the key manually.
UITS staff and local UITS support people:
See
Back up the key manually
.
Verify that a key has been escrowed
Even if the account you're using doesn't have access to view the recovery key directly, you still can verify that the device's BitLocker key is escrowed.  In Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC), in the entry for the device, check the
Bitlocker Recovery
tab.  You'll see one of the following results:
Key not escrowed:
"No Items in this view. To search for a recovery password, right-click on the domain object in tree view, and select 'Find Bitlocker Recovery Password...'"
Key escrowed, but the viewer does not have rights to see the key:
"Cannot retrieve recovery password information. Cannot get the password attribute of a recovery password record. Make sure you have sufficient permission to access the recovery password."
Key escrowed and viewer has rights to see the key:
The date added and password ID will be visible, and the details section will be filled in, including the recovery password (typically eight sets of six digits).
View the key in Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory)
IU's Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory or AAD) syncs BitLocker keys from Active Directory as another recovery option. The recovery password is stored with the computer object as a confidential attribute.
To view the key in Entra ID:
Go to
Entra ID
>
Devices
.
If you have the BitLocker key ID:
Choose
BitLocker keys (Preview)
.
Enter the BitLocker key ID.
Find the machine and click
Show Recovery Key
.
If you have the device name:
Search for the device by name and select it.
Find the BitLocker key ID.
Choose
Show Recovery Key
.
Save recovery keys
Recovery keys are essentially hardware passwords. During the beginning of the encryption process, you are required to either generate a file containing the key, or print the key. UITS strongly recommends that you keep the keys in a secure location, such as a password vault. KeePass is a free utility that can meet this need.
Tips and troubleshooting
Suspend BitLocker before making major system configuration changes. If you need to update the BIOS/UEFI, modify the boot order, or make any other major changes, suspend BitLocker first or you may be prompted for the 48-digit recovery key.
Be sure to back up any critical information before encrypting or decrypting a drive. Encryption can be rough on physical media, especially older drives.

title: Fulfill common accommodations related to digital materials
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Alternative format text
Textbook conversions
PDF content
Large print
Print-only
Braille
Tactile graphics
Audio description
Closed captioning
Live captioning (CART)
Notetaking
Permission to record
Additional resources
Overview
The
Assistive Technology and Accessibility Centers
(
ATAC
) at Indiana University provide a wide range of services for qualifying students, faculty, and staff with disabilities, as well as comprehensive course accessibility evaluation, consulting, presentations, and training for the IU community.
The
Assistive Technology and Accessibility Centers
(
ATAC
) specializes in sourcing and creating alternative formatted media that provide the highest levels of accessibility and usability for students with authorized alternative media accommodations.
While every instructor should attempt to meet
minimum digital accessibility guidelines for course content
, an instructor also may receive a course accommodation memo from their campus Accessible Educational Services (AES) office detailing a student's need for digital course materials to be made further accessible.
This page covers each type of accommodation related to digital material that an instructor might receive. For information related to pedagogy, group work, student presentations, or teaching strategies, consult your campus
AES office
. If you have received a notification with more than one of the accommodations listed on this page, you will need to look at each relevant entry. To receive a consultation on how to request the appropriate services, submit the
Accessibility Consultation
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
. Also via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
, anyone at IU may submit the
Canvas Course Accessibility Review
request form.
Alternative format text
The alternative format text accommodation indicates all classroom materials and exams must be provided to the student, if desired, in an alternative format prior to use. This can include print copies, ePub, braille, and tactile graphics.
All course documents must be provided in an accessible format. Instructors should use
Ally
to evaluate their course materials on Canvas and make any of the recommended changes to those documents.
Providing alternative formats to some students with accommodations does not fulfill the need to ensure materials meet the
minimum digital accessibility guidelines for all students
. Handwritten materials (whether scanned, on a board, or on an overhead), materials shown via camera during a videoconference, and materials displayed with a projector in-person are all examples of material that do not meet the accessibility standard on their own. Ways to make these types of content accessible include giving thorough descriptions during a presentation, recording a presentation so that additional descriptions can be added later, and providing the same content in a Microsoft Word document, on a Canvas page, or in Pressbook format.
Textbook conversions
Students with an alternative format text accommodation will automatically receive a Bookshare account and a link to approved readers. Bookshare is a collection site for accessible textbooks. Students also can submit the
Alternative Format Textbook
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
for any textbooks they cannot find as an ePub on Bookshare, or for textbooks they need in either physical large print or braille format.
Note:
After a student determines what textbooks are needed for their courses, it may take 10 weeks for them to get the first chapter of an alternative version. Because IU eTexts are not listed on the IU Bookstore website, instructors need to provide the textbook's title and ISBN number to the student listed in the accommodation memo.
PDF content
Students with an alternative format text accommodation also may need PDF content remediated. If you have a PDF that is not available through the IU library, and you do not have access to the source document (Word file), you can either create or request an alternative format through Ally in Canvas.
To improve the accessibility of the PDF yourself, see
Improve the accessibility of PDF documents in Canvas
.
To request PDF remediation from the
ATAC
:
Locate the item in your Canvas course.
Select the dial icon in front of the item.
Select
How to tag a PDF
.
Answer the series of questions presented.
At the end of the workflow, select
Help
.
In the text box provided, indicate that you need an accessible copy of the item.
Select
Send
.
The request will be routed to the
ATAC
for processing. If the item is not available in the IU library system, proof of legal access may be requested to fulfill the request. Scanned documents submitted for remediation should follow the recommendations listed in
Create a high-quality document scan
.
PDF remediation can take up to four weeks to complete.
Large print
The large print accommodation indicates that instructors must provide classroom materials, if desired, in a large print format at the font size specified in the accommodation memo. If possible, send presentation files to the student so that they can be opened on a personal computer and magnified.
Students who have this accommodation are automatically added to the ZoomText reservation list. For assistance with printing large font, across pages, or at a magnified scale using
tabloid printing
, contact your campus
Support Center
or
teaching and learning center
.
Print-only
Students who have a print-only accommodation are not able to endure prolonged screen use and will need to print out all digital materials. Since students with this accommodation can print materials on their own, instructors need only provide digital course materials to the student far enough ahead of time to give the student time to print them.
Braille
Braille is a system that conveys information using raised dots on specialized paper so it can be read by the fingers.
An alternative format text accommodation indicates a student is eligible for braille services, but it does not indicate whether a student will be able to, or want to, use braille for your exams or in-class materials. Check with the student and the
AES office
to clarify what will be needed in braille (for example, math, foreign language, chemistry, music, exams, and/or presentation printouts).
If braille services are needed, submit the
Accessibility Consultation
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
), and follow the directions in
Request braille and tactile graphics for approved accommodations
.
Note:
Braille requests require a 10-week lead time for in-class materials and a four-week lead time for exams. Submissions must already be digitally accessible. Canvas Quizzes (if requested in print format) must be converted to another document type before submission. In situations where circumstances, such as late enrollment, have made the lead time impossible to meet, make sure to discuss alternatives with the campus
AES office
while the braille versions of your materials and/or exams are being produced.
Tactile graphics
Tactile graphics make use of specialized paper to produce raised images that can be felt with the fingers; they often accompany braille or large print.
An alternative format text accommodation indicates a student is eligible for tactile graphics, but it does not indicate whether the student will want them for your class. If your course uses images that contain unique shapes (for example, graphs with unpredictable curves), images that will be heavily explored (for example, a flowchart or technical drawing), or images that are representative of other images they will come across in the class (for example, an introductory Venn diagram), you may need to submit those images for tactile graphic production.
Check with the student and
AES office
to determine whether tactile graphics will be useful to the student. If tactile graphic services are needed, submit the
Accessibility Consultation
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
, and follow the directions in
Request braille and tactile graphics for approved accommodations
. During your consultation with
ATAC
, you will receive more information about how to submit an image for tactile graphic production.
Note:
Tactile graphics requests require a 10-week lead time for in-class materials and a four-week lead time for exams. Submissions must include alt text or accompanying descriptions (and/or slide titles for PowerPoint presentations) so the student can have a way to connect the tactile references with the appropriate course materials. In situations where circumstances, such as late enrollment, have made the lead time impossible to meet, make sure to discuss alternatives with the AES office.
Audio description
The audio description (AD) accommodation is also called "verbal description of visual content". It involves verbalizing visual content, such as videos, images, and whiteboard drawings, in a way that conveys the essential elements to the listener.
The amount of AD needed is dependent on the complexity of the visuals in a presentation or video. This may be provided by the instructor as an explanation during a presentation, by an in-class sighted assistant, or by a supplier service through the
ATAC
. To request video description for videos that cannot be understood purely through listening to the audio, submit the
Audio Description for Video
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
.
Note:
Video description can take up to one week to produce.
Closed captioning
All videos required for a course must contain completely accurate captioning. The automated captioning provided by services such as YouTube, Vimeo, and Kaltura are not sufficient to fulfill this requirement.
If you receive a closed captioning accommodation, submit the
Accessibility Consultation
request form via the
IT Accessibility Service Catalog
so that
ATAC
staff can review your video content and explain the process.
Note:
Closed captioning can take up to five business days to produce.
Live captioning (CART)
Live captioning, or Communication Access Realtime Translation (CART), is the real-time display of spoken dialog for a synchronous classroom setting (in-person or via a videoconferencing platform). The captioner is usually a trained stenographer who joins the class via video and provides the captions through the student's laptop or mobile device.
The live captioning accommodation indicates that virtual synchronous or in-person course lectures must have transcriptions available in real time. To request live captioning, contact your campus
AES office
directly for scheduling.
Note:
Live captioning can take a week or more to schedule for your course.
Notetaking
The notetaking accommodation indicates that copies of class notes from a peer must be made available to the student unless the notes are posted by the instructor to Canvas.
Permission to record
The permission to record accommodation indicates that the student is allowed to record class lectures and discussions using approved software (
Genio Notes
, smart pen, or OneNote). The student may not share the recordings with other students. Sharing recordings would result in the removal of this accommodation; using direct quotes would be considered plagiarism and subject to referral to the Office of Student Conduct. When students have this accommodation, they also are eligible for notetaking tools, such as Genio Notes, and technical training.
Additional resources
IU Expand
courses:
Creating an Accessible Syllabus using Microsoft Word
Creating Accessible Documents at Work
Improving the Accessibility of Your Canvas Course
Teaching Online Series
(Module 8 is about accessibility)
Ally documentation:
Ally instructor guide
Ally alternative formats for students
General accessibility documentation:
Accessibility resources at IU

title: About the port group upgrade in IU's Intelligent Infrastructure environment
content:
During the first quarter of 2020, as a follow-up to the
Intelligent Infrastructure stretched cluster
project, the UITS Storage and Virtualization (SAV) team will enable additional security enhancements to the distributed port groups to align with current VMware best practices.
The specific change depends on the original port group configuration; the majority of the changes involve disabling
MAC Address Changes
,
Forged Transmits
, and
Promiscuous Mode
. These features historically were required for certain older load balancers and clustered workloads. Most modern load balancers and clustered workloads do not require these features.
To minimize potential operational impact of the change:
On December 30, 2019, the SAV team created new port groups that use the new settings and denoted pre-existing port groups with settings that don't meet the updated standard by appending
-Legacy
to their names. For example, an existing port group named
DPortGroup-VLAN-123
would be relabeled
DPortGroup-VLAN-123-Legacy
(with all of its settings remaining the same), and a new
DPortGroup-VLAN-123
port group would be created with the new, hardened security settings.
Targeted email notification was sent to VM owners of the deprecated port groups. The message included directions to self-service port group migrations during their scheduled maintenance windows.
The SAV team is providing a self-service tool to enable bulk updates to multiple VMs at a time. To help VM admins with multiple VMs, the SAV team has published a PowerShell script that lets you identify and control the VM network adapter port group changes. It creates a
CSV
file containing the VM network adapters that need port group updates. VM admins can edit the CSV file, and the script will programmatically update the indicated VM network adapters instead of requiring VM admins to manually log into the GUI to make each change.
Download the bulk update PowerShell script from GitHub:IU
(log in with your
IU username
and
passphrase
).
Note:
To run the script, your workstation must be connected to the IU network, and have the
VMware.VimAutomation.Core
PowerCLI module and the PowervRA PowerShell module installed.
Before March 1, 2020, organizations should update each NIC on any of their VMs that are attached to a legacy port group:
To check whether your organization has any VMs attached to a legacy port group,
log into vRealize Automation (vRA)
and
request a VM information report
. This creates a CSV file containing all the VMs belonging to your organization. Check the "VLANs" column for any port groups marked with
-Legacy
.
For any VMs attached to a legacy port group, use the
Change NIC (Add, Change, Remove)
action in vRA (see
Interact with a VM in the Intelligent Infrastructure (II) self-service portal
) to update each NIC to the corresponding new port group. For example, if your VM is using
DPortGroup-VLAN-9999-Legacy
, switch to
DPortGroup-VLAN-9999
. This may occur with the VM powered on.
Note:
SAV recommends that you test the migration with pre-production systems first, and then perform the modifications during a scheduled maintenance window.
A small percentage of workloads (particularly, some load balancers) may require non-standard port group configurations to function as expected. If you encounter issues after migrating to a new port group, use the
Change NIC (Add, Change, Remove)
action to reconfigure the NIC(s) back to the legacy port groups and restore functionality, and then email the SAV team at
sav-request@iu.edu
with the VM name, the service(s) running on the VM, a description of the issues you are experiencing, and the name of VLAN that requires the exception. SAV will work with you to create a purpose-built exception port group for your workload.
At 12:01am on March 1, 2020, any VMs that have not been migrated off legacy port groups will be migrated automatically by the system. On March 4, 2020, all legacy port groups will be removed from the II environment.

title: About the IUIE (Indiana University Information Environment)
content:
Table of contents
Overview
General information and support
IUIE access and login information
Navigating and searching the IUIE
IUIE catalogs
Reporting in the IUIE
Mailing functions
IUIE publishers
Data managers
Overview
The Indiana University Information Environment (IUIE) is a centrally maintained, enterprise-wide, web-based operational reporting environment. It provides a collection of reports, tools, and information to assist the university in providing access to
institutional data
. In the IUIE, a developer creates a report object, and then it becomes available to all authorized IUIE users.
Note:
All IUIE users can see all the report objects in the Master Catalog, but not all users have access to all objects. For more, see

title: Developer tools: Web Framework hosted brand and search assets
content:
Important: SiteKube is replacing Sitehost. For more, see About SiteKube . Table of contents Overview Branding requirements Branding header Footer Search Use the branding header, footer, and search Asset types Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) assets JavaScript assets Static HTML assets Asset location HTML sites Asset implementation Making alterations to the brand assets Page boilerplate Footer Implementation examples Hosted assets Global CSS Global JS GitHub repositories Overview Developers must follow all branding requirements when building and maintaining IU sites. Developers can use a predefined set of CSS components and Javascript functionality by pointing to global assets. Anything you see in the page parts is included in these global assets. Note: This article is about assets that developers can use to create IU-branded content outside of the WCMS. Using these assets is no longer recommended, and they will be retired in summer 2027. Instead, use the Rivet Design System for creating websites and web applications if they're outside of the WCMS. If you need the assets described below, such as for an existing site, continue reading. Branding requirements If you have a school, program, department, affiliated unit, or other official IU site, you must have the branding header (also called the branding bar) and footer on each page. Search is an optional component. All branding bars must extend across the page, and the name of the university or campus should function as a link to its home page. No other graphics, text, or features can be added to the branding bars without approval from University Communications and Marketing (UCM). Branding header The header branding bar features the Block IU in a red bar and goes at the top of every page of your website. Each campus has its own branding bar, but only the name and link change. These centrally hosted static HTML elements can be accessed by using a specific URL . Footer The branding footer should feature the IU trident with links to accessibility information, the College Scorecard, the site's privacy notice, and copyright. If you have an IU Web Framework site or your site points to the global brand footer, your site should automatically update. If you have a Web Framework site that does not utilize server-side includes, you may need to republish your site to receive the update. To see if your Web Framework site uses includes, check the Settings block . Search The IU search function appears as a small white magnifying glass within the branding header. When users click on it, the Google Programmable Search box opens. The search box assets are also centrally hosted. However, you may need additional configuration to correctly implement the search function on your site. Use the branding header, footer, and search To learn more about the assets that make up the branding header, view the asset types section. For more information about where these branding assets are located, view the asset location section. For instructions on how to implement these assets within your website, view the implementation section. If you would like to use the global IU Framework CSS and JS assets within your website, check out those instructions in the global CSS and JS section. Asset types The branding assets found in the branding package are divided into the following types: Cascading Style Sheets: These contain Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) code to describe the look and format of the branding elements. JavaScript file: This file contains JavaScript code that enables search interaction and Google search implementation for the site. Static HTML elements: These elements contain HTML markup code for rendering branding elements on the page. Cascading Style Sheet (CSS) assets The branding package includes the following pre-compiled Cascading Style Sheets: brand.css: This CSS file contains styles to format the header and footer elements on the HTML page. search.css: This CSS file contains styles to format the search box and results on the search results page of the site. JavaScript assets The branding package contains only one JavaScript file: search.js . This file contains JavaScript functions to implement search toggle and Google Custom Search implementation for the site. Static HTML assets The static HTML elements provide the markup code to render the header and footer assets on the page. The static HTML files available in the branding package are listed below. Header The header element contains the HTML markup that renders the trident and the campus name for your site. The branding package includes header elements to support all the IU campuses. The naming convention followed is the linking of the word header with the campus name. For example, the Indiana University Bloomington header is the file named header-iub.html . The table below describes the list of headers that have been built and are available through the branding package. Branding header assets File name Campus Domain name header-iu.html Indiana University iu.edu header-iub.html IU Bloomington bloomington.iu.edu header-iue.html IU East east.iu.edu header-iuk.html IU Kokomo kokomo.iu.edu header-iun.html IU Northwest northwest.iu.edu header-iui.html IU Indianapolis indianapolis.iu.edu header-ius.html IU Southeast southeast.iu.edu header-iusb.html IU South Bend southbend.iu.edu header-iufw.html IU Fort Wayne fortwayne.iu.edu header-iuc.html IU Columbus columbus.iu.edu Footer The footer element contains the HTML markup code required to render the footer on your site. The footer element consists of the tagline, copyright information, and privacy link. Search The search element contains the HTML markup code that describes a search box. The search box is used to accept user input for search implementation. Refer to the Asset location section of this article to learn how to find the assets you need. To learn how to implement these assets, refer to the Implementation section. Asset location IU branding assets are centrally hosted and are available through specific URLs. The URLs needed to brand your website depend on your campus and your version of HTML. HTML sites These assets support sites that are written using HTML5 syntax specifications. You will need to include six URLs to appropriately brand your content. In the header URL below, "*" represents the campus value for your site. Branding assets for HTML5 sites Asset type URL Cascading Style Sheet https://assets.iu.edu/brand/3.3.x/brand.css https://assets.iu.edu/search/3.3.x/search.css JavaScript https://assets.iu.edu/search/3.3.x/search.js Static HTML elements https://assets.iu.edu/brand/3.3.x/header-*.html https://assets.iu.edu/brand/3.3.x/footer.html https://assets.iu.edu/search/3.3.x/search.html Versioning of the assets: The assets are versioned following the convention of major.minor version depending upon the bug fixes or improvements. To avoid confusion related to the usage of the latest versions, URLs are numbered as major version. x . The version is symbolically linked to the latest version on the server. Site widths The branding header and footer elements are set to 1020 pixels. If you have a site that is of a different width, you can still use the header and footer elements. They will just be a little narrower or wider than your content. If you need to match the width of your site, you can add the following CSS rules within your site’s CSS. (Be sure to update with the correct value.) #branding-bar-v1 .wrapper, #footer-v1 .wrapper { max-width: 965px !important; } Asset implementation To implement the header and footer branding assets on your site, you will need to do two things: Point to the brand.css stylesheet Include the header-*.html and footer.html markup elements on your site's pages You may not include tools, social media icons, other links, or anything else in the header, footer, and search branding assets. Making alterations to the brand assets The header, footer, and search brand assets must be implemented as they are unless search is a primary function of your site. If that is the case on your site, you may make limited alterations. No other alterations are allowed. Search The search in the branding bar is optional. For example, if your site doesn't need search, or if your site includes the Google Programmable Search function within the primary content area of your site, you can remove the search functionality by simply not including the search asset and associated script. Implement Google Programmable Search on your site To implement the Google Programmable Search assets on your site, you will need to include a placeholder for rendering the search form in the site header section and initialization for Google Programmable Search. To learn how to customize search results for your website, see Set up a Custom Google Search Engine for your IU website . The elements needed for search implementation are: search.css search.js search.html Search initialization The search module can be initialized using following code. This code can be included in a local file, inline inside the $(document).ready block, or as a standalone script inside the document without being wrapped inside the $(document).ready block. /*! * Site Specific IU Search Init */ var IUSearch = window.IUSearch || {}; var searchOptions = { CX: { site: 'xxxx:xxxx', // Replace this with a site CX value all: 'xxxx:xxxx' // Replace this with campus CX value }, wrapClass: 'row pad', searchBoxIDs: ['search', 'off-canvas-search'] } /* Initialize global search */ IUSearch.init && IUSearch.init( searchOptions ); The search.js file should be included in the document prior to initialization of search code shown above. Search functions in the search.js file implement the Google Programmable Search Engine functions. As shown below, CX values for both the site and campus can be passed during the search initialization. If your site doesn't have a CX ID, refer to the Google search engine documentation to find it. Google Search CX values for a few IU campuses Campus names and corresponding CX values Campus name CX IU 016278320858612601979:ddl1l9og1w8 IU Bloomington 016278320858612601979:w_w23ggyftu IU Indianapolis 016278320858612601979:pwcza8pis6k IU Fort Wayne 014162612540646926707:vjfmkkqguyo Search results page Create a search results page and include the following markup. Remember to replace * with your campus name. This will allow you to toggle between search results for your site and your campus.
Page boilerplate All the elements described above should be included on your page as described in this HTML boilerplate:
Footer The branding footer should feature the IU trident with links to copyright and accessibility information, as well as a link to the site’s privacy notice. If your site does not use the IU Web Framework, update your footer’s markup to use the latest footer markup . Then, update your CSS to include the latest footer CSS. The styles required in this case are all of the selectors which include #footer .tagline (such as #footer .tagline.bicentennial), and they can be found within this CSS file . Please note that the second set of styles with these selectors are within a media query. Update the privacy link in the footer The footer branding element also includes a link to the privacy policy for your site. The link defaults to an index page of the root-level ‘privacy’ folder of the site; virtualhostname/privacy/. To modify this link, use the following javascript code: var newPrivacyURL = 'http://site.iu.edu/privacy.html'; (oldPrivacyURL = document.getElementById('privacy-policy-link')) ? (oldPrivacyURL.href = newPrivacyURL) : ''; Social media icons and tools If you currently house social media channels, quick links, or tools in your header or footer, you must find another place for them after installing the new brand assets. IU Studios has created a solution for sites using a mobile-first framework. We developed a “skirt” area above the footer where these types of links can be housed. You can see it in action on the IU Bloomington home page . Implementation examples The following section describes a few methods that can be used for including IU branding assets on your site. The branding implementation method that will work best for you will depend on your hosting environment, site development technology, and other factors. Examples for sites residing on IU Linux web hosting environment (Sitehost) For sites residing in the IU Linux web hosting environment (Sitehost), the branding assets can be symbolically linked to the gwassets folder and implemented using the following steps. Create a symbolic link to the branding assets folder that is under the account "gwassets" by running the following command: ln -s /groups/gwassets/web gwassets Use a PHP include script or server side include script to include the HTML markup elements that are inside the gwassets folder. To use the PHP include method: In order to avoid using the dot patterns to match the filenames created in the include path, the following lines should be added to the php.ini file. To use the SSI (Server Side Includes): The Apache server allows you to place SSI directives that enable including elements on a HTML page. Here is an example of a Server Side Include statement. Examples for sites requiring a local copy of the branding markup For sites requiring a local copy of the branding markup: Refer to the asset location section to determine the URLs that are appropriate for your site. Create local copies of the contents of the asset files. Copy the source markup and include it in your page as indicated above. Hosted assets This section describes implementing Global CSS and JS. Global CSS You can use the current version of global CSS by including the following in the of your page. Global JS The current version of global JavaScript depends on a custom implementation of Modernizr and jQuery > 2.0. You should include Modernizr in the portion of your page. Using the tags, add the following to the opening tag: src="http://assets.iu.edu/web/1.5/libs/modernizr.min.js" Once you have included Modernizr, you can use the current version of global JavaScript by including the following script. Since the global JavaScript depends on jQuery, you must include this file after your implementation of jQuery. Using the tags, add the following to the opening tag: src="//assets.iu.edu/web/3.3.x/js/iu-framework.min.js" Finally, for global JavaScript to be in initialized, use the following after the global JavaScript file: /*! * Initialize IU JS */ (function($, window, document, undefined) { $(document).ready(function() { Foundation.OffCanvas.defaults.transitionTime = 500; Foundation.OffCanvas.defaults.forceTop = false; Foundation.OffCanvas.defaults.positiong = 'right'; Foundation.Accordion.defaults.multiExpand = true; Foundation.Accordion.defaults.allowAllClosed = true; // Initialize Foundation $(document).foundation(); var IU = window.IU || {}; // Delete modules if necessary // delete IU.uiModules['accordion']; IU.init && IU.init(); }); })(jQuery, window, window.document); GitHub repositories To see the GitHub repositories for the Global CSS and JS, contact the UITS Web team ( webhelp@iu.edu ).

Overview
1Password

Request a 1Password vault
To request a shared 1Password vault for your IU department, fill out the
1Password Vault Creation
form. On the form, you will need to specify an ACM group with
Acceptable Use Agreement
compliance enabled for the vault's Edit group (the people who will have the ability to read, create, edit, and delete passwords in this 1Password vault). Optionally, you can specify an additional ACM group for people who should have read-only access. If different groups need access to separate sets of passwords, you will need to create more than one vault.
Set up 1Password
When group members are added to a 1Password vault, they receive an invitation via email. They then have five days to follow the link in the email to set up their 1Password account.
Important:
To prevent account lockout and the need for account recovery, it is crucial that members sign into 1Password using the desktop application or mobile app in addition to the web browser. This ensures that they can access their accounts if their web sessions expire. Due to 1Password's built-in two-factor authentication, using at least two of the provided options (web browser, desktop application, and/or mobile app) is highly recommended.

title: About organizational units in Active Directory
content:
An organizational unit (OU) is a subdivision within an
Active Directory
into which you can place groups, computers, and other organizational units.
The term "organizational unit" is often shortened to "OU" in casual conversation. "Container" is also often applied in its place, even in Microsoft's own documentation. All terms are considered correct and interchangeable.
At Indiana University, most OUs are organized first around campuses, and then around departments; sub-OUs are then individual divisions within departments. For example, the
BL
container represents the Bloomington campus; the
BL-UITS
container is a subdivision that represents the
University Information Technology Services
(UITS) department on the Bloomington campus, and there are subcontainers below that. This method of organization is not an enforced rule at IU; it is merely chosen for convenience, and there are exceptions.
Some of this information was adapted from
Microsoft support documentation
.
Note:
For help with
Active Directory
, contact your
local UITS support person
.
