title: About non-standard computer approvals at IU
content:
Table of contents
Overview
UA Lifecycle Request form
IT Equipment Order form
Independent orders for computer equipment
Lab instruments purchased with a computer
Overview
IU has created a list of standard computers that can be bought, without the need for approval, through both the Dell and CDW catalogs in the
One.IU
tab of
One.IU
. Since these computer models and configurations are meant to meet the needs of 80%-90% of staff and faculty, there are times when faculty, researchers, developers, video editors, and BI analysts might need computers other than the standard devices in the Dell and CDW catalogs.
To buy a non-standard computer, a request must be submitted and approved. The process is different depending on whether you use one of the existing computer equipment order forms through Endpoint Lifecycle, or if you place the order independently. All three processes are covered below.
UA Lifecycle Request form
The
UA Lifecycle Request
form is used primarily by the UA-VPIT groups to order computer equipment. It provides five standard devices with a standard configuration: an Intel Ultra 5 processor (8C-10C silicon processor for Mac computers), 16GB of RAM, and a 512GB SSD.
If the standard configuration doesn't meet the needs of the person requesting a computer, they can select
Other - none of these above options work for me
to see a list of non-standard devices with the following configuration: an Intel Ultra 7 processor (or 14C-30C silicon processor for Mac computers), 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD.
You can also create a custom computer request. If you select
Custom Request
, a notification will display and provide a link to a KB document that explains the process of going to the IU Dell or CDW catalogs.
If you select
Other - none of these above options work for me
or
Custom Request
, the automated approval workflow will be triggered.
The approval workflow has two steps. In the first step, the request is reviewed by the manager of Endpoint Lifecycle to determine if:
The computer is from an approved supplier (Dell, Apple, or Microsoft).
The model is supported by the EMS team and can be imaged using the IU Common Build or the HTS computer image.
If the computer meets both requirements, it is approved and the ticket moves on to the second stage of approval. However, if the request does not meet the above requirements, the request will not be approved and a suitable alternative will be suggested in an email to the requester. The ticket is then automatically closed.
In the second stage of approval, an email is sent to a director or director-level equivalent of the person the computer has been requested for. The director is asked to approve the device based on the use case and business need for the employee the device has been requested for. The director must then approve or deny the request; if the request is approved, the device is ordered. If the request is not approved, an email is sent to the person who submitted the request stating that the request was not approved, and the ticket is then closed.
IT Equipment Order form
The IT Equipment Order form is used by Health Technology Services (HTS), legacy
UA Technology Support
customers, Executive and Internal Technology Support (EITS) and a few Client Technology Support (CTS)
client
s.
It provides three standard devices with a standard configuration: an Intel Ultra 5 processor (8C-10C silicon processor for Mac computers), 16GB of RAM, and a 512GB SSD. It also provides four non-standard computer models with the following configuration: an Intel Ultra 7 processor (or 14C-30C silicon processor for Mac computers), 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD.
In the first step of a non-standard or custom-computer request approval, the request is reviewed by the manager of Endpoint Lifecycle to determine if:
The computer is from an approved supplier (Dell, Apple, or Microsoft).
The model is supported by the EMS team and can be imaged using the IU Common Build or the HTS computer image.
If the computer meets both requirements, it is approved and the ticket moves on to the second stage of approval. However, if the request does not meet the above requirements, the request will not be approved and a suitable alternative will be suggested in an email to the requester. The ticket is then automatically closed.
In the second stage of approval, an email is sent to the person that is appointed to review computer requests for the department of the person the computer has been requested for (typically a financial officer or administrative assistant). The device is then approved based on that department's policy. If the request is approved, the device is ordered. If the request is not approved, an email is sent to the person who submitted the request stating that the request was not approved, and the ticket is automatically closed.
Independent orders for computer equipment
If a computer is requested and is not listed on the Dell "Standard Configurations" page or the CDW navigation pane of the CDW-G for Indiana University catalog landing page, the requester must fill out the
Non-Standard Device Selection Process form
.
To fill out the Non-Standard Device Selection Process form, you must have local UITS support person credentials. If you don't have local UITS support person credentials, your local IT support person will need to submit this form on your behalf. You will need to provide them with the following:
The manufacturer of the computer.
The model number of the computer, and the configuration (processor, RAM, hard drive, video card, etc.).
The number of computers you would like to purchase with this configuration.
The cost per device.
The use case or business need for why this specific device is needed, and why one of the standard computer models will not suffice.
Lab instruments purchased with a computer
If you are purchasing a lab instrument that includes a computer, you will need to fill out the Non-Standard Device Selection Process form as described
above
. Once you receive approval, attach it to the requisition for the lab instrument. If the approval for the Non-Standard Device Selection Process is not included with the requisition, the lab instrument purchase may be delayed.

title: Technician instructions: IU Common Build Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Steps
Things to consider
Overview
The Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer will create a new AD computer object and place it in an EMS-managed OU at
ads.iu.edu/IU/IU-UEMS/Production/Pre-Configured Systems
. The old AD computer objects will be abandoned and will remain in place but inactive until manually deleted.
This is a rebuild on the machine, while keeping data from user profiles. The data is backed up to a file server during the rebuild, and then placed back on the machine after the build. While the data transfer is very reliable, it is important to do a manual backup of the user's profile as well, as some files may not be saved in traditional locations.
For the upgrade to appear in Software Center, the system must either
either be under the Common Build already or
be added to a collection in SCCM that has been sent to EMS for this purpose. EMS recommends using a collection that contains only devices about to be rebuilt.
Note:
The Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer must be run by a qualified local UITS support person rather than the user. If the logged in user is not a local UITS support person, the rebuild will be visible but will not run.
The upgrade must be performed on a wired connection. It will not succeed if connected to WiFi. If you are going to use a USB network adapter, contact the EMS team to register the USB network adapter in SCCM. If you build a device with USB network adapters that have not been registered in the SCCM console, duplicate devices can appear in the console.
Devices will multiple hard drives are not supported for rebuild with data transfer. If you begin the install on a system with multiple hard drives, it will start but eventually fail.
For an overview of the IU Common Build process, see
Get started with the IU Common Build for Windows
. To install a clean IU Common Build, see
Technician instructions: Clean IU Common Build for Windows
.
Steps
Bookmarks from browsers will
not
be automatically transferred, and you should export the user's bookmarks prior to starting the process. To export bookmarks:
Chrome:
Open Chrome from the user's profile, and select the three dots in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Bookmarks
and then
Bookmark manager
.
In the Bookmark manager, select the three dots in the top right corner of the manager.
Select
Export bookmarks
.
Choose where you want to save the exported bookmarks file and select
Save
.
Microsoft Edge:
Open Edge from the user's profile, and select the three dots in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Favorites
and then
Manage favorites
.
In the Favorites manager, select the three dots in the top right corner of the manager.
Select
Export favorites
.
Choose where you want to save the exported bookmarks file and select
Save
.
Firefox:
Open Firefox from the user's profile, and select the three lines in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Library
and then
Bookmarks
.
In the Bookmarks manager, select
Import and Backup
.
Select
Export bookmarks to HTML
and choose where you want to save the file.
Select
Save
.
Back up files from the following locations:
Userprofile\Appdata\*.pst
EXCLUDED -
Userprofile\*\Sharepoint.pst
(ignores any SharePoint
.pst
files)
Userprofile\Appdata\*\Signatures\
(grabs the user's Outlook signature file)
Userprofile\Appdata\*\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\*Bookmarks*
(grabs bookmarks from the default Google Chrome browser profile)
Userprofile\Appdata\*\Packages\*\MicrosoftEdge\User\Default
(grab a legacy MS Edge browser profile)
Userprofile\Appdata\*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\*Bookmarks*
(grabs bookmarks from the default MS Edge Chromium browser profile)
Userprofile\Desktop\*
Userprofile\Favorites\*
Userprofile\Documents (My Documents)\*
Userprofile\My Pictures\*
Userprofile\My Music\*
Userprofile\My Videos\*
Userprofile\Downloads\*
(sometimes used as a repository)
Program Files (incl x86)\*.enl
(grabs any EndNote libraries that might be stored there)
Start the build process:
Open Software Center.
In Software Center, select
Operating Systems
.
You should see an option that says
Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer
. Select that, and then choose
Install
.
You will see a warning giving you more information about the Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer. Review this, and then select
Install
.
Note:
The rebuild with data transfer does not support an OSD wizard (unlike the clean install from a thumb drive described in
Technician instructions: Clean IU Common Build for Windows
). Legacy devices being rebuilt to common build will automatically land in the "Pre-Configured Systems" OU (
ads.iu.edu/IU/IU-UEMS/Production/Pre-Configured Systems
).
The "Pre-Configured Systems" OU does not allow standard user login. Only Common Build local UITS support people are allowed local login. Move the AD computer object to the correct departmental OU to allow the user to log in.
Use the OU move tool (
\\iu-sccm-cmfs1\UEMS$\Tools\Common Build Device OU Move Tool.exe
) to move devices into the correct OU (see the "Computer object management" section of
IU Common Build: Windows management tasks
). Move the system to
ads.iu.edu/IU/IU-UEMS/Production/
campus
/
site name
/Workstations
.
Once the rebuild is complete, you should meet with the
client
while they first log into the new build.
The initial login may look different, depending on the GPOs linked to the machine's previous OU.
Verify the
client
's data was moved correctly. If not, use the backups you created prior to starting the rebuild process.
Have the
client
try to sign into Outlook.
You may see error indicating the license is not valid. There are a few different solutions for this:
From cmd or PowerShell run the command
dsregcmd /join /debug
.
Restart the machine.
Create a new mail profile.
Import saved bookmarks back into the
client
's browser:
Chrome:
Open Chrome and select the three dots in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Bookmarks
and then
Bookmark manager
.
In the Bookmark manager, select the three dots in the top right corner of the manager.
Select
Import bookmarks
.
Choose the bookmarks HTML file you want to import, and select
Open
.
Microsoft Edge:
Open Edge and select the three dots in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Settings
and then
Profile
.
Select
Import browser data
.
Choose
Bookmarks HTML file
as the data type to import.
Select the
Import
button, and choose the HTML file that contains your exported bookmarks.
Select
Open
to begin the import process.
Firefox:
Open Firefox and select the three lines in the top right corner of the browser.
Select
Library
and then
Bookmarks
.
In the Bookmarks manager, select the
Import and Backup
button.
Select
Import bookmarks from HTML
.
Choose the bookmarks HTML file you want to import, and select
Open
.
Ensure the
client
can sign into any software that they use/need.
Things to consider
The IU Common Build process supports only Dell, Microsoft Surface, and Lenovo ThinkPads manufactured within the past four years.
Be sure to keep open communication with the
client
during this process.
The Windows Wipe and Rebuild with Data Transfer takes some time (as it copies entire contents of the
C:
drive), so it is best to start it overnight, or at a point when the
client
will not need the machine for at least six or more hours.

Overview
Following is information about compiling serial and parallel C, C++, and Fortran programs using the GNU Compiler Collection, the Intel Compiler Suite, the NVIDIA HPC compilers, and the MVAPICH compilers available on
Quartz

Quartz
uses the Lmod module management system to allow users to customize their software environments. For more about Lmod, see
Use modules to manage your software environment on IU research supercomputers
.
GNU Compiler Collection
Set up your user environment
The GNU Compiler Collection (the
gnu
module) is added by default as part of the standard user environment. It includes compilers for C, C++, and Fortran codes:
GNU Compiler Collection
Language
Compile command
Manual page
C
gcc
man gcc
C++
g++
man g++
Fortran
gfortran
man gfortran
With the
gnu
module loaded, the GNU Scientific Library (GSL) numerical library for C and C++ programs is available. To add it to your user environment, load the
gsl
module:
module load gsl
FFTW compiled with GNU and MVAPICH is available if you also load the
openmpi
module. To add both to your user environment, enter:
module load openmpi fftw
Optimize your code
Adding the
-O
option to your compile command enables various optimization flags that tell the compiler to try to improve your code's performance. A higher
-O
level indicates higher optimization, but can add compilation time and potentially alter the semantics of your program:
UITS
recommends using
-O2
or
-03
for production runs:
Optimization level options
Optimization level
Description
-O0
No optimization (this is the default)
-O
or
-O1
These levels are identical; the compiler tries to reduce code size and execution time, but doesn't perform optimizations that take a lot of compilation time.
-O2
This level turns on all
-O1
optimization flags plus others that increase both performance and compilation time.
-O3
This turns on additional optimization flags along with those specified by
-O2
.
Examples
UITS recommends using the
mtune=native
and
march=native
options with the GNU compilers to generate instructions for the machine and CPU type. Compile by default in 64-bit. Add the
-m32
switch to your compile command to compile in 32-bit; add the
-m64
switch to return to 64-bit.
Following are example commands for compiling optimized serial programs with the GNU compilers:
To compile a serial C program (for example,
my_program.c
) and create an optimized executable (for example,
my_program.exe
), on the command line, enter:
gcc -O2 -mtune=native -march=native my_program.c -o my_program.exe
To compile a serial C++ program (for example,
my_program.cpp
) and create an optimized executable (for example,
my_program.exe
), on the command line, enter:
g++ -O2 -mtune=native -march=native my_program.cpp -o my_program.exe
To compile a serial Fortran program (for example,
my_program.f
) and create an optimized executable (for example,
my_program.exe
), on the command line, enter:
gfortran -O2 -mtune=native -march=native program.f -o my_program.exe
To enable support for shared-memory multi-threaded (OpenMP) parallel programs, you must pass the
-fopenmp
flag to the compiler; for example:
gcc -fopenmp my_omp_program.c -o my_omp_program.exe
For distributed-memory examples, see the
MVAPICH compiler
section below.

Quartz

Intel Compiler Suite
Language

Optimize your code
Adding the
-O
option to your compile command enables various optimization flags that tell the compiler to try to improve your code's performance. A higher
-O

Optimization level options
Optimization level
Description
-O1
Optimize for maximum speed, but disable some optimizations that increase code size for a small speed benefit.
-O
or
-O2
These levels are identical. Optimize for maximum speed. This is the default.
-O3
Optimize for maximum speed and enable more aggressive optimizations that may not improve performance on some programs.
-O0
Disable optimizations.
UITS recommends using
-O2
for production runs. You can also try the

Following are example commands for compiling optimized serial programs with the Intel compilers (compile by default in 64-bit):
To compile a serial C program (for example,
my_program.c

my_program.exe

my_program.cpp

my_program.exe

To compile a serial Fortran program (for example,
my_program.f

my_program.exe

ifort -O my_program.f -o my_program.exe
To enable support for shared-memory multi-threaded (OpenMP) parallel programs, pass the
-openmp
flag to the compiler; for example:
icc -O2 -openmp my_omp_program.c -o my_omp_program.exe
For distributed-memory examples, see the
MVAPICH compiler
section.

content:
Table of contents
Overview
Before you begin
Use Guest Mode
Guest Mode vs. anonymous access
Learn more
Get help
Overview
Top Hat Guest Mode allows instructors to conduct polls with participants who are not registered Top Hat students, making it ideal for use in conferences, meetings, training sessions, and similar events. Previously, polling non-Top Hat users required special arrangements with the vendor. However, starting in May 2025, instructors can enable Guest Mode in any Top Hat course without enrolled students, with no special setup needed.
Before you begin
Before attempting to use Guest Mode, keep the following limitations, requirements, and recommendations in mind:
You must have a Top Hat instructor account in order to administer polls with Top Hat Guest Mode. For instructions on creating an account, see
Indiana University - Single Sign-On Account Setup
. IU students are not permitted to create instructor accounts.
You can't use Guest Mode to take attendance or to assign asynchronous content and questions to participants.
You should never use Guest Mode in regular academic courses with enrolled students nor in any course synced with the Canvas Gradebook.
If you use the same Top Hat course and questions at multiple separate sessions, the stored and live on-screen results will be cumulative rather than broken out by session. To avoid this problem, UITS recommends creating a new Top Hat course for each session or event in which you plan to use Guest Mode. This will ensure that the on-screen question results will include only the respondents at the current session.
Alternatively, if you'd prefer to keep all related content in one Top Hat course, store your content in a folder, and create a separate copy of the folder each time you need to present it. As long as you use copies instead of reusing the content in the original folder, the data for each session will be kept separate.
Points are not recorded in the Top Hat gradebook or student manager for guests. However, it is possible to export individual responses by navigating to the desired question in the Gradebook and selecting
Export Responses
. The exported results include the names entered by guests when joining the session.
Faculty participants who are already logged into Top Hat with an instructor account are not able to respond to Guest Mode polls. To participate in the Guest Mode session, they can either:
Go to
app.tophat.com/logout
in their default browser and choose
Yes
. After that, they should be able to access the guest poll via the URL or the QR code.
Open a private/incognito browser tab and go to
app.tophat.com/guest
, then enter the join code.
To view all the content available to you here,
log into the Knowledge Base
near the top of the page.
IU community:
Contrary to the information in the
Guest Mode
article on the Top Hat support site, there are no limits on sessions or enrolled students for Guest Mode at Indiana University. Guest Mode will continue to function regardless of the number of enrolled students or the number of Guest Mode sessions initiated in any given Top Hat course.

title: Protect data in copiers and multifunction devices
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Purchase or lease new equipment
Maintain and protect existing equipment
Determine whether your equipment retains digital data
Inquire about a replacement
Purchase add-on equipment and/or software
Harden the device and develop departmental cleanup policies
Dispose of, transfer, or retire old equipment
Learn more
Overview
Use the information below to help you make appropriate and informed risk-based decisions for handling information contained on office, unit, or departmental copiers and multifunction office devices.
Purchase or lease new equipment
When beginning the search for new equipment, engage and work closely with
IU Purchasing
. They have negotiated contracts with vendors to ensure the university receives the best prices on equipment, as well as additional protection for data processed by the machine, whether by keeping the cache encrypted, securely deleting the cache periodically, or (ideally) not keeping a cache at all.
If you have specific questions about purchasing this type of equipment,
contact IU Purchasing
.
Maintain and protect existing equipment
If your existing copier or multifunction device does not yet need to be replaced, you have several options for maintaining and protecting its data.
UISO
recommends you carefully evaluate the options and choose one commensurate with your perceived risk.
Determine whether your equipment retains digital data
Before you do anything else, determine whether your equipment is actually retaining digital copies on a hard drive. To do this, you may want to contact your sales/leasing vendor, review the manufacturer's website, or consult
IU Purchasing
.
Inquire about a replacement
Contact either
IU Purchasing
or your vendor directly to inquire about replacement equipment. All equipment contracts are different, and you may be able to replace your equipment at no cost to you.
Purchase add-on equipment and/or software
Some vendors or manufacturers produce add-ons to their equipment for additional purchase that either regularly destroy or encrypt the cache copies stored on the equipment's hard drive. This option may be viable if you have a large, expensive piece of equipment that can't be replaced at this time.
Note:
It has been speculated that several manufacturers have contributed to the media frenzy on this subject in an attempt to sell these add-ons. Though discussing options with a vendor is not discouraged, you should consult with
IU Purchasing
before making any final purchasing decisions.
Harden the device and develop departmental cleanup policies
Your best option may be to keep your current equipment and attempt to secure the data within the devices as you go. UISO recommends you take the following steps:
Review all the functionality of the device, decide how it is to be used (or receive that information from others), and harden the configurations. Disable every service and feature except those identified as required on an everyday basis, including how accessible the machine is via the network. Revisit the requirements of the device as often as necessary, because offices are often organic environments with changing needs.
Determine if your make and model of equipment offers a "disable" option with respect to maintaining digital cache copies. If so, disable that option.
If you can't disable the option to maintain digital cache copies, determine whether your equipment allows periodic deletion of this data. Automatic deletion at specific intervals is preferable, but manual deletion will suffice.
If your equipment only allows for manual deletion, determine which person in your office will be responsible for this task. Copiers and related devices have not traditionally been considered IT equipment, so an office manager or other administrative personnel may oversee your equipment.
If a department head wants to learn more before assigning staff hours to this task, see:
Protecting Data & Privacy
About secure data removal
Dispose of, transfer, or retire old equipment
Since it has become public knowledge that copiers and multifunction office devices may contain sensitive personal information, you must handle their disposal carefully. IU already has the following existing resources related to the disposal of hard drives and the secure removal of data, and you should apply the same standards to this type of equipment:
Disposal and Redistribution of University Property (FIN-PURCH-11)
About secure data removal
IU Surplus: Data Security and Computer Disposal or Resale
(IU Bloomington)
Surplus Hard Drive/Data Shredding Program
(IU Indianapolis and regional campuses)
Learn more
For more, see
Auditing and Securing Multifunction Devices
from the SANS Institute Information Security Reading Room.

title: About secure data removal
content:
Table of Contents
IU policy
Simple deletion of data is not enough
Methods of secure deletion
Wiping utilities
Destruction
Degaussing
Destruction of data on paper
Examples
Learn more
IU policy
Before a department may redistribute, sell, or dispose of computing equipment to another entity, all data must be removed from the storage device(s) to comply with
Disposal and Redistribution of University Property (FIN-PURCH-11)
.
Departments must choose and correctly use a tool that performs at least a one-pass
wipe
of the storage device. If a storage device is inoperable or cannot be wiped using an approved tool, your remaining options include degaussing and drive destruction.
Additionally, if a computer or mobile device is viable for reuse or resale, you should follow all guidelines at
Departmental disposal of equipment at IU
before it leaves your department.
Simple deletion of data is not enough
When a file is deleted using the usual methods inherent in an operating system, these methods typically only remove the pointers to the files,
not
the actual files themselves. The data remains on the hard drive as unallocated space and can easily be recovered with readily available tools.
A common misconception is that using system utilities like
fdisk
and reformatting a hard drive will securely delete all data on the hard drive. Like
rm
and
del
, these utilities modify file system attributes but do not remove the actual data.
CD-ROMs, since they are read-only, present a different challenge in that there is no way to programmatically and securely delete the contents of the CD. Inoperable hard drives are also a challenge since they cannot be connected to a system and accessed through software.
Methods of secure deletion
Wiping utilities
Disk wiping is a term used to describe a method that writes a series of ones and/or zeros over the disk to securely remove the data. Since tools that do this have to overwrite the entire disk, this process can be time-consuming.
UISO
has verified that DBAN and the macOS Disk Utility,
if used correctly
, can be successfully used to securely remove data from a disk; for details, see
Securely wipe disk drives
.
Note:
For devices with a solid-state drive (SSD), instead see
Securely erase a solid-state drive
.
Destruction
For media that has contained highly sensitive data or for media that cannot be wiped (for example, inoperable hard drives or DVDs) or degaussed (for example, CD-ROMs), destruction of the media is the most effective means of ensuring that the data cannot be recovered.
In order to be effective, the destruction has to be thorough. For example, a simple whack with a hammer leaves the majority of data on the media readable.
For detailed guidelines for inoperable devices, see
About disposing of failed devices and media containing data
.
Degaussing
Degaussing is a process by which magnetic storage media is subjected to a powerful magnetic field to remove data on the media. It is appropriate for magnetic tape, but is ineffective with optical media such as DVDs and CDs. For guidelines, see
About disposing of failed devices and media containing data
.
Destruction of data on paper
Information classified as
Critical data
, when stored in paper form, must be properly destroyed by shredding. For low-volume paper document destruction, units may consider purchasing a small cross-cut paper shredder. For high volume needs, a document destruction vendor may be the best solution. IU Purchasing currently lists the following contracted vendors for document destruction:
IU Bloomington:
Shredding & Storage Unlimited
Email:
Chrisy Gornall (
chrisy@shreddingunlimited.com)
Website:
Shredding and Storage Unlimited
IU Indianapolis:
GRM Document Management
Email:
Customer service (
indorders@grmdocument.com)
Website:
GRM Customer Service & Sales
Examples
Scenarios and recommendations
Scenario
Recommended action
You have an inoperable hard drive that contains sensitive data.
Since disk wiping can't be used on inoperable drives, physical
destruction
is the best alternative.
You are transferring a computer, which has been used to store FERPA-protected student records, to another user.
Disk
wiping
is the best alternative.
You are transferring a computer to another department on campus. The computer was bought new and used as a public access terminal; it has never maintained sensitive data, but has applications installed on it that were licensed from a software vendor.
Since data storage is not an issue, you can
fdisk
the system and reformat the hard drive, ensuring that any individually licensed software is unusable.
You are transferring a computer, which has been used to store sensitive data, to another department on campus.
Secure disk
wiping
is the best alternative.
Your computer has reached the end of its life and no other IU department wants it.
See:
Disposal and Redistribution of University Property (FIN-PURCH-11)
Sale of Computing Equipment (FIN-PUR-14.1)
Departmental disposal of equipment at IU
Your hard drive containing sensitive data has a mechanical failure, and the manufacturer requests that the drive be returned for replacement under warranty.
Inform the manufacturer that the drive contains sensitive data and you'd prefer not to return it. If the manufacturer insists on return of the damaged drive before sending a replacement, request a formal letter from the manufacturer stating that they will ensure all data is securely removed from the hard drive. If the vendor refuses to comply, purchase a replacement drive and destroy the damaged disk using one of IU's destruction services (see
About disposing of failed devices and media containing data
).
You have a very large volume of media to be retired that contains sensitive data.
IU Purchasing
can contract with a professional shredder company to come to campus and shred the media. When finished, they will provide a certificate of destruction.
You are replacing an old smartphone.
Remove all data from smartphones, tablets, and other mobile devices that have been used to access, store, or manipulate institutional data. See:
Secure your Android OS device
Secure your iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch
You may have sensitive data cached in your office copier or multifunction device.
See
Protect data in copiers and multifunction devices
.
Learn more
To learn more, see the following policies and documents:
Disposal and Redistribution of University Property (FIN-PURCH-11)
Sale of Computing Equipment (FIN-PUR-14.1)
NIST Special Publication 800-88: Guidelines for Media Sanitization
Effectively Erasing Files
, US-CERT National Cyber Awareness System Security Tip (ST05-011)

title: IU Data Center Access Control Policy
content:
Table of contents
Overview
1.0 Scope
2.0 Purpose
3.0 Responsibility
4.0 Communication of policy
5.0 Categories of access
6.0 Faculty, staff, and student access
7.0 IU affiliate access
8.0 Daily access
9.0 Visitor/tour access
10.0 Card visibility
11.0 Conduct of authorized users
12.0 Data Center Access Review Board
Overview
Due to the sensitive nature of the data and information systems maintained within its facilities, security and access are important aspects of the Office of Vice President for Information Technology/University Information Technology Services (OVPIT/UITS) environment. In most cases, Indiana University is contractually and legally obligated to limit access to only those who have IT responsibilities requiring frequent access.
Security cameras are located throughout OVPIT/UITS buildings. These cameras record footage for follow-up in the case of a security incident. They also provide an effective deterrence function in the safe operation of the building. IU Data Centers use two layer authentication smart cards and biometric hand scanners to grant access to the facilities.
These increased security protocols follow guidelines from NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, SOC 2 and other sources, and are modeled on best practices by other universities such as the BTAA partners.
1.0 Scope
1.0.1
Document the policy and procedures for requesting, reviewing, authorizing, assigning, and maintaining access rights for those who need to perform services or visit University Information Technology Services (UITS)-managed data centers at Indiana University.
2.0 Purpose
2.0.1
In support of IU data centers, data center access and physical security, these policies and procedures provide a strong security strategy that protects IU employees, data, and resources entrusted to UITS by IU and its customers. These procedures are intended to clarify access requirements for all UITS-managed data centers.
3.0 Responsibility
3.0.1
UITS Data Center Operations is responsible for assigning access rights to individuals for secured areas under its control based on management-approved requests and adherence to IU Data Center Access Policy. Public Safety and Institutional Assurance is the owner of the card access system and is responsible for its system administration. Data Center Operations manages and provides operational support for the IU data centers.
4.0 Communication of policy
4.0.1
All sponsors of individuals with authorized access to IU data centers are responsible for ensuring those individuals are aware of and comply with the policies and procedures identified in this document.
4.0.2
All personnel who are authorized to access IU data centers must read, understand, and comply with the policies and procedures identified in this document.
4.0.3
All individuals applying for access to IU data centers must comply, understand and acknowledge that they have read the IU Data Center Access Policy and the
IU Data Center Standards
.
5.0 Categories of access
There are four categories of access to IU data centers: faculty, staff, and student access, IU affiliate access, daily access, and visitor/tour access.
5.1 IU faculty, staff, and student access
For IU employees with a business need to provide services in IU data centers
Requires a valid Indiana University ID card (CrimsonCard)
Requires a IU supervisor as a sponsor
No escort required
A review will take place verifying the data center's access list every 60 days (refer to
section 12.0
for details).
Access will expire on an annual basis and must be renewed by completing the form and obtaining the appropriate approvals (refer to
section 12.0
for details).
Refer to
section 6.0
for details regarding the acquisition of faculty, staff, and student access.
5.2 IU affiliate  access
Affiliates are individuals who require an ID card to access services or facilities but are not registered students or employees of Indiana University.
Must be sponsored by a department
For contractors/vendors who have long-term support agreements to provide services for equipment in IU data centers. Includes external co-location clients
No escort required
A review will take place verifying the data center's access list every 60 days (refer to
section 12.0
for details).
Access will expire on an annual basis and must be renewed by completing the form and obtaining the appropriate approvals (see
section 12.0
for details).
Refer to
section 7.0
for details regarding the acquisition of IU affiliate access.
5.3 Daily access
For external co-location customers or contractors without IU affiliate access
For those with limited-term engagements to provide a defined service
For individuals who are familiar with IU data center standards
Requires Data Center Operations Manager sponsorship
Visitor badges are issued at the Data Center Operations Center at the time of access.
Requires escort by individual with IU faculty/staff/student access
Access expires in 24 hours.
Refer to
section 8.0
for details regarding the acquisition of daily access.
5.4 Visitor/tour access
For individuals with no primary business need to access IU data centers other than for education or demonstration purposes
Tour appointments must be scheduled at least 24 hours in advance.
Visitor badges are issued at the DC Operations Center.
Requires escort by individual with IU faculty/staff/student access at all times while in IU data centers
Refer to
section 9.0
for details regarding the acquisition of Visitor/Tour access.
6.0 Faculty, staff, and student access
6.0.1
Faculty, staff, and student access is generally approved for IU staff when job duties require access to IU data centers.
6.1 Obtaining faculty, staff, and student access
6.1.1
In order to be granted faculty, staff, and student access to IU data centers, the applicant must:
6.1.1.1
Complete the required faculty, staff, and student data center access request form and submit it.
6.1.1.2
Access form will be routed for approval from the requester's supervisor, the DCOPS manager, the Enterprise Infrastructure Director and Data Center Access Control.
6.1.1.3
Must have a valid Indiana University ID (CrimsonCard).
6.1.1.4
The applicant must visit DCOPS with card to register in the hand geometry scanner system and have approved access areas assigned.
6.2 Maintaining faculty, staff, and student access
6.2.1
Cards must not be altered or defaced in any way; cards must not be bent, written on, have anything affixed to, or have holes punched in them.
6.2.2
The individual's supervisor must immediately report any change in job duties or employment status that would eliminate the need for data center access to DC Access Control (
dcaccess@iu.edu
).
6.2.3
The individual must retain sole possession of the card for the duration of their approved use. The individual is responsible for card use. Card use is not transferable and cannot be shared. Anyone caught allowing another individual to use their card will have their data center access immediately deactivated.
6.2.4
Faculty, Staff, and Student access must be renewed on an annual basis.
6.3 Replacing Faculty, Staff, and Student access cards
6.3.1
Lost or stolen cards must be immediately reported to IU Data Center Access Control via email (
dcaccess@iu.edu
) or call 812-855-9910.
6.3.2
For damaged, lost, or stolen cards, a replacement card will be assigned with the previously approved access areas.
6.4 Returning Faculty, Staff and Student access cards
6.4.1
Upon termination of employment or change in job responsibilities, it's the supervisor/sponsors responsibility to return access cards to DC Access Control and access will be removed.
7.0 IU Affiliate access
7.0.1
IU Affiliate access is generally granted to vendors who have annual support contracts to perform routine and emergency support of hardware and software used in IU data centers.
7.1 Obtaining IU Affiliate access
7.1.1
Requests for IU Affiliate access must be initiated by an IU sponsor using the IU Affiliate access request form.
7.1.2
The cost of an affiliate card is $25. To receive a card, present a completed Affiliate Card Request Form along with a valid, government-issued photo ID, at any CrimsonCard office location.
7.1.3
DC Access Control will process each request.
7.1.4
The applicant must visit DCOPS with card to register in the Biometrics hand scanner system and have approved access areas assigned.
7.2 Maintaining IU affiliate access
7.2.1
Cards must not be altered or defaced in any way; cards must not be bent, written on, have anything affixed to, or have holes punched in them.
7.2.2
The individual's IU sponsor must immediately report any change in job duties or employment status that would eliminate the need for data center access to DC Access Control (
dcaccess@iu.edu
).
7.2.3
The individual must retain sole possession of the card for the duration of their approved use. The individual is responsible for card use. Card use is not transferable and cannot be shared. Anyone caught allowing another individual to use their card will have their data center access immediately deactivated.
7.2.4
IU affiliate access must be renewed on an annual basis.
7.3 Replacing IU affiliate access cards
7.3.1
Lost or stolen cards must be immediately reported to IU Data Center Access Control; email
dcaccess@IU.edu
or call 812-855-9910.
7.3.2
If a card is damaged, lost, or stolen, a replacement card will be assigned with the previously approved access areas.
7.4 Returning IU affiliate access cards
7.4.1
Upon termination of employment or change in job responsibilities, it's the individual's responsibility to return access cards to DC Access Control and access will be removed.
8.0 Daily access
8.0.1
Daily access is generally assigned to those who only require data center access for short-term project work.
8.1 Obtaining daily access
8.1.1
Requests for short-term cards must be initiated at the direction of the DCOPS manager using the data center sign-in form available from DCOPS.
8.1.2
DCOPS will process each request.
8.1.3
DCOPS will issue approved short-term cards.
8.1.4
The applicant must visit DCOPS to obtain the card. The applicant will have to present government-issued identification.
8.2 Maintaining daily access
8.2.1
Cards must not be altered or defaced in any way; cards must not be bent, written on, have anything affixed to, or have holes punched in them.
8.2.2
The individual must retain sole possession of the card for the duration of their approved use. The individual is responsible for card use. Card use is not transferable and cannot be shared. Anyone caught allowing another individual to use their card will have their data center access immediately deactivated.
8.2.3
Daily access cards expire in 24 hours.
8.3 Replacing daily access cards
8.3.1
Lost or stolen cards must be immediately reported to IU Data Center Access Control via email (
dcaccess@iu.edu
) or call 812-855-9910.
8.3.2
If a card is damaged, lost, or stolen, it must be reported immediately to DC Access Control. A replacement will be issued by going to DCOPS. Refer to
section 8.0.1
.
8.4 Returning Daily Access Cards
8.4.1
Surrender the card to DCOPS upon signing out and leaving the DC.
9.0 Visitor/tour access
9.0.1
Visitor/Tour Access for an IU data center is granted under limited circumstances. Tours are for educational purposes and are for viewing only.
9.1 Obtaining Tour Access
9.1.1
Requests for tours must be arranged with DCOPS in person, by phone, or via email. Include the purpose of the tour, names of those attending, and preferable dates and times.
9.1.2
Tours must be approved by the DCOPS manager (or designee).
9.1.3
Tours must be requested at least 24 hours in advance.
9.1.4
A data center team tour guide will coordinate the tour.
9.1.5
Approved tour groups will meet their tour guide at DCOPS, sign in, and be issued their visitor badge(s). Individuals in the tour group will be required to present government-issued photo identification.
9.1.6
The tour will be escorted at all times when in IU data centers.
9.2 Returning visitor badges
9.2.1
When the tour is finished, the individuals must return their visitor badge(s) and sign out at DCOPS.
10.0 Card visibility
10.0.1
While in IU data centers or related secured areas, ID badges must be worn and visible at all times. Acceptable card display areas are on the chest or front hip.
11.0 Conduct of authorized users
11.0.1
No food or drink is allowed within IU data centers.
11.0.2
Visitors may not tamper or interact with equipment that is not theirs.
11.0.3
Individuals must comply with all Data Center Operations team instructions while in IU data centers.
11.0.4
Cards are non-transferable and may not be used by anyone other than the person to whom the card was assigned.
11.0.5
Individuals must present their access credentials at each access control point to ensure a valid access event is registered (that is, no tailgating).
12.0 Data Center Access Review Board
12.0.1
The Data Center Access Review Board is an authoritative governing body that reviews and approves all data center access requests.
12.0.2
UITS Data Center Access Control assigns and maintains access to IU data centers.
12.0.3
A review will take place verifying the ICTC and IU Bloomington data centers access list every 60 days. Data center access will be deactivated after 60 days of inactivity.
12.0.4
The Data Center Access Review Board will review any justifications for renewing expired access. If it is determined that Data Center access is no longer needed the access will not be renewed.
12.0.5
An audit log of all data center access provisioning and deprovisioning will be kept for at least 90 days.
12.0.6
Upon termination of employment or in the event of a disciplinary action, data center access will be immediately deactivated and suspended. In the case of disciplinary action, a justification and review process will be required for future access.
12.0.7
Data Center Access Review Board can be reached by phone at 812-855-9910 or via email at
dcaccess@iu.edu
.

title: Migrate from a personal ChatGPT account to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace
content:
Table of contents
Overview
What to expect when you request access to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace
Access the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace
Migration prompt for iu.edu personal accounts
Migration options
Recommendations

Overview
Note:
Access to the Indiana University ChatGPT Edu workspace is currently limited to selected users participating in a pilot program. At present, users not participating in the pilot who are using a personal ChatGPT associated with their IU email accounts can continue doing so and should continue following
Precautions about using ChatGPT at IU
.
If you previously created a personal ChatGPT account using your
@iu.edu
email address and want to be added to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, you will be prompted to either migrate your existing ChatGPT data to IU’s environment or download your existing data for storage. Once you join the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, your personal account associated with your
@iu.edu
email address will be deleted and replaced by the IU-managed version.
ChatGPT does not provide options for changing the email address of an existing personal account or for transferring data from a personal account associated with your IU email address to a personal account associated with a non-IU email address.
Before requesting access and migrating your chat data to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, UITS strongly recommends reviewing your chat history and deleting any sensitive or personal conversations that you do not want to be associated with your IU account.
This article outlines what to expect when joining the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace and how to decide between the two migration options.
Note:
This migration process does not apply to personal OpenAI accounts created with non-IU email addresses. Those accounts remain unaffected.
What to expect when you request access to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace
Before accessing the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, you should understand what will happen behind the scenes and what decisions you may need to make ahead of time. This applies especially if you already use ChatGPT with your IU email address.
When your
@iu.edu
email address is added to IU's ChatGPT Edu workspace:
OpenAI will check whether your IU email address is already associated with a personal ChatGPT account.
If it is, you will be prompted to choose what to do with your existing account before you can proceed.
You will need to either migrate your existing content (for example, chats and saved GPTs) into the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, or export and delete your content to start fresh.
Important:
Your IU email address can belong to only one workspace at a time. If it is already used in a personal account, you will be required to resolve that before joining the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace.
Once you are added to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, your IU ChatGPT usage will be managed by the university and subject to institutional policies. Any personal OpenAI activity linked to your IU email account will become part of that managed workspace. Your personal account associated with your
iu.edu
email address will be deleted.
UITS recommends reviewing your account beforehand so you can decide what action is best for your needs when prompted.
Access the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace
Once you are added to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, follow these steps to access the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace:
On the
ChatGPT
website, in the top right corner, select
Log in
.
In the "Email address" field, enter your IU email address (for example,
username@iu.edu
), and then select
Continue
.
Select
Indiana University
.
On the
IU Login
page, enter your
IU username and passphrase
, and then complete a
Two-Step Login (Duo)
authentication.
After authenticating, you will be placed into the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace.
Migration prompt for iu.edu personal accounts
When your IU email address is added to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, OpenAI will detect that your IU email address is already associated with a personal account. As a result, you will see a prompt asking what you would like to do with your exiting data. This prompt appears only if your IU email address is already linked to a personal OpenAI account. To complete enrollment in the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, you must choose between the two migration options outlined in the next section of this document.
Migration options
When you join the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace with an IU email address that is already associated with a personal OpenAI account, you will be prompted to resolve that conflict before proceeding. You will be presented with the following options for handling your existing personal account:
Option 1: Transfer
This option allows you to merge your personal account data into the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace. It lets you retain your chat history, saved custom GPTs, and other activity by migrating them to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace.
Certain personalized features, such as plug-ins and custom instructions, may be removed during this process.
If you have an active ChatGPT Plus subscription, it will be canceled and refunded once the account is transferred.
After migration, ChatGPT data associated with your IU email address will be fully managed by IU.
Option 2: Export and Delete
This option deletes your personal OpenAI workspace tied to your IU email and clears the way for your IU email address to be used in the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace; however, it does not let you transfer your personal workspace data to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace.
You will be offered the ability to export your chat history before it is deleted.
If you have an active ChatGPT Plus subscription, it will be canceled and refunded once the account is transferred.
Important:
Once you finalize your selection, the action is permanent and cannot be reversed. Make sure to use the
Settings
menu in the ChatGPT interface to export anything you wish to retain before proceeding. For more on exporting data, see
Exporting ChatGPT Data
.
Recommendations
If you want to retain past chats or custom GPTs, choose Option 1.
If you prefer to start fresh or already use another email address for personal use, choose Option 2.
You cannot change the email address associated with your personal ChatGPT account. You must either transfer or delete your data tied to your
@iu.edu
email address.
Before requesting access to the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace, UTITS strongly recommends reviewing your chat history and deleting any sensitive or personal conversations that you do not want to be associated with your account in the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace.
If you are unsure, use the
Settings
menu in the ChatGPT interface to export anything you wish to retain before proceeding. For more on exporting data, see
Exporting ChatGPT Data
.
Frequently asked questions
Will I lose access to my chat history after migrating my data?
No, unless you're removed from the IU workspace. As long as you're active, your migrated history remains available. If your account is later deactivated (for example, if you leave the university or the workspace is removed by IU), your history will be deleted.
Can I keep or create a personal OpenAI account?
Yes, as long as it is associated with a different (non-IU) email address.
Can I reverse the migration?
No. Once you choose to transfer or delete your personal workspace, the action is irreversible.
Get help
If you have questions or concerns about accessing the IU ChatGPT Edu workspace or migrating your personal ChatGPT account,
contact your campus Support Center
.

title: Use a cable longer than 15 feet in campus housing requiring the IU-specific Ethernet cable
content:
If you wish to use a cable longer than 15 feet in campus housing with proprietary Ethernet cables, you have two options:
Purchase a straight-through cable and an RJ45 coupler from a computer or electronics store. Attach one side of the coupler to the end of the pre-installed IU cable, and plug the straight-through cable into the other side of the coupler and into your computer.
If your IU cable can be removed from the wall (not all can), you can purchase an IU proprietary network cable of the desired length from a local computer or electronics store. Ask specifically for an IU wall cable; if you are not specific, you may receive a straight-through cable, which will not work. Once you have your longer cable, unplug the provided IU cable from the jack and plug in your new cable. Leave the pre-installed cable attached to the wall.
Note:
UITS calculates its networking needs based on industry-standard specifications, and so will support cables of only 15 feet or less connected to a university data jack. Installing a longer cable on a data jack may exceed the specifications and cause data transfer problems if the total length of the cable from your computer to the switch port exceeds the capability of the electrical signal. (In some areas, you may experience no problems with a longer cable if the distance to the switch port does not yet violate the standard.)

content:

Overview
Indiana University requires electronic documents to be accessible to people with disabilities and now has contracts with two suppliers for document remediation services.
Electronic documents include, but are not limited to, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, InDesign, and PDF files.
Electronic document remediation is the process of ensuring that documents are accessible to individuals with disabilities. This includes providing appropriate alt text for images and graphics, verifying the tag structure of PDF documents, and checking color contrast, among other tasks.
Supplier information
IU has service-level agreements with two suppliers that can remediate electronic documents. These agreements lock in system-wide pricing. Both suppliers provide document remediation services, but exact services may vary. They are also rated for different data classification levels.
Allyant T-Base Communications:
This supplier specializes in converting documents to accessible PDFs. The standard turn-around time is five business days. The pricing listed below is based on remediating an existing PDF into an accessible PDF. There are additional costs for rush service.
Contact: Kim Gilmer (
kgilmer@allyant.com
)
Allyant services at a glance:
$5 per page for standard pages
$7 per page requiring Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
Fillable forms start at $50 per page
BarrierBreak Solutions 247 Accessible Documents:
This supplier works with a variety of document types. The standard turn-around time is five to seven working days. There are additional costs for rush service.
Contact: Shashank Kapur (
shashank@barrierbreak.com
, +91 9920076289)
BarrierBreak services at a glance:
$7 per page for PDFs
$4.50 per page for Word and PowerPoint files
$4.50 per page for Excel files
$27.50 per page for fillable PDF/Word forms
How to choose a supplier
Important:
Before choosing a document remediation supplier, you must determine the
data classification
level of your documents. If your documents contain
Restricted
or
Critical
data, you will need to use Allyant T-Base Communications and take additional steps to securely transfer documents. Documents containing only
Public
and/or
University-internal
data can be remediated by either supplier.
To choose the best supplier for your documents, consider the following:
What type(s) of documents do you need remediated?
Allyant specializes in remediating PDFs but can work with other document types. BarrierBreak can remediate a variety of document types.
In what format do you want the remediated document(s)?
Allyant specializes in creating accessible PDFs. BarrierBreak can remediate documents in the same format they were created in or convert other document types to PDF.
Do your documents include languages other than English?
If your documents include languages other than English, there may be additional costs for remediation. You may need to provide any alt text in other languages. BarrierBreak may use Google translate for any translations.
Do your documents include STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Math) images and graphics?
If your documents include STEM images and graphics, you should plan to provide alt text and image descriptions that require subject matter expertise.
Transfer documents
IU Secure Share
is the recommended method for transferring documents to suppliers. Your supplier contact will provide any additional information needed for transferring your documents to them.
Overview of the purchasing process
Each department-driven request for services will require a formal quote from the supplier. Use the contact information above to request a quote from your chosen supplier. Each quote must include the following:
Declaration that "This Quote is subject to the Framework Services Agreement between the parties."
Reference to the effective date of the agreement
Begin and end dates of the work to be completed
Itemized pricing
Description of services
Once a formal quote is obtained, the department must submit a non-catalog requisition in
BUY.IU
. The department must attach the quote to the non-catalog requisition for supporting documentation of the cost and services. The quote number should be referenced in the line item description.

Work should not begin until an IU purchase order is received by the supplier for the services requested.

Overview
The IU Common Build provides a standardized platform for operating system installation and configuration on IU devices. This includes Windows, Apple, and Linux devices. The goal is to improve client experiences by simplifying user and device setup, optimizing performance, ensuring security compliance, eliminating duplicate management tools, and enhancing supportability across all IU workstation devices.

SerialNumber

Devices must be (re)built into the Common Build (IU-UEMS) OU structure.
Devices still on a legacy build should never be moved into the IU-UEMS OU structure as it can cause problems with the legacy build.
Devices must always remain managed and joined to Active Directory (AD) with the OCS agent and SCCM client installed and functional.
Devices' AD computer objects must remain under the IU-UEMS OU structure.
IU Common Build devices found outside of the IU-UEMS OU structure may be moved back into the correct OU without notice.
IU Common Build AD computer objects should never be added to AD computer groups.
AD computer objects found to be a member of an AD computer group may be removed from that AD group without notice.
Do not disjoin, rename, and rejoin IU Common Build devices outside of the IU-UEMS OU structure.
LSP and departmental expectations
All group policy printer and drive map policies submitted to EMS for migration must be configured for AD user group targeting.
Printer policies for IU Print secure release printers may be granted exceptions.
Windows OSD build and rebuild process should only be performed by IU LSPs.
Institutional data should not be stored on Common Build workstations or mobile devices; see
About institutional data at IU
.
Support requests
Submit support tickets through the
EMS Ticket Submission form
Note:
Tickets submitted to Tier 2 (
sct2@iu.edu
) may be delayed reaching EMS as they are routed through Tier 2 support.
Submit support tickets for the Linux Common Build through the
EMS Linux Support Request form
.
User-level functionality tickets should be triaged by the originating departmental on-site CTS support and, if necessary, a secondary ticket submitted to EMS for communication with the LSP to track and troubleshoot the larger issue.
EMS does not support and does not have the ability to support users at the user level; that is, EMS does not have access to Bomgar or any other screen share utility to see what the user is seeing. This type of troubleshooting should be performed by on-site CTS personnel and, when requested, communicated back to EMS.
Tickets regarding IU Common Build support issues must always be submitted by an IU LSP.
Tickets submitted to EMS with a non-IU LSP as the caller may have the ticket reassigned back to the originating assignment group.
Access to IU Common Build IT resources
Individual LSP access is maintained via ACM groups set up by EMS and maintained by IT managers; see
Local UITS Support People admin accounts for the IU Common Build
.
ACM admin groups for device administration should not contain primary user accounts.
Only secondary LSP admin group accounts may be used to access IU Common Build resources.
EMS expectations
Changes to global policies (top-level GPOs and Jamf Pro policies applying to all IU Common Build devices) will be submitted to and tracked through UITS Change Management.
Operating system build and functionality
The IU Common Build does not restrict local user logon without a documented functional need.
All university owned devices must be managed.
Windows devices must be domain joined and managed by SCCM or managed by Intune.
Apple devices will be managed under Jamf Pro.
Linux devices must be domain-joined and managed by Landscape.
Apple devices must be assigned to Mobile Device Management (MDM) via Apple School Manager (ASM) prior to delivery to a user or setup by department IT staff.
Local administrative accounts should not be created on Windows, macOS, or Linux ADS-joined devices.
All Windows secondary administrative accounts are applied to devices exclusively through group policy.
Linux devices operate on a "deny all, allow some" methodology. As such, accounts must be individually authorized on each system.
Follow the "Account management" steps in
Linux IU Common Build administrative tasks
to authorize and de-authorize accounts and to assign and restrict
sudo
privileges.
Secondary administrative accounts must be ADS group accounts.
Requests for a standard user (non-LSP) secondary administrative account policy must be submitted to EMS by an LSP.
Locally created admin accounts will be removed from Administrators by policy on Windows and ADS joined macOS devices.
Application of the admin account is based on the computer name, so LSPs should update EMS if a computer is ever repurposed for a different user.
Disabled and deleted group accounts will be removed from policy at the discretion of EMS.
Windows LAPS is used to manage the local administrator account password on all IU Common Build Windows devices.
Windows LAPS Overview
Windows Laps vs legacy Microsoft LAPS
Jamf LAPS is used to manage the local administrator passwords for accounts created by pre-stage enrollment on all macOS Common Build computers.
Jamf LAPS Overview
Windows, macOS, and Linux devices must always remain encrypted with BitLocker, FileVault, or LUKS.
BitLocker is enforced using a combination of SCCM Microsoft BitLocker Administration and Monitoring (MBAM) and group policy.
Information about BitLocker on the IU Common Build
Multi-user macOS devices will not use FileVault unless requested by the department. All Apple devices are encrypted at rest regardless of FileVault status.
Printer and SMB file shares should never be created on workstation devices.
Windows updates and third-party updates will be deployed as they are released with a maximum two-day installation deadline.
Update reboot maintenance windows occur weekly on Thursday nights from 11pm to 5am
Zero-day remediations may be applied outside of the standard installation deadlines and reboot maintenance windows.
Windows servicing updates will be maintained with the latest version of the Windows operating system with servicing updates occurring approximately every 6 months.
Due to the Microsoft design of Windows servicing, exceptions to Windows servicing updates cannot be granted. Devices that cannot be upgraded to the latest Windows operating system will need to be rebuilt to a Windows LTSC version.
Linux and third-party security updates will be deployed every day at 5am. If necessary, the system will be rebooted after updates are installed.
Linux and third-party feature and bugfix updates will be deployed once per week. The first attempt will take place Saturday at 10pm. If the system is offline or updates are unsuccessful, a second attempt will be made on Sunday at 10pm. If necessary, the system will be rebooted after updates are installed.
macOS system updates will be pushed after a week delay (see
IU Common Build macOS updates
).
Common Build Macs check for needed application updates daily from 5pm to 8am.
Zero-day remediations will be applied as soon as they become available.
Windows OSD build
Only Microsoft Surface and Dell business line models, primarily the standard models offered on Buy.IU, are supported for the IU Common Build OSD process.
Non-standard device models are not supported for OSD, and drivers cannot be added.
If necessary, EMS will assist directly with ensuring non-standard device models receive IU Common Build policies and configurations.
Devices must be (re)built using the custom IU Common Build ISO
The device name is automatically set to "IU-SerialNumber" when using the IU Common Build ISO.
Serial numbers longer than 12 characters will automatically have any non-alphanumeric characters removed and will be truncated to use the last 12 characters of the serial.
Manually configuring the device name
will not work
to make a device use the IU Common Build OSD process.
All IU Common Build devices should be built with Windows 11 or higher operating system.
Devices requiring Windows 10 will need to demonstrate a documented functional need, such as application computability restrictions, to be granted an exception to use Windows 10. In such cases, Windows 10 LTSC will be used to prevent future servicing updates.
Drivers/firmware/BIOS
EMS does not actively update OSD drivers with current versions unless there is a known issue; EMS may update drivers for a specific device model upon request. Only supported device models with drivers included in the Dell Enterprise OSD Driver Packs will be added to the OSD process. All post-build driver installations and/or updates must be completed by the on-site technician; drivers for external devices, such as monitors and docking stations, will not be added to the OSD process. Any post-build firmware and/or BIOS updates and configurations also must be performed by the on-site technician.
For Dell devices, use the Dell Command Update tool available in Software Center (or in the
Intune Company Portal app
). For Microsoft Surface devices, use the Microsoft Surface app (available in the Windows Store) to open Windows Update; use the drop-down next to the
Check for updates
button, and then select
Check online for updates through Microsoft Update
.
Post-OSD build
Post-build scripts are not supported on the IU Common Build.
Post-build scripts created for legacy builds can cause problems and create conflicts with IU Common Build policies.
The Windows [Easy] Files and Settings Transfer Wizard should never be used.
It is not supported by Microsoft on Windows 10 or Windows 11.
"Cleaner" applications, such as CCleaner, should never be used on the IU Common Build.
These applications commonly remove cached MSI files that are often required to update and uninstall applications. This could cause third-party application updates to fail resulting in a device rebuild.
Windows LAPS passwords can be accessed on the LAPS tab of the Active Directory computer object device properties.
Manage and monitor Windows LAPS
The legacy Microsoft LAPS UI executable will not work to retrieve the Windows LAPS password.
The legacy version of Microsoft LAPS (LAPS UI and LAPS GPO extension) that required a manual install has been deprecated and is no longer supported on any current version of Windows.
Deprecation of legacy Microsoft LAPS
Windows LAPS is built-in to Windows and does not require any manual installation. Legacy Microsoft LAPS should never be installed on Common Build devices.
Manually installing legacy Microsoft LAPS will cause problems with Windows LAPS and should not be installed on Common Build devices.
Jamf LAPS passwords can be access in the Jamf console.
Using LAPS in the Jamf Pro Interface
Software installation
The Software Center and Jamf Self Service should be used for software installation whenever possible.
Frequently used software is packaged, and current versions are maintained as available in the Software Center and Jamf Self Service.
Global applications that are available in Jamf Self Service, the Software Center, and/or OSD will not be deployed as required without a documented functional need.
While
apt
is available for installing software packages on Linux devices, UITS highly recommends using
snap
. These packages are designed to automatically update and do not conflict with system software or configurations. Installing software with
apt
may result in unintended negative effects.
Apple and Jamf functionality
macOS computers residing on campus full time should bound to ADS.
macOS computers not residing on campus full time will not be bound to ADS.
This is to mitigate known issues with AD authentication using cached credentials including FileVault authorization errors.
University-owned macOS, iOS, and iPadOS devices not deployed as a university owned personal device such as one to one deployment or lifecycle replacements will be managed in Jamf Pro under the direction of EMS Apple Team and in coordination of the department.
Legacy Casper Jamf Pro managed devices must be reassigned to the Common Build Jamf Pro service and rebuilt; they cannot be migrated.
macOS computers must have Microsoft Defender installed.
macOS laptop users must have access to privilege escalation options. Departments must vet and account for this configuration.
One to one deployments of iOS or iPadOS devices will require that user of the device do the initial setup. Technicians should not do the setup for the user.
Department IT staff are responsible for printer and network share setup on devices.
Where possible EMS can make IU Print printer configurations available to departments for devices assignments.

title: About the IU Science DMZ
content:
The Indiana University Science DMZ is a dedicated computer network optimized to accommodate the vast amounts of research data produced by applications
critical to scientific discovery and innovation. Unlike networks optimized for general-purpose, enterprise IT services, the IU Science DMZ is engineered specifically to support high performance, data-intensive science applications.
The IU Science DMZ's high performance network hardware is used exclusively for transferring research data between IU systems, and between IU and external networks. Its custom security policies are tailored to ensure maximum performance and baseline security. Real-time monitoring and testing systems are used to closely monitor traffic, performance, and security.
The IU Science DMZ is based on the
Science DMZ network model introduced by the Energy Sciences Network (ESnet)
.

These Terms of Use apply to all contributors, approvers, publishers, and managers of the Indiana University Web Content Management System (WCMS) service.

Purpose of Terms of Use
IU expects the WCMS and related information technology resources will be used in a lawful manner and in support of the university's mission of research and creative activity, teaching and learning, and civic engagement.
Terms of Use
Unless otherwise specified in these Terms of Use or other university policies, use of the WCMS is restricted to purposes related to the university's mission of research and creative activity, teaching and learning, and civic engagement. Eligible individuals are provided access in order to support their studies, instruction, duties as employees, official business with the university, and other university-sanctioned activities.
WCMS accounts are provided to individuals with university accounts that authenticate through
IU Login
. The WCMS Administrators require unique user identification when accessing the WCMS and its related applications. Group accounts may not be used for authentication and access. Unique user identification is required for auditing, security, and HIPAA requirements. Individuals may not share with or transfer their university accounts to others including network IDs, passwords, or other access codes that allow them to gain access to the WCMS.
The WCMS may not be used in a manner that violates the law, for private commercial activities that are not approved by the university, for personal private gain, or for political campaigning and similar activities that are inconsistent with the university's tax-exempt status.
Data storage
Only Public and University-Internal data are suitable to be stored in the WCMS. Restricted and Critical data cannot be stored in the WCMS. For definitions of Public, University-Internal, Restricted, and Critical data, see
Classification levels of institutional data
. In addition, federally and state-protected data, human subjects research data, passwords, and protected health information cannot be stored in the WCMS. For more about protected health information, see
About protected health information (PHI)
. For more about data classifications, see
About sensitive data at IU
.
Group name change
The Web Content Management System, Cascade CMS, does not allow users to change group names. Site Managers can create a new group with the desired name and delete the old group. To request the deletion of manager groups, email the UITS Web team at
webhelp@iu.edu
.
Site names
Site names exist for the WCMS Administrators to locate and organize sites. Site names follow a naming convention of
Campus-Organization-Department.siteName
(for example,
BL-COLLEGE-PSY.tomlab
). Site Managers may request a site name change. However, if a site name is changed, access rights for all assets will be reset to the default state. It is the responsibility of the Site Manager to recreate groups and assign them to the appropriate assets.
Web standards
Sites within the WCMS must meet accessibility, visual design, content, and navigation guidelines outlined by the
IU Brand Guidelines
for electronic media.
Web domains
Requesting a
departmental domain, subdomain, or designer domain name
is the responsibility of the school, department, division, or unit.
Web Services
Web Services should not be used for publishing. Possible exceptions should be evaluated by WCMS Administrators. The WCMS team does not provide development support for custom Web Services applications. Use of Web Services API Keys instead of a Web Services user is preferred whenever possible.
Enforcement
IU will handle reports of misuse or abuse of information and the WCMS in accordance with existing policies and procedures issued by appropriate authorities. Depending on the individual and circumstances involved, this could include the offices of Human Resources, Vice Provost or Vice Chancellor of Faculties (or campus equivalent), Dean of Students (or campus equivalent), Office of the General Counsel, and/or appropriate law enforcement agencies. For more, see
Misuse and Abuse of Information Technology Resources (IT-02)
.
Failure to comply with the WCMS Terms of Use may result in sanctions relating to the individual's use of the WCMS (such as suspension or termination of access, removal of online material, or disabling of the individual's WCMS site). WCMS Administrators are authorized to define violations of and enforce the Terms of Use. For more, see
Appropriate Use of Information Technology Resources (IT-01)
.
