title: Best practices for Microsoft Teams meetings in PC-based conference rooms
content:
Instead of a dedicated videoconferencing (Cisco or Polycom) unit, many Indiana University conference rooms use a standard PC for collaboration, sometimes referred to as PCVC equipment (Personal Computer for Video Conferencing). These rooms provide flexibility by allowing participants to choose the app needed for each meeting. However, this flexibility requires the user who logs into the conference room PC to take steps to maintain privacy and to ensure a quality meeting experience.
Consider the following tips for a successful meeting when using
Microsoft Teams
in a PCVC room.
To adjust your privacy settings for the
Microsoft Teams
application, choose one of the following options:
Note:
The lobby function in
Microsoft Teams
is turned off by default for future and recurring meetings. If you want to modify that setting, see
About the lobby in Microsoft Teams meetings at IU
.
Set your
Microsoft Teams
status to
Do not disturb
; for instructions, see
Change your status in Microsoft Teams
. This will prevent desktop notifications (pop-up messages at the lower right) from appearing during your meeting.
Turn off pop-up chat notifications for the
Microsoft Teams
app; for instructions, see
Only get notifications in the app
.
Log into the conference room PC with an administrative group account (if available) instead of your personal credentials; this will ensure that personal account information is not displayed. The group account will need to be invited to the meeting or the meeting will need to be joinable by any IU account.
Close unneeded applications such as email, chat, or any documents that may contain private or sensitive information or that may require restricted access. For more about data classification at IU, see
Classification levels of institutional data
.
To reserve the physical room, include the Outlook account for the room in the meeting invitation; for more, see
Schedule meetings and reserve rooms at IU
.
If you know that a conference room with a Cisco or Polycom unit may be joining the
Microsoft Teams
meeting, verify that the invitation includes "Join with a video conferencing device" information within the
Microsoft Teams
meeting dialing instructions. These instructions only appear in
Microsoft Teams
meeting invitations that were created on or after July 11, 2021.
Other participants in the physical conference room can share their screen wirelessly by joining the meeting from the
Microsoft Teams
application on their personal device. When these in-room participants join, have them choose the video and audio option
Don't use audio
to prevent audio feedback in the conference room.
If you wish, you may add a second device to the
Microsoft Teams
meeting. When you are logged into the
Microsoft Teams
application on the conference room PC, and you join from the
Microsoft Teams
app on your personal device to wirelessly share that device's screen, you'll see a prompt to either
Add this device
or
Transfer to this device
; choose
Add this device
. For more, see
Join a Microsoft Teams meeting on a second device
.

content:

Overview

Migration of physical servers to EWA
Overview
Enterprise Windows and Azure Administration (EWA) can assume management of a pre-existing server, or deploy a new one to replace it. Migrating an existing server may be preferable in cases where deploying a new one would be prohibitively complex or expensive. To migrate a server to EWA, submit a ticket to
ewahelp@iu.edu
.
Completing the steps below will help expedite this process; pre-migration tasks cannot begin until EWA has access to the server and related resources.
For all servers
Add
ads\iu-ewa-admins
to the local administrator group.
Work up an inventory listing the following:
Server name
What the server does
Test/production? EWA will migrate test workloads first, if available.
Local contact(s) for the server. Who can answer questions EWA might have and test before/after EWA migrates it?
Stored data classification (public, university-internal, restricted, critical). If restricted or critical, describe the type of data being stored.
Any special considerations EWA might need to be aware of related to scheduling of maintenance. By default, all production servers are patched on the third Sunday of the month between 12am-8am; non-production servers patch the evening of the prior Wednesday. Decisions about patching at other times are case-by-case depending on business requirements and EWA staff overhead.
If the server hosts vended software, include the name of the software and any information you have about the vendor. All software deployed on EWA-managed servers needs to be actively maintained and patched at regular intervals. The EWA AppAdmin team will help with scheduling and implementing these upgrades. If vendor technicians need remote access to your servers, EWA has tools to facilitate that.
What users or groups will need local admin permissions on the servers once migrated? EWA will ask you to submit a FireForm post-migration to formalize this and recertify on a yearly basis, but it's helpful to know in advance.
Your preferred window for the actual migration to occur. The server will be intermittently available while EWA cut it over; the server will be rebooted, and it EWA may need to troubleshoot if services fail to start or if there are other obvious problems.
Is the server located in II?
If so, provide the billing account(s) associated with your current resource pool(s). EWA will create new pools billed to these same accounts for the migrated servers and move the VMs at migration time. You may decommission the old pools if they are empty post-migration.
If it's a physical machine, provide management addresses for any iDRAC or similar out-of-band management interfaces; EWA will also need login credentials or permissions assigned to
ads\iu-ewa-admins
. Also provide the rack and U location of the server.
If this is a fileserver, how do your users access its shares? If you have the shares behind DFS-N, provide the details on the namespace: is it hosted locally on the server(s), or in AD? Do you have any client devices that are not standard Windows or Mac workstations (for example, scanners) that might have problems with newer SMB features like encryption?
For all Active Directory OUs
Grant full control to
ads\iu-ewa-admins
.
For the Campus Network Portal
Either add all members of
ads\ewa-cnp
to your CNP AD group(s), or grant EWA control over the AD group so EWA can do that for you.
Migration of physical servers to EWA
Customers who wish to transfer existing bare-metal servers to EWA management may do so; EWA's ability to support the server may be limited by factors such as:
Absence of a hardware maintenance contract with the vendor
Absence of an out-of-band management interface (for example, iDRAC)
Age of the server
Customers transferring out-of-support/end-of-life hardware to EWA assume all risks related to system failure. EWA strongly recommends prioritizing virtualization of these workloads to mitigate these risks. II supports "P2V" (physical-to-virtual) migrations of Windows servers, which may allow for expedited migrations when compared to a full rebuild. New hardware is subject to the terms of the EWA standards and practices related to physical servers.

Overview
The Records Retention Schedule Database (RRSD) is the official repository of records retention and disposition schedules for all Indiana University campuses, schools, and departments. It organizes retention and disposition instructions for materials by record series, a group of logically related records with the same retention and disposition instructions that support a specific business or administrative activity (for example, a personnel file consisting of an application, reference letters, etc.).
All units, university-wide, are to follow the records retention and disposition instructions in the RRSD.
To suggest a change or addition to the records retention schedules in the RRSD, email
archives@iu.edu
.
Access
Access the database through
One.IU
, or directly at
https://rrs.iu.edu.
.
Anyone with an
IU username and passphrase
can log in.
If you're on campus, you must be connected to the wired campus network,
eduroam
, or
IU Secure
, and if off campus, you must use the
IU VPN
.
Navigation
After login, the default view is the Simple view, which displays a limited set of fields. To display all fields, check
Advanced view
.
The default sort order of the entire database is reverse creation date.
To search in a field, use the funnel, choose
contains
or another limiter, and enter the search term.
To sort a field alphabetically or numerically, select the field name.
Database fields and values
Type:
Records Series that are common to more than one unit are called a General Schedule (G); Unit-Specific Schedules (U) are for records that are only handled/held by one unit.
General
Unit-specific

University-wide
IU Bloomington

Records Retention Area:
These are standard values kept in the list of records coordinators by area linked from
Records Coordinators
.
Example: Financial, Intercollegiate Athletics, etc.
Records Retention Sub-Area:
These are standard values determined by the Records Coordinator for this area, kept in the University-Wide Records Areas and Records Coordinators spreadsheet.
You may leave this blank if none.
Area/Sub-Area Description:
The Records Coordinator for this area may choose to describe or clarify the scope of the area and/or sub-area here.
Record Series Code:
This is a unique alphanumeric identifier for each record series, similar to IU Policy codes. This can be helpful when referring to a particular record or record series on other documents (for example, a destruction certificate), or if the name of the record series changes but still refers to the same documents. Use letters from the Office of Record's Org Code, which is helpful for sorting and exporting by Office of Record.
Examples:
UA-HUMM -001 = University Human Resource Services
UA-TREA-001 = Office of the Treasurer
The first two digits represent the campus scope.
The second set of digits represents the functional or organizational area.
The third set of digits represents the chronological listing of record series in the schedule a particular scope and area.
Record Series:
This is a prose identifier for each record series, which can be helpful to clearly identify a particular record series.
Example: Prospective Student Athlete Forms, or Tenure Packet
Record Description:
Provides a definition/description of the record series, such as what documents it includes, etc.
Vital:
This is a Business Continuity term, and indicates records very important to the function of the unit.
Yes
No
Event Code:
Standard codes for IU that indicate an event that starts the disposition, such as
FYE
for Fiscal Year End. (If a record should be retained for seven years after the current fiscal year, the retention policy would be
FYE + 7
.)
Retention Period:
Standard time period that indicates how long the record should be retained after the event indicated by the event code.
To determine how long to keep the record, note when the event must occur (reach end of fiscal year, for example), and then add the time period here to that time. You would keep the records for the fiscal year that just ended, PLUS seven years more (add the time period to the event).
If kept indefinitely, this field will indicate
Permanent
.
Disposition:
Directions for how to dispose of the records. Disposition may include destruction or transfer to another office, including the campus archives.
If the official record medium is paper, and the records
do not
contain sensitive data, the value will be
Recycle
.
If the official record medium is paper, and the records
do
contain sensitive data, the value will be
Securely Shred
.
If the official record medium is electronic, and the records
do not
contain sensitive data, the value will be
Delete
.
If the official record medium is electronic, and the records
do
contain sensitive data, the value will be
Securely Delete
.
If the record is to be kept indefinitely, the value will be
Not Applicable
.
This field may also indicate if records are to be transferred to Archives or to another location.
Based On:
Describes the source of information that assisted IU in choosing the retention period and disposition.
Governing Statutes:
Describes which overarching law on which the retention period is based.
Governing Regulations:
Describes the specific citation of the regulation, where the retention information is communicated.
Governing IU Policies:
Describes the IU policy where the retention information is communicated.
Reason for Retention Period:
To record any information about why this retention period was chosen and disposition instructions, especially if it is based on business need.
Official Record Medium:
The format the official copy of the records is kept in.
Paper
Electronic (if you scan a paper version to store and shred the paper, then choose electronic)
Paper and electronic
Office of Record:
The office/person ultimately responsible for decisions regarding the retention/disposition instructions for this record series for IU.
Can Units Retain Copies?:
Provide instructions to units as to whether they may retain copies, or if they need to retain originals, and for how long if this differs from the official copy retention period.
Example: Yes, up to two years post termination
Requires Certificate of Destruction:
Used only where a statute or regulation
requires
it.
Yes
No
Records Coordinator:
Email address of the IU Records Coordinator relevant to this record series.
Data Steward Domain:
If the record series can be mapped to a Data Steward Domain, it is entered here.
Creation Date:
This field is populated by the system when the record is created.

title: SMTP servers for external email services
content:

Overview
Exemptions

Server applications that do not support authenticated SMTP

Alternative authentication methods

"Too many recipients" error message
Overview
Indiana University requires
SSL
(Secure Sockets Layer) encryption and
authentication
for the university
SMTP servers
(
mail-relay.iu.edu
) to increase security and stem the flow of email messages propagating
spam
,
viruses
, and worms. SSL protects outbound email by encrypting it before sending it to an SMTP server. Authentication ensures that only legitimate IU users are able to send email messages through the SMTP server to email addresses outside IU.
If your group's service needs to send email outside the Indiana University network, you generally must set up SMTP authentication.
All SMTP authentication to
mail-relay.iu.edu
is restricted and requires prior authorization before being able to send authenticated email. To submit an authorization request, fill out the
Mail Relay Authorization form
. After your submission is processed, you will be authorized to send authenticated email.
Exemptions
Internal email
Email messages sent from a server on the IU network to addresses within the IU system do not require authentication. Authentication is required only for messages sent through the SMTP server to email addresses outside IU.
Server applications that do not support authenticated SMTP
If your server does not support authenticated SMTP, you can request an exemption for it by filling out the
Mail Relay Authorization form
.
SMTP authentication account
UITS
recommends requesting a separate service account for authenticating against the SMTP server. This way, if your server is compromised, the attackers may get the
passphrase
for the service account, but will not gain access to an account that has administrative privileges in your environment.
Alternative authentication methods
The IU SMTP server supports GSSAPI (Generic Security Services Application Program Interface) authentication in addition to authentication using a username and password. However,
Tier 2 Support
does not currently support this method, meaning you must implement it yourself.
SMTP server protocols and ports
TCP ports 25/587
TLS ports 25/587
Note:
Do not use Port 465. This port will be disabled as of March 27, 2025. It was a Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) port originally used for SMTPS (SMTP over SSL). Port 465 was deprecated after STARTTLS was introduced.
"Too many recipients" error message
If you see the error message "4.5.3 Too many recipients", your email message originated from an off-campus IP address and included more recipients than
mail-relay.iu.edu
permits. The maximum number of recipients per email message is 30. This limit does not affect email messages sent from on-campus connections or messages sent within Exchange. If you need to email more than 30 recipients, you will need to compose additional messages for the remaining recipients.
Note:
If an IU List address is a recipient, it counts as one recipient, regardless of how many subscribers are included on the IU List.

content:

Set up a DFS namespace

Set up a DFS namespace
These instructions assume you are running Server 2008 R2 or higher.
In
Server Manager
, add the
File Services
role. Enable the
File Server
and
Distributed File
System
role services, and select the option to create a namespace later.
Note:
This will open several DFS-related items in the firewall (including
File and Printer Sharing
). To restrict access, include the IP addresses and domain controllers of your servers that will be participating in DFS;
File and Printer Sharing
should remain open.
Assign a name to your DFS namespace (typically your campus-dept code, for example,
IU-ITPS
; see
Recommended naming conventions for IU Windows computers and groups
).
Verify that the firewall rules created in step 1 are still open and domain admins are administrators on your machine. Make sure the name you want for your DFS namespace (for example,
\\server\IU-ITPS
) has not already been assigned to a share on the server.
Including the name of your namespace, the FQDN of the server initially hosting the namespace, and the group to be assigned as the namespace administrator (typically it's your OU Admin group),
contact Tier 2
.
After the ADS admins have created the domain-based namespace on your server:
The local path of your namespace will be
C:\DFSRoots\{namespace}
(for example,
C:\DFSRoots\IU-ITPS
).
This folder will be shared as
\\server\{namespace}
(for example,
\\server\IU-ITPS
).
You'll be able to access this namespace using the following path:
\\ads.iu.edu\{namespace}
(for example,
\\ads.iu.edu\IU-ITPS
).
Add redundant roots to an existing namespace
With redundant roots, clients will be redirected seamlessly to another DFS namespace server in the event of a server outage.
Note:
These instructions assume you have set up a domain-based namespace.
In
Server Manager
, add the
File Services
role. Enable the
File Server
and
Distributed File
System
role services, and select the option to create a namespace later.
Note:
This will open several DFS-related items in the firewall (including
File and Printer Sharing
). To restrict access, include the IP addresses and domain controllers of your servers that will be participating in DFS;
File and Printer Sharing
should remain open.
Make sure the
DFS Management snap-in
is installed on the management server. This does not have to be the server you're using for DFS.
Run the
DFS Management
snap-in
. Right-click
Namespaces
, and add your namespace to the display.
Right-click your namespace, select
Add Namespace Server...
, and enter the name of the server you configured above. The local path will automatically be created, along with the proper sharing permissions.
Select
Edit Settings
. Select
Administrators have full
access; other users have read-only permissions
, and then select
OK
twice. The wizard will finish, creating the folders on your server, along with the share.
DFS folders and folder targets
After you've set up your DFS namespace, you can create DFS folders that point to existing file shares on servers (folder targets). The folder targets do not have to be on the same server as the DFS namespace roots.
A DFS folder can have folder targets to more than one server. To set which folder target is the preferred server, select the
Folder
Target
tab, and select
Properties
. Then select the
Advanced
tab, and select
Override referral
ordering
.
Note:
Specifying a preferred server doesn't guarantee that all client referrals will be to that server.
DFS replication
At IU, in order to allow for the most flexibility with DFS replication, the standard Microsoft recommendation isn't followed. Instead, SCT2 will create a single replication group for a department. Within that replication group, you may have multiple sets of replicated folders. You may add additional servers if desired.
Notes:
Although they often go hand in hand, DFS replication does not require the use of DFS namespaces.
Standard DFS replication does not work well for files that can be opened and written to by multiple people or locations at the same time. Frequently, people want to use DFS to "automatically back up" user/group directories; however, this process is not as simple as putting two servers in a DFS link, enabling replication, and telling users to access it via the DFS link. For more, contact SCT2 or see
DFS Step-by-Step Guide for
Windows Server 2008
.
Set up DFS replication
Choose two initial servers that will be in the replication group; you can change the servers later.
Create a folder on each server (for example,
C:\Test_Folder
) that will be the initial folder to be replicated. Although not required, giving the folder the same name on each server is easier to manage.
If you haven't already done so, go to
Server Manager
, and add the
File Services
role. Enable the
File Server
and
Distributed File System
role services, and select the option to create a namespace later.
Assign a name to your DFS namespace (typically your campus-dept code, for example,
IU-ITPS
).
Verify that the firewall rules created in step 1 are still open and domain admins are administrators on your machine; your firewall needs to allow connections on all ports from the ADS domain controllers.
Email
sct2@iu.edu
with the following:
Your replication group name
The name of the AD group that will administer the replication group
You can add a new server to your replication group, or even add two new servers that will replicate data between each other, without affecting your initial two servers. When adding new servers, you will also need to create new
Connections
between the servers for replication to occur.
Replicate folders with data
Go to the
DFS Management Console
and add your replication group.
Right-click your group, and select
New Replicated Folders
.
Choose the primary member (server). This will be the authoritative server for the initial transfer.
Add the folder on the primary server that is to be replicated.
Select the secondary server, select
Edit
, add the local path on that server, and then select
Finish
.
Note:
You can also change NTFS permissions or make one partner "read only" from within the wizard.
To save time, you can pre-stage the existing data on the second server; see
Use Robocopy to pre-seed files for DFS Replication
.

When your Indiana University website is no longer needed, it is best practice to retire it from the web and archive any necessary content. This retirement process removes the site and associated services, and ensures compliance with IU policy.
As the Site Steward (the person responsible for the website), you can either ask UITS to handle the website retirement process for you or retire the site yourself.
Option 1 (preferred): UITS-managed website retirement
You can ask UITS to retire your website and associated services on your behalf. This is the preferred method for retiring an IU website.
You may request a snapshot of your website to be stored on archive-it.org, however submitting a request does not guarantee your site will be archived.
Before submitting a retirement request, make sure to download and save any files or data you want to keep, as it is your responsibility to preserve this content locally.
Email the UITS Web team (
webhelp@iu.edu
) with the following information:
The URL of the website you want to retire
Whether the group account should also be retired
Whether you need a redirect from the old URL
Whether you want an archival copy of the site
Option 2: Manual website retirement (self-service)
To retire your IU website on your own:
Back up your website:
Save a copy of your site files to an IU-provided file storage or another location recommended by your department's IT staff. If you want an official archive, complete the
Request to Archive Site
form.
Note:
Submitting an archival request does not guarantee that the website will be archived.
Retire associated services:
Depending on how your site is set up, complete some or all of the following:
Virtual host:
Delete or transfer the virtual host. To request a redirect (recommended for six months), email
webhelp@iu.edu
with the URL being retired and the destination URL for the redirect.
WCMS:
Email
webhelp@iu.edu
with the WCMS site name and a request to archive the site.
Siteimprove:
Go to the
Siteimprove Request Form
and select
Other
to notify the Siteimprove team your site has been retired.
Finalize website retirement:
After completing all applicable tasks, email
webhelp@iu.edu
to confirm that your website has been retired. The UITS Web team will finalize the process by confirming that all associated services are retired and marking the site as non-operational in the
IU Website Directory
.
Additional recommendations
Use a
backlink checker
to find other sites that link to yours, and then let them know your site will be taken offline.
Use a 301 redirect to redirect content to a relevant site for at least six months.

title: Medium-level review of a VPAT, stage 2
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Criteria tables
Additional resources
Overview
This document will help you perform final checks and reviews of the Accessibility Compliance Report (ACR) portion of the VPAT for a small number of finalist products that remain under your consideration after performing
stage 1 of the medium-level review
. It contains the success criteria not addressed in stage 1.
All Level A and AA criteria are covered in
Perform a full review of a VPAT
. You may want to skip to a full review if you have only one or two products to compare and have not already performed a medium-level review.
If you are comparing many potential options and can perform a hands-on review of the products or services, you should use the
quick review of the VPAT
as an initial filter. You can then perform a
medium-level review of the VPAT
with software or applications that pass the quick review (If a hands-on review is not possible, skip straight to the medium-level review). The quick and medium-level reviews are intended to help you establish the reliability of each vendor's accessibility documentation and gain a general sense of the overall accessibility of their product.
Criteria tables
The tables may represent information about three standards:
WCAG
Revised Section 508
EN 301 549
For the purposes of this document, we are only looking at the WCAG standards and accompanying tables. The WCAG standard contains three conformance levels, A, AA, and AAA, which each have an individual table. There may be references to the other standards within these tables as there are matching criteria from all three standards.
The tables include three columns:
Criteria
Conformance Level
Remarks and Explanations
Criteria
will list the specific standard targeted by the evaluation.
Conformance Level
gives you the opportunity to gauge the possible accuracy of the submission. The conformance level column can have one of four different values:
Supports
Partially Supports
Does Not Support
Not Applicable (N/A)
Note:
There has been a language change with the release of VPAT 2.3 where "Supports with Exceptions" was replaced with "Partially Supports". This change took place in December of 2018. So, make note of the language and the date, which can tell you whether the vendor's submission is based on recent testing or may have been copied and pasted from an older version.
Remarks and Explanations
should ideally be as detailed as possible about the specific problems encountered. Look for:
Specific examples of how the product supports, partially supports, or doesn't support the criterion
Remarks and explanations for all criteria
Responses that should concern you:
Explanations that duplicate the wording of the criteria
All criteria marked as "Supports"
Language like "this product was designed to...", which doesn't indicate if it actually does
Table 1: Success Criteria, Level A
2.1 - Keyboard Accessible
These guidelines should be considered the starting point in the evaluation process and the most critical within the standard.
This doesn't preclude an application that has "partially supports" from being considered. However, they should be flagged and then sent for more in-depth testing before purchase. View a
1-minute video on testing keyboard support
.
2.1.4 - Character Key Shortcuts (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: If custom keyboard shortcuts have been implemented, they shouldn’t use a single character (letter, number, punctuation, or symbol) without modifier keys, such as Ctrl or Alt, or there should be a way for the user to change the shortcut.
Priority: High
2.2 - Enough Time
2.2.1 - Timing Adjustable
Summary: If there is a time limit of less than 20 hours, the user needs to be able to turn it off, adjust it, or extend it. For example, if a session times out after a period of inactivity, there should be a way for the user to indicate they are still active and stop the timeout. There is an exception for real-time events, like an auction.
Priority: High
2.4 - Navigable
2.4.3 - Focus Order
Summary: Someone using a keyboard should be able to navigate through the content in an order that is logical and meaningful.
Priority: High
2.4.4 - Link Purpose (In Context)
Summary: The text of a link should give users an idea of where the link will take them.
Priority: High
2.5 - Input Modalities
Complementary to the guidelines for keyboard users, these guidelines address barriers for people who use a pointer (mouse, touch) or their voice (voice control).
2.5.1 - Pointer Gestures (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion requires a single pointer alternative for any path-based or multipoint gestures. An example is zoom in and out buttons as an alternative to the multipoint pinch zoom gesture.
Priority: High
2.5.2 - Pointer Cancellation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion is about preventing accidental pointer input. If an action happens with a single pointer (mouse or touch), it can be cancelled or reversed.
Priority: High
2.5.3 - Label in Name (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: If there is visual text for a link or control, the accessible name contains that text.
Priority: High
2.5.4 - Motion Actuation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: For functions activated by moving a device, such as shaking or tilting it, or by gesturing towards the device, there is another way to perform the action, for example, a button as an alternative to shaking the device to undo. It also requires a way to turn off these functions, such as by supporting system settings.
Priority: High
3.2 - Predictable
3.2.6 - Consistent Help (2.2 only)
Summary: If help is provided in the form of contact information, self-help, or a fully automated help mechanism, it is consistent across pages within a set. For example, a link to a help page is always in the same relative location.
Priority: High
3.3 - Input Assistance
3.3.7 - Redundant Entry (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easy for users to complete processes. If the same information is needed again within the same session, the user shouldn't have to enter it again. There is an exception for security information, such as re-entering a new password.
Priority: High
4.1 -  Compatible
4.1.1 - Parsing
Summary: This requires a web-based application's markup language (generally HTML) to be appropriately structured. These can include properly opening and closing tags, appropriate specifications for nested list elements, and input fields with associated attributes. Essentially, this requirement assures the proper valid syntax (format) of the markup language.
Priority: High
Table 2: Success Criteria, Level AA
1.2 - Time-based Media
1.2.4 - Captions (Live)
Summary: There must be
captions
provided for any live video content. This is critical for a hearing-impaired user.
Priority: High
1.2.5 - Audio Description (Prerecorded)
Summary: Video content is given additional
audio descriptions
during pauses in the audio. Audio descriptions describe visual content for people who are blind or have low vision.
Priority: High
1.3 - Adaptable
1.3.4 - Orientation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Devices can be used in any orientation. Content shouldn't be locked in landscape or portrait orientation.
Priority: High
1.3.5 - Identify Input Purpose (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Autocomplete is used on certain form fields to identify what information goes in the field, such as a person's name or address.
Priority: High
1.4 - Distinguishable
1.4.3 - Contrast (Minimum)
Summary: Text has enough contrast so it can be seen. There are different standards for regular text and for large or bold text.
Priority: High
1.4.4 - Resize Text
Summary: The user should be able to make the text larger, up to double the default size, without content disappearing or overlapping.
Priority: High
1.4.5 - Images of Text
Summary: Real text should be used instead of images of text. This is related to the previous success criterion on resizing text because images of text become blurry when made larger.
Priority: High
1.4.10 - Reflow (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Content doesn't require both horizontal and vertical scrolling. This is related to the previous success criterion on resizing text. As text is resized or the content zoomed, it should reflow, usually into a single column. There is an exception for content like a map or a table where the two-dimensional presentation is needed for usage and meaning.
Priority: High
1.4.11 - Non-text Contrast (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Just as text should have enough contrast to be seen, user interface components and graphics should have enough contrast to be seen. User interface components are things like buttons and text input boxes. The graphics referred to here include icons without text and the parts of a complex graphic needed to understand the content, such as the lines on a graph.
Priority: High
1.4.12 - Text Spacing (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: The user can override the spacing of text to make it easier to read.
Priority: High
2.4 - Navigable
2.4.5 - Multiple Ways
Summary: This is about making sure there is more than one way to get to a page. It might be hard for some people to find a particular page in a large navigation list, for example, but they can find the page using a site search.
Priority: High.
2.4.6 - Headings and Labels
Summary: This success criterion requires headings or labels to be descriptive. It does not require headings or labels, which are covered by other guidelines.
Priority: High
2.4.11 - Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: Keyboard focus indicators should be at least partially visible. At least some portion of the focused item should be visible on screen and not hidden behind other content. This builds on the previous success criterion on visible focus.
Priority: High
2.5 - Input Modalities
Complementary to the guidelines for keyboard users, these guidelines address barriers for people who use a pointer (mouse, touch) or their voice (voice control).
2.5.7 - Dragging Movements (2.2 only)
Summary: This requires an alternative in addition to dragging movements. For example, buttons move an item in a list up or down instead of having to press, hold, move and release with a mouse.
Priority: High
2.5.8 - Target Size (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easier for people to tap or click the correct item. It requires interactive items to be big enough or have enough space around them so that someone would not accidentally use the wrong one.
Priority: High
3.1 - Readable
3.1.2 - Language of Parts
Summary: If parts of a web page are in a different language than the main language, the language for those parts is programmatically defined for assistive technologies to access.
Priority: High
3.2 - Predictable
3.2.3 - Consistent Navigation
Summary: If there is navigation used throughout a website or application, the items should be in the same order on each page.
Priority: High
3.2.4 - Consistent Identification
Summary: This is about making it easy for someone to understand the interface by making sure things are named consistently. For example, if a magnifying glass is named "search" in one location, it should be "search" in other locations, not "find".
Priority: High
3.3 - Input Assistance
3.3.3 - Error Suggestion
Summary: If there is an error, an error message should suggest how to correct the error.
Priority: High
3.3.4 - Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
Summary: This is about helping people avoid serious consequences of making a mistake when an action involves legal or financial commitments or could cause the permanent loss of data.
Priority: High
3.3.8 - Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easier to authenticate or log in without needing to remember a password or solve a puzzle.
Priority: High
4.1 - Compatible
4.1.3 - Status Messages (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion is about making sure important changes are shared with assistive technology users without moving their focus.
Priority: High
Additional resources
To learn more about reviewing a VPAT/ACR, see:
A quick guide to reviewing a VPAT ACR
by Karl Groves
How I Evaluate an ACR (VPAT)
by Adrian Roselli
Making VPATs and ACRs more effective in procurement
from WebAIM
To learn why a VPAT completed by a reputable third party is more trustworthy than one completed by the vendor, see
Why a third party should prepare your VPAT
by Karl Groves.

title: Perform a full review of a VPAT
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Compare a VPAT and an ACR
Overview of an Accessibility Compliance Report (ACR)
Additional resources
Overview
This document will help you perform a review of vendor provided accessibility documentation. It is most useful to perform a full review on a small number of finalist products.
If you are comparing many potential products, you should start with a
quick review of the VPAT
as an initial filter. You can perform a
medium-level review of the VPAT
with software or applications that pass the quick review. The quick review and medium-level reviews are intended to help you establish the reliability of each vendor's accessibility documentation and gain a general sense of the overall accessibility of their product.
Compare a VPAT and an ACR
Before starting, you should understand the difference between a VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) and the accompanying ACR (Accessibility Compliance Report).
VPAT
The VPAT is the entire template with all the pages of instructions and resources to help gain a comprehensive understanding of the document.
ACR
The ACR is the report portion of the VPAT after the instructions and resources are removed. The ACR contains only the introduction form and the details of the criteria tables.
Overview of an Accessibility Compliance Report (ACR)
The vendor may send an entire VPAT or just the ACR portion of it. The ACR contains the important parts to review. You need to examine the introduction form and the criteria tables.
Introduction form
The introduction form contains general information about the product and the evaluation.
Pay attention to the version of the VPAT.  Version 2.4rev or newer indicates the vendor follows more current standards. Version 2.5rev is the current version, released in April 2025.
Verify the product and version. Make sure the VPAT is for the version you are interested in purchasing, especially if there are multiple versions of the product. There may also be multiple reports for a single product. If the product is complex, separate reports may exist, for example, for different interfaces (user versus administrator).
Four specific fields in this introduction help establish the reliability of the form as a whole:
Evaluation methods used:
The evaluation methods are perhaps the most critical aspect to the introduction. Look for:
Assistive technology used during the testing process
Multiple methods, including both manual and automated testing
Third party evaluators that can be vetted to certify their value
Specific methodology references
Answers that should concern you:
Similar to another evaluated product
Use of a vendor-proprietary testing method, unless the method can be vetted appropriately
Automated testing with no manual testing
General product knowledge
Other similar responses
Applicable standards and guidelines:
What standards were used to create this report? This field requires at least one standard. However, it is better if multiple standards were used and listed. Look for:
WCAG 2.1 or 2.2, A and AA conformance
WCAG 2.0, A and AA conformance, is older and does not cover as much as WCAG 2.1 or 2.2
Additional standards that show more detailed knowledge and commitment by the vendor:
Revised Section 508
EN 301 549
Note:
WCAG 2.1, released in December 2018, is the standard required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) Title II. WCAG 2.2, released in October 2023, indicates the vendor follows more current standards. The level of conformance is also important, which exists as Level A, AA, and AAA. This document focuses on level AA, which is a common standard and should be the minimum goal.
Contact information:
The name of the tester, their position within the organization, and specific contact information should be provided.
The tester's position is usually more reliable if they are:
On the vendor's accessibility team
From a third-party accessibility firm
Be more cautious if the tester's position is from the vendor's:
Marketing team
Sales team
Marketing and sales people may have little knowledge of the product and thus any details of any testing that may have been done. They are also likely to have a biased purpose.
Date:
This field should contain the date the VPAT was issued. Look for a date within the last six to nine months.
Be cautious of anything over one year. You may need to request an updated report.
Note:
This is highly dependent on the type of application it is and how frequently the vendor releases regular updates. Therefore, this is a general guideline, not a gold standard.
Criteria tables
The tables may represent information about three standards:
WCAG
Revised Section 508
EN 301 549
For the purposes of this document, we are only looking at the WCAG standards and accompanying tables. The WCAG standard contains three conformance levels, A, AA, and AAA, which each have an individual table. There may be references to the other standards within these tables as there are matching criteria from all three standards.
The tables include three columns:
Criteria
Conformance Level
Remarks and Explanations
Criteria
will list the specific standard targeted by the evaluation.
Conformance Level
gives you the opportunity to gauge the possible accuracy of the submission. The conformance level column can have one of four different values:
Supports
Partially Supports
Does Not Support
Not Applicable (N/A)
Note:
There has been a language change with the release of VPAT 2.3 where "Supports with Exceptions" was replaced with "Partially Supports". This change took place in December of 2018. So, make note of the language and the date, which can tell you whether the vendor's submission is based on recent testing or may have been copied and pasted from an older version.
Remarks and Explanations
should ideally be as detailed as possible about the specific problems encountered. Look for:
Specific examples of how the product supports, partially supports, or doesn't support the criterion
Remarks and explanations for all criteria
Responses that should concern you:
Explanations that duplicate the wording of the criteria
All criteria marked as "Supports"
Language like "this product was designed to...", which doesn't indicate if it actually does
Table 1: Success Criteria, Level A
1.1 - Text Alternatives
1.1.1 - Non-Text Content
Summary: This is mostly about
alternative text for images
, charts, tables, and so on. Most products should support this. The use of CAPTCHA elevates this success criterion to critical. CAPTCHAs are an element of controversy in the accessibility community because of their potential barrier to access. If CAPTCHAs are included within a vendor's submission, there must be more than one option (for example, visual and auditory) as a minimum.
Priority: Critical
1.2 - Time-based Media
1.2.1 - Audio Only & Video Only (Pre-recorded)
Summary: There must be text alternatives to pre-recorded audio or video content, usually in the form of
text-based transcripts
. This is critical for accessibility as these text transcripts can then easily be translated into different modes for different user needs.
Priority: Critical
1.2.2 - Captions (Pre-recorded)
Summary: There must be
captions
provided for any pre-recorded audio/video content. This is critical for people who are D/deaf or hard of hearing. "Does not support" or "Partially supports" indicate the product should be flagged for further testing. View a
1-minute video overview about captions
.
Priority: Critical
1.2.3 - Audio Description or Media Alternative (Pre-recorded)
Summary: Video content is either given additional
audio descriptions
within the confines of the audio track or in an entirely separate audio track that contains the entirety of the video content described in audio format. Alternatively, there is a full text version of all visual and audio content. Exceptions here could be expected as full conformance seems a rarity in this area. However, it should still be viewed as a critical component.
Priority: Critical
1.3 - Adaptable
1.3.1, 1.3.2, 1.3.3 - Info and Relationships, Meaningful Sequence, Sensory Characteristics
Summary: These three success criteria are related to meaning and how the structures of applications can be read, and thus interpreted, with assistive technology. For this reason, they should be viewed more as a whole than as individual sub-sections. This area is as critical to accessibility as any on this list. However, because these are design guidelines, it is also the one with the largest room for interpretation. The good news is most modern web-based applications generally conform to these concepts during their initial design phase. Answers here should generally list "Supports". Possible exceptions should be very detailed if they exist.
Priority: Critical
1.4 - Distinguishable
1.4.1 - Use of Color
Summary: This deals with the
use of color
within an application.
If color is used in a defining way (for example, click the red button), there must be alternative ways to identify that element or color identification.
This success criterion is critical as it has the potential for significant barriers to access.
Priority: Critical
1.4.2 - Audio Control
Summary: If audio content is to be automatically played, there must be a way for the content to be stopped or paused, and the volume must be operated independently from the system volume.
Priority: Critical
2.1 - Keyboard Accessible
These guidelines should be considered the starting point in the evaluation process and the most critical within the standard.
This doesn't preclude an application that has "partially supports" from being considered. However, they should be flagged and then sent for more in-depth testing before purchase. View a
1-minute video on testing keyboard support
.
2.1.1 - Keyboard
Summary: This success criterion deals solely with the ability to
navigate the application with keyboard controls
, which is crucial to the use of assistive technologies.
Priority: Critical
2.1.2 - No Keyboard Trap
Summary: This success criterion deals with the process of navigating to a specific element and then becoming "trapped" on the element and not being able to navigate away from it.
Priority: Critical
2.1.4 - Character Key Shortcuts (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: If custom keyboard shortcuts have been implemented, they shouldn’t use a single character (letter, number, punctuation, or symbol) without modifier keys, such as Ctrl or Alt, or there should be a way for the user to change the shortcut.
Priority: High
2.2 - Enough Time
2.2.1 - Timing Adjustable
Summary: If there is a time limit of less than 20 hours, the user needs to be able to turn it off, adjust it, or extend it. For example, if a session times out after a period of inactivity, there should be a way for the user to indicate they are still active and stop the timeout. There is an exception for real-time events, like an auction.
Priority: High
2.2.2 - Pause, Stop, Hide
Summary: The user needs to be able to pause, stop, or hide any content that moves, blinks, or scrolls automatically. This applies if the movement, blinking, or scrolling lasts longer than 5 seconds and there is other content on the screen at the same time.
Priority: Critical
2.3 - Seizures and Physical Barriers
2.3.1 - Three Flashes or Below Threshold
Summary: This success criterion restricts the flashing of content to no more than three flashes per second within an application. Considering its impact, its critical importance is clear.
Priority: Critical
2.4 - Navigable
2.4.1 - Bypass Blocks
Summary: This success criterion deals with "skip to" links at the top of web pages which allow quicker navigation to those critical areas. View a
short video on checking skip links
.
This is a very basic function that is included in most web-based applications today. If unsupported, this should be a red flag.
Priority: Critical
2.4.2 - Page Titled
Summary: This success criterion simply requires an appropriate and descriptive title for each web page. View a
short video on checking page titles
.
This is a very basic function that is included in most web-based applications today. If unsupported, this should be a red flag.
Priority: Critical
2.4.3 - Focus Order
Summary: Someone using a keyboard should be able to navigate through the content in an order that is logical and meaningful.
Priority: High
2.4.4 - Link Purpose (In Context)
Summary: The text of a link should give users an idea of where the link will take them.
Priority: High
2.5 - Input Modalities
Complementary to the guidelines for keyboard users, these guidelines address barriers for people who use a pointer (mouse, touch) or their voice (voice control).
2.5.1 - Pointer Gestures (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion requires a single pointer alternative for any path-based or multipoint gestures. An example is zoom in and out buttons as an alternative to the multipoint pinch zoom gesture.
Priority: High
2.5.2 - Pointer Cancellation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion is about preventing accidental pointer input. If an action happens with a single pointer (mouse or touch), it can be cancelled or reversed.
Priority: High
2.5.3 - Label in Name (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: If there is visual text for a link or control, the accessible name contains that text.
Priority: High
2.5.4 - Motion Actuation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: For functions activated by moving a device, such as shaking or tilting it, or by gesturing towards the device, there is another way to perform the action, for example, a button as an alternative to shaking the device to undo. It also requires a way to turn off these functions, such as by supporting system settings.
Priority: High
3.1 - Readable
3.1.1 - Language of Page
Summary: This ensures that a web page's language is programmatically defined for assistive technologies to access. Exceptions should be rare.
Priority: Critical
3.2 - Predictable
3.2.1 - On Focus
Summary: This success criterion essentially prohibits the context change of a web element when it receives system focus through standard navigation. An example could be the automatic submission of a web form when the button receives focus, or the automatic launch of a new browser tab when a link gets focus.
Priority: Critical
3.2.2 - On Input
Summary: This success criterion addresses changes in context when a user changes the state of a component, and the change will persist after interaction stops. An example of a state change would be checking a checkbox or entering text in a text box. These are elements where a user must be alerted to a context change to validate that element's status.
Priority: Critical
3.2.6 - Consistent Help (2.2 only)
Summary: If help is provided in the form of contact information, self-help, or a fully automated help mechanism, it is consistent across pages within a set. For example, a link to a help page is always in the same relative location.
Priority: High
3.3 - Input Assistance
3.3.1 - Error Identification
Summary: This ensures that input entry
errors are identified in a clear and descriptive manner
to all users. While slightly ambiguous, the intent here is that any error message must be immediately identifiable and accessible to any user using any type of assistive technology. The error should also be described in a way that the user can figure out what is wrong.
Priority: Critical
3.3.2 - Labels or Instructions
Summary: There must be proper labeling and instructions for any application input fields. Examples include search fields or a web form. This is a barrier to access, so exceptions should be viewed cautiously.
Priority: Critical
3.3.7 - Redundant Entry (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easy for users to complete processes. If the same information is needed again within the same session, the user shouldn't have to enter it again. There is an exception for security information, such as re-entering a new password.
Priority: High
4.1 - Compatible
4.1.1 - Parsing
Summary: This requires a web-based application's markup language (generally HTML) to be appropriately structured. This success criterion does not apply in WCAG 2.2, where it is obsolete and removed. It is always supported in WCAG 2.0 and 2.1, per the September 2023 errata.
Priority: High
4.1.2 - Name, Role, Value
Summary: This success criterion targets custom user interface elements created with scripting components instead of the standard markup language elements. It requires that these custom components' name, role, attributes, and any change of status be identifiable by assistive technologies. An example would be a custom checkbox being identified as "checkbox checked" after it has been marked by a user.
Priority: Critical
Table 2: Success Criteria, Level AA
1.2 - Time-based Media
1.2.4 - Captions (Live)
Summary: There must be
captions
provided for any live video content. This is critical for a hearing-impaired user.
Priority: High
1.2.5 - Audio Description (Prerecorded)
Summary: Video content is given additional
audio descriptions
during pauses in the audio. Audio descriptions describe visual content for people who are blind or have low vision.
Priority: High
1.3 - Adaptable
1.3.4 - Orientation (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Devices can be used in any orientation. Content shouldn't be locked in landscape or portrait orientation.
Priority: High
1.3.5 - Identify Input Purpose (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Autocomplete is used on certain form fields to identify what information goes in the field, such as a person's name or address.
Priority: High
1.4 - Distinguishable
1.4.3 - Contrast (Minimum)
Summary: Text has enough contrast so it can be seen. There are different standards for regular text and for large or bold text.
Priority: High
1.4.4 - Resize Text
Summary: The user should be able to make the text larger, up to double the default size, without content disappearing or overlapping.
Priority: High
1.4.5 - Images of Text
Summary: Real text should be used instead of images of text. This is related to the previous success criterion on resizing text because images of text become blurry when made larger.
Priority: High
1.4.10 - Reflow (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Content doesn't require both horizontal and vertical scrolling. This is related to the previous success criterion on resizing text. As text is resized or the content zoomed, it should reflow, usually into a single column. There is an exception for content like a map or a table where the two-dimensional presentation is needed for usage and meaning.
Priority: High
1.4.11 - Non-text Contrast (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: Just as text should have enough contrast to be seen, user interface components and graphics should have enough contrast to be seen. User interface components are things like buttons and text input boxes. The graphics referred to here include icons without text and the parts of a complex graphic needed to understand the content, such as the lines on a graph.
Priority: High
1.4.12 - Text Spacing (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: The user can override the spacing of text to make it easier to read.
Priority: High
1.4.13 - Content on Hover or Focus (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This deals with hovering over or focusing on an item to activate extra content. Hover action elements are notorious for accessibility problems.
Priority: Critical
2.4 - Navigable
2.4.5 - Multiple Ways
Summary: This is about making sure there is more than one way to get to a page. It might be hard for some people to find a particular page in a large navigation list, for example, but they can find the page using a site search.
Priority: High.
2.4.6 - Headings and Labels
Summary: This success criterion requires headings or labels to be descriptive. It does not require headings or labels, which are covered by other guidelines.
Priority: High
2.4.7 - Focus Visible
Summary: There must be an indicator for keyboard focus within a web-based application. This is critical for multiple reasons. This focus indicator is the primary way testers evaluate the keyboard access and tabbing order of an application. So, this can not only act as evidence of that testing process, it will also be critical for future testing of the application during update cycles.
Priority: Critical
2.4.11 - Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: Keyboard focus indicators should be at least partially visible. At least some portion of the focused item should be visible on screen and not hidden behind other content. This builds on the previous success criterion on visible focus.
Priority: High
2.5 - Input Modalities
2.5.7 - Dragging Movements (2.2 only)
Summary: This requires an alternative in addition to dragging movements. For example, buttons move an item in a list up or down instead of having to press, hold, move and release with a mouse.
Priority: High
2.5.8 - Target Size (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easier for people to tap or click the correct item. It requires interactive items to be big enough or have enough space around them that someone won't accidentally use the wrong one.
Priority: High
3.1 - Readable
3.1.2 - Language of Parts
Summary: If parts of a web page are in a different language than the main language, the language for those parts is programmatically defined for assistive technologies to access.
Priority: High
3.2 - Predictable
3.2.3 - Consistent Navigation
Summary: If there is navigation used throughout a website or application, the items should be in the same order on each page.
Priority: High
3.2.4 - Consistent Identification
Summary: This is about making it easy for someone to understand the interface by making sure things are named consistently. For example, if a magnifying glass is named "search" in one location, it should be "search" in other locations, not "find".
Priority: High
3.3 - Input Assistance
3.3.3 - Error Suggestion
Summary: If there is an error, an error message should suggest how to correct the error.
Priority: High
3.3.4 - Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
Summary: This is about helping people avoid serious consequences of making a mistake when an action involves legal or financial commitments or could cause the permanent loss of data.
Priority: High
3.3.8 - Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (2.2 only)
Summary: This is about making it easier to authenticate or log in without needing to remember a password or solve a puzzle.
Priority: High
4.1 - Compatible
4.1.3 - Status Messages (2.1 and 2.2)
Summary: This success criterion is about making sure important changes are shared with assistive technology users without moving their focus.
Priority: High
Additional resources
To learn more about reviewing a VPAT/ACR, see:
A quick guide to reviewing a VPAT ACR
by Karl Groves
How I Evaluate an ACR (VPAT)
by Adrian Roselli
Making VPATs and ACRs more effective in procurement
from WebAIM
To learn why a VPAT completed by a reputable third party is more trustworthy than one completed by the vendor, see
Why a third party should prepare your VPAT
by Karl Groves.

title: Install Python packages on the research supercomputers at IU
content:
Table of contents
Overview
Install Python packages for personal use
Set up your user environment
Install a package using
pip
Install a package using its
setup.py
script
Understand the module search order
Supported packages
Supported packages in the Python modules
Supported packages in the
python/gpu
modules
Overview
Python packages are collections of modules (reusable code) that extend and enhance the functionality of the core Python language. Python developers contribute to the official Python Package Index (
PyPI
) repository, making their packages available to the Python community under open source license terms. The Python Packaging Authority (
PyPA
) manages the repository, and maintains a standard set of tools for building, distributing, and installing Python packages.
On Indiana University's
research supercomputers
, many third-party packages already are installed to supplement commonly used Python builds. For the most commonly used packages that are supported at IU, see the
Supported packages
section; for a complete list, type
pip freeze
after loading the Python module to see what packages are installed. If you have a unique need for a third-party Python package that is not already installed, you can use
pip
or
setup.py
to install the package in your home directory or in your
Slate
storage space.
Note:
Space on
Slate
is available to all IU
research supercomputer
users. To create a
Slate
account, follow the instructions in
Get additional IU computing accounts
.
If you know several researchers are interested in using a Python package that is not already installed, you can request to have it installed as a system-wide site package.
Install Python packages for personal use
Set up your user environment
The IU
research supercomputers
use module-based environment management systems that provide a convenient method for dynamically customizing your software environment.
To install Python packages, you must have Python added to your user environment. To check which modules are currently loaded; on the command line, enter:
module list
If Python is not among the list of currently loaded modules, use the
module load
command to add it; for example:
To add the default version, on the command line, enter:
module load python
To add a non-default version:
Check which versions are available; on the command line, enter:
module avail python
Load the preferred version; on the command line, enter (replace
version_number
with the preferred version number):
module load python/
version_number
If Python is listed among the currently loaded modules, but you prefer or need to use another version, you must remove the currently loaded module before loading the other version. To do this with one command, use
module switch
; for example, on the command line, enter (replace
current_version
with the version number of the currently loaded
python
module and
new_version
with the preferred version number):
module switch python/
current_version
python/
new_version
You can save your customized user environment so that it loads every time you start a new session; for instructions, see
Use modules to manage your software environment on IU research supercomputers
.
Install a package using
pip
The
pip
package management tool, one of the standard tools maintained by the Python Package Authority (PyPA), is the recommended tool for installing packages from the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository.
To install a package from the PyPI repository (for example,
foo
), use the
pip install
command with the
--user
flag; for example:
Python package installation commands
To install:
Use the command:
The latest version
pip install foo --user
A particular version (for example,
foo 1.0.3
)
pip install foo==1.0.3 --user
A minimum version (for example,
foo 2.0
)
pip install 'foo>=2.0' --user
The
--user
option directs
pip
to download and unpack the source distribution for your package (for example,
foo
) in the user
site-packages
directory for the running Python (for example,
~/.local/lib/python3.6/site-packages/foo
). Python automatically searches this directory for modules, so prepending this path to the PYTHONPATH environmental variable is not necessary. If you omit the
--user
option,
pip
will try to install your package in the global
site-packages
directory (where you do not have the necessary permissions); as a result, the installation will fail.
Alternatively, you can use the
--prefix
option to install your package in your
Slate
storage space; for example, to install your package (
package_name
) in an existing subdirectory (
python-pkgs
) in your
Slate
space, enter:
pip install --prefix=/N/slate/$USER/python-pkgs package_name
If you install your package to a location other than the user
site-packages
directory, you will need to prepend the path to that directory to your PYTHONPATH environment variable; for example:
export PYTHONPATH=$PYTHONPATH:/N/slate/$USER/python-pkgs/lib/python3.x/site-packages
Note:
In the above example,
3.x
represents the first two elements of the Python version number you are using. For example, if your Python version is 3.10.5, replace
3.x
with
3.10
.
This line can be added to your
.bashrc
file to avoid having to add it every time you log in.
For more about using
pip
, see the
pip install
page in the
pip User Guide
.
Install a package using its
setup.py
script
To install a Python package from a source other than the PyPI repository, you can download and unpack the source distribution yourself, and then use its
setup.py
script to install the package in the user
site-packages
directory:
Set up your user environment (as described in the
previous section
).
Use the
wget
command to download the distribution archive (for example,
foo-1.0.3.gz
) from the source (for example, http://pythonfoo.org); for example:
wget http://pythonfoo.org/foo-1.0.3.gz
Use
tar
to unpack the archive (for example,
foo-1.0.3.gz
); for example:
tar -xzf foo-1.0.3.gz
The distribution should unpack into a similarly-named directory in your home directory (for example,
~/foo-1.0.3
).
Change (
cd
) to the new directory, and then, on the command line, enter:
python setup.py install --user
The
--user
option directs
setup.py
to install the package (for example,
foo
) in the user
site-packages
directory for the running Python (for example,
~/.local/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages/foo
).
Python automatically searches this directory for modules, so prepending this path to the PYTHONPATH environmental variable is not necessary.
If you omit the
--user
option,
setup.py
will try to install the package in the global
site-packages
directory (where you do not have the necessary permissions); as a result, the installation will fail.
Alternatively, you can use the
--home
or
--prefix
option to install your package in a different location (where you have the necessary permissions); for example, to install your package in a subdirectory (for example,
python-pkgs
):
Within your home directory, enter:
python setup.py install --home=~/python-pkgs
In your
Slate
storage space, enter:
python setup.py install --prefix=/N/slate/$USER/python-pkgs
Note:
If you install your package to a location other than the user
site-packages
directory, you will need to prepend the path to that directory to your PYTHONPATH environment variable. For more about PYTHONPATH, see
Understand the module search order
below.
Understand the module search order
Knowing how the Python interpreter responds to
import
statements can help you determine why a particular module or package isn't loading, or why an unexpected version of a package is loading, even though the correct version is installed and the path to its location is listed in your PYTHONPATH environment variable.
When Python launches, it searches the paths found in
sys.path
, a list of directories that determines the interpreter's search path for modules. The
sys.path
variable is initialized from the following locations, in this order:
The directory containing the script used to invoke the Python interpreter (if the interpreter is invoked interactively or the script is read from standard input, this first item,
path[0]
, remains an empty string, which directs Python to search modules in the current working directory first)
The directories listed in PYTHONPATH
The version-specific
site-packages
directory for the running Python installation; for example
<sys.prefix>/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages
, in which
<sys.prefix>
represents the path to the running Python installation and
X.Y
represents the version number of the running Python installation
By default, Python also imports the
site.py
module upon initialization, which adds site-specific paths to the module search path (
sys.path
), including the path to your user
site-packages
directory within in your home directory (for example,
~/.local/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages
).
As
site.py
adds paths to
sys.path
, it scans them for path configuration (
.pth
) files, which contain additional directories that are added to
sys.path
. If a directory contains multiple
.pth
files,
site.py
processes them in alphabetical order.
However, some
.pth
files contain embedded commands that insert directory entries at the beginning of the module search path (ahead of the standard library path). As a result, a module from one of the inserted directories will load instead of the module of the same name from the standard library directory. This can be undesired and confusing behavior unless such a replacement is intended.
Note:
If your
import
requests are consistently disrupted by
site.py
and
.pth
files, try invoking the Python interpreter with the
-S
(uppercase "S"):
python -S
This disables the automatic import of
site.py
and, as a result, prevents it from manipulating
sys.path
. However, it also prevents
site.py
from adding your user
site-packages
directory to
sys.path
. To import
site.py
without adding your user
site-packages
directory to
sys.path
, invoke Python with the
-s
(lowercase "s") option:
python -s
To see which directories Python scans when you issue
import
commands, on the command line, enter:
python -c "import sys; print ('\n'.join(sys.path))"
Alternatively, launch Python in interactive mode, and then invoke the same commands in this order (
>>>
is the Python primary prompt):
>>>import sys
>>>print ('\n'.join(sys.path))
Note:
The
sys.path
variable is only an editable list of strings that you can edit like any other Python list. Avoid editing the first item in the list (
path[0]
), because many packages assume it refers to the directory containing the script used to invoke the Python interpreter.
Supported packages
Supported packages in the Python modules
Following are the most commonly used packages available in the Python modules. To see a full list of available packages, after loading a Python module, type:
pip list
or
pip freeze
astropy
biopython
cryptography

PySocks

scikit-learn
scipy
seaborn
tensorflow
tornado
Supported packages in the
python/gpu
modules
Following are the most commonly used packages available in the Python modules. To see a full list of available packages, after loading a
python/gpu
module, type:
pip list
or
pip freeze
accelerate
bs4
causality
cupy-cuda117
dask
editdistance
GraphViz
